**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 22, verse 1:**

(Surat al-Hajj, 22) Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it was revealed in Medina, and this is the view of al-Dahhak. It was also said that the whole surah is Meccan. Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas narrated from Mujahid, from Ibn 'Abbas, that it is Meccan except for three verses, ﴿These two adversaries dispute﴾ [al-Hajj: 19] to the end of the three verses, for those were revealed in Medina. In another report from Ibn 'Abbas, the exception is four verses, from ﴿These two adversaries dispute﴾ to His saying, ﴿the punishment of the Fire﴾ [al-Hajj: 22].

[p. 110]

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatada that it is Medinan except for four verses, from ﴿And We did not send before you any messenger﴾ to ﴿the punishment of a barren day﴾ [al-Hajj: 52–55], for those are Meccan. The more correct view is that it is mixed, containing both Medinan and Meccan material, although there is disagreement about which verses are which. This is the view of the majority. The number of its verses is ninety-eight according to the Kufan count, ninety-seven according to the Meccan count, ninety-five according to the Basran count, and ninety-four according to the Syrian count. The connection between it and the surah before it is clear. Concerning its virtue, Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from 'Uqba ibn 'Amir, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, has the Surah of al-Hajj been given preference over the rest of the Qur'an by two prostrations?' He said: 'Yes. So whoever does not prostrate in them, let him not recite them.'"

The reports that it contains two prostrations are numerous and are mentioned in al-Durr al-Manthur. However, Ibn Abi Shayba narrated through the route of al-'Uryan al-Mujashi'i, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "In al-Hajj there is one prostration, and it is the first," as is found in another report.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord﴾. This is an address whose ruling encompasses those who were obligated at the time of revelation, and those who will be included among them later from among those present who have not yet reached the level of legal obligation, and those who come into existence after that until the Day of Resurrection. However, according to us, this is not in the strict literal sense, but rather by way of predominance (taghlib) or by generalizing the ruling through an external proof. The direct address (khitab al-mushafaha) does not include those who have not yet been obligated, and it is specific to the obligated people present at the time of revelation. This differs from the Hanbalites, some of the Salafis and jurists, who held that it includes all of them in the strict sense. There is no disagreement that women are included in such phrases as "people" (al-nas) and similar plural forms that show plurality without a sign of masculine or feminine gender. The disagreement concerns whether women are included in pronouns such as the pronoun in ﴿fear﴾ (ittaqu) and in the words "the Muslims." The Shafi'ites, the Ash'arites, and the majority of the Hanafites and Mu'tazilites held that they are not included, while the Hanbalites, Ibn Dawud and a few outliers held that they are included. The inclusion here, according to us, is by way of predominance.

Some have claimed that the address is specific to the people of Mecca, but this is not so. What is commanded is taqwa in its absolute sense, which is abstaining from everything that incurs sin, whether an act or an omission, and it includes faith in Allah and the Last Day, as the Law has stated, being included initially but in a way that encompasses both the establishment and the continuation (of that taqwa). It would fit specifying the address to the people of Mecca to take taqwa to mean its first level, which is guarding oneself against polytheism. The mention of the title "Lord" together with the attribution to the pronoun of those addressed serves to reinforce the command and to emphasize that compliance is obligatory, by way of warning and encouragement. That is, "beware of the punishment of the Master of your affairs and the One who nurtures you."

His saying, ﴿Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing﴾, gives the reason for the obligation of the command by mentioning a terrifying matter. Reflecting on the greatness and horror of that, and on the dreadfulness of what precedes it and its beginnings, of conditions and terrors from which there is no refuge except to clothe oneself in the garment of taqwa, necessarily requires greater care in being attached to it and in constant adherence to it. The zilzal (convulsion) is a violent shaking and a fierce disturbance by repetition, to the point of removing things from their places and displacing them from their centers. Its attribution to the Hour is either the attribution of a verbal noun (masdar) to its agent, but in a metaphorical sense of attribution, as was said regarding His saying, ﴿Rather, the plotting of the night and the day﴾ [Saba': 33], because the one who actually causes the shaking is Allah, and the object is the earth or the people. Or it is the attribution of the noun to its object, but with it treated as the object in a broad sense, as in the verse: "O thief of the night, (stealing from) the people of the house." It is also permissible that the attribution be in the sense of "in" (fi), and some have affirmed this and held it regarding the previous verse. According to some, that is what is mentioned in His saying, ﴿When the earth is shaken with its (final) convulsion﴾ [al-Zalzala: 1], and according to what was said, it occurs at the second blast and the establishment of the Hour. Indeed, it has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the convulsion of the Hour is its establishment.

Ahmad, Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Nasa'i, al-Tirmidhi and al-Hakim narrated, and the last two declared it sound, from 'Imran ibn Husayn [p. 111] who said: "When ﴿O mankind﴾ down to ﴿but the punishment of Allah is severe﴾ was revealed, the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, was on a journey. He said, 'Do you know what day that is?' They said, 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'That is the day when Allah will say to Adam, peace be upon him, "Send forth the group for the Fire." He will say, "O Lord, what is the group for the Fire?" He will say: "Out of every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine to the Fire, and one to Paradise."' Then the Muslims began to weep, and the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, said: 'Be close to the mark, be steadfast, and rejoice, for prophethood has never existed except that before it there was a period of ignorance (jahiliyya). The number is taken from the ignorance; if it is complete, well and good, and if not, it is completed from the hypocrites. Your likeness among the nations is only like the mark on the leg of a beast, or like the mole on the flank of a camel.'" Then he said: "Indeed, I hope that you will be half of the people of Paradise," so they proclaimed takbir. Then he said: "Indeed, I hope that you will be a third of the people of Paradise," so they proclaimed takbir. Then he said: "Indeed, I hope that you will be half of the people of Paradise," so they proclaimed takbir. (The narrator) said: "I do not know whether he said 'two-thirds' or not."

The hadith about the sending forth is mentioned in the two Sahihs and elsewhere, but with a different wording. Its content, as mentioned, supports the view that this convulsion takes place on the Day of Resurrection, and this is what is narrated from al-Hasan.

Ibn al-Mundhir and others narrated from 'Alqama, al-Sha'bi and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr that it will occur before the sun rises from its west. According to this view, the attribution to the Hour is because it is one of its signs. Many reports have come about a great earthquake occurring before the Hour, which is among its portents. However, there is a question about whether that earthquake is what is meant here, since it does not suit the sentence to be a reason for the command to all people to fear Allah. Furthermore, according to this view, it retains its literal meaning, which is the violent movement of the earth. This movement happens by the stirring of an angel, based on what is reported, that in the earth there are veins that extend to Mount Qaf, and an angel there holds them. When Allah, mighty and majestic, wills a matter, He moves a vein, and when it is moved, the earth quakes.

According to the philosophers, when vapor (bukhar) is trapped in the earth and becomes thick, to the point that it cannot pass through its channels because of their great density and compactness, it gathers seeking to escape and cannot, and so the earth quakes. Sometimes the quake intensifies and the earth collapses, and fire comes out due to the violence of the movement, which causes the vapor and smoke to ignite, especially if they mix in a manner approaching oiliness. Sometimes the matter becomes strong enough to split the earth, and tremendous sounds occur. Sometimes the quake is caused by the falling of high places, and it subsides in the interior of the earth, so the trapped air surges within it and the earth quakes because of it. Rarely does the earth quake from the collapse of mountain peaks upon it, for some reasons.

Among what is cited in support of the view that its cause is the trapping of thick vapor and its seeking to escape, and its failure to find an outlet, is that earthquakes are more frequent in hard land and more severe there than in soft land. It is not hidden that if a sound hadith explaining the cause of the earthquake exists, one should not deviate from it. Otherwise, there is no harm in holding the philosophers' opinion on this, and it does not contradict the belief in the Free Agent, as some have supposed. As for those who hold that it is the Day of Resurrection, some said it is in its literal sense as well, and others said it is a metaphor for the terrors and hardships that will occur on that day. Describing it as "a thing" indicates that minds are incapable of comprehending its reality, and that expression is too narrow to encompass it except in a general, vague way. In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit) it is said that applying the term "thing" to it, even though it has not yet come into existence, indicates that it may be applied to what does not exist. Whoever prohibits that says that its being called a thing is because its occurrence is certain and it will inevitably come into existence.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 2:**

﴿On the Day you see it, every nursing mother will be distracted from what she nursed.﴾ The apparent reading is that the pronoun in (تَرَوْنَها, "you see it") refers to the earthquake (al-zalzala), since it is the subject being spoken of. It has also been said that it refers to the Hour (al-sa'a), but that is, as you see, weak. (يَوْمَ, "the Day") is in the accusative case, governed by (تَذْهَلُ, "will be distracted"), and it is placed before its verb for emphasis. It has been said that it is governed by (عَظِيمٍ, "great"), and it has been said that it is governed by an implied (اذْكُرْ, "remember"). It has also been said that it is a substitute (badal) for (السّاعَةِ, "the Hour"), and it is given the fatha vowel because it is indeclinable, as was said regarding the verse ﴿This is a day when truthfulness benefits﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 119] according to the reading of (يَوْمَ) with fatha. It has been said that it is a substitute for (زَلْزَلَةَ, "earthquake") or is governed by it, if the separation between the verbal noun and its adverbial complement by the predicate is permitted. The clause (تَذْهَلُ, "will be distracted") on these possibilities is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the object pronoun, and the returning pronoun is omitted, i.e., "will be distracted in it." Al-dhuhul (distraction) is a preoccupation that produces sorrow and forgetfulness.

(الْمُرْضِعَةُ, "the nursing mother") is the one who is in the act of nursing, putting her breast to the child's mouth. This differs from (الْمُرْضِعُ, "the wet-nurse") without the ta' marbuta, which refers to one whose nature it is to nurse, even if she is not actually nursing at the time it is applied to her. Some Kufan grammarians restricted (مُرْضِعَةٌ, with the ta') to the child's mother and (مُرْضِعٌ) to a hired wet-nurse, but this is refuted by the poet's words:

*"Like a nursing woman who nurses the children of others and neglects the children of her own womb; this is error far from the aim."*

The use of this form here serves to show the severity of the matter and the intensity of the terror. The apparent reading is that (ما, "what") is a relative pronoun and the returning pronoun is omitted, i.e., "from that which she nursed." The use of (ما) emphasises the distraction, and that the nursing infant is such that it does not occur to her what it is, since she knows its thingness but does not know specifically who it is. It has been said that (ما) is a verbal-noun particle, i.e., "she is distracted from her nursing." The first reading indicates the severity of the terror and the completeness of the alarm. The speech is according to the method of tamthil (figurative illustration), meaning that if there were a nursing mother and an infant, the mother would be distracted from her infant while nursing it, because of the severity of the terror, and likewise what follows. This is apparent if the earthquake is at the second blast, or on the Day of Resurrection when Adam, peace be upon him, is commanded to send forth the company of the Fire and the company of Paradise, unless we say that every person is resurrected in the state in which he departed the world, so that a nursing mother is resurrected as a nursing mother and a pregnant woman as a pregnant woman, as is reported in some traditions. But if we say that, or that the earthquake is in this world, then the speech may be literal, and the fact that the matter then is more intense, greater and more dreadful than what is described, and more widespread, does not harm its being a figurative illustration, since what has been mentioned is for the sake of terror, as is not hidden from the fair and noble judge.

It was read (تُذْهَلُ) from the causative (al-idhhal) in the passive voice, and Ibn Abi 'Abla and al-Yamani read (تُذْهِلُ) from it in the active voice, with (كُلَّ) in the accusative, meaning "the day the earthquake distracts every nursing mother." It has been said that the subject is the Hour. (وَتَضَعُ كُلُّ ذاتِ حَمْلٍ حَمْلَها) ﴿and every pregnant female will drop her burden﴾, i.e., every pregnant female will cast off her foetus before its full term. The reason he did not say (وَتَضَعُ كُلُّ حامِلَةٍ ما حَمَلَتْ, "every pregnant woman will drop what she carried"), in the pattern of what preceded, is that that is not explicit about the intended meaning, which is the delivery of the foetus, whereas the sublime wording here is explicit in it, because (الْحَمْلُ), with fatha, is what is carried in the womb of the child, and its application to something like a fruit on a tree is by analogy with the pregnancy of a woman. For the sake of explicitness on this from the outset, He did not say (حَمْلَها) in the form of "every pregnant woman her burden." This is what has been said. It has been objected that the claim that (الْحَمْلُ) is restricted to what is carried in the womb as a child, and that its application to something like a fruit on a tree is by analogy, is a matter for investigation. In al-Bahr: al-hamlu with fatha is what is in a womb or on the top of a tree.

In al-Qamus: al-hamlu is what is carried in the womb of the child; its plural is himal and ahmal. (حَمَلَتِ الْمَرْأةُ تَحْمِلُ) means she became pregnant; it is not said (حَمَلَتْ بِهِ), or it is rare. She is (حامِلٌ) and (حامِلَةٌ). Al-hamlu is also the fruit of a tree, and it may be pronounced with kasra or fatha: fatha for what is hidden inside its fruit, and kasra for what is visible; or fatha for what is in a belly or on the top of a tree, and kasra for what is on a back or top; or (ثَمَرُ الشَّجَرِ, the fruit of the tree) with kasra is what has not yet grown, and once it has grown it takes fatha. Its plurals are ahmal, humul and himal. End of quotation.

It has been said: what is obvious is the dropping of the foetus, whatever expression is used; however, (ذاتُ حَمْلٍ, "one possessing a burden") is more forceful in terror than (حامِلٌ, "pregnant") or (حامِلَةٌ), because it implies companionship, which implies constancy, so the speech implies that the pregnant woman at that time drops the foetus which was settled and established in her womb. This is in addition to the gentleness of combining what implies companionship with what implies separation, which is dropping. So reflect, for the path of the mind has room.

(وَتَرَى النّاسَ) ﴿and you see people﴾ is read with fatha on the (تَاء) and (رَاء), addressing each one of the addressees with the seeing of the earthquake. The difference between the plural and the singular is that what is seen in the first instance is the earthquake, which all witness, while in the second instance it is the state of those other than the addressee among them. So there must be a singular addressee in a way that covers each one of them, but without considering his being characterised by that state, since the purpose is to show the effect of the earthquake on the one seen, not on the seer by the variation of his feelings, because its ruling is the aspect of his seeing the earthquake, not anything else. It is as if it were said: "and the people will become drunk," etc. What is in the revelation was preferred over this to indicate the complete manifestation of that state in them and its reaching such clarity that it is hardly hidden from anyone. This was said by more than one scholar.

Some have permitted that the address is to the Prophet ﷺ, but the first is more forceful in terror. The seeing is visual (baṣariyya), with (النّاسَ) as its object; and His saying (سُكارى, "drunk") is a circumstantial clause from it, i.e., each one sees them resembling the drunk. His saying (وَما هُمْ بِسُكارى, "yet they are not drunk") means in reality, and it is also a circumstantial clause, but an emphatic one, and an emphatic circumstantial clause is joined by the particle (وَاو, "and"), especially when it is a nominal clause. So it is not said: if the meaning of His saying "you see people drunk" is by way of comparison, then "yet they are not drunk" in the stated sense would be dispensed with, and there is no basis for making it an emphatic circumstantial clause because of the waw. It is permitted that (تَرَى) means (تَظُنُّ, "you think"), so (سُكارى) is a second object, and then it is permitted that the speech is by way of comparison and the nominal clause is in the position of an emphatic circumstantial clause, and it is permitted that it is literal, in which case there is no emphasis here. The matter of the singular address and its exaggeration by a state is in its own right. In any case, what is meant in His saying (وَما هُمْ بِسُكارى, "yet they are not drunk") is the continuation of negation, and it is emphasised by the addition of the particle (بِ, "bi") to alert that what they are in is nothing like what is customary, but is a matter they had never experienced before. Its cause is indicated by His saying: ﴿But the punishment of God is severe.﴾ That is, the severity of His punishment makes them as you see. This is an exceptive (istidrak) continuation of what al-Intisaf said regarding His saying (وَما هُمْ بِسُكارى). Abu Hayyan claimed that it is an exceptive continuation of an implied clause, as if it were said: "This, i.e., the distraction, the dropping, and seeing people as drunk, are light states; but the punishment of God is severe and is not light." This is very contrary to the apparent meaning.

Zayd ibn 'Ali, may God be pleased with both of them, read (تُرِي) with damma on the (تَاء) and kasra on the (رَاء), meaning the earthquake makes all of creation see people as drunk. Al-Za'farani read (تُرى) with damma on the (تَاء) and fatha on the (رَاء), with (النّاسُ) in the nominative, by attributing the passive verb to it, and the feminine form is according to the interpretation of the group. Abu Hurayra, Abu Zur'a, Ibn Jarir and Abu Nuhayk read the same, except that they put (النّاسَ) in the accusative; and (تَرى) on this reading is transitive to three objects, as in al-Bahr. The first is the hidden pronoun, which is the deputy subject; the second is (النّاسَ); and the third is (سُكارى). Abu Hurayra and Ibn Nuhayk read (سَكارى) with fatha on the (سِين) in both places; it is a broken plural whose singular is (سَكْرانُ). Abu Hatim said it is the dialect of Tamim. Al-Tabarani and others transmitted from 'Imran ibn Husayn that the Messenger of God ﷺ read (سَكْرى) like (عَطْشى) in both places, and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri also transmitted this. It is the reading of 'Abd Allah and his companions, and Hudhayfa, and with it read the two brothers (al-Akhawan), Ibn Sa'dan and Mas'ud ibn Salih. The adjective is made into the pattern fa'la when it denotes afflictions and diseases, like (قَتْلى, "slain"), (مَوْتى, "dead") and (حَمْقى, "foolish"). Because drunkenness functions like these, in that it disables the powers and senses, it is pluralised in this pattern; so it is the plural of (سَكْرانُ). Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said it may be the plural of (سَكِرٌ), like (زَمْنى) of (زَمِنٌ). Sibawayh reported that (رَجُلٌ سَكِرٌ) means (سَكْرانُ). Al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Abu Zur'a, Ibn Jubayr and al-A'mash read (سُكْرى) with damma on the (سِين) in both places. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is rare. Abu al-Fath said: it is a singular noun, like (البُشْرى, "good news"), and Abu 'Ali [al-Farisi] gave me this ruling when I asked him about it. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi also held that it is a singular noun, saying: (فُعْلى) with damma on the (فاء) is an attribute of a single female, but since it has been made an attribute of people, who are a group, the group is treated as a singular feminine. From Abu Zur'a: (سَكْرى) with fatha on the (سِين), and (بِسُكْرى) with damma. From Ibn Jubayr: (سَكْرى) with fatha on the (سِين) without alif, and (بِسُكارى) with damma and alif as in the reading of the majority. The dispute over whether (فَعالى) is a plural or a collective noun is well known.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 3:

﴿Among the people is one who disputes about God without knowledge﴾. It was revealed as Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Malik, may God be pleased with him, concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who was a contentious disputant and who said: "The angels, peace be upon them, are the daughters of God, glory be to Him, and the Qur'an is the tales of the ancients," and that God, exalted is His state, is not able to bring back to life one who has decayed and become dust. It was also said to be about Abu Jahl, and it was said to be about Ubayy ibn Khalaf. The verse is general in meaning for everyone who engages in disputation about what is and is not permissible for God, glory be to Him, regarding His attributes and actions, and who does not refer to knowledge, proof, or fairness. The specificity of the occasion of revelation does not remove it from generality. Its mention came right after the explanation of the great importance of the Hour, which announces the Resurrection, in order to describe the condition of some of those who deny it. The place of the prepositional phrase is in the nominative case as a subject (mubtada', the subject of a nominal sentence), either by taking it according to its meaning, or by supposing what it is connected to. The phrase ﴿without knowledge﴾ (bi-ghayri 'ilm) is in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal, a word indicating the state of the subject at the time of the action) from the pronoun in (yujadilu, disputes), to clarify what disputation implies of ignorance. That is: "and some of the people, or some of them who are among the people, is one who disputes concerning the affair of God, mighty and majestic, and says what has no good in it of falsehoods, accompanied by ignorance." (And he follows) in what he undertakes of disputation, or in everything he does and neglects of the false affairs, of which this is part, ﴿every rebellious devil﴾: stripped bare for corruption, devoid of good. It derives from their saying: "a marda tree" (shajarah mardá'), meaning one without leaves, and from it it is said: "a marda sand-dune" (ramlah mardá'), when it produces nothing, and from it comes al-amrad (the beardless youth), because he is bare of hair. Al-Zajjaj said: the origin of marid and marid is the elevated, smooth thing, and in it is the meaning of being bare and stripped. What is meant by it is either Iblis and his soldiers, or the leaders of the disbelievers who call those beneath them to disbelief. Zayd ibn Ali, may God be pleased with them both, read (wa-yatba'u), with a light pronunciation (khafifan).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 4:

﴿It is decreed for him that whoever takes him as a friend, he will lead him astray and guide him to the punishment of the Blaze﴾. The pronoun in (ʿalayhi) refers to the devil (shayṭān), and likewise the object pronoun in ﴿tawallāh﴾, the pronoun in (fa-innahu), and the two hidden pronouns in ﴿yuḍilluhu wa-yahdīhi﴾. The pronoun in (annahu) refers to the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn, the pronoun of the matter), and all the remaining pronouns refer to whoever (man).

There is disagreement over the grammatical analysis (iʿrāb) of the verse. It has been said that ﴿annahu man tawallāh﴾ and so on is the deputy subject (nāʾib fāʿil) of (kutiba), and the clause is in the position of a second attribute of shayṭān. Here (man) is conditional (jazāʾiyya), and its response is omitted, while ﴿fa-annahu yuḍilluhu﴾ and so on is conjoined to (annahu) together with what falls under its scope and what is connected to it. The meaning is: it is decreed upon the devil that the matter is that whoever takes him (atakhadhahu) as a friend (waliyyan) and follows him, [the devil] will destroy him; for he will lead him astray from the path of Paradise and its reward, and guide him to the path of the Blaze and its punishment. The fa' indicates the detailing of the destruction, as in His saying: ﴿So repent to your Creator and kill yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 54]. Al-Ṭībī interpreted the words of al-Kashshāf in this way, and it is a good view, except that whether this is what al-Zamakhsharī intended is unclear.

It has also been said that (man) is a relative pronoun (mawṣūla), the subject (mubtadaʾ), and the clause ﴿tawallāh﴾ is its relative clause (ṣila), with the hidden pronoun as its returning pronoun. (Annahu yuḍilluhu) is, in interpretation, a verbal noun (taʾwīl maṣdar), the predicate of an omitted subject, or a subject whose predicate is omitted, and the clause is the predicate of the relative. The entry of the fa' into its predicate is by analogy with the conditional: the meaning is, it is decreed upon him that the matter is that whoever takes him as a friend, so his matter is, or it is due, that he will lead him astray, and so on. It is also permissible for (man) to be conditional and the fa' to be a response particle, with what follows it together with the implied element being the response of the condition.

It has been said that the pronoun in (annahu) refers to the devil, and it is the subject of (anna), while (man) is relative or qualifying. The first is more apparent. Its predicate is the hidden pronoun in (tawallāh), which refers to some of the people, and the explicit pronoun refers to whoever, and the clause is a relative clause or a qualifier. His saying, exalted is He: (fa-annahu yuḍilluhu) is conjoined to (annahu man tawallāh). The meaning is: he follows every devil about whom it is decreed that he is the one whom [the person] took as a friend after the people, and that he misleads whoever takes him as a friend; so the first serves as a preparation for the second. That is, he follows a devil specific to him, about whom it is written that he is his friend and that he misleads him, so he spares no effort in misleading him. This meaning is more eloquent than the previous meaning, given the possibility that man is conditional, because it indicates that each of the two disputants has one of the rebellious devils. Al-Kashshāf's commentator (al-Kashf) approved this and took the intent of the author of al-Kashshāf to be this.

It has been reported from some virtuosi that the pronoun in (annahu) refers to the disputer, i.e., it is decreed upon the devil that the disputer is whoever takes him as a friend. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿fa-annahu﴾ and so on is conjoined to ﴿annahu man tawallāh﴾. It has been objected that the devil's being characterized by the disputer's taking him as a friend is what the context requires, not the reverse; and that if (man) in ﴿man tawallāh﴾ were made a relative pronoun, as is apparent, it would follow that no one takes him as a friend except the disputer, and this restriction defeats the intensification.

In al-Baḥr: the apparent view is that the pronoun in (ʿalayhi) refers to whoever (man), because it is the one spoken of; and in (annahu), (tawallāh), and (fa-annahu), it refers to him as well, the subject of (tawallā) being the pronoun of man, and likewise the hāʾ in ﴿yuḍilluhu﴾. It is also permissible that the hāʾ in (annahu) on this reading be the pronoun of the matter, and the meaning is that this disputer, because of his much disputing in falsehood and his following of the devil, has become a leader in misguidance for whoever takes him as a friend, so the matter is that he misleads whoever takes him as a friend. End of quotation. On this reading, the clause (kutiba ilakh) is a fresh sentence and not an attribute of shayṭān. The more apparent view is to make the pronoun in (ʿalayhi) refer to the devil, and this is what is narrated from Qatādah. In any case, (kutiba) is in the sense of "passed" (maḍā) and "was decreed" (qudділа), and it is also permissible that it be taken in its literal sense. In al-Kashshāf: the "writing upon him" is like an expression (ayy), as if that was written upon him because it is evident in his condition.

The metaphorical, mocking allegorical metaphor (al-istiʿāra al-tamthīliyya al-tahakkumiyya) in (yahdīhi) is not hidden.

It was also read as «kataba» in the active voice, i.e., God decreed (kataba Allāh). It was read «fa-innahu» with a kasra on the hamza, so the clause is the predicate of man or its response. Al-Aʿmash and al-Juʿfī, from Abū ʿAmr, read «innahu» and «fa-innahu» with a kasra on the hamza in both places. The reason for the kasra in the second is clear; as for its reason in the first, it is, as Abū Ḥayyān favored, that (kutiba) is ascribed to the clause in a verbal sense: it was written upon him this statement, as you say "I wrote that God the Exalted commands justice and benevolence," or by supposing a saying (taqdīr qawl) and making the clause an object of it, or by imputing to the verb the meaning of that: it was decreed upon him, said concerning his matter, that whoever takes him as a friend...

[Page 115]

﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection...﴾ and so on. This is an establishment of proof which silences those who dispute about the Resurrection, following an indication of what their affair will come to. It has been inferred that the intended sense of "mankind" here is the disbelieving disputants who deny the Resurrection. The expression of their belief concerning it as "doubt" (*rayb*), that is, uncertainty, is used even though they are firmly convinced of its impossibility. This is either to make known that the most that can proceed from them, even though they are in the utmost obstinacy and stubbornness, is wavering concerning its matter. Or, if they are certain of its impossibility, then that lies outside the circle of possibility. Likewise, the indefinite form of the word and its introduction with the word of doubt (*shakk*) indicate that its proper status is to be weak and of doubtful occurrence. Or it is to alert to the fact that their offence in this regard is like a weak doubt, because the evidences for its possibility are so clear and their strength so complete. The text does not say "if you doubt about the Resurrection" in order to emphasise the removal of any trace of the occurrence of doubt from its matter, and to indicate that if doubt does occur, it comes from their side and not from its side. Considering that they are settled in it and it surrounds them does not contradict considering its weakness and scarcity, because what that requires is the continuance of their involvement with it, not its strength or abundance. The *min* here is for origin (*ibtida'iyyah*), attached to an omitted element that stands as a description of *rayb*. It has been inferred that the intended sense is doubt about the possibility of the Resurrection, since that is what what follows requires. It has also been allowed that the intended sense is doubt about the actual occurrence of the Resurrection. It has been objected that the proof alluded to afterwards only shows possibility, together with the redundancy that results with His saying, exalted is He, to come, ﴿and that Allah will raise those who are in the graves﴾. There is room for reflection here, so reflect.

[Page 116]

Al-Hasan (al-Hasan al-Basri) read *min al-ba'ath* with a fatha on the ʿayn (*al-ba'ath*), which is a dialect form of the word, like *al-jalab* and *al-tarad* for *al-jalb* and *al-tard* according to the Basrans. According to the Kufans, the sukun on the ʿayn is a lightening, and it is analogical in every noun whose middle letter is a throat letter, such as *al-nahr* and *al-nahar*, *al-sha'r* and *al-sha'ar*.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed We created you from dust﴾, it is the indication of the response of the condition, or it is the response by interpretation, meaning: "And if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then look at the origin of your creation, so that your doubt may vanish: indeed We created you..." and so on. It has been said that the implied sense is: "then I inform you and make you know that We created you..." and so on, but this is not the right reading. Their creation from dust is within the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, from it, or it is by the creation of the foods from which the seed is formed, which, though formed from all the elements together with it, is the greatest of the parts according to what has been said. Therefore it was singled out for mention from among them. The first view was preferred, and the meaning taken is: We created you with a general creation from dust, ﴿then﴾ We created you with a detailed creation ﴿from a drop﴾, that is, seed, from the *nutaf*, in the sense of dripping. Al-Raghib said: the *nutfah* is clear water, and it is used to express the man's water. It has been said that the restriction on this basis, although creation is from two waters, is because the majority of the human's parts are created from the man's water. The truth is that *nutfah*, just as it is used to express the man's seed, is also used to express seed in general, and al-Raghib's statement is not an explicit denial of that. The apparent meaning is the drop from which each one is created without intermediary. It has been said that the intended sense is the drop of Adam, peace be upon him, and this has been related from al-Naqqash, and it is extremely remote.

﴿Then from a clinging clot﴾, that is, a solid piece of blood formed from the seed. ﴿Then from a lump of flesh﴾, that is, a piece of flesh formed from the clot, and its original sense is a piece of flesh the size of what can be chewed. ﴿Formed﴾ in the genitive is a description of *mudghah* (lump), and likewise His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and unformed﴾.

Ibn Abi ʿAblah read both with the accusative as a *hal* (circumstantial clause) from the preceding indefinite noun. This is rare, and Sibawayh made it analogical. The well-known and immediately understood view is that *mukhallaqah* means the one whose creation is manifest, that is, a lump whose creation and form are manifest, and a lump whose creation and form have not yet become manifest. The intention is to detail the state of the lump, and that it was at first a piece in which none of the organs had appeared, then they appeared gradually, bit by bit. The order based on gradual progression from remote beginnings to near ones would require that the unformed be mentioned first, but it was delayed because it is a privation (*'adam malakah*). The form *taf'il* is for the multiplicity of organs, each of which is specific to a creation and a form. It has also been said that *mukhallaqah* means the one that is levelled and smooth, free from defect and fault. It is said: he *khalaqa* the siwak or the stick, meaning he levelled it and smoothed it, and a rock is *khalqa'*, that is smooth, and a mountain is *akhlaq*, that is smooth. So the meaning is: from a levelled drop, without deficiency or fault in the beginning of its creation, and a drop that is not levelled, in which there is a fault. Thus the drops from which a human is created vary: some are of perfect creation, smooth from defects, and others are the reverse. Following this variation is the variation of people in their creation, forms, height, shortness, completeness and deficiency. It is related from Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Sha'bi, Abu al-ʿAliyah and ʿIkrimah that the *mukhallaqah* is the one for which the full term of pregnancy has been completed, and upon which creation has been successively formed, and the *ghayr mukhallaqah* is the one for which this has not been completed and which has miscarried. This is supported by what al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in *Nawadir al-Usul*, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: When the drop settles in the womb, the angel of the wombs takes it in his palm and says: "O Lord, is it formed or unformed?" If it is said "unformed," it is not a living soul, and the womb ejects it as blood. If it is said "formed," he says: "O Lord, male or female? Wretched or blessed? What is its term, what is its trace, what is its provision, and in what land will it die?" The report continues, and it has the ruling of what is traced back to the Prophet. The intended sense is that they were created from the kind of this drop described as complete or miscarried, not that they were created from a complete drop and from a miscarried drop, since it is not conceivable to create from a miscarried drop, which is evident. It seems that the mention in this view is for describing it with what has been mentioned, to magnify the matter of divine power. In making each of these stages a starting point for their creation, and not for the creation of the stages that come after it, is an additional indication of the greatness of His power, exalted is He, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We made the drop a clot, then We made the clot a lump, then We made the lump...﴾ and so on.

﴿So that We may make clear to you﴾ is connected to *khalaqna* (We created), and the object is omitted for its magnification in quantity and quality. That is, We created you in this wondrous pattern so that We may make clear to you what expression cannot encompass of realities and subtleties, among which is the matter of the Resurrection. For whoever reflects on what has been mentioned of gradual creation is certain that He who was able to create the human at first from dust, and who never tasted the water of life, and who made him in a form that makes him fit to generate his like again and again, by directing him through the stages of creation and transforming him from one state to another, together with the difference and contrast between those stages and states, is able to restore him. Indeed, restoration is easier by analogy. Some have estimated the object as specific, meaning: so that We make clear to you the matter of the Resurrection, but this is not the right reading.

Much more remote is the one who claimed that the meaning is: so that We make clear to you that the shaping is a choice of the choosing agent, and that were it not so, some individuals of the lump would not become unformed. Ibn Abi ʿAblah read *liyubayyin* with the *ya'* by way of *iltifat* (a shift of grammatical person), and likewise he read His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and We cause to remain in the wombs what We will﴾. The majority read it with the *nun*. The clause is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*) brought to explain their condition after the completion of their creation and the succession of stages upon them. That is: and We cause to remain in the wombs after that what We will to make remain in them, ﴿for an appointed term﴾, which is the time of delivery. Its minimum is six months and its maximum, according to us, is two years, and according to al-Shafiʿi, may Allah have mercy on him, four years. It is related from Yaʿqub that he read *wa-nuqirru* with a fatha on the *nun* and a damma on the *qaf*, from *qarartu al-ma'*, when I poured the water. Yahya ibn Wathhab read *ma nishaʾu* with a kasra on the *nun*.

﴿Then We bring you forth﴾, that is, from the wombs after your being made to remain in them, when the appointed term is complete. ﴿As infants﴾ is a *hal* (circumstantial clause) from the pronoun of the addressees. The singular form is either by considering each one of them, or by intending the genus which applies to the many, or because it is a verbal noun (*masdar*), in which the singular and the plural are alike, as al-Mubarrad said, or because the intended sense is "infant by infant," which was abbreviated, as al-Jalal al-Suyuti related in *al-Ashbah al-Nahwiyyah*.

ʿUmar ibn Shabbah read *yukhrijukum* with the *ya'*. ﴿Then that you may reach your full strength﴾, that is, your full maturity in strength, intellect and discernment. In the *Qamus*: "until he reaches his *ashudd*, and its first letter may be dammed," that is, his strength, which is between eighteen years and thirty. It is a singular form that came in the pattern of a plural, like *ka'annaka*, and there is no parallel to these two; or it is a plural with no singular from its own form; or its singular is *shiddah* with a kasra, although *fi'lah* is not pluralised on the pattern *af'ul* by analogy, so *ni'mah* and *an'um* is not an objection; or *shadd* like *kalb* and *akluhb*, or *shidd* like *dhi'b* and *adhu'ub*. These two are not heard, but are analogical. (*Wa-li-tablughu*) Abu al-Suʿud, the Allamah, said: it is a cause (*'illah*) for *nukhrijakum* (We bring you forth), coordinated with another cause suitable to it. It is as if it were said: "then We bring you forth so that you may grow little by little, then so that you may reach your full strength," and so on. It has also been said that the cause is of an omitted element, and the estimate is: "then We grant you respite so that you may reach your full strength," and so on.

Al-Allamah al-Tibi allowed that the estimate is: "(then so that you may reach your full strength) that stay and that bringing forth took place." It has also been said that it is coordinated with *nubayyin* (We make clear). Al-Allamah objected that this disrupts the eloquence of the noble composition, and he treated it, like others, as coordinated with it on the reading of *nuqirru*. *Nukhraja* with the accusative is the reading of al-Mufaddal and Abu Hatim, except that the first read with the *nun* and the second with the *ya'*. Likewise making the two verbs coordinated with it, and he said: The meaning is: We created you by the stated gradation for two matters. One is that We make clear our affairs, and the second is that We cause you to remain in the wombs, then bring you forth as infants, then that you may reach your full strength. The placement of the making clear before what follows, although its occurrence in fact is after all of them, is to indicate that it is the ultimate end and intended in itself. The repetition of the *lam* in *li-tablughu*, while the *lam* is stripped from *nuqirru* and *nukhriju*, is to indicate the primacy of reaching maturity in relation to the causing to remain and the bringing forth, since the obligation that leads to happiness and misery depends on it. The choice of attributing reaching maturity to the addressees, rather than attributing the making to reach to Him, exalted is He, like the preceding verbs, is because it is more suitable for explaining their state of being characterised by perfection and their independence through the originating of effects and actions. End of quotation.

[Page 117]

What he mentioned about the coordination of *nuqirru* and *nukhraja* (with the accusative) on *nubayyin* was not accepted by Shaykh Ibn al-Hajib. He said in the commentary on *al-Mufassal*: it is among the things in which the accusative is impossible, because if it were put in the accusative as coordinated with *nubayyin*, the meaning would be weak, since the *lam* in *li-nubayyin* is for causation of what came before it, and what came before is a cause for making clear. So if *wa-nuqirru* were coordinated upon it, it would fall within the causal relation of ﴿Indeed We created you﴾ and so on, and the creation from dust followed by what came after it is not suitable as a cause for causing to remain in the wombs. Al-Zajjaj said: in *wa-nuqirru* only the nominative is permitted, and it is not permitted that its meaning be "We did that so that We might cause to remain in the wombs," because Allah, exalted is He, did not create mankind so that He might cause them to remain in the wombs, but He created them to guide them to their right course and their welfare. This is a view that the coordination on *nubayyin* is not permitted.

[Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 5 (part 2 of 2)]

It is answered that the purpose in reality is reaching full maturity (bulugh al-ashudd) and fitness for legal responsibility (taklif). However, since the affirming (al-iqrar) and what follows it are among its preliminaries, it is valid to include it in the causal clause. As for his claim that coordinating (al-'atf) ﴿لِتَبْلُغُوا﴾ with ﴿لِنُبَيِّنَ﴾ on the reading with raf' (ﷺ) harms the eloquence of the noble arrangement, the apparent meaning is that it is an allusion against al-Zamakhshari, who made the coordination with that, and said: "If you say: how can ﴿لِتَبْلُغُوا أشُدَّكُمْ﴾ be coordinated with ﴿لِنُبَيِّنَ﴾ when there is no correspondence (tibaq)? I say: the correspondence is present, because His saying, exalted is He, ﴿ونُقِرُّ﴾ is a companion of the causal clause, and its being joined to it and bound to it makes them, as it were, one thing. So it returns from this aspect to the strength of the reading with nasb." End of quote. In this there is what hints that the reading with nasb is clearer as well as stronger. The verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) did not accept this. In al-Kashshaf (the commentary of al-Zamakhshari, as cited by Alusi) it is said that the reading with raf' is the well-known one, established among the Seven Readings, and it is the preferable one. It has been hit by its composition in this manner, like the aim of an archer, so that the affirming in the wombs is not made a cause; rather, the purpose of it is made to be reaching full maturity, which is the state of completion in knowledge and action. Since ﴿ونُقِرُّ﴾ was not coordinated with ﴿لِنُبَيِّنَ﴾ except after it had been placed before it, then ﴿نُخْرِجُكُمْ﴾ was made ﴿نُقِرَّ﴾ coordinated with "Indeed We created you" (﴿إنّا خَلَقْناكم﴾). The turn to the present tense serves to develop the state and indicate increased particularity. So the correspondence is present both verbally and in meaning. Moreover, in separating the two causes there is a subtlety that is not hidden from one of sound intellect whose appreciation of its place becomes good after reflection. Likewise, in the use of "then" (thumma) in His saying, glorified is He, ﴿ثُمَّ لِتَبْلُغُوا﴾, there is an indication that this is the principal purpose for which man was created: ﴿وما خَلَقْتُ الجِنَّ والإنْسَ إلا لِيَعْبُدُونِ﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56]. And since the earlier items were the more evident in indicating resurrection, His saying, exalted is He, ﴿لِنُبَيِّنَ﴾ was placed before the affirming and the bringing out. End of quote.

From this one learns what is in the statement of the 'Allamah (al-Alusi's reference to the author of the source), that the coordination of "li-tablughu" and so on upon "li-nubayyina" harms the eloquence of the noble arrangement, and that it is not necessary to take ﴿ونُقِرُّ﴾ as a fresh sentence (isti'naf). In it also is that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿ومِنكم مَن يُتَوَفّى﴾ and so on is a fresh sentence explaining the divisions of bringing forth from the womb, as He fully covered the divisions of the first. In it is also a clarification of the excellence of the state of reaching full maturity, and that it is the most deserving to be the intended goal of the creating. But among you is one who is caused to die before reaching it, so he is brought to the point of death, and among you is one who passes beyond it, so he is brought to abasement. That is: among you is one who dies before reaching full maturity. ﴿ومِنكم مَن يُرَدُّ إلى أرْذَلِ العُمُرِ﴾, that is, the most degraded and lowest of life, and what is meant is that he is returned to a time like childhood. ﴿لِكَيْلا يَعْلَمَ مِن بَعْدِ عِلْمٍ﴾, that is, after much knowledge, ﴿شَيْئًا﴾, that is, anything of things or anything of knowledge. The lam is connected to "yuradd" and it is the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah), and what is meant is exaggeration in the diminishing of his knowledge and the reversal of his condition. There is no fixed limit for the time of that return; rather, it varies with the variation of temperaments, according to what is in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit of Abu Hayyan). The mention of the return (radd) and the causing to die (tawaffi) in the passive form is for conformity with the manner of divine majesty, since the agent is determined, as in Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim (of Abu al-Su'ud). In Sharh al-Kashshaf of al-Tibi, after permitting that ﴿ثُمَّ لِتَبْلُغُوا﴾ be taken as ... (that) this affirming and bringing forth [occurred], the benefit of that is the announcement that reaching full maturity is the best of states, bringing forth is the most wondrous of them, and return to the lowest of life is the worst of them. The change of expression for this is why the bringing forth was attributed to His holy essence, and the cause was omitted in the second, and the third was not attributed to its agent, and in it was negated what was affirmed for man in that state of possessing knowledge and power, which is indicated by "ashudd." It is as if it was said: then He brings you out from those base stages as a child, a wondrous creation, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿فَتَبارَكَ اللَّهُ أحْسَنُ الخالِقِينَ﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14]. Then, ﴿لِتَبْلُغُوا أشُدَّكم﴾, He arranged that wondrous arrangement, because it is the time of the firm establishing of knowledge and understanding and of being able to act, which are the two aims of the creating. Then He causes you to die or returns you to the lowest of life, in which knowledge and the power to act are removed. End of quote.

From this it is understood that it is permissible that what is meant by ﴿ومِنكم مَن يُتَوَفّى﴾ is death after reaching full maturity. Some people permitted that what is meant is death at the time of reaching maturity. It was said that this would make the clause a circumstantial clause (hal) and that it would be from the present tense, and that is, as you see, weak. It has been read as "yatawaffa" in the active form, with its subject being the pronoun of God, exalted is He, meaning: whom God causes to die. It is also permitted that the pronoun refers to "man" (man), meaning: he who completes the duration of his life. It is narrated from Abu 'Amr and Nafi' that the mim of "al-'umr" is pronounced with sukun. This is the discussion. Then, what is in the variation of the human states after being brought out from the womb of admonition regarding the soundness of resurrection is not hidden, just as in the variation of them before. So reflect on all that has been mentioned. And to God, exalted is He, belongs the pearl of the revelation, how many its possibilities are!

﴿وتَرى الأرْضَ هامِدَةً﴾ is another proof of the soundness of resurrection, coordinated with ﴿إنّا خَلَقْناكُمْ﴾. It is a cosmic proof (ayah afaqiyyah), and what came before is an internal proof (ayah anfusiyyah). The address is to everyone from whom sight is possible. It was also said: it is to the disputant. The present-tense form serves to indicate renewal and continuity, and it is a sight of the eye, not of knowledge, as was said. "Hamidah" is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from "al-ard," meaning: dead and dry. It is said: "hamadat al-ard" when it dried up and became effaced, and "hamad al-thawb" when the garment wore out. Al-A'sha said:

"Qutaylah said: what is wrong with your body, pale,
and I see your garments worn out, decayed."

Its origin is from "hamadat al-nar," when the fire became ashes.

﴿فَإذا أنْزَلْنا عَلَيْها الماءَ﴾, that is, the water of rain. It was said: it includes that and the water of springs and rivers, though the apparent sense of "sending down" requires the first.

﴿اهْتَزَّتْ﴾: its vegetation moved. The attribution is then metaphorical (majaz 'aqli). Or: it became loose-textured, and some of its parts separated from others because of the emergence of plants. Taking "ihtizaz" as movement in quality is far-fetched.

﴿ورَبَتْ﴾: it increased and swelled because of the water and vegetation that penetrate it.

Abu Ja'far, 'Abd Allah ibn Ja'far, Khalid ibn Ilyas, and Abu 'Amr in one narration read "wa-rabat" with the hamzah, meaning: it rose up. It is said: "Fulan yarba' bi-nafsihi 'an kadha," meaning: he raises himself above such-and-such. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is from "rabi'tu al-qawm," when I ascended a height of the land as a lookout over them. So it is as if the land, with water, stretches out and rises.

﴿وأنْبَتَتْ مِن كُلِّ زَوْجٍ﴾, that is, kind, ﴿بَهِيجٍ﴾, beautiful, pleasing to the beholder.

[Page 119]

﴿That is because Allah is the Truth﴾. This is a resumptive statement (kalam mustaʾnaf), brought after establishing the truth of the resurrection (al-baʿth, the raising of the dead) and confirming the proof for it in the most complete manner. It explains that what has been mentioned of the creation of man through different stages, His directing him through various conditions, and His giving life to the earth after its death, which reveals the truth of this, are among the effects of His divinity (uluhiyyah) and of the rulings of His essential, attributive and active affairs (shu'un). It also explains that what they deny, namely the coming of the Hour and the resurrection, is among the causes of those wondrous effects, which are known to them, and among the origins of their issuing from Him, exalted is He. In this there is an indication of the strength of the proof and the originality of what it proves in its realisation, and a manifest demonstration of the falsity of their denial. For denying the realisation of the cause while being certain of the realisation of the effect is something that, by the immediate judgment of minds, necessitates its falsity. The demonstrative ﴿That﴾ refers to the creation of man through different stages and what accompanies it. The singular form is used in view of what is mentioned, and the sense of distance in it is to indicate the distance of its rank in perfection. It (ḏālika) is the subject (mubtadaʾ), and its predicate (khabar) is the prepositional phrase (al-jarr wa-l-majrur). By "the truth" (al-ḥaqq) is meant that which is established and whose establishment is necessary, because it is so in its essence, not merely that which is established in any sense. Thus the restriction (ḥaṣr) is evident: that is, what has been mentioned of wondrous creation comes about because He, exalted is He, is the Truth alone in His essence, His attributes and His acts, the One who realises all other things.

﴿And that He gives life to the dead﴾. That is, it is His affair and His habit, exalted is He, to give life to the dead. The summary of this is that He, exalted is He, is able to give them life at the beginning and in return, for otherwise He would not have given life to the drop of semen and to the dead earth again and again. What the imperfect verb form indicates of renewal is only in respect of the connection of the power and what it is connected to, not in respect of the power itself, because personal eternity (al-qidam al-shakhṣi) contradicts that.

﴿And that He is Able over all things﴾. That is, He is exceedingly powerful. Otherwise He would not have brought into being these existing things, which are numerous, and among which is what has been mentioned. The specific mention of giving life to the dead, although it is among the things over which He has power, is to make explicit that which is in dispute and to repel it into the throats of the deniers. Its being placed first is to highlight the importance attached to it.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 7:**

﴿And that the Hour is coming﴾, meaning: in what is yet to come. The expression is used in this form, rather than as a verb, to indicate the certainty of its arrival and its definite establishment, since wisdom necessarily requires it. His saying, ﴿there is no doubt about it﴾, is either a second predicate (khabar thani) of inna (indeed), or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "al-sa'ah" (the Hour) in the predicate. The meaning of negating doubt about it is that its matter is so evident and its signs so clear that there is no ground for anyone to doubt its coming.

*Anna* and what follows it are in the sense of a verbal noun (masdar), coordinated with the verbal noun governed by the causal *ba'* (the particle of cause). They fall within its scope together with it, like the two verbal nouns derived from His saying ﴿and that He gives life to the dead﴾ and His saying, glorified is He, ﴿and that He is powerful over everything﴾. Likewise is His saying, mighty and majestic is He, ﴿and that God will raise those in the graves﴾. However, this is not on the basis that the coming of the Hour and the raising of those in the graves are an effect of the power of God in the things mentioned among His acts; rather, it is on the basis that each of them is a cause that calls Him, mighty and majestic, to act, in accordance with His compassion towards His servants, which is founded upon far-reaching wisdoms, including the creation of humankind and the revival of the dead earth in a wondrous manner suitable for being cited as evidence of the possibility of these two, so that they may reflect upon this and derive proof from it regarding that possibility, or regarding their occurrence, and believe in it, so that they may attain eternal happiness. Were it not for that, He would not have done it; rather, He would not have created the world at all. This, as you see, is among the rulings of the truth of His, exalted is He, in His acts and their being founded upon manifest wisdoms, just as what precedes it is among the rulings of the truth of His, exalted is He, in His attributes and their being in the utmost perfection. This is what the scholar Abu al-Su'ud chose in explaining this, and it is what sound disposition inclines towards. The author of *al-Kashshaf* also took the reference to be to what has been mentioned, but apparently he made the coming of the Hour and the raising of those in the graves a metonymy (kinayah) for wisdom, since these are among its consequences. So the implied meaning is that this is established by the fact that God is the Truth, the existent and established, that He is able to revive the dead and over every possible thing, and that He is wise. He thus dispensed, by means of what wisdom requires, with describing Him as wise, because of the point contained in the metonymy, especially since the discourse is addressed to those who deny the resurrection, in order to repel it from their throats. Yet this is not free from remoteness. Al-Naysaburi reported the wording of *al-Kashshaf* and objected to it with things whose refutation is not hidden. He put forward an interpretation of the verse which he said had not occurred to anyone else, and he hoped it would be correct. However, apart from its requiring that the *ba'* be understood as covering both the efficient causal sense and the final causal sense, it has problems that are not hidden.

It has been said: that refers to what has been mentioned, except that His saying, ﴿and that the Hour is coming﴾ etc., is not coordinated with what is governed by the *ba'*, nor does it fall within the scope of causation; rather, it is a predicate, and the subject is omitted because the meaning is understood. The implied sense is: "the matter is that the Hour is coming," etc. Abu Hayyan confined himself to this view, but in it the discourse is cut off from its coherence.

It has been said: that refers to what has been mentioned, except that the *ba'* is a complement (silah) of a particular verb-like notion (kawn khass), and is not causal. It indicates that God is the Truth, etc. In this there is the objection that there is no indication of this particular notion.

It has been said: the meaning is "that is so that they may know that God is the Truth," etc. In this there is a certain allusion to the meaning of the well-known sacred hadith on people's tongues and in the books of the Sufis, although it is not established according to the hadith scholars: "I was a hidden treasure, so I loved to be known, so I created creation that I might be known." This, as you see, is [problematic].

It has been said: the reference is to the resurrection, which is inferred from what came before, and some have favoured this view. It is not hidden from you how much contrivance it requires.

It is reported in *al-Bahr* that this is in the accusative (mansub) by a hidden verb, meaning: "We did that because," etc. Abu 'Ali confined himself to saying that it is in the nominative as a subject (mubtada'), with the prepositional phrase as its predicate, and he said: "No other possibility is permissible." It seems that by "other" he meant what has been mentioned. What al-'Ukbari transmitted, that it is a predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "the matter is that," is permissible in principle, but it is very much contrary to the apparent sense.

Then, as for the intended meaning of "the Hour": it has been said that it is the Day of Resurrection, which includes the raising and the gathering and other things. Sa'di Jalabi said: what is meant here is the complete annihilation of the world, lest it be repeated together with the resurrection. As for the statement of al-Tibi that the path of His saying, ﴿and that the Hour is coming﴾, relative to His saying, glorified is He, ﴿and that God will raise those in the graves﴾, is the path of His saying, exalted and high is He, ﴿and that He is over everything powerful﴾, relative to His saying, mighty and majestic is He, ﴿and that He gives life to the dead﴾, but He placed the latter first and the former second for the sake of observing the rhyme endings (fawasil), it is evident in the first sense.

This is so. In *al-Itqan* by al-Jalal al-Suyuti, [it is recorded] that the Islamic logicians mentioned that in the beginning of surah al-Hajj, up to His saying, ﴿and that God will raise those in the graves﴾, there are five conclusions (natijah) deduced from ten premises. He then explained that in a manner that is strange and indicates the shortcomings of his command of that science. It may be said in explaining this that the five conclusions are the coordinated clauses that fall within the scope of the *ba'*. The deduction of the first is: if God, glorified is He, were not the Truth, i.e., the Necessarily Existent in Himself, then some of the possibles, such as humankind, plants, and others, would not have been witnessed; and the consequent is evidently false; therefore God, exalted is He, is the Truth. The ground for the implication is the proof of mutual exclusion (burhan al-tamanu'). The deduction of the second: if God, glorified is He, were not able to revive the dead, He would not have developed humankind through various stages until He made him alive, and would not have sent down water from the sky, reviving the earth after its death; and the consequent is evidently false, since the opponent does not deny that He, exalted is He, gave life to humankind and gave life to the earth. Therefore God, exalted is He, is able to revive the dead. The ground for the implication is clear. The deduction of the third: if God, exalted is He, is able to revive the dead, then He, glorified is He, is powerful over everything; but He, exalted is He, is able to revive the dead; therefore He is powerful over everything. The ground for the implication is that by "thing" is meant the possible, and the reviving of the dead is possible, and power over some possibles but not others contradicts the necessity of His essential existence, exalted is He. Moreover, the reviving of the dead is the most difficult of matters according to the disputing opponent, to the extent that he claimed it is one of the impossibles. Therefore, when it is established that He, glorified is He, is able to do it by what has preceded, it is established that He, exalted is He, is able over the rest of the possibles all the more so. The deduction of the fourth: the Hour is a possible matter, the True One (al-Sadiq) promised its coming, and every possible matter the True One promised to come is coming; therefore the Hour is coming. As for the Hour being a possible matter, it is because no impossibility follows from supposing its occurrence. As for it being something the True One promised to come, it is because of the Quranic verses by which He challenged. As for every possible matter the True One promised to come being coming, it is because of the impossibility of lying. The deduction of the fifth is in a similar manner. The deduction of each need not be confined to what has been mentioned; rather, it is possible by other than that, and the choice of it is because it comes to mind quickly. Perhaps one may confine oneself to three of these five, based on what you have come to know, between His saying, ﴿and that He gives life to the dead﴾ and His saying, ﴿and that He is powerful over everything﴾, and likewise between His saying, glorified is He, ﴿and that the Hour is coming﴾ and His saying, glorified is He, ﴿and that God will raise those in the graves﴾. Among the five is counted His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, the quaking of the Hour is a tremendous thing﴾, and its deduction is by saying: the quaking of the Hour distracts every nursing mother from what she has nursed, and everything of which this is the state is a tremendous thing; therefore the quaking of the Hour is a tremendous thing. And piety is obligatory upon you, which is indicated by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Fear your Lord﴾, and its deduction by saying: piety is that by which the harm of the Hour is averted, and everything by which harm is averted is obligatory upon you; therefore piety is obligatory upon you.

It is not hidden that what has been mentioned first is preferable, except that if this were their intended meaning, it would be more apparent for them to say: in His saying, ﴿That is because God is the Truth﴾ up to His saying, glorified is He, ﴿and that God will raise those in the graves﴾, there are five conclusions, rather than saying: in the beginning of surah al-Hajj up to its end. What was mentioned second would suit this statement, except that it is objected to: the apparent meaning of their words is that each of the conclusions is explicitly mentioned, and there is no doubt that "piety is obligatory upon you" is not mentioned in that way; rather, what is mentioned is what indicates it in a general sense, and that too is not a proposition, as is not hidden. Some people have contrived an explanation for this other than what we have mentioned, and we have judged that leaving its mention is preferable. So reflect.

Page 121

Among people is one who disputes about God without knowledge. It was revealed, according to what has been narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, and according to what has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning Abu Jahl. Some scholars held that it was revealed concerning al-Nadr, like the preceding verse. If the disputant is the same in both verses, then the repetition is for emphasis in censure, or because each of the two verses contains an addition not found in the other. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The verse was repeated in the manner of rebuke, as if it were said: these examples are in the utmost clarity and explanation, yet among people there is still one who disputes," and so on to its end. Here the *waw* is the *waw* of circumstance (*wāw al-ḥāl*), whereas in the preceding verse it is the *waw* of conjunction (*wāw al-ʿaṭf*), which conjoined the sentence to what came before it in the sense of narration, not of rebuke. End of quotation. And it is as you see.

In *al-Kashshaf* it is stated that the more apparent reading in the wording, and the more suitable to the context, is that this verse concerns those who follow (*muqallidīn*, those who practise *taqlīd*, uncritical adherence to others' authority), with the *lām* pronounced with a fatḥa, while that verse concerns those who are followed (*muqallidīn*, with the *lām* pronounced with a kasra). Thus the *waw* is for conjunction with the first verse. By "knowledge" is meant necessary knowledge (*ʿilm ḍarūrī*), just as by "guidance" in His words, exalted is He, ﴿nor guidance﴾ is meant reasoning and sound inquiry that leads to knowledge, ﴿nor an illuminating Book﴾, meaning a revelation that makes the truth manifest. That is, he disputes concerning the matter of God, exalted is His standing, without holding to any necessary premise, nor to any proof, nor to any evidence from revelation.

Ṡāniya ʿiṭfihi (turning away with his side): a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) from the pronoun in yujādilu, like the preceding prepositional phrase, meaning "turning his side away." It is a kinaya (metaphor) for his not accepting. This is what Ibn ʿAbbas meant by "arrogant," al-Ḍaḥḥāk by "lofty in his nose," and Ibn Jurayj by "turning away from the truth."

al-Ḥasan read ʿaṭfihi with a fatḥa on the ʿayn, meaning preventing his compassion and mercy (taʿaṭṭuf wa-taraḥḥum).

Liyuḍilla ʿan sabīli llāh (so that he may lead astray from the way of God): this is connected to yujādilu as its purpose (ʿilla), since his aim in disputing is misguidance from His path, even if he does not admit that it is misguidance. Abu al-Baqa' permitted its connection to thāniya, but that is not the right view. The misguidance may be meant as either: leading from guidance into error, in which case the object is whoever he disputes with among the believers, or people in general, with the believers given precedence over others; or as confirming them in error or increasing them in it, figuratively, in which case the object is specifically the disbelievers.

Mujāhid, the people of Mecca, and Abu ʿAmr in one narration read liyaḍilla with a fatḥa on the yā', meaning that he himself goes astray. The use of the imperfect form, although he was not guided before, treats his capacity for guidance as if it were guidance, since it is guidance in potential. It may mean that he persists in error or that his error increases. It has also been said that this is because his earlier error is treated as misguidance. In either case the lām is the lām of consequence (lām al-ʿāqibah).

Lahu fī l-dunyā khizy (for him in this world is disgrace): a resumptive clause explaining the outcome of the path he took. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be a predicated circumstantial clause (ḥāl muqaddara) or a concomitant one (ḥāl muqārina), meaning that he deserves it, but the first is more evident: that is, humiliation and abasement are established for him in this world because of what he did. The intended meaning, according to those who say this disputer was al-Naḍr or Abu Jahl, is what befell him on the day of Badr. Whoever generalizes, and this is preferable, understands it as the believers' condemnation of him and their silencing him when debating, and his failure to produce any proof at all, or as this together with the punishment he receives, such as death, but in relation to some individuals.

Wa-nudhīquhu yawma l-qiyāmati ʿadhāba l-ḥarīq (and We shall make him taste on the Day of Resurrection the punishment of the Burning): that is, the Fire that burns intensely. The idāfa (construct) is, as some say, an idāfa of the cause to the effect (muwaḥḥid), and ḥarīq has also been explained as one of the layers of Hell. It is also permitted that the idāfa be of the qualified to the qualifier, meaning the burning punishment, that is, extremely scorching. Zayd ibn ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, read wa-uḏīquhu with the hamza of the first-person speaker.

﴿That﴾, meaning what has been mentioned of his being humiliated in this world and made to taste the punishment of the Burning in the Hereafter. The demonstrative ﴿that﴾ carries the sense of distance, indicating that the matter is at the furthest extreme of terror and dreadfulness. It is the subject (mubtada') of a sentence whose predicate (khabar) is the statement of the Exalted: ﴿for what your hands have sent forth﴾, meaning because of what you have earned of disbelief and sins. The attribution to the two hands is because earning (iktisab) is customarily done by the hands. It is also permitted that ﴿that﴾ be the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada' mahdhuf), meaning "the matter is that," and that it be the object (maf'ul) of an omitted verb, meaning "We did that," and so on, though this is contrary to the apparent meaning. The clause is a resumptive new sentence (isti'naf), having no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis). It is also permitted that it be in the accusative position as the object of an omitted saying that occurs as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning "saying," or that it be what is said to him, "that," and so on. According to the first view, there is an iltifat (shift in grammatical person) in the speech, to emphasize the warning and intensify the threat.

﴿And that Allah is not an oppressor of the servants﴾. Apparently it is conjoined (ma'tuf) to "what," and this is the view of some scholars. Its benefit is to indicate that the causal relation of what they committed of sins to their punishment is conditioned by the addition of the negation of the Exalted's oppression to it. For were it not for this, it would be possible for Him to punish them for something other than what they committed, except that He would not punish them for what they committed. The summary is that the punishment of sinners may be due to their sins, or it may be merely the will to punish them without any sin. So this was mentioned to eliminate the second possibility and to specify the first as the cause, not to eliminate the possibility that He would not punish them for their sins, because that is permissible. Indeed, some verses indicate that this has occurred regarding some sinners. Its return in the Hereafter is to rebuke and reprove the disbelievers, that there is no cause for punishment except from their side, as if it were said: That punishment arose only from your sins which you earned, not from anything else.

Allamah Abu al-Su'ud chose that the place of "that" (inna) and what follows it is nominative (raf'), as a predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "and the matter is that He, the Exalted, does not punish His servants without a sin from their side." The clause is then a concluding parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD tadhyili), confirming the content of what precedes it. Regarding the conjunction, he said that its benefit is to indicate that the causal relation, etc. is not correct, because the possibility of His punishing His servants without sin, or even its occurrence, does not contradict the punishment of these specific disbelievers being due to their sins, such that it would need the consideration of its absence alongside it. Yes, if the claim were that all of His punishments were due to the sins of those punished, then it would need that qualification.

His statement "the possibility, etc." was challenged on the grounds that the discussion is not about the contradiction of those two matters in themselves, but about the contradiction of the possibility of punishment without sin, since the causality of sins is determined. His statement "Yes, if the claim were, etc." was challenged on the grounds that the need for that qualifier in each of the two cases is only to rebuke the sinners, that there is no cause for their punishment except from their side. So the claim of needing it in the case of all, and not needing it in the case of the specific, is extremely weak. It was also challenged in other ways. The view of the parenthetical insertion, although it is not free from remoteness, is further from being a parenthetical insertion.

As for expressing the negation of His punishing His servants without sin by the negation of oppression, although punishing them without sin is not oppression according to the principle established by the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah), this is to show the complete purity of the Exalted from that, by depicting it in a form of what is impossible for Him, the Glorified, to do: oppression. The intensive form (sigha al-mubalaghah) is for emphasizing this meaning, by presenting what was mentioned of punishment without sin in the form of exaggeration in oppression. It has been said that it is for observing the plurality of the servants, so it is an intensification in quantity, not in quality. It was objected that negating intensification in any form suggests the impossible. It has also been said: It is permitted that the intensification be considered after the negation, so that this is an intensification in the negation, not a negation of intensification. It was objected that this is not like the detached qualifier, which may be considered either to precede or follow, as they stated concerning the qualifiers occurring with negation. Making it a qualifier in the estimation, because it means "not possessing great or much oppression," is an artificial stretch with no parallel. It has also been said that "zallam" (intensive form) is for relativity (nisbiyyah), meaning "not one possessing oppression," and this is not restricted to the pattern of the active participle (fa'il), for it has come in the verse:

"And she is not one possessing a spear, nor am I an archer."

It has been said other than this.
