Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 11:

﴿And among the people is one who worships Allah on an edge.﴾ This begins the discussion of the state of the wavering ones (al-mudhabdhabin). That is: among them is one who worships Him, the Exalted, while being on a fringe of the religion, without any firmness in it, like one who stands at the edge of an army: if he senses victory he stays, and otherwise he flees. So in the expression there is a metaphor of representation (isti'arah tamthiliyyah). His words, the Exalted: ﴿But if good befalls him﴾ etc., are an explanation of this and a clarification of the aspect of resemblance. By "good" is meant worldly good, such as ease, well-being and children. That is: if what he desires befalls him, ﴿he is reassured by it﴾, meaning he remains upon what he was outwardly, not that he is reassured by it with the reassurance of the believers, whom no storm can move and no gale can turn back. ﴿But if a trial befalls him﴾, meaning something by which one is tested, of an unpleasant kind that afflicts him in his person, his family or his property, ﴿he turns back on his face﴾, meaning he becomes intent on the direction he faces, not looking to right or left, and unconcerned with whatever he encounters of heat and mountains. This is the meaning of the words in al-Kashshaf: "He flew upon his face," and he took it in al-Kashf as a metaphor for defeat. It was also said that here it is an expression for anxiety, since it stands in contrast to "reassured." Whichever it is, the meaning is that he apostatized and returned from his religion to disbelief.

Al-Bukhari, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas that he said concerning this verse: A man would come to Medina, and if his wife bore a boy and his mares foaled, he would say, "This is a good religion." But if his wife did not bear and his mares did not foal, he would say, "This is an evil religion."

Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Sa'id, who said: A Jewish man embraced Islam, then his sight, his property and his child were lost, so he blamed Islam as an omen. He came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said, "Release me from it." The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "Indeed Islam is not to be retracted." He said, "I have gained no good from my religion: my sight is gone, my wealth is gone, and my child has died." The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "O Jew, Islam purifies men as fire purifies the dross of iron, gold and silver." Then this verse was revealed. Ibn Hajar judged this report weak. It was also said that it was revealed concerning Shayba ibn Rabi'ah, who embraced Islam before the Prophet (ﷺ) prevailed and apostatized after he prevailed; this is related from Ibn Abbas. And from al-Hasan that it was revealed concerning the hypocrites.

﴿He has lost the world and the Hereafter.﴾ This is a resumed sentence, or a substitute for "turns back" (inqalaba), as Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said, or a circumstantial clause from its subject, with "qad" implied or without it, as is the view of Abu Hayyan. The meaning: he lost the world and the Hereafter and wasted both, since he missed what would have gladdened him in both.

Mujahid, Humayd, al-A'raj, Ibn Muhaysin (through al-Za'farani), Qa'nab, al-Jahdari and Ibn Muqsim read ﴿khasira﴾ in the pattern of the active participle, in the accusative as a circumstantial clause, since its genitive construction is verbal only. It was also read ﴿khasirun﴾ in the nominative, as the subject of "inqalaba," and in it the explicit noun is placed in the position of the pronoun to indicate that his turning back is caused by his loss. It was also said that this is a form of tajrid, and therefore it carries emphasis. It is also permitted that it be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "he is a loser," and the sentence then conveys blame and reproach.

﴿That﴾, meaning what has been mentioned of loss. The distance-marker in it indicates that it is at its utmost degree. It was also said that the distance-particle is used because the thing referred to is not explicitly mentioned. ﴿That is the manifest loss﴾, meaning clearly a loss and nothing else.

﴿He calls upon, besides Allah,﴾ it was said that this is a resumptive clause (istinaf, a new sentence that begins afresh) censuring some of his ugly deeds. It was said that it is a resumptive clause explaining the magnitude of the loss. It is permissible that it be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring back to the subject of ﴿turns over﴾, with what precedes it being a parenthetical interjection (i'tirāḍ). Whatever the case, this makes it unlikely that the verse refers to any of the Jews, because they do not call upon idols, even though they took their rabbis and monks as lords besides Allah.

The apparent meaning is that what is called upon is idols, given His words, Exalted is He: ﴿what neither harms him nor benefits him﴾. The meaning of "calling upon" here is worship: that is, he worships, going beyond the worship of Allah, Exalted is He, that which neither harms him if he does not worship it nor benefits him if he does. It is also permissible that "calling upon" means "calling out," i.e., he calls out to it to rescue him from the trial that has afflicted him, calling upon an inanimate object that is not of the nature of harm and benefit. The repetition of the word "what" (mā) hints that the intended object is such an inanimate thing, as in Irshad al-Aql al-Salim (the commentary of Abu al-Su'ud).

﴿That﴾, i.e., the calling, ﴿is the far-off error﴾ from the truth and guidance. It is a metaphor taken from the error of one who wanders far into the wilderness, lost from the path.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 13:

﴿He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*, a new sentence that is not grammatically dependent on what precedes it), which explains the outcome of his calling upon and worshipping other than God, the Exalted, and establishes that this is "far error." It also removes any suspicion that the denial of harm from his deity is meant in the direct sense, while the denial of it is meant in the sense of causation. So "calling" (*al-du'a'*) here means "saying," as in the verse of 'Antara:

*They call out "'Antar!" while the spears are like the ropes of a well*
*in the chest of the dark bay horse.*

The *lam* is prefixed to the clause that is the object of "saying," and it is the *lam* of the beginning (*lam al-ibtida'*). *Man* is the subject (*mubtada'*), and "his harm is nearer" is a subject and predicate, and the clause is the relative clause (*sila*) of *man*. God's words, ﴿Wretched is the patron, and wretched is the companion﴾, are the answer to an implied oath, and the *lam* in it is the *lam* of answer. The clause of the oath and its answer is the predicate of *man*. The meaning is: the unbeliever will say on the Day of Resurrection, raising his voice and crying out, when he sees the harm that his deity has brought upon him and his entry into the Fire because of it, and sees no trace of the benefit he used to expect from it: "By God, wretched is the one taken as a helper, and wretched is the one kept as a companion and associated with, so how much more so is that which is pure harm, wholly devoid of benefit?" In this there is an extreme degree of condemnation of the state of the idol and a thorough censure of it that is not hidden. This is the secret of choosing *man* over *ma*, and of using the comparative form. This mode of i'rab was chosen by al-Sijawandi, and its meaning is free of any difficulty.

Jar Allah (al-Zamakhshari) also adopted this view. It is also permitted that "he calls" here is a repetition of the earlier "he calls," for emphasis and as a preparation for what follows of the explanation of the evil state of his deity, after the explanation of the evil state of his worship, by God's words ﴿That is the far error﴾. It is as if it were said, from Him, glory be to Him, after mentioning the worship of the unbeliever of what neither harms nor benefits him: "He calls upon that, then it is said of one whose harm, by being an object of worship, is nearer than his benefit, by being an intercessor: wretched is the patron..." and so on. There is no contradiction in this either, since the harm that is denied is that which happens directly, and the harm that is affirmed is that which happens by causation. Likewise, the benefit that is denied is the actual benefit, and the affirmed is the expected benefit. It has been said that it is for this affirmation that the expression *man* is used, since harm and benefit are things that can proceed from rational beings. In *Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim* it is said that the word *man* and the comparative form may be intended if this is a report from Him, glory be to Him, about the evil state of the deity of the unbelievers, for the purpose of mockery of it. I see no objection to its being, as in the first estimation, for the sake of the extreme condemnation of the state of the idol and the thorough censure of it.

Ibn Hisham objected to this view, saying that it involves two claims contrary to the basic rule: the basic rule is the absence of emphasis, and the basic rule is that the emphasized should not be separated from its emphasis, especially in verbal emphasis. Al-Akhfash said: "*Yad'u*" means "*yaqulu*" (says), the *lam* is the *lam* of beginning, *man* is a relative pronoun serving as subject, its relative clause is the clause after it, and its predicate is omitted, its estimate being "a god" or "my god," and the clause is quoted after the verb of saying. It was objected that this meaning is corrupt, because this statement by the unbeliever occurs only in this world, and in this world he does not believe that the idols' harm is nearer than their benefit.

It was answered that what is meant is the denial of their saying that the idols are divine, except that God, exalted is He, expressed it by what He mentioned, for mockery. Yes, it is better to estimate the predicate as "a patron," because God's words ﴿Wretched is the patron, and wretched is the companion﴾ point to it more clearly. Nevertheless, the remoteness of this view is not hidden.

It has been said that "*yad'u*" is taken to include the meaning of "*yazʿumu*" (claims), and it is assimilated to verbs of the heart, because a claim is a saying together with belief. The *lam* is the *lam* of beginning, suspending the verb, and *man* is the subject, and its predicate is omitted as in the earlier view, and the clause is in the place of an accusative after *yad'u*. Al-Farisi pointed to this view, and it is not hidden from you what is wrong with it.

Al-Farra' said: the *lam* has entered a place other than its own, and the estimate is "he calls upon the one whose harm is nearer than his benefit," so *man* is in the place of an accusative governed by *yad'u*. Abu Hayyan and others criticized him, saying that this is remote, because what is in the relative clause cannot precede the relative pronoun.

Ibn al-Hajib said: it has been said that the *lam* is extra for emphasis and *man* is the object of *yad'u*, but this is not correct, because the open *lam* is not added between a verb and its object. However, the view that it is extra has been strengthened here by the reading of Abdullah: "*yad'u man darruhu*" without the *lam*. It has also been said that "*yad'u*" means "*yusammi*" (names), with *man* as its first object and its second object omitted, meaning "a god." It is not hidden from you what is wrong with this.

It has been said that "*yad'u*" does not govern what follows it, but governs what precedes it, and *man* is a relative pronoun in the sense of *alladhi* (who). This is reported from al-Farisi too, and although it is remote, it is not valid except according to the view of the Kufans, who permit a demonstrative pronoun in general to be a relative pronoun. As for the Basrans, they permit this only with *dha*, on condition that it is preceded by the interrogative *ma* or *man*.

It has been said that it governs a pronoun omitted that refers back to that, meaning "call them," and the clause is in the place of a circumstantial phrase, the estimate being "that is the far error," called upon. In this there is, besides its remoteness, the point that "*yad'u*" is not estimated as "called upon," but as "calling," and what is estimated as "called upon" is only "is called" in the passive.

It has been said that "*yad'u*" is conjoined to the first "*yad'u*," and the conjunction particle is dropped for the purpose of enumerating the states of that wavering person. The *lam* is extra, and *man* is the object of "*yad'u*," and it refers to a rational being. The calling in both places is either in the sense of worship or in the sense of invocation. The intention is either to explain the state of a group of them, meaning that at times they call upon what neither harms nor benefits, and at times they call upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit; or to explain the state of the genus with respect to what is under it, meaning that among them is one who calls upon what neither harms nor benefits, and among them is one who calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit. That, as you see, is remote. In sum, the best of these views is the first.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 14:

﴿Indeed, Allah will admit those who have believed and done righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) explaining the perfection of the good state of the believers who worship Him, and that He, exalted is He, bestows upon them everlasting bliss, following the explanation of the extreme evil state of the disbelievers. The clause "tajri" (flowing) and what follows is an attributive description (sifah) of "jannat" (gardens). If by "gardens" is meant the dense trees whose branches extend over what is beneath them, then the flowing of the rivers from beneath them is evident. If by them is meant the land, then a genitive noun (mudaf) must be assumed, that is, "from beneath their trees." And if it is made to denote the whole of the land and the trees together, then the "beneath" is considered in relation to the visible part, which justifies applying the name "garden" to the whole, as in Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does whatever He wills﴾ is a reason (ta'lil) for what precedes it and an affirmation by way of verification (tahqiq). That is, He, exalted is He, certainly does every act He wills, among the perfectly executed acts founded on exquisite wisdoms, of which is the rewarding of one who believed in Him and affirmed His Messenger (ﷺ), and the punishing of one who disbelieved in Him and denied His Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 15:

﴿Whoever thinks that Allah will never help him in this world and the Hereafter...﴾ The pronoun in (yansurahu, "help him") refers to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, according to what has been related from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Kalbi, Muqatil, al-Dahhak, Qatadah, Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi, and it was chosen by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. It is as if, when He mentioned the one who disputes concerning Allah without knowledge and his being forsaken in this world, because he does not put forward any proof, whether necessary (daruriyyah), theoretical (nazariyyah) or transmitted (sam'iyyah), and because of the punishment that his affair leads to, and in the Hereafter with what is greater and more severe. Then He, glorified is He, mentioned those who follow them, and generalized their loss in both abodes; He mentioned in contrast to them the believers, and followed it with mention of the one who disputes on their behalf and on behalf of the religion of Allah, the Exalted, in the best manner, and that is His Messenger, upon whom be prayers and peace. He emphasized his being helped with what admits of no addition, and he abbreviated the speech to indicate that he ﷺ is the sign that is not confused, and that the discourse is about him, concerning him, and with him, even if others are mentioned by way of following his mention. So the meaning is that Allah, the Exalted, helps His Messenger ﷺ in this world by exalting his word and manifesting his religion, and in the Hereafter by exalting his rank and admitting those who believed him into gardens beneath which rivers flow, and by taking vengeance upon those who denied him and making them taste the punishment of the Burning. Nothing turns Him, glorified is He, from that, and no one who inclines Him away from it. So whoever is enraged by that, from among his enemies and envious ones, and thinks that He, the Exalted, will not do it because of his repelling it with some matters and engaging in the schemes he wants, let him exert every effort and go beyond every known limit in earnestness. Yet the ultimate outcome of his endeavor is the failure of his efforts and the barrenness of his beginnings and origins, and the remaining of what enrages him in its state, and the continuance of his grief and distress. This is placed in the position of this recompense.

His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Then let him stretch a rope﴾ etc., means: then let him stretch a rope ﴿to the sky﴾, that is, to the ceiling of his house, as 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from al-Dahhak. ﴿Then let him cut off﴾, that is, let him choke himself, as Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, explained it. From qata'a, when one chokes, its origin being qata'a nafasahu (with two fathas), or ajalahu (his life); then the object was dropped as something forgotten, so it became in the sense of ikhtanaqa (he choked), intransitive of khanaqahu. They mentioned that cutting off the breath is a metaphor for choking. It was also said that the meaning is: let him cut the rope after choking, the intent being the supposition of cutting, and its depiction, as the intent of looking in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then let him look: will his scheme remove what enrages him?﴾ is the supposition of looking and its depiction, since after choking such a thing cannot be done by him. That is: let him imagine in himself the looking, whether his scheme will remove his rage or that which enrages him of the victory. It is permissible that what is intended is: let him now look whether, if he does that, what enrages him will go away. It is also permissible that the one commanded to look is other than the first one commanded, from among those who can look. And it is permissible that the speech is outside its literal path, as an expression of mockery, just as it was said that calling his act a scheme is outside this path. A group said: the application of the term scheme to that is because of its resemblance to it, for the schemer, when he schemes, brings about the utmost of what he is able to do, and that act is the utmost of what that enemy, the envious one, is able to do.

It was reported from Ibn Zayd that the meaning is: let him stretch a rope to the sky that shades, and let him climb upon it, then let him cut off the revelation from him, may Allah, the Exalted, bless him and grant him peace. It was said: let him cut the distance until he reaches the clouds of the sky, then let him strive to repel his help, upon him be prayers and peace, descending from its direction. Abu al-Su'ud, the Mawla, objected to this, saying that the arrangement of the noble composition rejects it, as the statement that matters supposed to occur, if they were realized and established, are far from removing what enrages; and it is clear that there is no sense in supposing the occurrence of impossible matters and ordering the command to look upon it, especially cutting off the revelation, for supposing its occurrence certainly undermines the aim. This was contested in a way that is not hidden from the reflecting one. Yes, the previous meaning is the more preferable. In any case, those who suppose that are the disbelievers envious of him, may Allah, the Exalted, bless him and grant him peace. It was said: they are Bedouins of Aslam and Ghatafan who were slow to accept Islam and said: "We fear that Muhammad will not be helped, so what is between us and our allies among the Jews will be cut off, and they will not host us or shelter us." It was also said: they are a group of Muslims who, out of extreme rage at the polytheists, were impatient for the victory that Allah, the Exalted, had promised His Messenger, may Allah, the Exalted, bless him and grant him peace. The meaning according to this, and likewise according to the previous view if it is said that those Bedouins also were impatient for the victory, is: whoever is impatient for the help of Allah, the Exalted, and seeks it quickly, let him kill himself, because He has a time in which wisdom requires its occurrence, so it does not occur at other than it. You know the remoteness of these two views, and that the second is more remote.

Abu Hayyan preferred that the pronoun in yansurahu refers to man (man), because it is the one mentioned, and the pronoun ought to refer to something mentioned. This is the view of Mujahid, and some have gone to it, and the help was interpreted as provision. Abu 'Ubaydah said: a beggar from Banu Bakr stopped at us and said: "Whoever will help me with the help of Allah, the Exalted?" They said: "A land that is mansurah," meaning rained upon. al-Fiq'asi said:

And you do not give a man beyond his right, nor do you possess the thing of which you are its helper.

That is, its giver. It seems to be borrowed from nasr in the sense of 'awn (aid). So the meaning is that provisions are in the hand of Allah, the Exalted, and are not attained except by His will; therefore the servant must be content with His distribution. So whoever thinks that Allah, the Exalted, is not his provider, and is not patient and does not submit, let him reach the utmost of distress, which is choking, for that does not reverse the distribution nor return him provided for. The purpose is to urge contentment with what Allah, the Exalted, has apportioned, not like one who worships Him on an edge. It seems that when He, glorified is He, mentioned the believers after them, as has passed, He warned them against the likeness of their condition, out of kindness toward them. This is not free from remoteness, though the connection of the verse with what precedes it is close to it. It was said: the pronoun refers to man, and the help is in its commonly understood sense, and the meaning is: whoever thinks that Allah, the Exalted, will not help him, so he is enraged at the absence of His help, let him employ the greatest stratagem in seeking Allah's help for him, and let him exhaust his effort in bringing the help to him; then let him look whether that will remove what enrages him of the absence of help. The connection in this view is not free from obscurity.

As we have indicated, man (whoever) is conditional. It is permissible that it be relative, with the fa' in its predicate because it includes the meaning of the condition. (Hal yudhhibanna, "will it remove") is in a place of nasb governed by (yanzur, "let him look"). It has been mentioned that it is by dropping the preposition. The Basrans, Ibn 'Amir and Warsh read (thumma liyaqta') with the kasra on the lam of the imperative, while the rest read it with sukun, treating thumma as like wa and fa, since all of them are conjunctions.

﴿And thus﴾, i.e., like that sending down, the wondrous one that contains profound wisdoms, ﴿We sent it down﴾, i.e., the Noble Qur'an in its entirety, ﴿as clear signs﴾, whose indications of their pleasing meanings are plain. So the thing referred to by the demonstrative is the sending down mentioned after it. It is also permissible that what is meant is the sending down of the preceding verses. Whichever is the case, it implies that the Noble Qur'an in all its chapters is fully clear, not in the matter of resurrection alone. ﴿Āyātin﴾ (signs) is in the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial qualifier) of the object pronoun. As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and that Allah guides whom He wills﴾, the lām (لامِ) is to be understood as omitted, and the phrase is connected to an omitted element that is to be understood as postponed, to make a restriction relative to a particular context (ḥaṣr iḍāfī). The meaning is: and because Allah, exalted is He, guides by it from the outset, or confirms in guidance, or increases in it, whomever He wills to guide, to confirm, or to increase in it, He sent it down thus. Or it is in the sense of a verbal noun in the nominative, as the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada', subject), i.e., and the matter is that Allah guides, etc.

It is also permissible that it be coordinated with the grammatical position (maḥall) of the object of ﴿We sent it down﴾, i.e., and We sent down that Allah guides, etc.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 17:

﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾, that is, in what has been mentioned of what was revealed by the guidance of God, the Exalted, or in everything that must be believed in. What has been mentioned enters into this in the first instance.

﴿And those who are Jews, and the Sabians﴾: according to what Ibn Jarir and others related from Qatada, they are a people who worship the angels, pray towards the qibla, and recite the Zabur (Psalms). In al-Qamus (the dictionary), they are a people who claim to follow the religion of Noah, peace be upon him, and their qibla is from the direction of the north wind at midday. In Kitab al-Milal wal-Nihal (The Book of Sects and Creeds) by al-Shahrastani, the Sabians (al-Sabi'ah) existed in the time of Abraham, peace be upon him, and their opponents were called the Hunafa' (monotheists). They used to say: "We need, in knowing God, the Exalted, knowing His obedience, His command and His rulings, a spiritual intermediary, not a corporeal one."

The basis of their doctrines is zeal for spiritual beings. They exalted them to the utmost degree and sought nearness to them. When they could not draw near to their essences or receive from them directly, a group resorted to their temples (hayakil), which are the seven wandering planets and some of the fixed stars. The Sabians of Rome relied on the wandering planets, and the Sabians of India relied on the fixed stars. At times they descended from the temples to the figures that neither hear, nor see, nor avail anything. The first sect are the worshippers of the stars, and the second are the worshippers of idols. Abraham, peace be upon him, silenced both sects and imposed the proof upon them.

It is mentioned in another place that their emergence was in the first year of the reign of Tahmuras, one of the kings of the Persians. The word Sabians is Arabic, from ṣabā, as in manaʿa and karuma: ṣabwan and ṣubūʾan, meaning he departed from one religion to another.

﴿And the Christians and the Magians (al-Majus)﴾: according to what was also related from Qatada, they are a people who worship the sun, the moon and fire. Some limited their description to the worship of the sun and moon, and others to the worship of fire. It was said: they are a people who separated from the Christians and wore woolen garments (al-masuh). It was said: they are a people who took some of the religion of the Christians and some of the religion of the Jews, and they hold that the world has two principles, light and darkness.

In Kitab al-Milal wal-Nihal there is something indicating that they are groups, that they existed before the Jews and the Christians, that they hold to laws unlike the Sabians, that they have a semblance of a scripture, and that they venerate fire. In it also: the fire-temples (buyut al-niran) of the Magians are many. The first temple that Afridun built was a fire-temple in Tus, and another in the city of Bukhara was Bardasun. Bahman took a temple in Sijistan called Karku. They also have a fire-temple in Bukhara called Qubadan, and a fire-temple called Kunashah between Fars and Isfahan, built by Kaykhusraw. Another is at Qumash called Jarir. The fire-temple of Kaykadar was built in the east of China, and another in Arjan of Fars, which Arjan, the grandfather of Gushtasp, took. All these temples existed before Zoroaster (Zaradusht). Then Zoroaster renewed the fire-temple of Baynisa after Gushtasp, when they sought the fire that Jam used to venerate, and they found it in the city of Khwarazm. He moved it to Darabjird, and the Magians venerate it more than others. Kaykhusraw, when Afrasiyab invaded, venerated it and prostrated to it. It is said that Anushirvan was the one who moved it to Karashan, and they left some of it there and carried some of it to Nasa. In the land of the Romans, at the gate of Constantinople, there is a fire-temple which Shapur ibn Ardashir took, and it remained so until the days of al-Mahdi.

The fire-temple of Basifita, near the city of Salam, belonged to Buran, daughter of Kisra. In India and China there are also fire-temples. The Magians venerate fire for several reasons, among them that it is a noble, lofty substance, and they suppose that this saves them from the punishment of the fire of the Day of Resurrection. But they did not realize that this is the greatest cause of their punishment. End quote.

There is in this what is not hidden from one who reviews the histories. In al-Qamus: Majus, like Sabur, is a man with small ears who devised a religion and called to it, arabicized from mīkh and kūsh. In al-Sihah: al-Majusiyyah is a sect, and al-Majusi is its adherent, and the plural is al-Majus. Abu ʿAli al-Nahwi said: al-Majus and al-Yahud were made definite on the pattern of Yahudi and Yahud, and Majusi and Majus. The plural was formed on the pattern of shaʿīrah and shaʿīr, then the plural was made definite by al-alif and al-lam. Were it not so, the alif and lam could not be attached to them, since they are two feminine definite nouns. So they are used in their speech like the two qiblas, and they are not treated like the two tribes (hayyayn) in the rules of inflection. He recited:

"O Hār, let me show you a lightning that blew at a distance, like the fire of the Magians blazing in borrowed light."
End quote.

Some have mentioned that Majus is arabicized from Mukush, and it was applied to those people because they used to let the hair of their heads grow down to their ears. It is related in al-Bahr that the mim is a substitute for the nun, and that it was applied to them because of their use of impurities, but this is a view not to be relied upon.

﴿And those who associated partners (with God)﴾: it is well known that they are the worshippers of idols. It was said that it includes them and all who worshipped another god alongside God, the Exalted, such as an angel, a star or others, of whom none became known by a specific name, like the Sabians and the Magians.

As for the words of God, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection﴾, the phrase is in the position of the nominative, as the predicate of the particle inna, which is preceded by (the particle) inna. Inna was introduced upon each of the two parts of the sentence for the increase of emphasis, as in the verse of Jarir:

"Indeed the Caliph, indeed God has clothed him with the garment of kingship, by which the seals are carried."

It was said: the predicate of the first inna is omitted, meaning "they will be divided on the Day of Resurrection" or something similar, indicated by His words, glory be to Him: ﴿Indeed God will judge between them﴾ etc. For your saying "Indeed Zayd, indeed ʿAmr strikes him is bad," the verse does not necessarily make the clause introduced by inna a predicate; rather it may be parenthetical, and the predicate is the clause "by which the seals are carried." After granting that it is bad, you should not overlook that the verse is not like the example mentioned, because of the long separation in it. In al-Bahr: the goodness of introducing inna before the clause that is a predicate in the verse is due to the long separation by the conjunctions. Al-Zajjaj said: some people claimed that your saying "Indeed Zayd, indeed he is standing" is bad, and that this verse is acceptable only because of the preceding relative pronoun. But there is no difference between a relative clause and other clauses in the rules of inna, and there is no disagreement among the Basrans that inna enters upon every subject and predicate. Accordingly, one should not depart from the apparent meaning.

The word "judgment" (fasl) here means decision: He, the Exalted, decides between the believers and the five groups united in disbelief, by making manifest the true from the false, and giving each of the two parties its due recompense, by rewarding the believers and punishing the other groups according to the deserts of the individuals of each. It was said: the meaning is that He, the Exalted, separates between the six groups in all their states and places. He does not recompense them with one single recompense without distinction, but rewards the believers with what befits them and the Jews with what befits them, and so on. He does not gather them in one place; rather He places the believers in Paradise and each of the disbelieving groups in one of the levels of the Fire.

His words, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed God is Witness over all things﴾ are an explanation of what precedes concerning the judgment, meaning: He, the Exalted, has knowledge of all things and watches over their conditions. Among the consequences of this is His comprehensive knowledge of the details of what proceeds from each individual of the groups mentioned, and His carrying out upon him the recompense that befits him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 22, verse 18 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do you not see that to God prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth﴾ etc. is an explanation of what necessitates the aforementioned separation of the groups in their deeds, with an indication of its manner and that it is by way of punishment, reward, honour and humiliation. It has also been allowed that it is an illumination of His being a witness over everything. It has been said that it is a rebuke for the disbelievers' disagreement and a declaring of it to be improbable, since there is an obstacle preventing it. The "seeing" here means knowledge, and the address is to everyone who is capable of it. By "prostration" is meant the subjection of things to His subjugation and His will, and their susceptibility to what He, mighty and majestic, brings about in them. The apparent sense of al-Amidi's words is that this is the literal meaning of prostration. In *Mufradat* of al-Raghib: "Prostration is originally lowering oneself and humbling oneself, and this has been made an expression for humbling oneself before God and worshipping Him, and it is general to humans, animals and inanimate things. It is of two kinds: prostration by choice, which belongs to humans, and by it one deserves reward; and prostration by subjugation, which belongs to humans and other animals and plants." It is restricted in the Sharia to the known pillar of the prayer and what follows its course, such as the prostration of recitation and the prostration of thanks. End.

Some have said that just as it is restricted in the Sharia to this, it is restricted in the usage of the language to it as well. Ibn Kamal said: its literal meaning, as stated in *al-Mujmal*, is placing the head (on the ground). The "second Allama" said: its literal meaning is placing the forehead, not the head, so that if the head is placed from the back side, one is not considered prostrating. On these two views, with their flaws, it has been said that prostration here is a metaphor for entering under His subjugation and submitting to His will, exalted is He. It has also been allowed that it is a metaphor for the implicit indication of the state of things through their humility and their need of their Creator and His greatness, exalted be His majesty. The illumination according to this is clear, and likewise the rebuke for the disagreement.

"Man" (*man*) is either specific to rational beings, or general to them and to others by way of *taghlib* (predominance of the rational over the non-rational), and this is the preferred reading, because it is the more fitting to the context, as it conveys the inclusion of the ruling

[Page 131]

for everything in them, either by way of residing in them or by way of being a part of them. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and the sun, the moon, the stars, the mountains, the trees, and the animals﴾ is a singling out of these by mention, for their fame, and for the improbability of this from them according to the apparent sense at first glance, as has been said; or because they have been worshipped besides God, exalted is He, either in their individual forms or in their kinds.

The sun was worshipped by Himyar, the moon was worshipped by Kinana, and among the stars al-Dabaran was worshipped by Tamim, al-Shi'ra by Lakhm and Quraysh, al-Thurayya by Tayy, and 'Utarid and al-Mirzam by Rabi'a. Most of the Arabs worshipped idols carved from mountains. Ghatafan worshipped al-'Uzza, which was a *samura* (a single acacia tree), a known tree. Among people there were those who worshipped cows. Al-Zuhri and Ibn Thabbab read *al-dawab* with a light *ba'* (without doubling). Ibn Jinni, in *al-Muhtasib*, restricted this reading to al-Zuhri and said: "I do not know of anyone who lightened it other than him, and it is rare and weak both by analogy and by transmission, because the meeting of two unvocalized letters is on its limit, and its excuse is the dislike of doubling; therefore they said *zalilt* becomes *zalt*, and they said *jan* with lightening." He mentioned many similar examples.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and many of mankind﴾ has been said to be in the nominative by an implied verb indicated by what has been mentioned, meaning: "and many of mankind prostrate to Him," the known prostration of obedience. It has been objected that al-Mughni explicitly states that the condition for a verbal indicator of an elided element is that it must match it in wording and meaning, or in meaning only and not in wording alone; so "Zayd is striking and 'Amr" is not permitted if the predicate of 'Amr is elided and is *darib* meaning "traveling in the land", i.e., "is traveling", while the mentioned one has its well-known meaning. Al-Khafaji replied that what was mentioned is not accepted, because the grammarians have stated that the elided element may be necessarily tied to the mentioned one, such as "Zaydan I struck, his servant," meaning "I humiliated Zayd." It is not shared as in the mentioned example, unless there is a suitability between them, so it is valid if they are identical in wording and are of the shared type, and there is a necessary connection between them that indicates the elided element; this is why the mentioned example is not valid. End.

Some have joined it to what precedes it, making the prostration in relation to it the known prostration, while in what came before it has the meaning of entering under subjugation or indicating the greatness of the Creator, exalted be His dignity.

It has been deduced from this the permissibility of using a homonym in both its meanings, or using a word in both its literal and metaphorical senses. The answer is what you know. It is not permitted to join and to make the prostration in all of them mean entering under subjugation or indicating greatness, because that is general to all people, so mentioning "many" is not fitting then. What is not general is only the prostration in the known sense, so mentioning "many" conveys that some of them do not possess it, and this is so. What has been said, that the restriction to the many may be for the purpose of the general prostration to indicate their nobility and distinction, is nothing, for how can distinction be achieved when non-rational beings like animals are joined with them?

Ibn Kamal said: those who permitted carrying a homonym on more than one meaning in a single usage have held onto His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do you not see that to God prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth﴾ and so on, on the basis that the prostration attributed to non-rational beings means submission, because the known prostration is impossible for them; and that attributed to rational beings is the known one and not mere submission, because submission is inclusive of all and not restricted to the many. But they have no argument in this, because each of the two justifications is open to objection. As for the first, the reality of prostration is placing the head, and there is no impossibility in attributing it to non-rational beings, and there is no need to establish the reality of the head for all, because *taghlib* is valid and common. As for the second, the unbelievers, especially the arrogant among them, have no share of submission, because what is meant by it is obedience to what has come concerning Him of commands, whether legislative or created, in the manner in which the command came; and assuming another verb in this context is from narrowness of view, as is not hidden from the discerning. End. In it is the saying that joining is permitted

[Page 132]

on both meanings of prostration, placing the head and submission, and an explanation of the benefit of restricting "many" on the second. It is not hidden that the apparent sense from the authoritative lexicographical books is that prostration is a literal linguistic term for submission in general, and that what he mentioned about *taghlib* is contrary to the apparent sense; likewise submission was interpreted according to what he mentioned. May God, exalted is He, have mercy on him: he took both meanings from *al-Tawdih*, and dropped from it what was unnecessary. What he claimed to be narrowness of view is what most of the people have gone to, and according to it "from mankind" is an attribute of "many." It was objected that then it follows that the known prostration of obedience is not restricted to many of mankind, for many of the jinn also possess it. And their not being obligated is contrary to the more correct view. Yes, it can be said that they were not commanded to prostrate at the time the verse was revealed, and the one who claims this must provide proof. The statement that "mankind" may be meant to include the jinn, since it is applied to them as the terms "group" and "men" are applied to them, is nothing. Some people answered this by saying that the implied "prostrates" is within the scope of "seeing," and they have said: what is meant by it is knowledge, and expressing it with it indicates the manifestness of the known. The manifestness of prostration in the sense of entering under subjugation, in the things to which it is attributed, is that which has no covering over it; likewise its manifestness in the known sense in many of mankind. As for the jinn, it is not so, and therefore the many is described as being of mankind. It was objected that the address in "Do you not see" is to whoever is capable of it, and there is no covering in the manifestness of the matter of prostration absolutely in relation to him. It was answered that the intent of the answerer that the prostration of the jinn is not manifest in reality, and regardless of the addressee, whoever he may be, the manifestness of entering under subjugation of the things mentioned first is clear, unlike the prostration of many of mankind, which is manifest as that is manifest in reality. Thus the many is restricted to being of mankind, so that what is within the scope of seeing is of one region of manifestness in reality.

It has been said that the context requires increasing the number of those who see what is mentioned within the scope of seeing, and the restriction is more suitable to that, so the many is restricted to being of mankind. All of this is as you see. The better view is that the restriction of the many of mankind by ascribing the known prostration to them, on the view that many of the jinn are likewise, is for the sake of distinguishing them, and this is not objected to by what passed, because non-rational beings are not joined with them in this prostration. So reflect. It has been said that "many" is in the nominative as a subject, its predicate elided, relying on the indication of the predicate of its counterpart, such as "the reward is due to him." The sentence conveys the multitude of both groups. The first view is preferable because it contains encouragement toward prostration and obedience to the True God who is worshipped. It has been allowed that "many" is a subject and "from mankind" its predicate, the definite article in it being for the reality and the genus, meaning: "and many of mankind, who are mankind in reality, and they are the righteous and pious." Al-Raghib said: "The word 'people' is sometimes mentioned and intended to mean the excellent, not everyone who falls under the name 'people,' metaphorically. That is when the meaning of humanity is considered, which is the existence of reason, mind, and the other faculties specific to it, for whatever lacks its specific function hardly deserves its name." The specifier of the indefinite subject is that it is an implied attribute in reality, and that the contrasting structure is one of the specifiers, as when you say: "men honoured and men humiliated," because it is a general distinction, so it is described implicitly; and because each of the two opposites is described by the difference from the other, so this falls under the implicit attribute. It is also permitted that "many" is a subject, "from mankind" its attribute, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and many﴾ is conjoined to it, and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿the punishment is due upon him﴾, meaning "is established and fixed," is the predicate. The sentence follows the pattern of your saying: "I have a thousand and a thousand," meaning "many thousands," a usage common in their speech. It thus conveys the multitude of those upon whom the punishment is due from mankind. These two views are remote; al-Bahr says they are weak.

The apparent sense is that the second "many" is a subject and the sentence after it is its predicate, and it has been placed in the position of "does not prostrate," so it is as if it were said: "and many of mankind prostrate, and many of them do not prostrate." There is no hiding the warning against abandoning prostration and obedience in that placement. Nor is it hidden that the lack of explicit restriction of the second "many" to being of mankind strengthens the claim that the restriction earlier was for distinction, and to take the absence of restriction as covering the many of the jinn is clearly contrary to the apparent sense.

It has been allowed that it is conjoined to "whoever," with prostration in one of the two earlier meanings, and the clause "is due" etc. is its attribute. An attribute is to be understood for the first "many," indicated by its counterpart, meaning: "for whom the reward is due," and "from mankind" is also its attribute. What is in it is not hidden. It was read "ḥuqqa" with a *ḍamma* on the *ḥā'*, and "ḥaqqan," meaning "the punishment is due upon him, in truth," so it is an absolute object emphasizing the content of the sentence.

His saying: ﴿And whomever God humiliates﴾, by God writing for him wretchedness according to what his essence has prepared him for of evil. "Whomever" is the elided object of "humiliates." ﴿then there is none to honour him﴾, that is, none who honours him with happiness.

Ibn Abi 'Abla read «mukrimin» with a fatha on the ra', taking it as a mimi (mim-prefixed) verbal noun, as in the Qamus, meaning: one for whom there is honour (ikram). It has been said that it is an ism maf'ul (passive participle) in the sense of a verbal noun, but there is no need to commit to this. It has also been said that it may remain as it commonly is in this form, an ism maf'ul, and the meaning is: he has no one who honours him and intercedes on his behalf so that he may be freed from humiliation. Its remoteness is not hidden. ﴿Indeed, Allah does whatever He wills﴾ among things, of which honouring and humiliating are part. This is better than restricting it to those two by the context.

These two adversaries who dispute concerning their Lord: this specifies the two sides of the dispute and clarifies their location. Thus "these two" refers to the group of believers and the group of disbelievers, which is divided into the five groups.

It has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, Mujahid, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, al-Hasan, 'Asim, and al-Kalbi, what supports this. On this basis it becomes determined that the preceding separation is between the believers and the whole group of those who are joined to them. Since each adversary is a group comprising a body of people, the verb ﴿اخْتَصَمُوا﴾ (they disputed) is in the plural form.

Ibn Abi Ablah read ﴿اخْتَصَمَا﴾ (the two disputed), taking into account the wording ﴿خَصْمانِ﴾ (two adversaries). This is the dual of ﴿خَصْمٌ﴾ (adversary). They mention that it is originally a verbal noun (maṣdar) in which the singular masculine and other forms are alike. Abu al-Baqa' said: "Most usage is in the singular, so whoever makes it dual or plural treats it as an adjective (ṣifah) and a noun (ism)." It is narrated from al-Kisa'i that he read ﴿خِصْمانِ﴾ with a kasrah on the kha'. The meaning of their dispute concerning their Lord is their dispute about His affair, glory be to Him. It is said: about His religion; it is said: about His essence and attributes. All of these are among His affairs, exalted is He. Each of the two groups believes in the truth of what it holds and the falsehood of what its opponent holds, and the building of its statements and actions upon this belief is sufficient for establishing its enmity toward the other group, and it does not stop from debating.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The believers and the Jews disputed. The Jews said: 'We are closer to Allah, exalted is He, and more ancient than you in scripture and prophethood, before your Prophet.' The believers said: 'We have more right to Allah, exalted is He. We believed in Muhammad (ﷺ) and we believed in your Prophet and in what Allah, exalted is He, sent down of scripture. You know our scripture and our Prophet, then you abandoned them and disbelieved in them out of envy.' So this was revealed."

A group narrated from Qatadah something similar to this. It has been objected that the dispute on this view is not concerning Allah, exalted is He, but concerning which of the two is closer to Him, glory be to His affair. It has been answered that this necessarily implies that, and it is as you see. It has also been said against it: specifying the Jews is contrary to the context of the speech in this place. In al-Kashf it is said: "They said that this does not contradict what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, that the verse refers to the people of the six religions in terms of its reality, because the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, al-Tabarani, and others narrated from Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, that he used to swear an oath that this verse ﴿هَذانِ خَصْمانِ﴾ up to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ يَفْعَلُ ما يُرِيدُ﴾ (Indeed, Allah does whatever He wills) was revealed concerning the three and the three who fought in single combat on the day of Badr. They are Hamzah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, 'Ubaydah ibn al-Harith, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, 'Utbah and Shaybah, the two sons of Rabi'ah, and al-Walid ibn 'Utbah. You know that this dispute is not a dispute concerning Allah, exalted is He, but its source is that. So reflect, and do not be heedless.

As for what has been said, that the two adversaries are meant to be Paradise and Hell, it should not be disputed that this is unacceptable, nor should two rams be butted over it. In the speech, as more than one has said, there is division, gathering, and separation. The division is ﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾ (Indeed, those who believe) up to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿والَّذِينَ أشْرَكُوا﴾ (and those who associate others with Allah). The gathering is ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ يَفْصِلُ بَيْنَهُمْ﴾ (Indeed, Allah will judge between them) up to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿هَذانِ خَصْمانِ اخْتَصَمُوا في رَبِّهِمْ﴾ (These two adversaries who dispute concerning their Lord). The separation is in His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿فالَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا قُطِّعَتْ لَهم ثِيابٌ مِن نارٍ﴾ (So those who disbelieve, garments of fire will be cut out for them), etc., meaning: that was prepared for them. It seems that He likened the preparation of the surrounding fire to the cutting and tailoring of garments for them according to the size of their bodies. So in the speech there is a mocking allegorical metaphor, and there is no cutting and no garments in reality. It seems that the plural of ﴿الثِّيابِ﴾ (garments) is to indicate the piling up of the fire surrounding them and that some of it is above some of it.

It is permissible that this is for matching a plural with a plural, but the first is more eloquent. The past tense is used because the preparation has already occurred, so it is not a case of expressing the past tense to indicate its certainty, as in ﴿نُفِخَ في الصُّورِ﴾ (the Trumpet will be blown).

A group narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that these garments are of molten brass, and there is nothing heated in the fire more intense in heat than it. So the garments are not of the very essence of fire, but of something resembling it, and these garments are a covering for them, and how ugly a covering it is. For this reason Wahb said: "The people of the Fire are clothed, and nakedness would be better for them." Al-Za'faranı in his choice read ﴿قُطِعَتْ﴾ with the lightened form, but the intensified form (﴿قُطِّعَتْ﴾) is more eloquent.

﴿يُصَبُّ مِن فَوْقِ رُءُوسِهِمُ الحَمِيمُ﴾ (Scalding water will be poured over their heads): that is, boiling water whose heat has reached its extreme. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that if a single drop of the scalding water fell upon the mountains of the world, it would melt them. Ibn Jubayr interpreted it as molten brass, but the well-known interpretation is the one mentioned earlier. Perhaps ﴿مَن﴾ (from) was used here only to indicate the severity of the pouring. The sentence is either a new (independent) sentence, or a second predicate of the relative pronoun, or in the position of a presumed circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿لَهُمْ﴾ (for them).

**(Yusharu bihi)** — that is, is melted — **(mā fī buṭūnihim)** — what is in their bellies — of the intestines and the entrails.

Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who declared it sahih), Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in his Zawa'id al-Zuhd, and a group of others transmitted from Abu Hurayrah that he recited this verse and said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Indeed, the boiling water is poured over their heads, and it penetrates the skull until it reaches their insides, and it strips away what is in their insides until it emerges from their feet. This is the ṣahr (melting). Then they are restored as they were.'"

Al-Hasan and a group read **yuṣahhar** with a fatha on the ṣād and a shadda on the hā'. The apparent meaning is that His words, **(wal-julūdu)** — and the skins — are a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon **mā** (what). Its being placed after it has been said to be either for the sake of observing the rhyme (fawāṣil), or to convey the utmost intensity of the heat, by giving the impression that its effect on the interior precedes its effect on the exterior, although its contact with them is the reverse. It has also been said that the effect on the exterior is too evident to need explanation, and it is mentioned only to indicate that the two are equal; and for this reason the interior is mentioned first, because it is the primary and more important concern. It has also been said that the implied sense is "and the skins are burned," because skins do not melt; rather they gather up upon the fire and shrink. In al-Bahr, it is said that this is of the type of "I fed it straw and cold water" (ʿalaftuhā tibnan wa-māʾan bāridan). Some have said: there is no need to adopt this, for the states of that world are a different matter. It has also been said that **(yuṣharu)** means "is cooked (yanḍaj)," and he cited the line: "The sun cooks it, yet it does not melt." In that case there is no difficulty in attributing it to the skins, and the clause is either a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to **al-ḥamīm** (the boiling water), or a resumptive new sentence.

(Page 135)

﴿And for them﴾, i.e., for the disbelievers. That the pronoun refers to the *zabaniyah* (the angels who guard Hell) is far-fetched. The *lam* here indicates entitlement, or benefit used sarcastically toward them. It has also been said that it indicates purpose, so the sentence is elliptical, meaning "for their punishment." It has further been said that it carries the sense of *'ala* (upon), as in His saying, ﴿And theirs is the curse﴾ [Ghafir: 52], i.e., "and upon them is the curse."

﴿garments of fire, and above their heads will be poured boiling water﴾ is not the verse under discussion. The verse under discussion is ﴿For them are hooks of iron﴾ (*maqami'a min hadid*). *Maqami'* is the plural of *miqma'ah* (a hook or goad), and its essential meaning is that with which something is restrained (*yuqma'* bihi), i.e., held back forcefully. In *Majma' al-Bayan*, it is said that it is a blunt-headed implement, from *qama'ahu* (he suppressed him) when he repelled him. Al-Dahhak and a group of scholars interpreted it as mallets, and some as whips.

In a hadith: "If one of them were placed in the earth, and then the two weights (*al-thaqalan*, i.e., jinn and humankind) gathered upon it, they would not be able to lift it from the earth."

﴿Whenever they wish to get out of it﴾ means they approached coming out of the Fire and drew near to it, according to what is related: it strikes them with its flame and lifts them up, and when they are at its top they are struck with maces (al-maqami', iron rods) and they fall back into it for seventy autumns (kharif, years). So "wish" (al-irada) is a metaphor (majaz, a figurative usage) for approaching and drawing near, as in His saying, ﴿it wants to collapse﴾ [al-Kahf: 77]. Some have made the pronoun in ﴿from it﴾ refer to the garments, but this is weak (rakik).

His saying, ﴿from distress﴾, is a badal ishtimal (substitution of inclusion, where the substitute is part of or contained in what it replaces) for the pronoun in ﴿from it﴾, with the preposition repeated. The connecting pronoun is omitted, and the indefiniteness is for emphasis (al-tafkhim), meaning great distress from its torments. Or it is a maful lahu (object of purpose) for "to come out," meaning: whenever they wish to come out of it because of great distress that befalls them from its punishment. Ghamm (distress) is the brother of hamm (worry), and it is well known. Some have said that here it is a verbal noun from "I covered the thing," meaning I concealed it, so the sense is: whenever they wish to come out from the covering of the punishment that is over them, or from what the punishment covers them with.

﴿They will be returned into it﴾ means they will be returned to its bottom, being sent back from its heights to its depths, without coming out of it, since for them there is no coming out, as is well known of their state. It has been cited as evidence by His saying, ﴿and they will not be people who come out of it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 167; al-Ma'idah: 37]. The choice of "in it" rather than "to it" hints at this. It has been said that the return is a metaphor for continuance. It has also been said that the meaning is: whenever they wish to come out of it and they come out, they are returned into it, so the return is conditional upon the coming out, and the condition is omitted to indicate how quickly the wish is followed by the return. It is also possible that this happens to them. As for His saying, ﴿and they will not be people who come out of it﴾, what is meant is the negation of continuity, meaning they will not persist in coming out, not the continuity of negation. The verb "return" is often followed by "fi" merely to indicate settling and permanence.

Some have said that the coming out is not from the Fire itself but from the places prepared for their punishment within it: the meaning is that whenever one of them wishes to leave his place in the Fire, prepared for him, for another place in it, and he comes out of it, he is returned into it. This, as you see, is far-fetched. This return, as has been said, is by the Zabaniyah (the angels of punishment) striking them with the maces.

His saying, ﴿And taste﴾, is understood as being in the sense of a saying that is conjoined with "they will be returned," meaning: and it will be said to them, "Taste ﴿the punishment of the burning﴾." The discussion of this has already passed, and the command is for humiliation (al-ihanah).

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 23:**

﴿Indeed, Allah will admit those who have believed and done righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow.﴾ This is a description of the good state of the believers, following the description of the bad state of the disbelievers. The style is varied here: the admission is attributed to the all-comprehensive Name (Allah), the sentence begins with the particle of confirmation (inna), and it is detached (as a fresh sentence, istin'af) to signal the complete contrast between their state and the state of the disbelievers, to show greater concern for the matter of the believers, and to indicate the certainty of the content of the statement.

﴿They will be adorned therein﴾ with the passive voice and the doubled form from "tahliyah" (adornment) with ornaments, meaning: the angels, upon them be peace, will adorn them by His command, may He be exalted. His saying, ﴿with bracelets﴾ (min asawira): it has been said that it is connected to "yuhallawna" (they will be adorned), with "min" being initial (ibtida'iyyah, marking the starting point), and the verb is transitive to one object, which is the deputy of the subject (na'ib 'an al-fa'il). It has also been said that it is connected to a deleted element that occurs as a qualifier of a deleted object, with "min" being explanatory (li-l-bayan), and the verb is transitive to two objects: one is the deputy of the subject, and the other is the deleted described noun, meaning: they will be adorned with ornaments, or with something of bracelets. On the view that this verb is transitive to two objects, it is permitted that "min" be partitive (lil-tab'id) occupying the position of the object, and that it be superfluous according to the opinion of al-Akhfash, who permitted its superfluous use in affirmative sentences. (Asawira) is the object of (yuhallawna).

His saying, ﴿of gold﴾ (min dhahabin) is a qualifier of (asawira), and "min" is explanatory. It has been said that it marks the starting point, meaning they were created from gold. It has been said that it is partitive. Its connection to (yuhallawna) is not hidden in its status.

It was read as "yuhlawna" with a damma on the initial letter and without doubling. According to what is in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit), it has the meaning of the doubled form. The statement of some scholars suggests that it is transitive to one object, which is the deputy of the subject, so "min asawira" is connected to it, and "min" is initial.

Ibn 'Abbas read "yahlawna" with a fatha on the ya' and the lam, and sukun on the ha', from "halat al-mar'ah" (the woman became adorned), when she put on her ornaments. Abu Hayyan said: when she became one who possesses ornaments. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: it is permissible that it be from "haliya bi-'aini" (he found it pleasing to his eye), "yahla," when you find something pleasing; and this is originally from sweetness (halawa), and in that case "min" is superfluous. The meaning is: they find the bracelets pleasing therein. It has been said that this verb is intransitive, and "min" is causal (sababiyyah), and the meaning is: some of them are pleasing in the eyes of others because of wearing gold bracelets.

Abu al-Fadl permitted that it be from "halaytu bihi" (I obtained it), when you succeed in it, and from this is their saying: "so-and-so did not achieve anything of value (lam yahl bi-ta'il)." In that case "min" carries the meaning of "bi" (with), meaning: they will obtain therein bracelets of gold.

Ibn 'Abbas read "min asworin" with a fatha on the ra' without an alif or a ha'. Its analogy would be to be declined (sarf), because its form has been reduced, so it became like "jandal" (a rock). However, the deleted element was treated as existing, so declension was prevented. The discussion of the like of this sentence has already been given in surah al-Kahf, so recall it.

His saying, ﴿and pearls﴾ (wa lu'lu'an) is coordinated with the position (mahall) of (min asawira), or with the deleted described noun. Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinni) interpreted it as the implication of a verb, meaning: "and they will be given pearls," or something similar to that.

Most of the Seven Readers, al-Hasan in one transmission, Talhah, Ibn Thabit, al-A'mash, and the people of Mecca read "wa lu'lu'in" with the genitive case (khafd), coordinated with (asawira) or with (dhahabin), because a bracelet may be of gold inlaid with pearls, and may be of pearls alone, as we have seen, and in our lands it is called "khasar," and most of it is from coral (marjan). They differed over whether there is an alif after the waw in the Imam (the 'Uthmanic codex). Al-Jahdari said: yes; al-Asma'i said: no. Yahya narrated from Abu Bakr the hamzing of the second and the changing of the first hamza into waw, while al-Mu'alla ibn Mansur narrated from him the opposite of that.

Al-Fayyad read "lu'liyyan," changing the two hamzas into two waws, so the second became a waw preceded by a damma. And since there is no declinable noun in their speech whose last letter is a waw preceded by a damma, the waw was changed into ya' and the damma before it into a kasra. Ibn 'Abbas read "wa li'liyyan," changing the two hamzas into two waws and then changing them into two ya's: the change of the second is for what you know, and the change of the first is for assimilation (ittiba'). Talhah read "wa lawlin," like "adlin" in the plural of "dalw" (bucket): the two hamzas were changed into two waws, then the damma of the lam was changed into a kasra and the waw into ya', then it was given the weak-letter treatment of "qadin" (judge).

﴿And their clothing therein is silk﴾ (wa libasuhum fiha harir): the style is varied, since it does not say "and they will wear therein silk," to indicate that the attribution of clothing to them is a certain matter, needing no explanation, since it is not possible for them to be free of it. What needs explanation is what their clothing is, unlike the adornment, which is not among their necessary attributes; therefore its explanation was made the primary purpose. Perhaps this is the secret of placing the explanation of the adornment before the explanation of the state of the clothing; so said the scholar Shaykh al-Islam. He did not accept what has been said: that the change is to indicate that silk is their customary clothing, or merely to preserve the form of the rhyming endings (fawasil). The apparent sense of their statements is that the sentence is coordinated with the preceding one. It is permitted that it be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of (yuhallawna).

Then, the apparent meaning is that this ruling is general for all the people of Paradise. It has been said that it is according to what is most common, due to what al-Nasa'i, Ibn Hibban, and others narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever wore silk in this world will not wear it in the Hereafter, and even if he enters Paradise, the people of Paradise will wear it and he will not wear it." The hadith that he does not wear it in the Hereafter is recorded in the two Sahihs from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, as a marfu' (raised) report.

[Page 137]

The apparent meaning is that the prohibition of men using silk, except in what has been excepted, is agreed upon by consensus (ijma') (ijma', scholarly consensus), and that whoever considers it lawful without interpretation (ta'wil) has disbelieved. Perhaps the report of al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan and others, from Ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with them both, as a marfu' report: "Whoever wore silk in this world will not wear it in the Hereafter, and will not enter Paradise," if it is authentic, is to be understood as referring to the case where the wearing is prohibited by consensus and its doer considers it lawful without interpretation; or it means that the intended meaning is that he will not enter Paradise along with the foremost (al-sabiqun). Otherwise, the non-entry of the wearer into Paradise absolutely is problematic.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 24:

﴿And they were guided to the good word﴾, which is their saying: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us and made us inherit the earth﴾ [Az-Zumar: 74], as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. It has also been said that it encompasses this and all the other speech exchanged among the people of Paradise with one another. It has also been said that this guidance is in this world, and the good word is the saying "There is no god but Allah." In another narration from Ibn 'Abbas, this is given along with the addition "and praise be to Allah." Ibn Zayd added "and Allah is greatest." From al-Suddi it is reported that it is the Qur'an. Al-Mawardi related that it is enjoining what is good and forbidding what is evil. It has also been said that it encompasses all of this and the other remembrances (adhkar). ﴿And they were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy﴾, that is, the One who is highly praised (al-Hamid, "the Praiseworthy"). The annexation of "path" to it has been said to be explanatory (bayaniyyah, an annexation in which the second term specifies the first). The path here is Islam, for it is a praiseworthy path, whoever treads it is praised, or it is itself praiseworthy, or its outcome is praiseworthy. It has also been said that the path is Paradise, and the term "path" is applied to it because it is a way to attaining what "no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived." It has also been said that "the Praiseworthy" is Paradise, and the annexation is in its literal sense, and its path is Islam or the tangible road leading to it on the Day of Resurrection. It has been inferred that "the Praiseworthy" refers to Allah, the Exalted, who deserves all praise in His essence. Its path, may He be exalted, is Islam, for it is a way to His pleasure, may He be exalted. It has also been said that the path is Paradise, for it is a way to attaining what was mentioned earlier, and it is attributed to Him for honour.

The sum of what they have said here is that the guidance may be in the Hereafter or in this world, and that "the Praiseworthy" may mean either Allah, may His majesty be exalted, or Paradise, or the path itself, and that "the path" may mean either Islam, or Paradise, or the tangible road leading to it on the Day of Resurrection.

They explained the delay of this clause relative to the first clause in two ways: at times, that it serves the rhyme endings (fawasil, the rhyming ends of verses); at other times, that mention of the praise contained in the first clause calls for mention of the One who is praised. It is not far-fetched to say that the guidance in both clauses occurs in the Hereafter after entering Paradise, that the annexation here is explanatory, that the good word is the speech that souls find delightful, exchanged among the people of Paradise with one another, and that the Praiseworthy path is what the people of Paradise follow in dealing with one another through actions for which they are praised, or through what is more general than that. Thus the sum of the first clause is the description of the people of Paradise by good speech, and the sum of the second is their description by good conduct, or by what is more general than both. It is as though Allah, after mentioning the goodness of their dwelling, their adornments and their clothing, followed this with the goodness of how they treat one another in speech and deed, indicating that what they are in does not lead them to harshness of speech or the vile conduct that would disgrace the goodness of their state and spoil the delight of their gathering. The reason for the order of precedence and delay on this view is not hidden from the discerning.

What he (al-Alusi) chose is that the good word is their saying after entering Paradise: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has removed from us all grief. Indeed, our Lord is All-Forgiving, Most Appreciative﴾, and ﴿who has settled us in the abode of permanence by His bounty; no fatigue touches us therein, nor does weariness touch us therein﴾ [Fatir: 34, 35], in accordance with His saying, may He be exalted, in Surah Fatir [33, 34], after His saying, glorified is He: ﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their clothing therein is silk﴾, and ﴿they will say: Praise be to Allah, who has removed from us all grief﴾, and so on. The Qur'an explains one part of itself by another. And he chose that the Praiseworthy path refers to what encompasses the sayings and actions passing among the people of Paradise that are praised in their conduct and association in those abodes, avoiding any trace of repetition (ta'kid, emphasis), as will not be hidden from a person of sound understanding. So reflect, may you be guided to the path of the Praiseworthy.

[p. 138]

Page 139

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar [others] from the way of Allah and the Sacred Mosque﴾: this is a threat against one category of disbelievers. The conjunction of the present tense (*mudari'*) with the past tense (*madi*) is good here, because the present tense is not meant to indicate the present or the future, as in the saying of people: "So-and-so is kind to the poor," where what is meant is the continuous existence of kindness. It has also been said that ﴿yasuddun﴾ (they bar) means "sadda" (they barred), but it is expressed in the present tense to bring the past scene vividly before the mind, to emphasise the gravity of the act of barring. It has also been said that there is no conjunction, rather the clause is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the whole is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the subject of ﴿kafaru﴾ (disbelieved), meaning: "while they bar." It has also been permitted that the clause be a circumstantial clause without the need to assume a subject, because it resembles a nominal clause in meaning. The predicate of ﴿inna﴾ (indeed) is omitted, indicated by the end of the noble verse, meaning: "We shall make them taste a painful punishment." Al-Zamakhshari estimated it to come after ﴿al-Masjid al-Haram﴾, but Abu Hayyan objected that this is not correct, because it involves separating the qualifier, which is ﴿al-Masjid﴾, from the qualified, which is ﴿alladhi﴾ (the one who).

It was answered that it is possible that he made ﴿alladhi﴾ a detached qualifier (*na't maqta'*). Ibn Atiyyah estimated it after ﴿wal-bad﴾ (and the desert dweller), which is better; but he estimated "khasiru" (they lost) or "halaku" (they perished), and the estimate "nudhiquhum" (We shall make them taste) is better than it. It has also been said that the *waw* in ﴿wa-yasuddun﴾ is superfluous, and the clause after it is the predicate of ﴿inna﴾. Ibn Atiyyah objected that this corrupts the intended meaning, and others objected that the Basrans do not permit the addition of *waw*; the view that it is permissible to add it is a Kufan view which is disregarded. The apparent reading is that ﴿al-Masjid﴾ is conjoined to ﴿sabil﴾ (way). It has also been permitted that it be conjoined to the noble name (Allah), and the verse, according to what is related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan ibn Harb and his companions when they barred the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions, may Allah be pleased with them, in the year of al-Hudaybiyah from the Sacred Mosque; so the Prophet (ﷺ) disliked to fight them, and he was in the state of ihram for 'umrah. Then they made a treaty with him that he should return in the following year.

The Sacred Mosque here means Makkah, and it is expressed by it because it is the principal intended object of it. This is indicated by His saying, ﴿which We have made for the people﴾, meaning: whoever he may be, without any distinction between a Makkan and an outsider; ﴿equal for the resident therein and the visitor﴾, meaning: the one who dwells there and the one who arrives there. Dwelling does not occur in the mosque itself, but in the houses of Makkah. Describing it thus adds to the reproach upon those who bar [people] from it. Some scholars have cited the verse as evidence for the impermissibility of selling and renting the houses of Makkah; otherwise the resident and the visitor would not be equal in them. This has been explicitly stated in some authentic hadiths: it was related by several chains that he (ﷺ) said: "Makkah, which Allah has made sacred, it is not lawful to sell its plots (*ribaʿ*) or to rent its houses." Ibn Sabit mentioned that the houses of the people of Makkah were without doors, until theft increased, so a man made a door, and Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, objected to him, saying: "Will you close a door in the face of the pilgrims to the House of Allah?" He said: "I only wanted to protect their goods from theft." So he left it, and the people made doors. Ibn Majah and Ibn Abi Shaybah related from Alqamah ibn Nadlah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) died, and Abu Bakr and Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, and the plots of Makkah were called only 'al-sawa'ib' (free to all); whoever needed, dwelt; and whoever was wealthy, let others dwell." Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "Whoever eats the rent of the houses of Makkah, he is only eating fire in his belly, because the people are equal in benefiting from them." Its beginning is found in a narration of al-Daraqutni traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). In al-Nihayah: there is no harm in selling the buildings of Makkah, but selling its land is disliked. This is the view of Abu Hanifah, and he said: there is no harm in selling its land; and this is also a narration from him. It is the view of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, and the fatwa is according to it. In *Tanwir al-Absar* and its commentary *al-Durr al-Mukhtar*: it is permissible to sell the buildings of the houses of Makkah and its land without disapproval; al-Shafi'i said this, and my teacher Ayni issues fatwas according to it. In *al-Burhan*, in the chapter on the tithe: the selling of its land is not disliked, just like its buildings, and by this one acts. In *Mukhtarat al-Nawazil* of the author of *al-Hidayah*: there is no harm in selling its buildings and renting them.

However, in *al-Zayla'i* and others, renting them is disliked.
