At the end of the fifth chapter of *al-Tatarkhaniyyah* and in the rent of *al-Wahbaniyyah*: Abu Hanifah said: "I dislike renting the houses of Makkah during the days of the season (*mawsim*)," and he used to issue fatwas permitting them to lodge in their houses, citing His saying, ﴿equal for the resident therein and the visitor﴾; and he permitted it outside the days of the season. End. So let this be memorised. I say: by this the distinction and reconciliation become clear. End.

What is understood from *Ghayat al-Bayan* is that the view of the disapproval of renting their houses during the days of the season is not something the Imam alone held; rather his two companions agreed with him on it, since it is related from *Taqrib* of the Imam al-Karkhi the following text: Hisham related from Abu Yusuf from Abu Hanifah that he disliked renting the houses of Makkah during the season and permitted it at other times; and Abu Yusuf said likewise. Hisham said: Muhammad informed me from Abu Hanifah that renting the houses of Makkah during the season is disliked, and he says to them that they may lodge in their houses if there is room in them, and if there is not, then no. This is the view of Muhammad. End.

What has been established from what we have seen in most of the reliable books of our masters of the Hanafi school is that the permissibility of selling the buildings of houses is agreed upon, because it is the property of the one who built it, like one who builds on waqf land with the permission of the trustee. It cannot be said that it is the building of a usurper, like one who builds a house in a congregational mosque, because the permission is evident here, but not there. Likewise is the disapproval of renting during the days of the season. As for selling the land, according to the two Imams it is permissible without disapproval, by one consensus; and from Imam Abu Hanifah there are two narrations: permissibility and non-permissibility, and the preferred view is permissibility. The basis for those who permit it from the noble Book is this verse.

The companions of al-Shafi'i answered it: the Sacred Mosque is the place of circumambulation (*mataf*), and the one who stays in seclusion (*'akif*) is the one devoted to worship, counted among the people of the mosque because of his constant presence there, which is more apparent. Likewise, equality in that it is one of the rites of Allah, the Exalted, set up for every devotee and visitor, is clearer, and this is the counterpart of the one described as barring from the way of Allah and the Sacred Mosque specifically. They were not barring [people] from Makkah, nor is barring [people] from it, for one who does not intend the rites, a sin. And what has the question of ownership and non-ownership to do with this context? As for the objection that it has a place by way of incorporation (*idmaj*) and an indication of the text (*isharat al-nass*), that is a statement of no use.

*Sawa'* (equal) has been explained in the manner that has been explained; so says *al-Kashf*. A debate took place in Makkah between al-Shafi'i and Ishaq ibn Rahawayh al-Hanzali, and Ishaq did not permit renting the houses of Makkah. Al-Shafi'i argued with His saying, ﴿those who were expelled from their homes without right﴾ (Surah al-Hajj 22:40), where the homes are attributed to their owners; and with His saying, peace be upon him, on the day of the conquest of Makkah: "Whoever closes his door is safe, and whoever enters the house of Abu Sufyan is safe." And also that Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, bought the prison house. Do you think he bought it from its owners or from non-owners? Ishaq said: "When I knew that the proof had become binding upon me, I abandoned my view." Some answered that the attribution is to the owners of the benefit of residence, and that Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, bought the building and not the land, and he satisfied with the price the one who had spent money on it for the public need, and the Imam has from that what is not for others. It was objected that argument by the apparent meaning, and deviation from the apparent meaning without a stronger basis, is not to be considered. Therefore Ibn Rahawayh said, and he is one of the pillars of the Muslims and a flag of the flags of the religion, what he said.

The apparent view is that the reports which explicitly prohibit selling and renting were not authenticated according to al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, and according to those who held a view like his. ﴿Sawa'﴾ is in the accusative as the second object of *ja'alna* (We made), and the first object is the attached pronoun of the third person, and *al-'akif* (the one who dwells) is in the nominative, depending on it, because it means "equal" (*mustawin*), even though originally it is a verbal noun. From their speech: "I passed by a man, equal, he and nothingness" (*sawa'an huwa wal-'adam*); and *al-lam* (the particle) is an adverbial complement (*zarf*) to what is in front of it.

It has been permitted that ﴿lil-nas﴾ (for the people) is in the position of the second object, meaning: We made it permissible for the people or a place of worship for them; and ﴿sawa'un﴾ (equal) is a circumstantial clause from the *ha'* (the pronoun); and likewise it is a circumstantial clause when the making is not transitive to two objects.

Al-Jumhur (the majority) read ﴿sawa'un﴾ with *raf'* (nominative), as the predicate, and ﴿al-'akif﴾ as the subject; the reverse was considered weak, because it involves giving information about a definite thing concerning an indefinite one. The clause is in the position of the second object or circumstantial clause. It has been permitted that it be explanatory of His making it for the people. A group, including al-A'mash in the narration of al-Qati'i, read ﴿sawa'an﴾ in the accusative and ﴿al-'akifi﴾ in the genitive; the basis of the accusative is what has preceded, and the basis of the genitive ﴿al-'akifi﴾ is that it is an apposition of detail (*badal tafsil*) from ﴿al-nas﴾ (the people); and it was said: it is an explicative apposition (*'atf bayan*). The reading ﴿wal-badi﴾ is recited with the *ya'* (yā') affixed in pause and in continuation, and it is recited without it in both, and with it in continuation and dropped in pause.

﴿And whoever intends therein﴾ with an object omitted in order to encompass every possible object, meaning: whoever intends therein something or some purpose. Ibn Atiyyah estimated the object as "the people," meaning: whoever intends the people therein.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿with deviation﴾ means: swerving from the intention, that is, moral rectitude; and its origin is *ilhad al-hafir* (the deviation of the digger, i.e., the digging of a side-tunnel). ﴿with injustice﴾, without right, are two synonymous circumstantial clauses, or the second is an apposition for the first by repeating the preposition; the *ba'* (with) in both is for association; or the first is a circumstantial clause and the second is connected to it, and the *ba'* in it is for causation, meaning: deviating because of injustice, such as associating partners with Allah and committing sins. Abu Ubaydah said: the *ba'* is superfluous, and *ilhad* is the object of *yurid*, and he cited as evidence the verse of al-A'sha:

"Our spears guaranteed the provision of our dependants."

It was supported by the recitation of al-Hasan: ﴿whoever intends its deviation with injustice﴾, and it has the meaning of "deviation therein," except that it has been widened so it is said "its deviation." Abu Hayyan said: it is better that *yurid* be understood as implying the meaning "to be clothed in" (*yatalabbas*), and the *ba'* be made for transitivity. A group read *yarid* with a *fatha* on the *ya'*, from *al-wurud* (arrival), and al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' related it, meaning: whoever comes therein with deviation, etc. The explanation of *ilhad* as mentioned is the apparent one, so it includes all sins, because the essential meaning of it is inclining from truth to falsehood, and this is realised in all sins. Likewise, according to a group, the meaning of injustice is included, and their combination on this view is for emphasis. It was said: the meaning of this is polytheism, but Ibn Abi Mulaykah did not accept this. Abd ibn Humayd related that he was asked about the saying of the Exalted: ﴿and whoever intends﴾ etc., and he said: "We did not doubt that it refers to sins, until non-Arab people of Basra came to non-Arab people of Kufa and claimed it was polytheism."

Abu Dawud and others related from Ya'la ibn Umayyah, from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, who said: "Hoarding food in the Haram is deviation therein." This is one of the instances mentioned because the situation calls for it. Some made from this the entering of it without ihram. It was related from Ata' that he explained deviation as this.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 25 (part 2 of 2):

It was narrated by Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) and a group of others, from Mujahid, who said: Abdullah ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both) had two tents (fustat), one in the al-Hill (the area outside the sacred precinct) and the other in al-Haram (the sacred precinct). When he wished to pray, he would pray in the one in al-Haram, and when he wished to rebuke his family, he would rebuke them in the one in al-Hill. He was asked about this, and he said: "We have been told that deviating (ilhad) in it [includes this]. No, by Allah, yes, by Allah." ﴿We shall make him taste a painful punishment﴾. The response (jawab) is for the conditional particle man (whoever). The apparent meaning is that the threat applies to the mere intention of this, in general. This indicates that whoever intends an evil deed in Makkah but does not do it will be held accountable for the mere intention. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Ikrimah and Abu al-Hajjaj.

Al-Khafaji said: The threat applies to an intention that accompanies the act, not to the mere intention. However, the expression of it (the intention) indicates the multiplication of evil deeds there. A firm (musammimah) intention is also something for which one is held accountable, even if it is said that it is not a major sin. It has been related from Malik that he disliked residing in Makkah permanently. End of quotation.

Mujahid also held the view of the multiplication of evil deeds in Makkah. Ibn al-Mundhir and others related from him that he said: "Evil deeds are multiplied in Makkah just as good deeds are multiplied." He (may Allah have mercy on him) also said: "I asked Ibn Umar, whose residence was in al-Hill and whose mosque was in al-Haram, 'Why do you do this?' He said: 'Because good deeds in al-Haram are more virtuous and sin in it is more grave. Therefore, whoever is in it should restrain himself and follow the path of rectitude in everything he resolves upon and intends.'"

The apparent meaning is that this tasting is in the Hereafter. It has also been said that it was before the family of the victim permitted it (istihlal), and that punishment is hastened in this world for whoever intends harm to it (Makkah).

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Rabi' ibn Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said regarding the verse: "A man who heard it from the descendants of the Emigrants (muhajirin) and the Helpers (ansar) told us that they informed him that whoever intends in it (Makkah) what the People of the Elephant intended, punishment will be hastened upon them in this world." He said: "Its (the sin's) recompense is only given through the permission of its people (istihlal min qibal ahlih)." What will benefit you in this matter will come soon, Allah willing.

Some of them defined the sacred precinct (al-Haram) with these lines:

"For the boundary of the Haram, of good land, is three miles, if you wish to master it,
and seven miles from Iraq and Ta'if, and Jiddah is ten, then nine is its Ji'ranah.
And from Yemen seven, with its sin (sin of sab'ah) placed first, and it is complete, so thank your Lord for His favour."

As for the Masjid al-Haram (the Sacred Mosque), according to Ata it applies to the entire sacred precinct, so its boundary is what was mentioned. In al-Bahr al-'Amiq (a commentary), from Abu Hurayrah, he said: "We find in the Book of Allah the Exalted that the boundary of the Sacred Mosque extends to the end of al-Sa'y (the place of running between al-Safa and al-Marwah)." From Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As he said: "The foundation of the Sacred Mosque, which Ibrahim (peace be upon him) laid, is from al-Hazwah to the outlet of the watercourse of Jiyad."

They have mentioned that the length of the mosque today is four hundred and four cubits, and its width is three hundred cubits. It has been related that it was not like this in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and it had no wall surrounding it. When Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) became caliph, he enlarged the mosque, bought houses, demolished them and included them in it. Then he built a short wall around it, below head height, and lamps were placed upon it. Then, when Uthman became caliph, he also bought houses, enlarged it with them, and built the mosque and the colonnades (arwiqah). Then Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, in the year sixty-something (sanah bid' wa-sittin), made a great addition to the mosque during his caliphate, and among it was part of the house of al-Azraqi, which he bought for seven thousand dinars. After that, Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan rebuilt it, but he did not expand it. However, he raised the wall of the mosque and brought to it columns of stone and marble. Then al-Mansur added to its Syrian side (shiqq al-shami) and built it, and placed in it columns of marble. Then al-Mahdi added to it twice after him. The Ka'bah had been on one side of the mosque, so he wished that it be in the centre; he bought houses, added to the mosque, and centred it. Thus al-Nawawi mentioned.

In al-Bahr al-'Amiq it is said that al-Mahdi's addition is the one adjacent to Dar al-Nadwah (the House of Assembly), behind the Maqam al-Hanafi (the Hanafi Station). Then, when the dynasty reached the sultans of the House of Uthman, may Allah keep their dynasty as long as the cycle of time endures, they spared no effort in serving it and striving for its maintenance.

Page 141

﴿And when We settled for Abraham the place of the House﴾: that is, remember for these disbelievers who bar others from the way of God, the Exalted, and from the Sacred Mosque, the time when We made the place of the House a dwelling-place (*msubah*) for their forefather Abraham, peace be upon him; that is, a place of return to which he would come back for its upkeep (*'imarah*) and worship. It is said: "He settled him (*bawwa'ahu*) in a dwelling (*manzilan*)" when he lodged him therein. Since it was necessary to make the second (Abraham) a dwelling for the first (the House), the preposition *lam* was used, so it is for transitivity (*lam al-ta'diyah*, the *lam* that makes the verb transitive), and "*makan*" (place) is the direct object.

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is "a House for him, in the place of the House, so that he may build it and it may be a dwelling for him and his descendants, to which they return and perform the pilgrimage." The first explanation is related from Ibn 'Abbas. It is also said that the *lam* is extra (*za'idah*) with the direct object, and "*makan*" is an adverb of place (*zarf*) for *bawwa'na* (We settled). This has been objected to, on the grounds that the *lam* is only added when the object is fronted or when the governing verb is a derived form (*far'*), and neither condition is met here; and that "*makan al-bayt*" is a specific place, so the verb should take *fi* (in) to govern it. There is room for discussion on this, as is known from the books of Arabic grammar. It is also said that the object of *bawwa'na* is omitted, meaning "We settled the people," and the *lam* in "*li-Ibrahim*" is the *lam* of cause (*lam al-'illah*), meaning "for the sake of Abraham," that is, as an honour to him. The reliable view is what we have already mentioned. The directing of the command to remember toward the time, even though the intended meaning is to remind of the events that took place in it, has already been mentioned more than once. "*Makan*" (place), in common usage, is that on which a thing rests and which prevents it from descending. The scholars have various views on it, but this is not the place to examine them.

[p. 142]

The root meaning of *bayt* (house) is the dwelling of a person at night. Then it may be used without regard to the night. Its plural is *abyat* and *buyut*, but *buyut* is more specific to a dwelling and *abyat* is more specific to poetry (a line of verse). The term applies to what is built of stone, of clay, of wool, or of camel's hair. The place of a thing may be expressed by its house. The "House" here is the House of God, the Mighty and Majestic, the Honoured Ka'bah. It has been built five times. The first was the building of the angels, peace be upon them, before Adam; it was of red ruby. Then that building was raised to the heavens during the time of the Flood. The second was the building of Abraham, peace be upon him. It is narrated that when God, the Exalted, commanded him to build the House, he did not know where to build it, so God sent him the *khujuj* wind (a wind that uncovers), which uncovered its ancient foundation, and he built upon it. The third was the building of the Quraysh in the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance). The Prophet ﷺ was present at it when he was a young man. When they wanted to lift the Black Stone, they disputed about it, and each tribe wanted to take on the task of raising it. Then they agreed that the first man to emerge from this lane (*sikkah*) would judge between them. The Messenger of God ﷺ was the first to come out, and he judged between them that they should place it in a cloak (*mirt*) and then all the tribes would lift it. They lifted it, and then he (ﷺ) climbed up and they raised it to him, and he placed it in its place. They used to call him, peace be upon him, "the Trustworthy" (*al-Amin*). This was, it is said, fifteen years before the Mission (*mab'ath*). The fourth was the building of 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr. The fifth was the building of al-Hajjaj, which is the building that exists today.

Its height in the sky is twenty-seven *dhira'* (cubits) and a quarter of a cubit. The cubit (*dhira'*) is twenty-four *isba'* (finger-breadths), and the finger-breadth is six barley-corns, and the barley-corn is six hairs of the horse's (*birdhawn*) hair. As for its length on the ground, it is from the Yemeni Corner to the Black Corner, twenty-five cubits, and likewise between the Yemeni and the Western Corner. As for its width, it is from the Yemeni Corner to the Black Corner, twenty cubits. The length of the door is six cubits and ten fingers, and its width is four cubits. The door is in its eastern wall, and it is of teak wood, plated with silver sheets. The height from the ground to below the threshold of the door is four cubits and three fingers. The gutter (*mizab*) is in the middle of the wall of the Hijr. The width of the Multazam, which is the space between the door and the Black Stone, is four cubits. The height of the Black Stone from the ground is three cubits less a seventh. The width of the *qidr* (the basin/enclosure) from which it projects is a span (*shibr*) and four fingers held together. The width of the *mustaja* (place of refuge), which is between the Yemeni Corner and the sealed door in the back of the Ka'bah, opposite the Multazam, is four cubits and five fingers. The width of the sealed door is three and a half cubits, and its length is more than five cubits.

As for the Hijr, also called the *Hatim* and the *Hazirah*, it is in the shape of a half-circle on the side of the Levant and the north, between the Iraqi and the Syrian Corners. Its boundary from the wall of the Ka'bah under the gutter to the wall of the Hijr is seventeen cubits and eight fingers, of which seven cubits, or six cubits and a span, are from the ground of the Ka'bah. The rest was a pen for the sheep of our lord Isma'il, peace be upon him, and they included it in the Hijr. The distance between the two doors of the Hijr is twenty cubits. The width of the wall of the Hijr is two cubits. The measurement of the circumference of the wall of the Hijr from the inside is thirty-eight cubits, and from the outside forty cubits and six fingers. The height of the wall of the Hijr is two cubits. Thus the measurement of the circuit alone around the Ka'bah and the Hijr is one hundred and twenty-three cubits and twelve fingers. This is according to what the Imam Husayn ibn Muhammad al-Amidi mentioned in a treatise he wrote on the subject, and the responsibility for it lies with him. We hope from the Lord of the House that He will grant us success in visiting His House and in verifying this by His kindness and generosity.

The *an* in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿that you associate nothing with Me﴾ is said to be explanatory (*mufassirah*), and the explanation is in view of the fact that the settling was for the sake of worship; so it is as if it were said: "We commanded Abraham, peace be upon him, to worship," and this carries the sense of speech without its letters. Or because "We settled him" carries the meaning of "We said to him: settle." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is the lightened form (*mukhaffafah*) of the heavy (*thaqilah*), and it is as if, by interpretation, "We settled him" meant "We informed him," so there is no objection to it, that it must be preceded by a verb of certainty or of preference.

[p. 143]

Abu Hayyan said: The preferable view is that it is the *an* governing the subjunctive (*al-nasibah*), and just as it is connected to the imperfect, it is also connected to the perfect, the imperative and the prohibitive, ending quote. In that case it does not govern the verb in form. Abu Hatim's statement that there must be a *nasb* (subjunctive case) on the *kaf* in this case was refuted in *al-Durr al-Masun*, meaning: "We did that so that you would not associate anyone with Me in worship." The apparent sense is that the address is to Abraham, peace be upon him, and this is supported by the reading of 'Ikrimah and Abu Nuhayk, "*an la yushrika*" with the *ya'* (third person). It is also said that the address is to the Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him.

﴿And purify My House for those who circumambulate, and those who stand, and bow and prostrate﴾: The intended meaning of purification (*tahharah*) includes both the physical and the spiritual; that is, purify My House from idols and filth for those who circle it and pray beside it. Perhaps the expression of prayer by its pillars, namely standing, bowing and prostration, is to indicate that each of them independently requires purification or settling, as it is said. "How is this, when they have been combined?" Or it is to specify this Muhammadan community, may the best of prayers and the most complete greetings be upon its Prophet, since the combination of these pillars is found only in their prayer. Prostration is not coordinated with bowing because it is of the same kind as bowing in humility. It is also possible that "*al-qa'imin*" (those who stand) means "those who reside" and "*al-ta'ifin*" (those who circle) means "those who come upon it (as visitors)," so that "*al-ruka' al-sujud*" alone means those who pray. However, what is understood first from "*al-ta'ifin*" is what was mentioned first.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 27:

﴿And proclaim among the people the Pilgrimage﴾ i.e., call out to them ﴿with the Hajj﴾ — with the summons to the Hajj and the command to perform it. Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "When Ibrahim, peace be upon him, finished building the House, he said: 'My Lord, I have finished.' He said: 'Proclaim to the people the Pilgrimage.' He said: 'My Lord, how will my voice reach them?' He said: 'Proclaim, and upon Me is the delivering.' He said: 'My Lord, how shall I say it?' He said: 'Say: O people, the Pilgrimage has been prescribed for you, to the Ancient House.' So the people of the heavens and the earth heard it. Do you not see that they answer from the farthest lands, saying the talbiyah?"

It is related in another narration from him that he, peace be upon him, climbed Abu Qubays, placed his two fingers in his ears, and then called out: "O people, indeed Allah, the Exalted, has prescribed the Hajj for you, so answer your Lord." They answered him with the talbiyah in the loins of men and the wombs of women. The first to answer were the people of Yemen. Therefore, from that day until the Hour is established, no pilgrim performs Hajj except one who answered Ibrahim, peace be upon him, on that day.

In another narration, he stood upon al-Hijr and called out. From Mujahid, he, peace be upon him, stood upon al-Safa. In another narration from him, he, peace be upon him, was made to stand tall until he was like the tallest mountain on earth, and then he proclaimed the Hajj. It is possible to reconcile these by the repetition of the proclamation. Whichever it was, the address is to Ibrahim, peace be upon him.

Some have claimed that it was addressed to our Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and that he was commanded with this at the Farewell Pilgrimage, and this has been related from al-Hasan. But this is clearly contrary to the apparent meaning, and there is no indication for it. It has also been said that the fact that the surah is Meccan refutes it, and you already know what is in its opening.

Al-Hasan, Ibn Muhaysin read «wa'dhin» with the long vowel and without doubling, i.e., "inform" (a'lim), as some have said. Others said that what is meant here is "cause the proclamation to be made" (awqi'i al-iidhan), because according to the first reading it should have been followed directly by its object rather than by "fi" — so it is like his saying: "yajrah fi 'arāqibihā naslī" (his blade wounds her hamstrings).

Ibn Atiyyah said: this reading has been distorted in the transmission to Ibn Jinni, for it has been transmitted from them as «wa-adhana» in the past tense, and he took it as conjoined to («bawwa'na»). Abu Hayyan refuted him, saying it is not a distortion; rather Abu Abd Allah al-Husayn ibn Khalawayh related it in his collection of irregular readings. Ibn Abi Ishaq read «bil-Hijj» with a kasra on the ha' wherever it occurs. The words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿they will come to you﴾ are in the jussive in response to the command, which is («adhdhin») according to the two readings, and («tahhir») according to the third, as the author of al-Lawami' said. The use of the verb of coming with His pronoun, peace be upon him, is because that occurs through his proclamation, and the meaning is "they will come to your House." His words, glorified is He, ﴿on foot﴾ are in the position of a circumstantial clause, i.e., walking, the plural of rajil, like qiyam, the plural of qa'im.

Ibn Abi Ishaq read «rujalan» with a damma on the ra' and without doubling. This is related from Ikrimah, al-Hasan, and Abu Mijlaz, and it is a collective noun for rajil, like tu'ar for ta'ir, or it is a rare plural. It is related from these and from Ibn Abbas, Muhammad ibn Ja'far, and Mujahid, may Allah be pleased with them all, «ruccalan» with a damma and doubling, as the plural of rajil like tajir and tujjar. From Ikrimah, he read «rujala» like sukara. It is the plural of rajul or rajil. From Ibn Abbas, Ata', and Ibn Hudayr, the same, except that they doubled the jim. His words, exalted is He, ﴿and upon every lean camel﴾ are conjoined to («rijalan»), i.e., riders upon every lean camel which the distance of the journey has worn out, so it became lean, or its leanness increased. «Dhamir» applies to the masculine and the feminine. He deviated from «rukbanan», which is more concise, to indicate the great number of those coming from distant places.

The verse is evidence for the permissibility of walking and riding in Hajj. Ibn al-Arabi said: Our scholars derived from placing («rijalan») first that walking is more excellent, and this has been related from Ibn Abbas. Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Bayhaqi, and a group narrated that he said: "I do not regret anything that has escaped me except that I did not perform Hajj on foot until old age overtook me. I hear Allah, the Exalted, saying: ﴿They will come to you on foot and upon every lean camel﴾, so He began with those on foot before the riders." There is also a marfu' hadith on this: Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Mardawayh, and others narrated from him that he said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'For the rider on Hajj, every step his mount takes is seventy good deeds, and for the one on foot, every step is seven hundred good deeds from the good deeds of the Sacred Precinct.' It was said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what are the good deeds of the Sacred Precinct?' He said: 'A good deed is a hundred thousand good deeds.'" Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from Mujahid that Ibrahim and Isma'il, peace be upon them both, performed Hajj while walking.

Ibn al-Faras said: Some have used the verse as evidence that Hajj is not obligatory upon one whose route includes a sea and who has no other way, because the sea is not mentioned in the verse. This was refuted as a weak argument, since Mecca is not on a sea; it is reached only by one of two means, walking or riding. Also, the argument from the absence of mention to the absence of obligation is open to question. The words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿coming﴾ are an attribute of («dhamir») or of («kull»), and the plural is in view of the meaning, as if it were said: "and riders upon lean camels coming." Here «kull» is for multiplicity, not for totality. What has been said — that when it is attached to an indefinite noun its meaning is rarely observed — they refuted with this verse and its parallels. Likewise what has been said — that it is permissible when they are in two separate clauses — since this is a single clause.

Abu Hayyan allowed that the pronoun might include both («rijal») and («kull dhamir»), with the clause being an attribute of them in the sense of groups and companies. This was refuted on the ground that it would entail giving precedence to non-rational beings over rational ones, and they have explicitly prohibited this. Indeed, Ubayd Allah and his companions, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Abi Abla read «ya'tūna», and the consideration of precedence there is in its proper place. The more well-known view is that the pronoun refers to («rijalan» and «rukbanan»), so there is no precedence. It was also permitted to make the pronoun refer to the people, with the clause being resumptive. ﴿From every deep ravine﴾, i.e., path, as related from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, and Abu al-Aliyah. Originally it is a gap between two mountains, and it is used for a wide path, but they stripped it of the sense of width, since that does not fit here; rather it would be somewhat defective. ﴿Deep﴾, i.e., distant, and by this the group also explained it. Its original sense is far downward, which is not suitable here.

Ibn Mas'ud read «mu'ayq». Al-Layth said: it is said "amiq mu'iq" for the Tamim tribe, and "a'maqtu al-bi'r" and "am'aqtuha", and it has become deep, and "ma'uqat" with "amaqah" and "mu'aqah", and it is a well of great depth.

[Page 145]

﴿That they may witness﴾ is connected to ﴿they will come to you﴾. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be connected to ﴿proclaim﴾. That is, to be present ﴿benefits﴾ of great importance and great number. Its indefiniteness, though it has no tanwin, indicates magnitude and abundance. It may also be indefinite for classification, meaning a kind of benefits, both religious and worldly. Generalizing the benefits so that they include both types is the view of a group, and it is related from Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him that he said about the verse: "Benefits in this world and benefits in the Hereafter. As for the benefits of the Hereafter, they are the good pleasure of God Most High. As for the benefits of this world, they are what they obtain of the flesh of the camels on that day, the slaughtered animals, and trade." Mujahid restricted the worldly benefits to trade, which is permissible for the pilgrim without disapproval if it is not the purpose of the journey. It has been objected that their calling and summoning to that is improbable, but there is room for discussion. Moreover, this only works according to what Abu al-Baqa' permitted. It is related from al-Baqir, may God be pleased with him, that the benefits are restricted to the otherworldly ones. In another narration from Ibn 'Abbas they are restricted to the worldly ones, but generalization is preferable. ( ﻟﻬﻢ ) is in the position of a qualifier for ﴿benefits﴾, meaning benefits belonging to them. ﴿And mention the name of God﴾ at the slaughter, ﴿on known days﴾, that is, specified days, which are the days of sacrifice (al-nahr), as held by a group including Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, may God have mercy on them both. Their number is three days: the day of the festival and two days after it, according to us, and according to al-Thawri, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, based on what is related from 'Umar, 'Ali, Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, Anas, and Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with them all, that they said: "The days of sacrifice are three, the best of them being the first." They said this by transmission, because reasoning cannot arrive at such measures. In the reports relied upon there is contradiction, so we adopted what is certain, which is the lesser number. Al-Shafi'i, al-Hasan, and 'Ata' said: four days, the day of the festival and three after it, based on his saying ﷺ: "All the days of tashriq (the days after the festival) are days of slaughter." According to al-Nakha'i, the time of sacrifice is two days; according to Ibn Sirin, one day; according to Abu Salamah and Sulayman ibn Yasar, the sacrifice extends to the new moon of Muharram. We have not found any reliable basis for that. It has been argued from the mention of days that slaughtering is not permitted at night. Abu Hayyan said: "This is the view of Malik and the people of opinion, end of quote." What is mentioned in the books of our companions is that slaughtering is permitted, but it is disliked because of the possibility of error in the darkness of the night.

As for the argument for non-permissibility from the mention of days, it is as you see. It has been said that the known days are the ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah, and this is the view of Abu Hanifah, may God have mercy on him. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Ibrahim, and Qatadah. Perhaps the intended meaning of mentioning His name according to this view is what has been said: His praise and thanks, may He be mighty and majestic. According to the first view, it is the words of the slaughterer: "In the name of God, and God is greatest," as related from Qatadah. It is mentioned that one also says with that: "O God, from You and to You, on behalf of so-and-so." Another view will come, God willing. It was preferred that it means thanks, because it is more suitable to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿over what He has provided them of the beast of livestock﴾. Al-Zamakhshari chose that the mention is over the beast of livestock, or in general, which is what the apparent wording of some of them implies, as a metonymy for slaughter. He mentioned that by this it indicates the primary purpose of slaughter and what distinguishes it from customs. He also hinted that all the rites of pilgrimage were legislated for the remembrance of God. It was also said that ﴿over what He has provided them﴾ to its end is an expression of eagerness regarding drawing near through the beast of livestock, meaning camels, cattle, sheep, and goats, to the Provider, and an easing for them in spending, along with the generality and detail that it contains. The temporal sense of the known days, on the view that they are the ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah, is for the slaughter, in consideration that the day of slaughter is among them. Something similar may be said on the assumption that the mention is restricted to what is understood from it. ﴿So eat from them﴾: a shift to address, and the fa' is eloquent, meaning:
[Page 146]
mention the name of God Most High over your sacrifices, then eat from their flesh. The command is for permission, based on the premise that eating was previously prohibited by law. They have said that a command after a prohibition implies permission. The prior prohibition is indicated by his saying, may God Most High bless him and grant him peace: "I had forbidden you from eating the flesh of the sacrificial animals, so eat from them and store (them)." It was also said that this is because the people of the Jahiliyyah used to consider it sinful, or that it is recommended, to show solidarity with the poor and to equalize them in eating from it. According to what al-Khafaji said, this is the view of Abu Hanifah, may God Most High be pleased with him.

﴿And feed the distressed﴾, that is, one who has been struck by distress (bu's), meaning hardship. It is related from Mujahid and 'Ikrimah that it is explained as the one who extends his hands to people asking. ﴿The poor﴾, that is, the needy. The command is for recommendation according to Imam 'Ali, also mentioned by al-Khafaji. It is recommended, as in the Hidayah (a Hanafi legal work), that what one feeds not fall below a third, because the purposes are eating and feeding, established by the verse, and storing, established by the hadith. So the udhiyah (sacrificial animal) is divided among them into thirds. Some have said there is no limit regarding what is eaten or fed, because the verse is unrestricted. The Shafi'is required feeding, and a group held that eating from the udhiyah is also obligatory. Restricting feeding to the distressed poor does not negate the permissibility of feeding the wealthy. Permissibility may be derived from the first command, since it indicates the permissibility of the slaughterer eating. And if it is permissible for him to eat while he is wealthy, it is permissible for him to feed a wealthy person.

﴿Then let them end their state of neglect (tafath)﴾. In its basic sense, *tafath* means dirt and filth. Qutrub reported that a man's *tafath* increases when his dirt accumulates during travel. Abu Muhammad al-Basri said that *tafath* derives from *taff*, which means the dirt under the nails, and that the *f* was changed to *th*, as in *mughthur*. A group of scholars here interpreted *tafath* as hair, extra nails, and similar things. *Qada'* (fulfilling, ending) originally means cutting off and separating. It is used here figuratively to mean removal, that is, ﴿let them remove that by clipping their nails, trimming their moustaches and sideburns﴾, as in a report from Ibn Abbas, ﴿plucking the armpit hair, shaving the head, and removing the pubic hair﴾. It is also said that *qada'* is the opposite of *ada'* (performing), and the sentence contains an omitted noun: ﴿let them fulfil the removal of their tafath﴾. The expression is used because, once the time for removing it has passed, the act is regarded as a making-up of what was missed.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with them) that he said: "Tafath is all of the rites (nusuk): the standing at Arafat, the running between al-Safa and al-Marwah, and the stoning of the pillars." On this view, *qada'* means *ada'* (performance), as if it were said: ﴿then let them perform their rites﴾. The rites are called *tafath* because the pilgrims are, until they leave the state of ihram, dishevelled and dusty. This is as you see. It may also be said that what is meant by removing the *tafath*, in the earlier sense, is the fulfilling of all the rites, since these cannot be completed except after it. So the fulfilling of the *tafath* is, by a kind of metaphorical extension, the fulfilling of all the rites. This is supported by what Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) reported, that he said: "The fulfilling of the *tafath* is the fulfilling of all the rites."

﴿And let them fulfil their vows﴾. These are the acts of righteousness that they vow during their pilgrimage. Ibn Abbas restricted this to what they vow concerning the slaughter of camels. Ikrimah said that it refers to the obligatory elements of the Hajj. Mujahid said it refers to what is obligatory of the Hajj and the sacrificial offering, and to anything a person vows that relates to the pilgrimage. Thus *nadhr* is used metaphorically in the sense of "obligation" in general. Shu'bah, reading from Asim, recited *"wal-yuwaffu"* with a doubled *waw*.

﴿And let them circumambulate﴾ the House of the *tawaf al-ifadah*, which is the circumambulation of visitation (*tawaf al-ziyarah*), one of the pillars of the Hajj, by which the complete exit from the state of ihram is achieved. It is the companion of the fulfilling of the *tafath* in the earlier sense. This was narrated from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak and a group of others. Al-Tabari even said, though this is not accepted for him: "There is no disagreement among the interpreters that it is the *tawaf al-ifadah*, and that this takes place on the Day of Sacrifice." It has also been said that it is the *tawaf al-sadr*, which is the farewell circumambulation, and there is disagreement regarding a number of the rites.

﴿By the Ancient House﴾. Al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh*, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it *hasan*, al-Hakim, who graded it *sahih*, Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani and others reported from Ibn al-Zubayr, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah named the House *'Ateeq* (ancient, freed) only because He freed it from the tyrants, so no tyrant ever prevailed over it." This view was held by Ibn Abi Najih and Qatadah. Tubba' had intended to demolish it, but he was struck with paralysis, and he was advised to desist from it. It was also said that it has a Lord who protects it, so he left it, clothed it, and he was the first to clothe it. Abrahah intended it and suffered what he suffered. As for al-Hajjaj, he did not intend to take control of the House, but Ibn al-Zubayr took refuge in it, and al-Hajjaj devised a way to force him out, and then rebuilt it. Perhaps what happened at the hands of the Qaramitah, even though they took the Black Stone and it remained with them for years, is of this kind. And it is said, regarding what will happen at the end of time, of the demolition of it by the Abyssinians and the throwing of its stones into the sea, if that is authentic, that it is one of the signs of the Hour, and it does not constitute a refutation of the matters that have been said to be consistent. It has also been said that the answer is other than this.

It was reported from Mujahid that it was named so because its site was never owned by anyone. In another report from him, it was named so because it was freed from drowning at the time of the Flood. Ibn Jubayr said that *'atiq* means "excellent," from the expression "noble horses" (*'ita q al-khayl*) and "noble birds" (*'ita q al-tayr*). It has also been said that it is in the form *fa'il* in the sense of *mufʿil*, that is, "one who frees the necks of sinners." The attribution of freeing to it is metaphorical, since Allah, exalted is He, frees their necks through circumambulating it. Al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd said: "*'Ateeq* means ancient, for it was the first house established for the people." This is the more apparent meaning, but you know that when the hadith is authentic, one should not depart from it. Furthermore, its protection from tyrants and its remaining, for a long time, as something revered, to which people come from every deep ravine, is by the sheer will of Allah, exalted is He, which is based upon dazzling wisdoms.

Some of the atheists claimed that it was built under the ascendancy of Saturn, with the ascending sign being Aquarius, one of its two houses. He had good debates on this, and so this required its protection from tyrants and its remaining revered for a long time. They call it for this reason "the House of Saturn." They have gone far astray in this. Allah willing, we will explain most fully the error of whoever holds that the ascending sign has influence. And Allah, exalted is He, is the One sought for help.

[Page 147]

**"That"**: meaning "the matter." This and similar demonstratives are used to mark a break between two statements, or between two aspects of one statement. The best-known use is in His saying, ﴿This! And indeed, for the transgressors is an evil place of return﴾ [38:55]. Likewise is the verse of Zuhayr, who had earlier described Harim's generosity and courage:

*"This! He is not like one who is unable to speak his speech in the midst of the assembly, when any speaker speaks."*

The choice of *dhalika* here signifies the magnitude of the matter and the loftiness of its rank. It is a form of *iqtidab* (abrupt transition), close to *takhallus* (the smooth transition between themes), because what follows fits what precedes. It has also been said that it is in the accusative position, governed by a deleted verb, meaning: "Comply with that." ﴿And whoever honours the sacred rites of Allah﴾: *Hurumat* is the plural of *hurmah*, which is that which is sacred in the Law. By it is meant all the obligations, including the rites of the Hajj and others. Honouring them means knowing that they must be observed and acting accordingly. A group said: they are what He has commanded of the rites. From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, it is reported that they are all the prohibitions of the Hajj: obscenity, disputing, sexual intercourse and hunting. Honouring them means not even approaching them. From Ibn Zayd it is reported that they are five: the Sacred Monument (al-Mash'ar al-Haram), the Sacred Mosque, the Sacred House, the Sacred Month, and the forbidden ones until one has been released from the state of consecration. ﴿Then it is better for him﴾, that is, then honouring them is better for him than other things, on the basis that *khayr* is an elative (*ism tafdil*, comparative/superlative form). Abu Hayyan said: "It is apparent that it is not meant as a comparison, so there is no need to supply a complement." The meaning of its being better for him ﴿with his Lord﴾ is that he will be rewarded for it on the Day of Resurrection. The mention of the title of Lordship together with the pronoun referring back to *man* (whoever) is to honour him and to indicate the reason for the ruling.

﴿And the grazing livestock has been made lawful for you﴾: that is, slaughtering them and eating them, because their essence is not described as lawful or unlawful. By them is meant the eight pairs in general. His saying, ﴿except what is recited to you﴾, that is, except what is recited to you as the verse forbidding it, is an *istithna' muttasil* (connected exception), as most have chosen, on the basis that *ma* refers to what is forbidden of them for an external cause, such as carrion and that over which the name of other than Allah has been invoked. It has been allowed that the exception is *munqati'* (disconnected), on the basis that *ma* refers to what is forbidden in His saying, ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ [5:3] and the rest of the verse, which includes things that are not of the type of livestock. In both cases the verb was not meant to refer to the future, because the recitation of the verse of prohibition came earlier. It is as if the use of the present tense was to bring the past scene to mind, for greater emphasis. It has also been said that the use of the present tense indicates a continuous, renewing state, which suits the context. The clause is a parenthetical insertion that confirms what preceded it, the command to eat and to feed others, and removes what might be suspected, namely that the state of ihram forbids this just as it forbids hunting. ﴿So avoid the filth﴾, that is, the foul thing, ﴿of the idols﴾, that is, which consists of idols, on the basis that *min* is explanatory (*bayaniyya*).

Defining *al-rijs* (the filth) with the generic *lam* (*lam al-jins*), together with the indefiniteness and the specification, and making the avoidance fall on the thing itself rather than on the worship of it, carries a clear emphasis in repelling people from worshipping them. It has been said that *min* is for the starting point (*ibtida' al-ghaya*), as if He commanded them to avoid filth in general, then specified for them its source from which it reaches them, since idol-worship encompasses every corruption and filth. In al-Bahr it is said that *min* may be partitive (*tab'idiyya*), meaning by the filth the worship of idols. This has been related from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jurayj, as if it were said: "Avoid, from among the idols, the filth, which is the worship, because what is forbidden of them is only the worship." Do you not see that it is conceivable to use an idol for building and other things that the Law has not forbidden? So the idol has aspects, one of which is worshipping it, which is what one is commanded to avoid, and worshipping it is only one of its aspects. Therefore Ibn 'Atiyya's statement, that whoever makes *min* partitive has reversed the meaning and corrupted it, is not appropriate. End of quote. There is no hiding the unnecessary strain in both readings, the starting-point and the partitive. There is another possibility here, which you will learn, with what is in it, God willing, shortly. The *fa'* (then) indicates that what follows is the consequence of what is implied by His saying, ﴿And whoever honours﴾ and so on, namely the obligation to observe the sacred things and to avoid violating them.

It has been mentioned that with the exception the transition to this was made gracefully, and this is the secret of not taking the livestock to mean only the known sacrificial animals and offerings, so that the exception is not needed, since there is nothing among them that is forbidden for an external cause. It is as if it were said: "Whoever honours the sacred things of Allah, it is better for him. The livestock are not among the sacred things, for they are lawful to you, except what is recited to you as the verse forbidding it, for that is among what must be avoided. So avoid what is the greatest of the matters that must be avoided, which is the worship of idols." It has also been said: the apparent meaning is that what follows the *fa'* is a consequence of His saying, ﴿The grazing livestock has been made lawful for you﴾, for that is a great blessing that calls for thanks to Allah, not disbelief and association. Indeed, it is not far-fetched that the meaning is: "Avoid the filth for the sake of the idols," with *min* being causal (*sababiyya*). This specifies what was invoked with the name of other than Allah, singling it out by mention, and so it follows from His saying, ﴿except what is recited﴾. This is supported by His saying later, ﴿Turning to Him as those who associate none with Him﴾, for if it is taken to mean what they had taken it to mean, it would be a repetition. End of quote. Regarding what he claimed was apparent, it was objected that the lawfulness of the livestock, though among the great blessings, is among the legal matters rather than the external proofs by which monotheism and the invalidity of association are known. So it is not fitting to consider the avoidance of idols as a consequence of it. As for his claim that it is not far-fetched, it is very far-fetched, and denying this is obstinacy. So reflect.

His saying, ﴿And avoid the saying of falsehood﴾, is a generalization after a specification, for the worship of idols is the head of falsehood, since it involves claiming a right that does not exist. As if He, when He urged the honouring of the sacred things, followed that with what refutes what the unbelievers were upon, namely prohibiting the *bahira* and *sa'iba* and the like, and inventing lies against Allah, claiming that He had ruled such things. He did not conjoin "the saying of falsehood" to "the filth" but repeated the governing verb for greater emphasis. By falsehood (*zur*) is meant any lie in general, and it is from *zur* in the sense of deviation, for a lie deviates from reality. The construction is explanatory (*idafa bayaniyya*). It has also been said that it is a command to avoid false testimony, based on what Ahmad, Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah, al-Tabarani and others related from Ibn Mas'ud: "The Prophet ﷺ prayed the dawn prayer, and when he finished, while standing, he said: 'False testimony is equal to associating partners with Allah,' three times. Then he recited this verse."

It has been objected that there is no explicit text in the report mentioned, along with what is in its chain in some routes of disputed reliability, to restrict the verse to this, since the verse may remain general and its recitation is for including this within it. Ibn Abi Hatim related from Muqatil that he said: "By the saying of falsehood is meant associating partners in speech. That is because they used to circumambulate the House and in their talbiyah would say: 'Here I am, O Allah, You have no partner, except a partner who is Yours, You own him and what he owns.'" This is a view of restriction. It is not hidden that generalization, or including this within it, though it suits the context, is like restricting it to some of them, saying this about the unbelievers' statement: "This is lawful and this is forbidden."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 31:

﴿Ḥunafāʾa lillāh﴾ [inclining towards God, turning away from every deviant religion towards the true religion, sincere to Him, exalted is He] ﴿ghayra mushrikīna bihi﴾ [not associating anything with Him], i.e., anything of things, so the idols enter into that by primary inclusion. These two are emphatic circumstantial clauses (ḥālān muʾakkidatān) from the waw of ﴿fa-jtanibū﴾ [so shun]. It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause from the waw of (wa-jtanibū), and the disavowal has been delayed after the turning away so that it connects with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever associates others with God, it is as if he had fallen from the sky﴾, which is a new (independent) sentence emphasising what precedes it of shunning association. The manifestation of the noble Name is to show the complete ugliness of association. Faith has been likened to the sky for its loftiness, and association to falling from it. So the associator has fallen from the peak of faith to the abyss of the disbelievers. If this falling concerns the apostate, its outward meaning is clear; and as for others, it is by consideration of the natural disposition (fiṭrah), and placing capability and strength in the position of the act, as was said regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their protectors are the Ṭāghūt, who bring them out of the light into the darkness﴾ [al-Baqarah: 257]. ﴿Then the bird snatches him away﴾, for the destructive desires scatter his thoughts. In this is a comparison of the scattered thoughts to the snatching of the talons of birds, and it is taken from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿God presents an example: a man in whom are partners at odds with one another﴾ [al-Zumar: 29]. The origin of khaṭf (snatching) is swift seizure.

Nāfiʿ read «﴿fa-takhṭafuhu﴾» with a fatḥah on the kha' and a shaddah on the ṭāʾ. Al-Ḥasan, Abū Rajāʾ and al-Aʿmash read «﴿fa-takhṭafuhu﴾» with a kasrah on the tāʾ, the kha' and the ṭāʾ with a shaddah. From al-Ḥasan also is the same, except that he put a fatḥah on the ṭāʾ with a shaddah. Al-Aʿmash also read «takhṭafuhu» without the fāʾ, with a sukūn on the kha' and a fatḥah on the ṭāʾ without a shaddah, and the sentence in this reading is in the place of a circumstantial clause. As for the first readings, the fāʾ is for coordination, and what follows it is coordinated upon ﴿kharra﴾ (fell). The choice of the present tense indicates the bringing to mind of that wondrous state in the sight of the addressee, to astonish him. Abū al-Baqāʾ permitted that the speech be by estimation "fa-huwa yakhṭafuhu", and the coordination is from coordinating a sentence upon a sentence. ﴿Or the wind carries him off﴾, i.e., drops him and hurls him. Abū Jaʿfar and Abū Rajāʾ read «al-riyāḥu» (the winds). ﴿To a far-off place﴾, distant, for the Satan has cast him far astray into error. In this is a comparison of the misleading Satan to the blowing wind, and it is taken from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen that We sent the devils upon the disbelievers, inciting them with incitement?﴾ [Maryam: 83]. So the comparison in the verse is divided (mufarriq).

The apparent view is that (tahwī) is coordinated upon «takhṭafu», and "aw" is for division, in the sense that his destruction is either a desire by which he is scattered in the valleys of loss, or a devil who casts him far into the wilderness of ruin. There is a difference between a passing thought of the soul and the devil, so what Ibn al-Munīr said is not objectionable, that thoughts are among the results of the whisperings of the devil, since the verse was brought to make them two things. In the Tafsir of al-Qadi, it is for choice, in the sense that you are free to liken the associator to one who fell from the sky and the birds snatched him, or to one who fell from the sky and the wind carried him from a far place. Or it is for variety, in the sense that the likened-to is of two kinds: the likened-to of the first kind, whose flesh is distributed in the bellies of the birds of prey, is the associator from whom there is no deliverance from association and no salvation at all; and the likened-to of the second kind, whom the wind hurled into the pits, is the associator whose deliverance is hoped for after a long time. Ibn al-Munīr said: The disbeliever is only of two kinds. The wavering one, constantly in doubt and not firm upon one misguidance; this is likened to one whom the birds snatched and scattered, so that whenever a bird seizes a piece of him, another takes it from it; and this is the state of the wavering one, who, whenever any imagining appears to him, follows it and leaves what he was upon. And the associator firmly resolved upon a false creed, who, even if he were sawn with saws, would not turn back nor return; there is no way to make him doubt, and no hope of moving him from what he is upon. He is joyful and delighted in his misguidance. This is likened, in his firm settlement upon disbelief, to the settling of one whom the wind has carried down to a lowest valley, the furthest of places from the sky, where he settled. End of quotation. And it is not hidden that what we have mentioned is more in accord with the apparent meaning.

Many have permitted that it be one of the compound (murakkabah) comparisons, so that it is as if He, glorified is He, said: whoever associates with God has destroyed himself with a destruction beyond which there is none, in that his state is depicted in the form of the state of one who fell from the sky, and the birds snatched him so that he was scattered into pieces in their crops, or the wind swept him until it dropped him in some far-off places. In al-Kashshaf, it was made that for this, "aw" is for choice, and it is not definitively so as far as appears. In both cases, the separation and composition of the comparison in the verse are two comparisons.

Al-Ṭībī mentioned that in it, on the compound reading, there are two comparisons, with (tahwī) coordinated upon (kharra); and on the separated reading, one comparison, with (tahwī) coordinated upon «takhṭafu». He claimed that the wording of al-Kashshaf indicates this, and this is not conceded.

﴿That﴾: meaning the matter is that, or comply with that. ﴿And whoever glorifies the sha'a'ir (rites and symbols) of Allah﴾: meaning the budn (camels brought as sacrificial offerings), as related from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and a group. Sha'a'ir is the plural of sha'ira or sha'ara, meaning a sign, like shi'ar. It was applied to the budn (sacrificial camels) because they are among the markers of the Hajj (pilgrimage), or signs of Allah's obedience and guidance.

Al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said: "Because they are made known (tush'aru), i.e., marked, by drawing blood from them with a sha'ira, i.e., an iron blade by which they are marked." The annexation (idafa) in the three possibilities is not obscure. Glorifying them means choosing them beautiful, fat, and of high price. It is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) sent one hundred camels as offerings, among them a camel for Abu Jahl with a gold ring in its nose. And it is related from 'Umar that he offered a noble camel which was requested from him for three hundred dinars, and he asked the Prophet (ﷺ) to let him sell it and buy sacrificial camels with its price, but he forbade him and said: "Rather, offer it." Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, used to drive sacrificial camels draped with cloth, and would give their meat and their coverings in charity. Zayd ibn Aslam said: "The sha'a'ir are six: al-Safa and al-Marwa, the budn, the jimar, the Masjid al-Haram, 'Arafat, and the Rukn. Glorifying them is completing what is done with them." Ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan, Malik and Ibn Zayd said: "The sha'a'ir are all the places of Hajj: Mina, 'Arafat, Muzdalifa, al-Safa and al-Marwa, the House, and other than these," and this is similar to Zayd's statement.

It was said: they are the laws (shara'i') of His religion, and glorifying them is adhering to them. The majority hold the first view, which is more suitable to what follows. ﴿Whoever (man)﴾ is either conditional or relative. In both cases, in His saying ﴿indeed it is from the piety of hearts﴾, there must be a pronoun returning to it, or something standing in its place. It was said that the estimated phrase is: "indeed their glorifying, etc." The glorifying is a verbal noun (masdar) annexed to its object, and it must have an agent, which can only be a pronoun returning to ﴿whoever﴾. So it is as if it were said: "indeed his glorifying of them." ﴿Min (from)﴾ may be causal, i.e., "indeed their glorifying is for the sake of the piety of hearts," or it may indicate the starting point, i.e., "indeed their glorifying arises from the piety of hearts." Estimating this annexed word (muḍaf) is necessary according to what has been said, since the sha'a'ir themselves cannot truthfully be described as being from piety in any sense.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "The estimate is: indeed their glorifying is from the actions of one of the piety of hearts, so these annexed words are omitted. The meaning is not sound except by estimating them, because there must be a returning pronoun from the answer (jaza') to ﴿whoever﴾ to link it." End of his quote.

Abu Hayyan criticised this: what he estimated is devoid of a returning pronoun to ﴿whoever﴾. Therefore, those who followed his path in estimating the annexed words before the estimate said: "indeed their glorifying is from him, from the actions, etc.," or "indeed their glorifying is from the actions of those of the piety of hearts among them," and so they brought a genitive pronoun returning to ﴿whoever﴾ at the end of the speech or within it. Some who took that path did not estimate "from him" or "from them," but committed to making the lam in ﴿the hearts﴾ a substitute for the pronoun annexed to it, according to the view of the Kufans, to serve as the link, i.e., "the piety of their hearts."

Al-Damamini made the link in al-Zamakhshari's estimate the agent (fa'il) of the omitted verbal noun, since the meaning is understood. So what he estimated is not devoid of a returning pronoun to ﴿whoever﴾, as Abu Hayyan claimed, because what is understood but omitted is like what is stated.

The author of al-Kashf (Sahib al-Kashf) also defended him, saying: "He meant that according to what he estimated, the generality of those of the piety of hearts takes the place of the pronoun. So estimating 'from him' as al-Baydawi did is not the correct approach." The author of al-Taqrib (Sahib al-Taqrib) objected to estimating the last two annexed words, i.e., "actions" and "those of," saying that this is only needed if ﴿min﴾ is taken as partitive; but if it is taken to indicate the starting point, it is not needed, because the meaning then is "indeed their glorifying arises from the piety of hearts," which is one of the two views you heard first.

The author of al-Kashf did not accept this, saying: "The estimate of 'actions' is because the meaning is that glorification is a branch (bab) of piety, and among its greatest branches, not that glorification proceeds from one who possesses piety. From this it appears that taking it to mean that glorification arises from the piety of hearts..." and then the objection that al-Zamakhshari's statement, "it is only sound if taken as partitive," is not as it should be. Moreover, if the piety is taken to include actions and abstentions according to the Shari'a usage, then glorification is definitely a part of it; but if piety is restricted to abstentions, the origin of glorification from them is not evident except by metaphor (tajawwuz). End of his statement.

It was objected that his claim, that the meaning is "glorification is a branch of piety" and not "glorification proceeds from one with piety," is a claim without proof; that the indication that it is among the greatest branches is not evident as he mentioned; that the view that no estimate is needed if glorification is a part is a compromise that the opponent would not accept; and that if the speech is sound by metaphor, al-Zamakhshari's statement "it does not stand" does not hold.

It was answered that this objection is not valid. As for the first point, the context is an exhortation to glorify the sha'a'ir, which requires counting it as piety, indeed among its greatest parts; and its arising from piety does not require that it be part of it, and may even suggest otherwise. As for the second point, the indication of its greatness is understood from the context, as when you say: "This is among the actions of the righteous, pardon is among the traits of the noble, and wronging is among the traits of base souls," as taste itself attests. As for the third point, he did not claim that no estimate is needed if glorification is a part; rather, he says the link is generality, as he said at first. As for the fourth point, the soundness of the speech without estimate by metaphor is because it is hidden, close to error, since there is no indicator for it; partition is what comes to mind, so there is no objection except to the view of the objector.

I say: It is not hidden that the less the estimate, the better. Thus the view of one who says "the estimate is: indeed their glorifying is from the piety of hearts" is better than the view of one who says "the estimate is: indeed their glorifying is from the actions of those who possess the piety of hearts." Here ﴿min﴾ is partitive. What the context requires, namely exalting this glorification, is understood from making it a part of the piety of hearts. This is based on the premise that restricting piety to the hearts indicates that piety is of two kinds: piety of the hearts, meaning the true, sincere piety with which the sincere believer is characterized; and piety of the limbs, meaning the false, outward piety with which the hypocrite is characterized, whose limbs often humble themselves while his heart is heedless and distracted. This structure is most similar to the saying: "Pardon is among the traits of the noble." So, when it is understood from it that pardon is among the greatest branches of noble traits, it should likewise be understood that glorification is among the greatest branches of piety, and the distinction is arbitrary. Perhaps making the annexation (to hearts) is for this indication is better than making it because the hearts are the source of piety and wickedness and that which commands them both, so reflect.

Some people did not require the estimate of glorification, and returned the pronoun in ﴿indeed it﴾ to the sanctity (hurma) or the quality (khasla), as was said in a similar way regarding His saying (ﷺ): "Whoever performs ablution on Friday, then by it (the sunna is fulfilled) and it is good." Or they returned it to a feminine verbal noun understood from ﴿glorifies﴾, i.e., the glorification (ta'zima).

This was objected to: the verbal noun contained in the verb is not made feminine unless its feminine form is well known, like rahma (mercy), and this is not the case here, so it is open to consideration.

Yes, taking this into account is something that sound taste does not relish, and from it one can know the situation regarding considering the glorifications in the plural form. Moreover, it was said against it that it implies a single glorification is not part of piety. This is not removed by saying that there is no consideration of what is implied, or that it is plural against plural, as is not hidden.

If the Kufan view regarding the lam in ﴿the hearts﴾ is considered, then no estimate at all is needed in the verse. Some of the eminent scholars held that the answer (jaza') is omitted, its estimate being "so they are truly pious," because the causal clause standing in its place indicates it. It was objected that omission goes against the original, and what has been mentioned is suitable to be an answer by way of information and announcement, as is known in similar cases. And you know that this estimate comes to mind, and the like of it is abundant in the Glorious Book.

﴿The hearts﴾ was read in the nominative (al-qulubu), as the agent of the verbal noun which is ﴿piety﴾. The Shi'a, and those who follow their path, used this verse as evidence for the legitimacy of glorifying the graves of the imams and other righteous people by lighting lamps over them, hanging objects made of gold and silver, and similar things, with which they surpass the worshippers of idols. And what is in this is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 33:

﴿For you therein﴾ means: in the rites (sha'a'ir) in the sense previously mentioned, ﴿there are benefits﴾, namely their milk, their offspring, their wool, and riding on their backs, ﴿until a specified term﴾, which is the time when one designates them and makes them an offering (hady, a sacrificial animal). From that point on, the owner has no share in their benefits. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas (ra) in a narration from Miqsam, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Dahhak. It is also the view of Imam Abu Hanifa, for the one who offers the hady, according to him, after designating and making it obligatory, does not own its benefits at all, because if he owned them it would be permissible for him to hire it out for riding, and it is agreed that this is not permitted for him. However, he may benefit from it in cases of necessity. On this is understood what is narrated from Abu Hurayrah (ra): "The Prophet (ﷺ) passed by a man who was driving his hady while he was on a campaign (jihad). He (ﷺ) said: 'Ride it.' The man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, it is a hady.' He (ﷺ) said: 'Ride it, woe to you.'"

ʿAta' said: the benefits of the offerings after they have been made obligatory and designated as hady are that they may be ridden and their milk drunk when there is need, until a specified term, which is the time they are slaughtered. Al-Shafiʿi (rh) took this view, and on it is based what is narrated from Jabir (ra) that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Ride the hady in a reasonable manner until you find a mount."

An objection to the previous view has been raised: the mawla (freed slave) of an umm walad (a slave woman who has borne her master's child) owns the right to benefit from her, yet he may not sell her. So why should it not be the case that the hady is similar: the one who offers it does not own the right to sell or hire it out, but does own the right to benefit from it in other ways?

It has also been said that the specified term is the time when it is marked (ishʿar), so that it may not be ridden at that time except in cases of necessity.

Abu Razin narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that the specified term is the time of departure from Makkah. In another narration from him, it is the time of departure and moving away from these rites to others. It has also been said that the specified term is the Day of Resurrection, but its weakness is evident.

﴿Then their place of sacrifice﴾ means: the obligation of slaughtering them, with maḥall being a mīmī verbal noun meaning "obligation," from ḥalla al-dayn (the debt became due) when it became obligatory; or the time of their slaughter, with maḥall being a noun of time. On both possibilities, it is conjoined with "benefits," and the sentence has an elided modifier (muḍāf) in its construction.

Page 153

The words of the Exalted: ﴿to the Ancient House﴾ are in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: ending at the House. By "the House" is meant what is adjacent to it, by the relation of nearness (ʿalāqat al-mujāwara), for they do not end at the House itself but at what is near to it. Mina has been made a place of sacrifice, and in the hadith: "All the paths of Makkah are a place of sacrifice, and all the paths of Mina are a place of sacrifice." Al-Qaffal said: this applies to the offerings that reach Mina. As for a voluntary hady that is disabled before reaching Makkah, its place of sacrifice is the place where it is. The Imamiyyah said: the place of sacrifice for the hady of Hajj is Mina, and the place of sacrifice for the hady of the single ʿUmrah is Makkah, opposite the Kaʿbah, at al-Hazwarah.

﴿Then﴾ (thumma) indicates a temporal or rank-based sequence, meaning: for you therein are worldly benefits until a specified term, and after that there is for you a religious benefit that brings about the reward of the Hereafter, which is the obligation of slaughtering them, or the time of their slaughter. In this there is an emphasis on the slaughter itself being a benefit. The sequence of rank is evident, while the temporal sequence is understood in reference to the first moment of its occurrence, so do not be heedless of this.

On the view that the rites (sha'a'ir) refers to the places of Hajj, the meaning is: for you in those places there are benefits, through the reward and recompense gained by performing what must be performed in them, until a specified term, which is the end of the days of Hajj. Then their place of sacrifice, that is the place where people leave their ihram (state of consecration), is to the Ancient House, meaning it ends there, by circling it in the Tawaf al-Ziyarah on the Day of Sacrifice after performing what is required in those places. Thus the attribution of the place to them is due to the slightest connection. Something similar is narrated from Malik in the Muwatta. Or: for you in them are the benefits of trade in the markets until the time of returning, then the time of leaving them, ending at the Kaʿbah by exiting ihram through the Tawaf al-Ziyarah. Or: for you are worldly and otherworldly benefits until the time of returning, etc. The same applies according to what is narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam, that it is specific to the six (days or matters).

On the view that the rites refers to the laws of the religion: for you in observing them are worldly and otherworldly benefits until the cessation of obligation. Then their place, to which they are conveyed when observed, ends at the Ancient House, which is Paradise. Or the place of their observance ends at the Ancient House, which is a sanctuary of the angels (peace be upon them). Its being the终 point is because deeds are raised to it. It has also been said that the place of their observance ending at the Ancient House means the Kaʿbah, as is the most apparent meaning, in view of the fact that the place of some of them, such as prayer and Hajj, ends at that. It has also been said: other than that. All of these are things that should not be attributed to the speech of even the least of people, let alone the speech of the Lord of the Worlds. The least objectionable of what has been said is that the discussion of those narrations is connected to the words of the Exalted: ﴿and cattle were made lawful for you﴾, and the pronoun in ﴿therein﴾ refers to them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 34:

﴿For every community We have appointed a rite (mansak)﴾ is conjoined to His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿Therein you have benefits﴾, or to His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And whoever honours﴾, etc., and what lies between them is a parenthetical objection to what has been said. You, I think, prefer the first, and the complete discussion of it will come, God willing, at the parallel verse. The mansak (the place of ritual devotion, or the ritual act itself, the noun of place or the verbal noun, respectively) is the place of nusuk (ritual sacrifice and worship) when it is a noun of place, or the nusuk itself when it is a verbal noun. Mujahid interpreted it here as slaughtering and shedding blood in order to draw near to God, so he took it as a verbal noun, and nusuk was understood as a specific act of worship. This is one of its usages, although originally it means worship in general, and it became common in the acts of the Hajj. Al-Farra' said: in the speech of the Arabs, the mansak is the customary place for good and righteousness, and he interpreted it here as the festival (ʿid). Qatadah said: it is the Hajj. Ibn ʿArafah said: ﴿mansakan﴾ means a way (madhhab) of obedience to Him, exalted is He.

Al-Zamakhshari chose what was narrated from Mujahid, and it is the most fitting, namely that He prescribed for every religious community that they slaughter for Him, exalted is He, in order to draw near to Him, and not for anyone else among them. Thus the placing of the prepositional phrase before the verb indicates exclusivity. The two brothers (al-Akhawan), Ibn Sa'dan, Abu Hatim on the authority of Abu ʿAmr, Yunus, Mahbub and ʿAbd al-Warith read ﴿mansikan﴾ with a kasra on the sin. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: this is anomalous in this respect and is not permissible by analogy, and it is likely that al-Kisa'i heard it from the Arabs. Al-Azhari said: the fath and the kasr in it are two attested dialects, ﴿that they may mention the name of God﴾, specifically and to the exclusion of any other than Him, exalted is He, as both the context (siyaq) and the immediate sequence (sibaq) make clear. In restricting the prescribing (ja'l) to this purpose alone, there is an indication that the most important purpose of the legislation of the rite is His mention, mighty and majestic is He, ﴿over what He has provided them of the beast of the cattle﴾ at the time of slaughtering it. And in this there is an indication that the offering must be from the cattle, so it is not permissible with horses and the like. The fa' in His words, exalted is He, ﴿so your God is one God﴾, is said to be for causation, and what follows it is the cause for restricting the mention to the name of God, exalted is He. The fa' in His words, glorified is He, ﴿so to Him submit﴾, is for the ordering of what follows it, namely the command to submit, upon His oneness, mighty and majestic is He.
