It is also said that the first fa' is for the ordering of what follows upon what precedes it, too, for His making for every community a rite indicates His oneness, exalted is He. The difficulty in the way of this indication is not hidden, and some have strained to explain it by saying that the legislation of a rite for every community so that they may mention the name of God necessarily implies that He, glorified is He, is their God, lest it be folly, and from His being their God it follows that He, mighty and majestic is He, is one, for whoever does not single Himself out for divinity does not deserve divinity at all, since partnership is a deficiency. But this is as you see. In al-Kashf: since the reason for His words, glorified is He, ﴿For every community We have appointed a rite﴾ is the mention of His name over the rites, and it is known that mention is only true mention when the heart is in agreement with the tongue, and the mention of the heart is an indication of exaltation, His words, exalted is He, ﴿so to Him submit﴾ came as a consequence of it, a fine causal connection. It was objected that His words, exalted is He, ﴿so your God is one God﴾ is a parenthesis, because it affirms the command to sincerity, strengthens the cause with a powerful strengthening, and also affirms that the mention is what is intended by the legislation of the rite. End of quotation. This indicates that the first fa' is for parenthesis and the second fa' is for ordering. Perhaps what was mentioned first is the more evident. As for what has been said, that the first fa' is for causation and the thing caused is omitted, and the meaning is that the obligations differed according to the differences of times and persons because of the differences of benefits and not because of a plurality of gods, for your God is one God, then this is not what should be attributed to the sublime speech of God, as is not hidden. It was said: ﴿one God﴾ and not merely ﴿one﴾, because the purpose is to explain that He, exalted is He, is one in His essence just as He is one in His divinity. The placing of the prepositional phrase before the verb is for restriction. The meaning is: devote the mention to Him, exalted is He, exclusively, and make it purely and sincerely for His face, unmixed with any association.

﴿And give good tidings to the humble (al-mukhbitin)﴾: the address is to him, may God's blessings and peace be upon him. The mukhbitun are those who are at rest (al-mutma'innun), as narrated from Mujahid, or the humble (al-mutawadi'un), as narrated from al-Dahhak. ʿAmr ibn Aws said: they are those who do not wrong people, and when they are wronged they do not seek retribution. Sufyan said: they are those who are content with God's decree. Al-Kalbi said: they are those who strive in expression, and it derives from ikhbat, whose root, as al-Raghib said, is the descent into a khabt, which is the low-lying part of the land. The fitness of this image here is not hidden, insofar as the descent into a low-lying place is suitable for the pilgrim.

Al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on surah 22, verse 35:

﴿Those who, when Allah is mentioned, their hearts tremble﴾, i.e., fear [of Him] (khafat), ﴿their hearts﴾ from Him, Mighty and Majestic, due to the radiance of the rays of majesty upon them. ﴿And the patient ones over what afflicts them﴾ of the hardships of obligations and the burdens of calamities, such as illnesses, trials, and estrangement from homelands. The excellence of this placement here is also not hidden. It is apparent that patience over adversities in general is praiseworthy. Al-Razi said: "Patience is obligatory over what comes from Allah the Exalted; as for what comes from the oppressors, it is not obligatory, but rather it is obligatory to repel it for whoever is able to do so, even by fighting." End of quote. And there is consideration in this. ﴿And those who establish the prayer﴾ at its times. Perhaps the mention of this here is because travel is a context where one may fall short in establishing the prayer.

Al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and Abu 'Amr, in one narration, read "al-salata" (الصلاة) with the accusative, as the object of "muqimi" (مُقِيمِي), and the nun was dropped from it for lightness, as in the verse of the Kitab (Sibawayh's book):

*al-hafizu 'awrata al-'ashirati la ta'tihim min warã'ihim nutafu*

with "'awrata" in the accusative. A similar example is his saying:

*inna alladhi hanat bi-falj dima'uhum* ∗∗∗ *hum al-qawmu kulla al-qawmi ya umma Malik*

and his saying:

*ibnay Kulayb inna 'ammiya alladhã* ∗∗∗ *qatala al-muluka wa-fakkaka al-aghlala*

Ibn Mas'ud and al-A'mash read "wa-l-muqimina al-salata" (والمُقِيمِينَ الصَّلاةَ) with the nun retained and "al-salata" in the accusative, according to the original form. Al-Dahhak read "wa-l-muqima al-salati" (والمُقِيمَ الصَّلاةِ) in the singular and with the genitive construction.

﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾ in the ways of good. Among that is the giving of gifts in which they go to excess.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 36 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And the camels (budn), We have made for you among the symbols (sha'a'ir) of God﴾, meaning: among the markers of His religion that God has legislated. Budn is the plural of badana, which, as al-Jawhari said, is a she-camel or a cow that is slaughtered in Mecca. In al-Qamus it is said: it is of the camel and the cow, like the sacrificial animal (udhiyya) of the sheep, sent as an offering (tuhda) to Mecca, and it applies to both the male and the female. It was so named for the bulkiness of its body (li-'izami badaniha), because they used to fatten it and then send it as an offering. That it belongs to both kinds is the view of the majority of the lexicographers (a'immat al-lugha), and it is the position of the Hanafis. Thus, if someone vows to slaughter a badana, a cow suffices for him according to them, and this is the view of 'Ata' and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab. 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with them both, that the badana is only known as being of the camel and the cow.

In Sahih Muslim, from Jabir, may God be pleased with him: "We used to slaughter the badana on behalf of seven." It was said to him: "And the cow?" He said: "And is it anything but of the budn?" Sahib al-Bari' among the philologists said: it is not applied to what is of the cow. This was related from Mujahid and al-Hasan, and it is the position of the Shafi'is. Thus, according to them, one who vows to slaughter a badana does not satisfy his vow by slaughtering a cow. This is supported by what Abu Dawud related from Jabir, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The badana is on behalf of seven, and the cow is on behalf of seven." For the conjunction (al-'atf) implies difference (al-mughayara), and what comes later [in the commentary] also supports this. The apparent point is that the use of badana for what is of the camel is more frequent, although the ruling on sufficiency is the same.

Perhaps Jabir's meaning in his saying about the cow, "And is it anything but of the budn?", is that its ruling is the same as its ruling [i.e., the cow is equal in ruling]. Otherwise it would be far-fetched that the questioner was ignorant of the lexical meaning so that he would need to be refuted by this. As for what was related from Ibn 'Umar, it may be said that his intended meaning of budn there is the legally prescribed budn. Perhaps, if it is said that the word is shared between both kinds, custom or something similar decides the specification in the case where a person vows a badana. This is indicated by what Ibn Abi Shayba and 'Abd ibn Humayd related from Ya'qub al-Riyahi, from his father, who said: A man made me his executor and bequeathed a badana. So I came to Ibn 'Abbas and said to him: "A man has made me his executor and bequeathed a badana; would a cow suffice for me?" He said: "Yes." Then he said: "From which of your people is your companion?" I said: "From Riyah." He said: "Since when have the Banu Riyah acquired cows along with camels? Your companion has erred. Cows belong only to Asad and 'Abd al-Qays. So reflect."

Al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Shayba and 'Isa read «al-budun» with a damma on the ba' and the dal. It was said that this is the original form, like khushub and khashaba, and the sukun of the dal is a lightening of it. This reading was related from Nafi' and Abu Ja'far.

Ibn Abi Ishaq also read with a damma on the ba' and the dal and with shadda on the nun. This may be a single noun formed on the pattern fu'l, like 'utull, or the shadda may be from the doubling permitted in pausal form (waqf), with the connected form treated as the pausal form.

The majority read «al-budna» (البُدْنَ) in the accusative under the rule of the verb being omitted (al-ishtighal), i.e., "and We have made the camels — We have made them." It is also read in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence (al-ibtida'). God's words ﴿for you﴾ are an adverbial phrase (zarf) attached to the verb "made," and ﴿among the symbols of God﴾ is in the position of the second object of it. God's words ﴿in them is good for you﴾ mean: benefit in this world and reward in the Hereafter, as related from Ibn 'Abbas, while from al-Suddi, restricting it to the reward alone. It is a resumed sentence (jumla musta'nafa) confirming what precedes it.

﴿So mention the name of God over them﴾, by saying at the time of slaughtering them: "In the name of God, God is greatest. O God, from You and to You." Several related this from Ibn 'Abbas. In al-Bahr it is: that one says at the time of the nahr (throat-cutting): "God is greatest, there is no god but God, and God is greatest. O God, from You and to You."

﴿Standing in rows (sawaff)﴾, meaning standing, having arranged their forelegs and hind legs. It is the plural of saffa, and its object is omitted. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Baqir, Mujahid, Qatada, 'Ata', al-Kalbi and al-A'mash, with a variant from him, read «sawafin» with a nun, the plural of safin. This is either from safana al-rajulu when he joins his two feet together, so that it means sawaff, or from safana al-faras when the horse stands on three legs with the tip of the hoof of the fourth touching the ground. This is because at slaughter the badana has one of its forelegs tied, so that it stands on three. Tying it at the time of the throat-cutting is a sunna. Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that he saw a man who had made his badana kneel and was slaughtering it, and he said: "Make it stand, tied, the sunna of Muhammad (ﷺ)."

Most scholars hold that the left foreleg is tied. Ibn Abi Shayba related from Ibn Sabit, may God be pleased with him, that "the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions used to tie the left foreleg of the badana and slaughter it standing on what remained of its legs." He also related from al-Hasan that he was asked: "How is the badana slaughtered?" He said: "Its left foreleg is tied when it is intended to be slaughtered." Some scholars held that the right foreleg is tied. Ibn Abi Shayba also related from Ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with them both, that he used to slaughter it while its right foreleg was tied. It was also said that there is no difference between tying the left and tying the right. Ibn Abi Shayba also related from 'Ata', who said: "Tie whichever of the two forelegs you wish."

Several related from Ibn 'Umar that he explained ﴿standing in rows﴾ as "standing, with one of their forelegs tied." According to this, there is no difference at all in meaning between sawaff and sawafin. However, it was related from Mujahid that sawaff are on four legs and sawafin on three.

Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Zayd ibn Aslam, Shaqiq, Sulayman al-Taymi and al-A'raj read «sawafiya» with a ya', the plural of safiya, meaning "purely for the sake of God, Mighty and Majestic, with nothing associated with them, as the pre-Islamic people used to associate." 'Umar and Ibn 'Ubayd gave the ya' tanwin, which is contrary to the apparent. This is because «sawafiya» is not declined (mamnu' min al-sarf) due to the form of the final plural (sigha muntaha al-judu'). It has been explained in two ways. The first: it was pausal with the alif of prolongation because it is in the accusative, then tanwin was added as tanwin al-tarannum (the tanwin of chanting), not the tanwin of declension replacing the alif. The second: it is according to the dialect of those who decline what is not declined, especially the final plural. For this reason someone said:

"Declension in the plural has come often, so much that some people claimed it is optional."

Al-Hasan also read «sawaf» with tanwin and lightening, according to the dialect of those who put a defective noun in the accusative with a presumed vowel and then delete the ya'. The original of ﴿sawaff﴾ is sawafiya; the ya' was deleted because of the heaviness of the plural, and the preceding kasra was retained, then tanwin was put in its place or something similar. Two verses:

"Even if a slanderer in al-Yamama had his home, and my home were on the heights of Hadramawt, he would be guided to me."

Sometimes the ya' remains with sukun, as in his saying:

"O maker of the bow, shaping it, you do not know how to do it well; do not spoil it, and give the bow to its maker."

On this basis is the reading of some «sawafi» with the ya' retained with sukun, on the assumption that, as in the well-known reading, it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ("over them"). Had it been taken, as some said, as an apposition (badal) from the pronoun, there would be no need to resort to an anomalous dialect.

﴿So when their sides fall﴾, meaning they collapse onto the ground, and this is a metaphor (kinaya) for death. The apparent meaning of this, together with the reports mentioned earlier, implies that they are slaughtered while standing. This was used to support the view that the budn are of camels and not of cows, because it is not customary to slaughter cows standing; rather, they are slaughtered lying on their side. Camels are rarely seen being slaughtered while lying down.

﴿So eat from them and feed the one who is content (al-qani') and the one who asks without being asked (al-mu'tarr)﴾. Al-qani' means the one who is satisfied with what he has and with what is given to him without asking or approaching. On this meaning is the verse of Labid:

"Among them is a happy one taking his share, and among them is a wretched one content with his livelihood."

﴿al-mu'tarr﴾ means the one who presents himself to ask, from i'tarra, if he approached him. This explanation was related from Ibn 'Abbas and a group. Muhammad ibn Ka'b, Mujahid, Ibrahim, al-Hasan and al-Kalbi said: ﴿al-qani'﴾ is the one who asks, as in the verse of 'Adi ibn Zayd:

"I did not betray a man of covenant, and I kept my covenant; and I did not refuse the desperate one when he came, asking."

﴿al-mu'tarr﴾ is the one who presents himself without asking. On the first view, al-qani' is said to derive from qani'a yaqna'u, like ta'iba yat'abu, qana'an, when one is satisfied with what he has without asking. On the second view, it derives from qana'a yaqna'u, like sa'ala yas'alu, both in form and meaning, qunu'an. On this is the verse of the poet:

"The slave is free if he is content, and the free man is a slave if he is greedy. So be content and do not covet, for nothing disgraces like covetousness."

Thus, on this view, al-qani' is not one of the contradictory words (al-adContent: "al-adSomething"), because the two verbs differ. Al-Khafaji stated this explicitly, judging against those who imagine otherwise. In al-Sihah, the view that it is one of the contradictory words is attributed to some scholars, and he did not follow it with anything. It is also reported from him that al-qani' may be the one who asks, called qani' because he is satisfied with what is given, whether little or much, and accepts it without refusing. The meaning of both words then returns to contentment, and to the idea that qani'a with kasra means "was satisfied," while qana'a with fatha means "asked." Al-Raghib adopted this, making the masdar of the first qana'a and qanaʿan, and the masdar of the second qunu'an. It is also reported from some that the root is from al-qina', which is what covers the head; so qani'a with kasra means he put on the covering, concealing his poverty, as they say khafiya when he puts on the veil, and qana'a when he lifts his veil, revealing his poverty by asking, like khafiya when he lifts the veil. The meaning of al-qani' as "the one who is satisfied" is supported by Abu Raja's reading «al-qani'» with the pattern of al-hadhir, on the basis that it does not occur in the sense of the asker, unlike al-qani' which occurs with both meanings, and the basic principle is agreement among the readings.

From Mujahid: al-qani' is the neighbor, even if he is rich. Ibn Abi Shayba related from him and from Ibn Jubayr that al-qani' is the people of Mecca and al-mu'tarr is all other people. It was also said that al-mu'tarr is the friend who visits. Of these views, the one I choose is the first.

Al-Hasan read «wal-mu'taree» as an active participle from i'tara, which means the same as i'tarra. Amr and Isma'il, as Ibn Khalawayh transmitted, read «al-mu'tari» with kasra on the ra' and without the ya'; al-Muqri related this from Ibn 'Abbas, and it also came from Abu Raja, with the ya' deleted for lightness, relying on the kasra in its place.

The verse is cited as evidence that the hady (sacrificial offering) is divided into thirds: one third for its owner, one third for al-qani', and one third for al-mu'tarr. This is related from Ibn Mas'ud. Muhammad ibn Ja'far, may God be pleased with them both, also held that it is divided into thirds, except that he said: feed al-qani' and al-mu'tarr one third, the wretched poor one third, and my family one third. There is some doubt about the soundness of this.

Ibn al-Musayyab said: the owner of the hady has only a quarter of it, apparently counting al-qani', al-mu'tarr and al-ba'is al-faqir as three. This is as you see. Ibn 'Atiyya said: all of this is on the basis of recommendation (istihsan), not obligation (fard). It seems he meant by istihsan the recommended (nadb), so he took both matters in the verse to be recommended.

In al-Taysir: the imperative ﴿kulu﴾ ("eat") is for permissibility (ibaha), so if he does not eat, it is permissible. The imperative ﴿at'imu﴾ ("feed") is for recommendation (nadb), so if he gives it all away for himself, he is not liable for anything. This applies to every hady of nusuk that is not an expiation (kaffara), and likewise the udhiyya. As for the expiation, he must give all of it in charity, so whatever he eats or gives as a gift to a rich person, he is liable for. In al-Hidaya: it is recommended for him to eat from the hady of voluntary offering, tamattu' and qiran; likewise it is recommended to give charity in the manner known for sacrifices. This is a view close to what Ibn 'Atiyya's statement implies in both matters. Malik permitted eating from the obligatory hady except the penalty for hunting, the expiation for injury (adha), and the vow. Ahmad permitted it except the penalty for hunting and the vow. According to al-Hasan, eating from all of these is permissible. The detailed treatment of this is in the books of fiqh.

﴿Thus﴾, meaning like that wondrous subjugation implied by God's words ﴿standing in rows﴾: ﴿We have subjected them to you﴾, despite their great size and immense strength. They are not so disobedient to you that you take them submissive, tie them, hold them standing on their legs, and then stab them in the chest. Had God not subjected them, you would not have been able to, and they would not be less powerful than some of the wild beasts that are smaller in body and weaker in strength. Enough as a constant witness and lesson is what persists of camels.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "Just as We have commanded you in this matter, all of it, We have subjected them (the camels) to you, and its remoteness is not hidden." ﴿So that you may be grateful﴾, that is, so that you may thank Us for Our favour upon you by drawing near (to Us) and by sincerity.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 37:

﴿It is not their flesh nor their blood that reaches Allah﴾; that is, the flesh given in charity and the blood poured out by slaughter do not reach the pleasure of Allah, the Exalted, insofar as they are flesh and blood. ﴿But it is piety from you that reaches Him﴾; but there reaches Him what accompanies it of the piety of your hearts, which calls you to magnify Him, the Exalted, to draw near to Him, the Glorified, and to be sincere toward Him, the Mighty and Majestic.

Mujahid said: The Muslims wished to do what the polytheists did, namely slaughtering, cutting up the meat, setting it up around the Ka'bah, and sprinkling it with blood, in glorification of it and seeking nearness to Allah, the Exalted. So this verse was revealed. A similar report is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas and others. Ya'qub and a group read "an tanala" and "wa-lakin tanaluhu" with the taa' (ta). Abu Ja'far read the first with the taa' and the second with the yaa' (the letter of the unseen). It is reported from Yahya ibn Ya'mur and al-Jahdari that they read the reverse of that. Zayd ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, read "lan yunala" and "wa-lakin yunaluhu" in the passive voice in both places, and "lahumaha wa-la dima'aha" in the accusative. ﴿Thus He has subjected them to you﴾: He, glory be to Him, repeated this as a reminder of the blessing and as a reason for what follows, His saying, ﴿that you may magnify Allah﴾; that is, that you may know His greatness through His power over what no one other than Him, the Mighty and Majestic, is capable of, so that you may declare Him one in greatness. It is said: that is, that you may say "Allahu akbar" at the time of the release (of the animal) or at the slaughter. ﴿for what He has guided you to﴾; that is, for His guidance and direction to you toward the way of subjecting them and the manner of drawing near by them. So "ma" is verbal-masdariyyah (the infinitive-forming "ma"). It is permitted that it be a qualifying (ma mawsufah) or a relative (ma mawsulah) with the returning pronoun omitted, and it must be regarded as in the accusative according to those who stipulate, for the omission of a genitive returning pronoun, that it be governed by the same governor as the relative in form, meaning, and reference. The preposition ("ʿala") is connected to "tukabbiru" because it includes the sense of thanks or praise, as if it were said: that you may magnify Him, the Exalted, giving thanks or praising Him for what He has guided you to. Some said: "ʿala" has the meaning of the causal "li" (for), and there is no need to posit the notion of inclusion (tadmin). This is supported by the saying of the one calling upon Allah on al-Safa: "Allahu akbar ʿala ma hadana, wa-l-hamdu lillahi ʿala ma awlana" (Allah is greatest for what He guided us to, and praise be to Allah for what He bestowed upon us). It is not hidden that not positing inclusion here has an aspect that is not present in what we are discussing, so understand. ﴿And give good tidings to the muhsinin﴾; that is, the sincere in everything they do and abandon in matters of their religion. And from Ibn 'Abbas: they are the monotheists.

* * *

Among the allusive (ishari) interpretations of the verses: ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord﴾ by turning away from what is other than Him and seeking reward (from Him). ﴿Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour﴾, which is the beginnings of the Greater Resurrection, ﴿on the Day you see it, every nursing mother will be distracted﴾, and these are the substrates (mawadd) of things, for every thing has a angelic substrate (madda malakutiyyah) that nurses its suckling from the Dominion and rears it in the cradle of readiness. ﴿And every pregnant one will deliver her load﴾, and these are the matters (haylulat), ﴿her load﴾, and these are the forms, ﴿on the Day the earth will be changed to other than the earth, and the heavens﴾. ﴿And you see people as intoxicated﴾ by bewilderment, ﴿but they are not intoxicated﴾ by love. It is said: the intoxication of the enemies comes from seeing the coercive things (al-qahriyyat); the intoxication of the adherents from seeing the wondrous acts; the intoxication of the seekers from the gleams of lights; the intoxication of the lovers from the unveilings of secrets; the intoxication of the longing from the appearance of the radiance of attributes; the intoxication of the ardent from the unveiling of the Essence; the intoxication of the near ones from awe and majesty; the intoxication of the gnostics from entering into the chambers of union; the intoxication of the unifiers from their immersion in the seas of primordiality; and the intoxication of the prophets and messengers, peace be upon them, from their awareness of the secrets of eternity:

A companion came upon us, beyond description, and in his glance is wine, and wine is on the palm.
He intoxicated my companions with the wine of his palm, and he intoxicated me, by Allah, with the wine of the glance.

﴿And among the people is he who worships Allah on an edge﴾, the verse. It includes whoever worships Allah, the Exalted, out of desire for marvels, the praise of creatures, and the attainment of their worldly goods. If he sees some of that, he is at ease in worship; if he does not see it, he abandons it and is careless about it. ﴿He loses the world﴾ by losing rank, acceptance, and being exposed before creatures, ﴿and the Hereafter﴾ by remaining veiled from witnessing the Truth and burning with the fire of distance. ﴿Whoever thinks that Allah will not help him in this world and the Hereafter, let him extend a rope to the sky﴾, the verse. In it is an allusion to the excellence of the station of submission and contentment with what the Wise, may His majesty be exalted, has done. ﴿And when We settled for Abraham the place of the House, [saying]: Do not associate anything with Me, and purify My House for those who circumambulate, stand, bow, and prostrate﴾. In it is much of the glorification of the matter of the Ka'bah. Allah, the Exalted, has made it an example of His Throne, and has made those who circumambulate it among mankind like the angels encircling the Throne, glorifying their Lord with praise. Except that the glorification of mankind and their praise of Him, the Mighty and Majestic, is with divine Quranic words, so they are, insofar as their glorification and praise with those words are concerned, deputies of Him, the Mighty and Majestic, in that; and the people of the Qur'an are, as in the hadith, the people of Allah and His special ones. The Ka'bah also has a distinction over the Throne and the other fourteen houses for a matter that has not been transmitted to us as being in the Throne or in any other of those houses, namely the Black Stone, which has come in a report to be the right hand of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Then He, the Exalted, made four corners for His House for a divine secret; in reality they are three, because the corner that is next to the Hijr is cubical like the Hijr in form, and for this reason it is called the Ka'bah, a likening to the knuckle-bone (ka'b). When Allah, the Exalted, made a House for it in the greater world, He made its counterpart in the lesser world, which is the heart of the believer. They have mentioned that it is more noble than this House: "My earth and My heaven did not contain Me, but the heart of My believing servant contained Me." He made the thoughts that pass over it like those who circumambulate, and in them is their like, the praiseworthy and the blameworthy. He made the locations of the thoughts within it like the corners of the House. The place of the divine thought is like the corner of the Black Stone; the place of the angelic thought is like the Yemeni corner; the place of the carnal thought is like the cubical one in the Hijr, and nothing more; and there is no place in it for the satanic thought. On this basis are the hearts of the prophets, peace be upon them. It may also be said: the place of the carnal thought is like the Syrian corner, and the place of the satanic thought is like the Iraqi corner. This was made for the Iraqi corner because the Lawgiver prescribed that one say at it: "I seek refuge in Allah, the Exalted, from discord, hypocrisy, and bad character." On this basis are the hearts of the believers other than the prophets, peace be upon them. Allah, glory be to Him, deposited in it a treasure that the Prophet, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, wished to remove, but he did not do so for a benefit he saw; likewise 'Umar wished to, but refrained, following the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Likewise, Allah, the Majestic and Exalted, deposited in the heart of the perfect person the treasure of knowledge of Him, the Mighty and Majestic.

The height of the House, according to what has passed, is twenty-seven and a quarter cubits. Some said: twenty-eight cubits, and accordingly that is the counterpart of the stations of the heart, which the planets of faith traverse in order to manifest events that occur in the soul, just as the planet traverses its stations in the sphere to manifest events in the elemental world, and other matters that only the people of unveiling know.

﴿For you in them are benefits until an appointed term; then their place of sacrifice is at the Ancient House﴾; that is, toward what is near it, for the slaughter is at Mina. They were made a place for offerings according to what the Shaykh al-Akbar Muhyi al-Din, may his secret be sanctified, mentioned, because it is from the attainment of the aspiration, and whoever attains the legislated goal has reached the end. In the slaughter of offerings is the destruction of spirits that manage animal bodies, so that human bodies may be nourished by them; their spirits look at them at the time of their separation, and so they manage them as human, after they had been managing them as camels or cows. This is a subtle matter that none has grasped except those whom Allah, the Exalted, has illumined in their insight from among the people of Allah, the Exalted, end. Its full understanding is entrusted to its people, so strive to be among them.

﴿And give good tidings to the mukhbitin﴾, ﴿those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned﴾, according to what occurs to them of manifestation at that time. Tranquility of the heart may also come from remembrance, since manifestation then requires it. Some mentioned that each name has a specific manifestation; so when Allah, the Exalted, is mentioned, it occurs according to readiness, and from here sometimes trembling occurs and sometimes tranquility. ("Idha," "when," does not imply totality; rather it is often used in the particular conditional.) It was said: the gnostic, whenever he hears the remembrance from other than Allah, the Exalted, his heart trembles, and whenever he hears it from Him, the Mighty and Majestic, he is at rest. It is understood from the apparent sense of their words that the hearer of remembrance is either trembling or at rest, and they did not state another category; if there is one, then the remainder remains in its state before hearing. Most of the shaykhs of our time dance upon hearing the remembrance, so I do not know whether their dancing arises from trembling before Him, the Exalted, or from tranquility? It will become clear on the day when secrets are tried and hidden things are made manifest.

﴿And the camels We have made for you among the symbols of Allah; in them is good for you; so mention the name of Allah over them, standing in ranks﴾. You have already been told that they slaughter the camels tied at the left foreleg, standing on the remaining legs. They mentioned as the secret of that that since their slaughter is an act of drawing near, the Prophet ﷺ desired harmony in the manner of their slaughter with oddness, so he had them stand on three legs, because Allah, the Exalted, is odd and loves odd numbers; three, or singularity, has the first rank in that, and primacy is also odd. He made them standing because the Self-Subsistence (qayyumiyyah), like oddness, is a divine attribute; so the one who slaughters them recalls the witnessing of the One who stands over every soul with what it has earned. It is established that the rites were prescribed only to establish the remembrance of Allah, the Exalted. The pairing of the two legs is due to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the leg is joined to the leg﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 29], which is the joining of the affair of this world with the Hereafter. The right foreleg of the camel was singled out so that it relies only on an odd one that has power. Standing is on the left foreleg because it is free of the strength that the right has, and standing does not occur except by strength.

Muslim has transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ prayed the noon prayer at Dhu al-Hulayfah, then called for his she-camel, and marked her on the right side of her hump, wiped the blood from it, and hung two sandals on her, then mounted his mount," the hadith.

The secret in his, peace be upon him, offering being of camels, although it has been reported of them that they are devils, and for this reason prayer in their resting places is disliked, is an allusion that his station, peace be upon him, returned those far from Allah, the Exalted, to the state of nearness. In marking her on her hump, which is the highest part of her, is a marking from him, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, that he came to them with the quality of greatness that they had in their souls, so let them avoid it, for the Last Abode is made only for those who do not desire exaltation in the earth nor corruption. The marking happened on the right side because the right is the place of power and strength, and the side (safha) is from pardon (safh); so in that is an allusion that Allah, the Exalted, pardons whoever has this quality when he seeks nearness to Allah, the Exalted, and removes from his greatness that which necessitated distance. He, peace be upon him, made the sandals a sign of removing pride in the satanic nature of the camels by hanging sandals on their necks, for one is struck with sandals only if he is of lowly and humiliated rank, and whoever is in this position has no pride left in him to be witnessed. He hung the sandals on necklaces of wool so as to remember by that what Allah, the Exalted, intended, and so that the mountains would be like carded wool. They have mentioned secrets of this kind for all the actions of the Hajj. In my view, most of them are ritual (ta'abbudi) matters, and most of what they have mentioned is of the nature of poetry. Allah, the Exalted, is the One who grants success to what is right.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 38:

﴿Indeed, Allah defends those who have believed.﴾ This is a resumed statement (kalam mustaʾnaf), brought to steady the hearts of the believers by explaining that Allah, exalted is He, is their helper against their enemies, to the extent that they cannot prevent them from performing the Hajj. It has been mentioned that this is connected to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar [others]﴾ [al-Hajj: 25]. And the mention of the rites (shaʿaʾir) that came in between is a digression (mustatradan) to further denounce their act and to condemn it, so that the ugliness of obstruction increases with the greater esteem of that from which they were barred. Its opening with the particle of confirmation (kalimat al-tahqiq) serves to show full concern with its content. The form of mufaʿalah (defend) is either for emphasis (lil-mubalaghah), or to indicate the repetition of the defending, since this form may be stripped of the sense of the act occurring reciprocally from both sides, so that its repetition remains like habitual practice (al-mumarasah). That is: Allah, exalted is He, exerts great effort in repelling the mischief and harm of the polytheists, of which obstructing the way of Allah, exalted is He, and the Sacred Mosque is a part, [exerting effort] like one who contends with it, or who repels it from them time after time, as their intention to harm them renews, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whenever they kindle a fire for war, Allah extinguishes it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64].

Abu ʿAmr and Ibn Kathir read "yadfaʿu" (He defends), with the object omitted, as has been indicated. In al-Bahr it is stated that He did not mention what He defends them from, so that it would be more majestic, greater and more general. But you know that the context does not require generality; rather, that is not correct.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love every treacherous ungrateful one﴾ is a justification (taʿlil) for what is implicit in the noble promise of a threat to the polytheists, and a notice that their repulsion is by way of subjugation and humiliation. It has been said: it is a justification for the defence of the believers by the hatred of those who are repelled, in a manner that implies that the cause of that is treachery and disbelief. The phrase "does not love" (la yuhibbu) was preferred over "hates" (yubghidu) as an indication of the place of allusion, and that the believers are the beloved of Allah, exalted is He. Perhaps the first is preferable, to give the impression that the verse is of the kind of your saying: "I repel Zayd from ʿAmr because of my hatred for Zayd," and there is not much concern for ʿAmr in that. That is: Allah, exalted is He, hates every treacherous one in His trusts, which are His commands and prohibitions, exalted is His majesty, or in all trusts, most of which is ungratefulness toward His blessings, mighty and majestic is He. The form of intensification in both words is to explain that the polytheists are like that, not to restrict it in a way that implies love for the treacherous or the disbeliever; or because the betrayal of the trust of Allah, exalted is He, and the ingratitude for His blessing are not trivial but are two great matters; or because of the abundance of what they betrayed of trusts and what they disbelieved of blessings; or for emphasis in negating love, by considering the negation first and then expressing the sense of intensification second, as has been said regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants﴾ [Fussilat: 46]. And you have known what is in it.

Whatever the case, the intended meaning is the negation of love from each and every individual of the treacherous, disbelieving ones.

﴿Uthina﴾ means: it was permitted (rukhkhisa). Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (udhina) in the active voice, meaning: Allah permitted (udhina Allahu ta'ala) ﴿for those who are fought against﴾, that is, those whom the polytheists fight. What is permitted is fighting, and it is in effect what has been mentioned, since the mentioned indicates it with a clear indication.

Abu 'Amr, Abu Bakr and Ya'qub read (yuqatilun) in the active form, meaning: they wish to fight the polytheists in the future and are eager for it. Its indication of the omitted element is therefore clearer. ﴿Because they were wronged﴾, that is, because they were wronged. The relative pronoun refers to the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) who were in Makkah. Al-Wahidi and others transmit that the polytheists used to harm them, and they would come to the Prophet (ﷺ), some beaten and some wounded, complaining of their oppression to him. The blessings of Allah and His peace be upon him would say to them: "Be patient, for I have not been commanded to fight until I migrate." Then this verse was revealed, and it is the first verse revealed about fighting after having been forbidden from it, in some seventy-odd verses, according to what al-Hakim narrated in al-Mustadrak (al-Mustadrak) from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. 'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir also related it from al-Zuhri.

Ibn Jarir related from Abu al-'Aliyah that the first verse revealed concerning it was ﴿And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19]. In al-Iklil (al-Iklil) of al-Hakim, it is stated that the first verse revealed on this matter was ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties﴾ [al-Tawbah: 111]. Al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il (al-Dala'il) and a group of others narrated that it was revealed concerning some believers who went out as emigrants from Makkah to Madinah, and the disbelievers of Quraysh pursued them, so Allah permitted them to fight against them. The oppressor is not explicitly named, in order to heighten the displeasure and to avoid mentioning him.

﴿And indeed, Allah is able to give them victory﴾: this is a promise to them of victory and an emphasis on what has preceded of the promise, and a clarification that what is intended is not merely their deliverance from the hands of the polytheists, but their dominance and their triumph over them. The statement has been expressed in the manner of royal majesty, for the gesture and the smile of a great king are sufficient to assure certainty of attaining what is sought. It has been emphasized with eloquent emphasis, to further settle the souls of the believers.

Page 162

﴿Those who have been expelled from their homes﴾ is in the genitive position (fi hayyiz al-jarr), as a qualifier (sifah) of the preceding relative pronoun, or an explanation (bayan) of it, or a substitute (badal) for it. It may also be in the accusative position as an expression of praise (madh), or in the nominative position by supposing an omitted subject (mubtada'), with the clause being nominative as praise. The intended meaning is those whom the polytheists expelled from Makkah. ﴿Without right﴾ is connected (muta'alliq) to the expulsion, meaning: they were expelled for something other than what would require their expulsion.

It is permitted that it be a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), meaning: they were expelled with an expulsion that had this attribute. al-Tabarsi preferred that it be in the place of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: while being without right, with a right that results from them and requires their expulsion. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿except that they say: Our Lord is Allah﴾, is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil) from (haqq, "right"). "That they say" and what follows it are, in interpretation, a verbal noun that is a substitute (badal) from it, because of the negative sense in "other than" (ghayr). The essential meaning is: there is no cause for their expulsion except monotheism (tawhid). This holds if by "the cause" is meant the cause in the real, objective sense, in the manner of the words of al-Nabighah:

"And there is no fault in them, save that their swords are notched from the clashing of the battalions."

It is also permitted that the substitution be from "other than," with a negative sense in "they were expelled," meaning: they were not left in their homes except on condition that they say, etc. This, as you see, is [weak]. It is permitted that the exception be disconnected (munqati'), and Abu Hayyan made this obligatory, meaning: but they were expelled because they said, "Our Lord is Allah." He made the accusative obligatory for what follows "except," as they made it obligatory in their saying: "It increased only what decreased," and "It benefited only what harmed." His view that it is connected was rejected, and his view that what follows "except" is a substitute from (haqq) was rejected with what is most like sophistry. It is understood from his speech that "except" may be in the sense of "other than" as a qualifier of (haqq), meaning: they were expelled without right, other than monotheism. Its essential meaning is: they were expelled by being monotheists.

﴿And were it not that Allah repels some people by means of others, there would have been demolished cloisters, churches﴾ is an incitement to fight, the fighting having been permitted, by informing that He, exalted is He, has established this custom among past nations, that by it the command is carried out and the laws are upheld and the acts of worship are safeguarded from demolition. So it is as if, when it was said, ﴿Permission has been given to those who are fought against﴾, etc., it was said: then let the believers fight. For were it not for fighting, and Allah's empowering the believers over the polytheists in every era and time, their places of worship would have been demolished and they would have gone in every direction. It was said: the meaning is, were it not that Allah repels some people by means of others, by empowering the believers of this nation over its disbelievers, the places of worship mentioned would have been demolished; but He, exalted is He, empowered the believers over the disbelievers, so these places of worship remained, some for the believers and some for those under their protection from the people of the dhimmah. This is not the right reading. Mujahid said: that is, were it not for the repelling of the oppression of a people by the testimony of trustworthy witnesses and the like, the places would have been demolished, etc.

Some said: that is, were it not for repelling the oppression of oppressors by the justice of rulers. A group said: that is, were it not for repelling punishment from the wicked through the supplication of the righteous. Qutrub said: that is, were it not for the repelling by retaliation (qisas) from souls. It was said: by the prophets, peace be upon them, from the believers. All of this is what the context does not require and what people of understanding do not accept.

The word "sawami'" (cloisters) is the plural of "sawma'ah," on the pattern fa'awalah, and it is a high building with a sharp top. "Al-asma'" among men means one who is sharp of speech. al-Raghib said: it is every building with a joined top, i.e., closely connected, and "al-asma'" is one whose ear is stuck to his head; this is close to close. As Qatadah said, before Islam it was specific to the monks of the Christians and to the worshippers of the Sabians, then it came to be used for the minaret of the Muslims. What is meant here is the place of worship of the monks according to Abu al-'Aliyah, and the place of worship of the Sabians according to Qatadah. It is not hidden that it is not appropriate to intend that, since the Sabians were never a community of true religion at any time. "Bi'a" (churches), whose singular is "bai'ah" on the pattern fi'lah, is the prayer place of the Christians, and it is not specific to their monks as "sawma'ah" is. al-Raghib said: if it is originally Arabic, the reason for naming it so is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their selves﴾ (9:111), etc. It was said it is the synagogue of the Jews.

The people of Madinah and Ya'qub read "wa-law la difa'" with an alif. The two Harams, Ayyub, Qatadah, Talhah, Za'idah from al-A'mash, and al-Za'faranI read "lahudimat" with the light pronunciation, and the doubled form (tadh'if) is according to the multiplicity of places.

﴿And synagogues﴾ is the plural of "salah," and it is the synagogue of the Jews. It was said: it is a place of worship of the Christians other than the bi'ah. The first view is more famous. The synagogue was named thus because prayer (salat) is performed in it, so it is a metonymy (majaz) of naming the place by the name of what is in it. It was said: it has its true meaning, and "hudimat" means "was rendered inoperative," or there is an omitted genitive (mudaf muqaddar) in the sentence, and this is not the right reading. It was said: "Salawat" is an arabicised form of "Salutha" with the unvoweled thaʾ (ث) and short vowel, and its meaning in Hebrew is "the place of prayer." It is narrated from Abu Raja', al-Juhdari, Abu al-'Aliyah, and Mujahid that they read it this way. The apparent meaning, on this view, is that it is a common noun (ism jins) and not a proper name, before arabicisation and after it. However, what Harun narrated from Abu 'Amr, that it is not nunated and is not declined because of proper-name status and foreignness, indicates that it is a proper name of a class (ism jins) since its being the name of one specific place, as was said, is far-fetched. On this basis it should have been left undeclined in the well-known reading. Therefore it was said that it was declined because of its resemblance to the plural in form, so it is like "'Arafat." The apparent meaning is that it is indefinite, since it was made general for what was arabicised. As for the claim that the one who holds this view does not nunate it, it is far-fetched, as al-Khafaji said.

Ja'far ibn Muhammad, may Allah be pleased with both of them, read ﴿salawat﴾ with dammah on the sad and the lam. Ibn Khalawayh related from him with kasrah on the sad and sukun on the lam, and it is related from al-Juhdari. It is also related from him "sula'wat" with dammah on the sad and fathah on the lam, and it is related from al-Kalbi. Abu al-'Aliyah in one narration read "salwat" with fathah on the sad and sukun on the lam. al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf read "sulawat" with dammah on the sad and the lam without an alif, and it is related from al-Juhdari as well. Mujahid read "sulawta" with two dammahs and a taʾ followed by an alif. al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi read "sulawth" with two dammahs without an alif and with a thaʾ. 'Ikrimah read "silwitha" with kasrah on the sad, sukun on the lam, a kasrah on the waw, a ya' after it, then a thaʾ, then an alif. It is related from al-Juhdari also "sulwath" with dammah on the sad, sukun on the lam, a fathah on the waw followed by an alif, then a thaʾ. It is related from Mujahid that he read likewise, except that the sad had a kasrah. Ibn Khalawayh and Ibn 'Atiyyah related from al-Hajjaj and al-Juhdari "sulub" with two dammahs and a ba' (b), as the plural of "salib," like "zarif" and "zurrf," and the plural of the form fa'il on the form fu'ul is anomalous. These are a number of readings which are rarely found in a single word.

﴿And mosques﴾ is the plural of "masjid," and it is a well-known place of worship for the Muslims. It was specified with this name out of concern for its matter, since prostration (sujud) is the closest the servant comes to his Lord, mighty and majestic. It was said: because prostration in prayer is specific to Muslims. This was refuted by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿O Mary, be obedient to your Lord, and prostrate and bow with those who bow﴾ (3:43). Taking prostration in it in the linguistic sense is far-fetched. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the names mentioned are shared by nations in their referents, except "bi'ah," which is specific to the Christians in the usage of every language. Most of them hold that the cloisters are for the monks, the churches for the Christians, the synagogues for the Jews, and the mosques for the Muslims.

Perhaps the delay in mentioning them, although the apparent order would be to put them first, is because of their nobility, since the existential order is thus; or so that it falls in the vicinity of praising their people; or to make distant the closeness of demolition. Perhaps the delay of "salawat" after "bi'ah," despite its contrary existential order, is because of its relation to the mosques; so it was said. It was also said that these acts of worship were arranged in this sequence for moving from the noble to the nobler: the churches are nobler than the cloisters, because many worshippers are in them, since they are places of worship for the monks and others, while the cloisters are a place of worship for the monks only. The synagogues of the Jews are nobler than the churches, because their origin is older and the time of worship in them is longer. The mosques are nobler than all of them, because Allah, exalted is He, has been worshipped in them with what has not been worshipped with in other than them. Perhaps the purpose of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿they would have been demolished﴾ etc., is to emphasize the appearance of corruption and the occurrence of disorder in the affairs of the servants, were it not for Allah's empowering the righteous over the falsifiers, not merely the demolition of places of worship for the adherents of religions. ﴿In which the name of Allah is mentioned much﴾ is in the place of a qualifier of "masajid." al-Dahhak, Muqatil, and al-Kalbi said: it is in the place of a qualifier for all of them. Abu Hayyan favored this. That the remembrance of Allah, mighty and majestic, being mentioned in the cloisters, churches, and synagogues is after their legislation was abrogated is not something the context requires, and it is nothing, because abrogation does not negate their remaining through the blessing of the remembrance of Allah, exalted is He, in them, and also because the meaning of the verse is general to what preceded abrogation, as has passed.

﴿And Allah will surely support those who support Him﴾, that is, Allah, exalted is He, will surely support whoever supports His religion, or whoever supports His friends. Allah, exalted is He, indeed fulfilled His promise, since He empowered the Emigrants and the Helpers over the chiefs of the Arabs, the kings of the non-Arabs, and the emperors of the Romans, and made them inherit their lands and their homes. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Powerful﴾ over everything He wills, of which among His wills is their support, ﴿Mighty﴾, none can resist Him, and nothing can repel Him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 41:

﴿Those who, if We establish them in the land, establish the prayer, give the zakat, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong.﴾ This is a qualifier (wasf) of "those who were expelled," either detached (maqta') or not detached. It is also permitted that it be a substitute (badal, an apposition that replaces the word it follows). Al-tamkin (establishment, i.e., empowerment) means authority and the execution of command. "The land" is meant generically, and it was said that it means Makkah. "The prayer" means the obligatory prayer, "the zakat" means the obligatory zakat, "what is right" means tawhid (affirmation of Allah's oneness), and "what is wrong" means shirk (associating partners with Allah), as narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam.

Perhaps the better view regarding the last two is generality. The description with what has been mentioned, as narrated from ʿUthman, may Allah be pleased with him, is praise before trial, meaning that Allah praised them before they introduced the good that they introduced. They said: In this there is evidence for the validity of the authority of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, may Allah be pleased with them all. This is according to what is in al-Kashshaf, because the verse is specific to the Emigrants (muhajirun), since they are the ones expelled without right, and those empowered in the land from among them are the caliphs and no others. So if the remaining attributes were not established, the statement would be contradicted, exalted is Allah above that, because it indicates that every one of them who is empowered is obliged to have the consequent, due to the generality of the wording. And since the empowerment has occurred, the argument is complete, without regard to the conditional's requirement of occurrence, like a statement introduced by "perhaps" (la'alla) and "perhaps" (ʿasa) from the great ones, for the consequent's necessity is inevitably required by the wording. And since the antecedent occurred, its occurrence is also necessarily required. In the establishment of the consequent is the establishment of the rightfulness of the caliphate absolutely, and it comes in the plural form, which is incompatible with restricting it to ʿAli alone, may Allah be pleased with him. And according to al-Hasan and Abu al-ʿAliyah, they are the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). On this view, it is better to make the relative clause a substitute for the phrase "whoever supports Him" in His statement, as al-Zajjaj parsed it. The same applies according to what is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, that they are the Emigrants, the Helpers, and the Successors, and according to what is narrated from Abu Najih, that they are the rulers.

[p. 165]

You know that the context requires only the first (view): ﴿And to Allah belongs the outcome of all matters﴾ exclusively, for its return is to His judgment and decree alone. In this there is an emphasis of the promise of exalting His word and manifesting His friends.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verses 42–44:**

﴿And if they deny you, [know that] the people of Noah, 'Ad, and Thamud have denied [their messengers] before them﴾ ﴿and the people of Abraham and the people of Lot﴾ ﴿and the companions of Madyan﴾. This is a consolation (*tasliyah*) for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The use of the present tense (*al-mudari'*) in the conditional clause, although the denial has already occurred, is either because the aim is to console him (peace be upon him) about the anxiety that is expected to follow from the denial, or to indicate that its occurrence is something that should not happen. The feminine marker (*ta' al-ta'nith*) is attached to the verb *kadhdhaba* (كَذَّبَ) because its subject, *qawm* (قَوْمُ), is a collective noun (*ism jam'*) which may be treated as masculine or feminine, and there is no need to interpret it as "the community" (*al-ummah*) or "the tribe" (*al-qabilah*), as Abu Hayyan and those who followed him did. In choosing the feminine form there is a lowering of the status of the deniers. The object of *kadhdhaba* is omitted because the intended meaning is fully evident.

It has also been permitted that the verb be treated as intransitive (*munazzal manzilat al-lazim*), meaning: they committed denial. For 'Ad and Thamud the word "people" (*qawm*) is dispensed with because they are well known by this shorter name. The original practice in such references is to use the proper name, which is why it is not said "the people of Salih" or "the people of Hud"; and there is no proper name (*'alam*) for other than these. It is not said "and the people of Shu'ayb" – it is said that this is because the people who denied him (peace be upon him) are these [groups] and not the people of al-Aykah, since although he (peace be upon him) was sent to them, those who denied him were outsiders to them. The denial of these [groups] is also earlier and more severe. The specification [of these peoples] is because the consolation is for the Prophet (peace be upon him) regarding the denial of his own people, i.e.: "And if your people deny you, know that you are not unique in this; the people of Noah, etc., denied before your people denied you."

﴿And Musa was denied﴾. Those who denied him (peace be upon him) were the Copts (*al-qibt*), and they were not his people. Rather, his people (peace be upon him) were the Children of Israel, and they did not all deny him; and whoever among them denied him repented, except a few. The denial of a few from a people is considered as no denial at all. Do you not see that the affirmation of a few from those previously mentioned was counted as no affirmation? For this reason it is not said "and the people of Musa," as is said "the people of Noah" and "the people of Abraham." As for the fact that it is not said "and the Copts," but rather the verb is repeated in the passive voice, this indicates that their denial of him (peace be upon him) was extremely grievous, because his signs were in the utmost clarity.

﴿Then I gave respite to the disbelievers﴾, i.e., I gave them time until the cords of their lifespans came to an end. The particle *fa'* (الفاء) indicates the sequence of granting respite to each group of deniers following the denial of that group, not the sequence of granting respite to all of them following the denial of all of them. The apparent noun is placed in the position of the implied pronoun referring to the deniers, in order to censure them for disbelief, and [the verse] explicitly mentions those who denied Musa (peace be upon him), since they were not explicitly mentioned previously.

﴿Then I seized them﴾, i.e., I seized each group of the deniers after the end of the period of their respite and reprieve. The seizing (*al-akhdh*) is a metonymy (*kinayah*) for destruction.

﴿So how was My rejection?﴾, i.e., My disapproval of them, by changing what they had of life, blessing, the flourishing of their lands, and replacing it with its opposite. It is a verbal noun (*masdar*) from *nakartu 'alayhi* when you do an act that deters him, in the sense of disapproval (*inkar*), like *nadhir* in the sense of *indhar* (warning). The yā' of the pronoun attached to it (i.e., the yā' in *nakīrī*) is omitted for the sake of the verse-ending (*fasilah*), though some reciters affirmed it. The interrogative is for exclamation (*li al-ta'ajjub*), as if it were said: "How severe was My disapproval of them!" In the sentence there is an intimidation (*irhab*) for Quraysh.

And the words of Him, exalted is He: ﴿So how many a town have We destroyed﴾ is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb that is explained by His words ﴿We destroyed it﴾. That is, "We destroyed many of the towns; We destroyed them." The clause is a substitute (badal) for His words ﴿so how was My denunciation﴾. Or it is in the nominative, with the beginning (mubtada') being ﴿how many﴾ and the clause ﴿We destroyed it﴾ as its predicate (khabar). That is, "So many of the towns, We destroyed them." Abu Hayyan chose this reading and said: "The better view in the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of ka-ayyin is that it is a mubtada', and its being in the accusative with an implied verb is weak."

Abu 'Amr and a group read ﴿I destroyed it﴾ with the first-person ta', in harmony with ﴿So I granted respite to the disbelievers, then I seized them﴾. The attribution of destruction to the towns is metaphorical, and what is meant is the destruction of their inhabitants. It is also possible that the speech contains an implied noun (taqdir mudaf). It was said: destruction is a metaphor for the loss of benefit from them through the destruction of their people.

His words ﴿while it was wrongdoing﴾ are a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya) from the object of ﴿We destroyed﴾. His words ﴿so it lies in ruins﴾ are coordinated (ma'tuf) upon ﴿We destroyed it﴾, so it has no place in i'rab, or its place is nominative like what it is coordinated upon. It is also permissible to coordinate it upon the nominal clause ﴿how many﴾ and so on, and some scholars chose this for the sake of consistency (tashakkul). The fa' does not prevent this, based on the order of the ruin following the destruction, since it is like "Zayd is your father, so he is kind to you." It was also permitted to coordinate it upon the circumstantial clause, but this was objected to on the ground that its ruin was not during the destruction of its people but after it. It was answered that it is a circumstance anticipated (haal muqaddara), and its coordination upon a concurrent circumstance is valid; or it may be said that it is also a concurrent circumstance, in that the destruction of the people occurred with its ruin upon them. It is not hidden that both answers go against the apparent meaning.

The word khawa' (ruin) may mean falling, from khawa al-najm (the star fell), and His words ﴿upon its roofs﴾ are connected to it. The roofs (‘uruush) here mean the ceilings, and the meaning is that its walls have fallen upon its ceilings: its buildings became idle, so its ceilings collapsed, then its walls were destroyed and fell on top of the ceilings. The attribution of the fall to the roofs is because the walls are the main part of the building, so they are treated as the whole building. Or the word may mean emptiness, from "the house became empty (khawat al-dar, takhwi khawa') when it was emptied of its people," and it is said: "the belly became empty (khawa al-batn, yakhwi khawan) when it was emptied of food." Al-Raghib made the original meaning of khawa' this, and made khawa al-najm derived from it, saying: "It is said khawa al-najm and akhwa when a star, at its setting, brings no rain," by analogy with that. Thus His words ﴿upon its roofs﴾ are either connected to it, or connected to an implied element functioning as a circumstance, with "upon" meaning "together with," that is, "it is empty while its roofs remain intact and sound." On the interpretation of khawa' as emptiness, it is also permissible that ﴿upon its roofs﴾ is a predicate after a predicate, meaning "it is empty, and it is upon its roofs," that is, standing, overlooking its roofs, since the ceilings have fallen to the ground while the walls remain standing, overlooking the fallen ceilings. The attribution of overlooking to the whole, though it is a state of the walls alone, is for the reason mentioned just above.

﴿And an abandoned well﴾ is coordinated upon ﴿town﴾. The word bi'r (well) derives from ba'artu, meaning "I dug." It is feminine in the pattern fi'l in the sense of maf'ul, though it may be masculine in the sense of qalib (a well). Its plurals are abar, aabar, ab'ur, a'bar, and biyar. Ta'til (abandonment) of a thing is the cancellation of its benefits, that is, "how many a well, thriving in the deserts, was left unused, with no water drawn from it, because its people perished."

Al-Jahdari, al-Hasan, and a group read mu'attala with the lighter form, from a'talahu, meaning ‘attalahu.

﴿And a lofty palace﴾ is also coordinated upon what came before, that is, "how many a palace of raised structure, or built with shid (gypsum plaster), we emptied of its inhabitants," as the context indicates, and the description of the well as "abandoned" before it. This supports the meaning of "khawiya 'ala 'uruushiha" as "empty while its roofs remain." In al-Bahr it is said that ﴿well﴾ should be the connection.

﴿And palace﴾, in that its coordination upon ﴿town﴾ places both of them with it within the sphere of destruction, reported of them with a kind of figurative extension: "how many an abandoned well and lofty palace, whose people We destroyed."

Some scholars claimed that they are coordinated upon ﴿its roofs﴾, but this is nothing. The indefiniteness in both suggests that no specific one is intended. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the well belonged to the people of 'Adan in Yemen, and it is the Rass. It is reported from Ka'b al-Ahbar that the palace was built by the second 'Ad.

[Page 167]

It is reported from al-Dahhak and others that the palace was on the top of a mountain in Hadramawt, and the well was at its foot, and that Salih, peace be upon him, descended there with four thousand men who believed in him, and God delivered them from the punishment. Hadramawt was so named, with fath on the ra' and the mim, and it may be pronounced with damma on both, and it may be indeclinable or declinable, because when Salih, peace be upon him, arrived there (hadara), he died (mata). Near the well there is a town named Hadur, which the people of Salih built. They appointed over it Jalhas ibn Julas, and they remained there for a time, then they disbelieved and worshipped an idol. God sent to them Handhala ibn Safwan as a prophet, but they killed him in the marketplace, so God destroyed them to the last one, and He, exalted is He, left their well and their palace abandoned.

It is permissible that this is intended by way of allusion (ta'rid), though this is far-fetched.

﴿Have they not traveled through the earth?﴾ This is an exhortation for them to travel, so that they may look and take heed from the final fates of those who were destroyed. This is if they have not traveled. If they have traveled, then it is an exhortation to reflect and take heed. The journeying is mentioned because reflection depends on it. It is also permissible that the interrogative is for denial (inkar) or for affirmation (taqrir). Whichever it is, the conjunction is upon an elided element that the context requires. As for His exalted saying, ﴿so that they would have﴾, it is in the accusative as the answer to the interrogative according to Ibn 'Atiyya, and as the answer to the affirmation according to al-Ḥawfi, and as the answer to the negation according to some. The position of the Basrans is that the accusative is by the implied "an" (idmar an), and from it and the verb a verbal noun is formed, which is conjoined to an assumed verbal noun (mașdar mutawahham). The position of the Kufans is that it is in the accusative by way of conversion (ṣarf), since the meaning of the speech is a statement; they converted it from the jussive (jazm) by way of conjoining it to (yasīrū), and returned it to the sibling of the jussive, which is the accusative. This, as you see, is [weak]. The position of al-Jurmi is that the accusative is by the fa' itself.

Mubashshir ibn 'Ubayd recited ﴿fa-yakūna﴾ with the yā' of the third person. ﴿Hearts with which they understand﴾, meaning, with them they know what must be known of monotheism. The object of (ya'qilūna) is elided because the context indicates it. Likewise is said regarding His exalted saying, ﴿or ears with which they hear﴾, meaning, with them they hear what must be heard of the revelation, or of the reports of the destroyed nations, from those among the people who neighbor them, for they know their condition better than others. ﴿For indeed, it is not the eyes that are blinded, but it is the hearts within the breasts that are blinded.﴾ The pronoun of (fa-innahā) refers to the matter (al-qiṣṣa), so it is explained by the sentence following it. In such a case it is permissible to use the masculine, by consideration of the affair (al-sha'n). On that basis is the reading of 'Abd Allah, "fa-innahu." The feminine was made acceptable here by the occurrence after it of something feminine. It was also said: it is permissible that it be an ambiguous pronoun explained by "the eyes," and it is as if the original was "indeed the eyes are not blinded," with the clause ﴿are not blinded﴾, composed of the verb and the concealed subject, being a predicate following a predicate. When the first predicate was dropped, the apparent noun was put in place of the pronoun, since there was nothing to which it could refer apparently, so it became a subject explaining the pronoun. Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying it is not permissible, because the pronoun explained by a singular noun following it is restricted to specific matters: the chapter of rubba, the chapter of ni'ma and bi'sa, the chapter of the operators (al-a'māl), the chapter of the substitute (al-badal), and the chapter of the subject and predicate; and what is here is not one of them. It was answered that it is from the chapter of the subject and predicate, like ﴿it is not but our life of this world﴾ [al-An'am: 29; al-Mu'minun: 37; al-Jathiya: 24], and the entry of the abrogating particle does not harm this. But there is consideration in this. The meaning is that the blindness of the eyes is not counted as blindness, and only the blindness of the hearts is counted; as if the blindness of the eyes is not blindness in comparison to the blindness of the hearts. So the speech is a concluding statement (tadhyīl) to magnify the state they are in of lacking understanding in the heart, and that it is the blindness after which there is no blindness, rather there is no blindness except it. Or the meaning is that their eyes are sound and intact, with no blindness in them, and the blindness is only in their hearts. So it is as if it was said: "Have they not traveled, so that they would have hearts possessing insights? For the affliction lies in the insights of their hearts, not in the sight of their eyes," and it is the affliction beyond which every other affliction is trivial. It is as if He is urging them to remove the disease and reproaching them for their inaction regarding it. The description of the hearts as "those which are in the breasts," according to what al-Zajjaj said, is for emphasis, as in His exalted saying, ﴿they say with their mouths﴾ [Al 'Imran: 167], and your saying: "I saw with my eyes."

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is well known and believed that blindness in its literal sense belongs to the sight, which is that the pupil is struck by something that extinguishes its light. Its use for the heart is a metaphor and an image. When it is intended to affirm what is contrary to the accepted belief, namely attributing blindness literally to the hearts and negating it from the eyes, this depiction needs additional specification and extra clarification, so that it is firmly established that the place of blindness is the hearts, not the eyes. As when you say: "The sharpness does not belong to the sword, but it belongs to your tongue that is between your jaws," and it is in the ruling of your saying: "I did not negate sharpness from the sword and affirm it for your tongue by a slip, nor by inadvertence from me, but I deliberately intended precisely that."

This verse, it is said, was revealed concerning Ibn Umm Maktum when he heard His exalted saying: ﴿And whoever is blind in this [life] will be blind in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Isra': 72]. He said: "O Messenger of Allah, I am blind in this world, so will I be blind in the Hereafter?" Perhaps the first meaning is preferred by this report, if it is authentic, since the answer by the verse to it is very evident. It is as if it was said to him: "You are not included in the generality of ﴿whoever is﴾ etc., because the blindness of the eyes in this world is not truly blindness in comparison to the blindness of the hearts. The one who is included in the generality of that is whoever is characterized by blindness of the heart." This suffices for the answer, whether the meaning of His exalted saying, ﴿And whoever is blind in this [life] will be blind in the Hereafter﴾, is "whoever is heart-blind in this world will be likewise in the Hereafter," or "whoever is heart-blind in this world will be blind of sight in the Hereafter, because in it the secrets will be tested, so the blindness of the heart will appear in the form of blindness of the sight." Yes, there is consideration regarding the soundness of the report.

In al-Durr al-Manthur: Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatada that he said regarding this verse: "It has been related to us that it was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Za'ida, meaning Ibn Umm Maktum." The ruling on a report transmitted in this manner is not hidden. Using His exalted saying, ﴿Have they not traveled﴾ etc., it was inferred that traveling across the earth and seeking out traces (of the past) is recommended.

Ibn Abi Hatim also related in the Book of Reflection (Kitab al-Tafakkur) from Malik ibn Dinar, who said: "Allah, exalted is He, revealed to Musa, peace be upon him, to take two sandals of iron and a staff, then to wander across the earth seeking traces and lessons until the two sandals wear out and the staff breaks." And using His exalted saying, ﴿so that they would have﴾ etc., it was inferred that the locus of intellect is the heart, not the head, as stated by al-Jalal al-Suyuti in Ahkam al-Qur'an al-'Azim.

Imam al-Razi said: In the verse there is an indication that intellect is knowledge, and that its locus is the heart. You know that the view that intellect is knowledge is the choice of Abu Ishaq al-Isfara'ini, and he argued for it by saying that one who understands something is said to know it, and one who knows something is said to understand it. On the assumption of difference, that would not be said, and this is not sound, because if by knowledge is meant every knowledge, it follows that whoever lacks some sciences is not intelligent, even if he has acquired the others; and if by knowledge is meant some sciences, then the definition is not attained due to lack of distinction. What was mentioned as evidence is not valid, because it is possible that knowledge is distinct from intellect while the two are mutually implicating. Al-Ash'ari said: There is no difference between intellect and knowledge except in generality and specificity, and knowledge is more general than intellect. So intellect, when it is known, is specific. It was said: it is the knowledge that restrains from ugliness and calls to beauty, and this is the saying of al-Jubba'i. It was said: it is the knowledge of the better of the two goods and the worse of the two evils, and this is also a saying of some Mu'tazila, and they have other sayings. What al-Qadi Abu Bakr chose is that it is some of the necessary sciences, like the knowledge of the impossibility of the joining of two opposites, that there is no intermediary between negation and affirmation, that an existent cannot be outside being either eternal or originated, and similar things. Imam al-Haramayn argued for the correctness of this and the invalidity of what is other than it, with what al-Amidi mentioned in Ibkar al-Afkar, with what is for it and against it. Al-Muhasibi, may God have mercy on him, chose that it is an innate disposition (gharīza) through which one reaches knowledge. This was refuted by saying: If by innate disposition he means knowledge, then what applies to the one who says it is knowledge applies to him; and if he means by it something other than knowledge, then it may not be granted that there exists something beyond knowledge through which one reaches knowledge.

[Page 169]

The author of al-Qamus, after relating several sayings on intellect, said: "The truth is that it is a spiritual light by which the soul perceives necessary and theoretical sciences. Perhaps we will verify this in another place, if God, exalted is He, wills." Then, regarding the locus of knowledge in the heart, there is disagreement among the intelligent. The well-known view of the philosophers is that the locus of knowledge concerning universals and abstracted particulars is the rational soul, and the locus of knowledge concerning material particulars is bodily faculties established in specific parts of the body, which are divided into five outward and five inward. The first are called the outer senses, and the second the inner senses, and the matter of each is well known.

Some later philosophizing scholars claimed that the perceiver of universals and particulars is only the soul, and the faculties in general do not perceive, but are rather instruments in the soul's perception. Some of us also held this view. In Ibkar al-Afkar, after relating the view of the philosophers, it is said: "As for our companions, a particular structure is not a condition for them; rather, every part of the human body in which perception and knowledge subsists is a perceiver and a knower. Whether that which subsists is in the heart or in something else is not necessary by reason, nor is it impossible. But the Law has indicated subsistence in the heart, by His exalted saying: ﴿Indeed, in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart﴾ [Qaf: 37], and His glorified saying: ﴿so that they would have hearts with which they understand﴾, and His mighty and majestic saying: ﴿Then do they not reflect upon the Qur'an, or are there locks upon their hearts?﴾ [Muhammad: 24]." End of quotation. It is not hidden that the argument from what was mentioned for the locus of knowledge being the heart is not free of problems. Yet it cannot be denied that the verses indicate that the human heart, by what has been deposited in it, has a complete role in perception, and experience testifies to the role of what is deposited in the brain in that as well.
