For this reason, I see no justification for saying that one of them has a role to the exclusion of the other. The fact that a person may be struck on the head and lose his intellect does not indicate that only what is deposited in the brain has a role in knowledge, as is not hidden from one who has a sound heart and an upright mind. So reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 47:

﴿They ask you to hasten the punishment﴾. The pronoun refers to the Quraysh. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to warn them of God's punishment and threaten them with its coming, but they denied this in the strongest terms. They asked for its coming in mockery and as a challenge to him (ﷺ), so God rebuked them for this. The sentence is a declarative in form, but in meaning it is interrogative and exhortative. God's words ﴿And God will not fail His promise﴾ form a circumstantial clause (jumlah ḥāliyyah), brought to show the falsehood of their denial of the punishment within their demand for it. It is as if it were said: "How do you deny the coming of the promised punishment, when God does not fail His promise, and the promise has already been made, so it must come?" Or it may be a parenthetical clause (i'tirāḍiyyah) for the same reason. God's words ﴿And indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count﴾ form a new independent clause (jumlah mustaʾnafah) if the first was circumstantial, and a coordinated clause (maʿṭūfah) on it if the first was parenthetical. It was brought to confirm the denial of hastening and to show their error in it, by showing the complete breadth of His forbearance (ḥilm) and the extreme narrowness of their own patience. This entails that a short period with Him is a long period for them, as His words indicate: ﴿Indeed, they see it as far off, but We see it as near﴾ [al-Maʿārij: 6–7]. Hence they regard its coming as distant, take this as a pretext to deny it, and dare to hasten it, not realising that the measure by which all matters are estimated, in their occurrence and in their report, is what is with Him.

The reading of al-Akhawayn (the two brothers) and Ibn Kathir is ﴿ya‘uddūn﴾ (يَعُدُّونَ) in the third person, meaning: "the hasteners count it", which fits this meaning better. In the reading of the majority, the address has also been made to them, by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person). But the apparent sense is that the address is to the Messenger (ﷺ) and those believers with him. It has been said that the meaning of "His promise" is what has been appointed for the destruction of each nation, a fixed term and a specified time, as in His words: ﴿They ask you to hasten the punishment; had there not been a term appointed, the punishment would have come upon them﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 53]. In that case, the first clause is an absolute statement showing the falsehood of hastening it, by showing the impossibility of its coming before its appointed time. The last clause is a demonstration of its falsehood by showing that it is based on the lengthening of what is short in His sight, in the manner already explained. In that case, there is no reference in the noble text to their denial of its coming, which they slipped in beneath the demand for hastening. The refutation of this is sufficed by showing the outcome of those before them who were like them. Whatever the case, the punishment that is demanded to be hastened is the worldly punishment, which is what the context (sibāq) and the wider setting (siyāq) require.

It has also been said that the punishment means the punishment of the Hereafter, and the day mentioned is the day of that punishment, which is lengthened because of its severity, for days of sorrow are long and days of joy are short, as it has been said:

*Enjoy the days of joy, for they are short,
while the days of sorrow are long.*

On this basis comes his saying:

*My night and Layla's night differ in my sleep
in length and length; how blessed if they were balanced.*

*My night grants length whenever Layla's night withholds it,
and if Layla's night grants length, my night withholds it.*

Thus the first clause answers their denial of the coming of the punishment, and the second rebukes them for hastening it, even though this is said in mockery. It is as if it were said: "How do you deny its coming, when the promise has already been made and God will not fail His promise, so it must come without fail? And how do you hasten it, when one day of its days, because of its severity, is seen as a thousand years of what you count?" The same may be said on the view that the day means one of the days of the Hereafter, for they are regarded as long, or because they are lengthened by the severity of their punishment.

It has been objected that this is something that neither the context (sibāq) nor the wider setting (siyāq) supports. Al-Farra' said: the verse includes both the punishment of this world and that of the Hereafter. The punishment demanded to be hastened is the punishment of this world, meaning: God will not fail His promise to send punishment upon you in this world, and indeed a day of your punishment in the Hereafter is like a thousand years of the years of this world. This is not without merit, but it contains some remoteness, as is not hidden.

The Mu'tazila (Mu'tazilites, a theological school) used God's words ﴿God will not fail His promise﴾ as evidence that God does not forgive the disobedient, since the "promise" here carries the sense of a threat, and God has informed us that He does not fail it, while forgiveness would entail failing it, which would entail lying, which is impossible for Him, exalted is He.

Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah, the orthodox majority) replied that the threats of the other disobedient sinners are either declarative statements or reports about their deserving what they were threatened with, not about its actual enactment. Where they are reports about its enactment, they are conditional on the absence of pardon, and the condition is omitted to increase the intimidation. This is not the case with the threats against the unbelievers, which are pure reports about the enactment, not conditional on any condition at all, like the promises to believers. The motive for the distinction is the reconciling of the verses. You know that the apparent sense of this is that the threats of the unbelievers with worldly punishment are like their threats with the punishment of the Hereafter: they are not open to non-fulfilment, so pardon for their punishment is not permitted in any case once it has been promised. In my view there is some hesitation in equating the two cases. It is known from this what the status of this reply is if the punishment in the verse is taken to be worldly punishment, which is most fitting to the context, and the promise is taken to be the promise of it.

Some have answered here that the promise meant is God's promise of respite and postponement, which is the opposite of a threat from the point of view of the one who postpones. There is no disagreement that God does not fail the promise that is the opposite of a threat, and that what is expressed by it is a pure report with no condition attached. It has also been said that the promise meant is God's promise to His Prophet (ﷺ) to send down the punishment that was demanded to be hastened upon them, and this is the opposite of a threat in that it contains good for him, upon him be blessings and peace. There is no barrier to one thing being good and bad at once in relation to two persons, as it has been said: "The calamities of one people are benefits to another." In that case, the Mu'tazila have no proof in the verse for their claim.

[Page 171]

﴿And how many a town﴾, that is, how many inhabitants of a town. ﴿I gave it respite﴾, just as I gave respite to these people, until they denied the coming of the punishment that He had promised and hastened it, mocking and challenging their messengers, peace be upon them, just as these people did. The clause is coordinated (ʿaṭf, grammatical coordination) with what precedes it. It was brought in to confirm the rebuttal, as has already been mentioned, and so the particle ﴿wa﴾ (and) is used. In its previous parallel instance, the particle used was ﴿fa﴾ (so). It has been said that this is because that clause was a substitute (badal) for a clause linked to it by ﴿fa﴾, and repeating ﴿fa﴾ confirms the relation of substitution. It has also been said that ﴿fa﴾ was used there because the clause follows from what came before it, whereas it was not used here because there is no such sequence. His statement, exalted is He, ﴿while it was wrongdoing﴾, is a circumstantial clause (ḥāliyyah, a clause describing the state of the subject) which conveys the perfection of His forbearance, exalted is He, and hints indirectly at the wrongdoing of those who hasten the punishment. That is: I gave it respite while it was in a state of wrongdoing, deserving the hastening of punishment, just as these people do. ﴿Then I seized it﴾ with punishment and retribution after a long period of respite and reprieve. ﴿And to Me is the destination﴾, that is, the return of all people, or of all the inhabitants of the town, is to My judgment, not to anyone other than Me, neither independently nor as a partner. So I will deal with them as is fitting for their deeds. This clause is a concluding parenthetical (iʿtirāḍ tadhyīlī, an appended clause that closes a passage with a general statement) which confirms what precedes it and explicitly states what was conveyed indirectly, namely that the end of those who hasten the punishment is also the severe seizure that has been mentioned.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 49:

﴿Say: O mankind, I am but a clear warner to you.﴾ The apparent context requires that by "mankind" (al-nas) the polytheists (al-mushrikun) are meant, for the discourse is directed at them. It is as if it were said: "Say, O polytheists who are hastening the punishment: I am but a warner to you, a clear warning, with what has been revealed to me (ilayya) of the news of the destroyed nations, without my having any part in bringing about the punishment you are hastening, the promised punishment, such that you could hasten me to it." The reason for restricting the role to warning is therefore evident.

The reason the believers and their reward are mentioned in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So those who believe and do righteous deeds, for them is forgiveness and noble provision﴾, is the increase in enraging the polytheists. So, in terms of its outcome, it is a warning. It is also permissible to say that His saying, glorified is He, ﴿So those who believe﴾ and what follows, is a detailing of those among the polytheistic people in whom the warning was effective, and of those who remained on their disbelief, in whom it was not effective. As if it were said: "Warn, O Muhammad, these disbelievers who seek to hasten the punishment, and press them hard. So whoever believes and turns back from what he is upon, for him is such-and-such; and whoever persists in his disbelief and continues in what he is upon, for him is such-and-such." Al-Tibi chose this, and it is, as in al-Kashshaf, good. Upon it, the division does not fall within what is said, unlike the first aspect.

Some of the verifiers said: "The people" is general, encompassing the believer and the disbeliever, and the one warned of is the establishment of the Hour. He, peace and blessings be upon him, was a clear warner only because his mission is among its portents. So warning was combined in him in speech and in state, by His saying: ﴿I am to you a clear warner﴾, like his saying (ﷺ), in the authentic collections of al-Bukhari and Muslim: "I am the naked warner." The context also indicates this, since the address is followed by a warning that details the condition of the two groups when it occurs. End of quotation.

There is no barrier to this, were it not for the apparent context. That the believers are not warned, especially since among them are the righteous and the wicked, is something without basis. Whoever prevented generality in this respect said: the estimate is "upon it a bringer of glad tidings and a warner." This is transmitted from al-Kirmani.

Then, forgiveness may be for what slipped from the believers of sins, and that does not contradict describing them as doing righteous deeds. It may also be for what preceded from them before faith and turning back from what they were upon. The noble provision here means Paradise, as its occurrence after forgiveness suggests, and likewise throughout the Qur'an, according to what Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi. The meaning of "noble" (karim) in attributes other than those of human beings is the one surpassing

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 51:

﴿And those who strive against Our signs﴾ i.e., they exert effort in nullifying them, calling them at one time sorcery, at another time poetry, and at another time "the myths of the ancients."

Page 172

The origin of sa'y (striving, effort) is hastening in walking, and it is also used for reform and corruption. One says: "He strove (sa'a) in the affair of so-and-so," if he reformed it or corrupted it by his striving in it. ﴿Seeking to frustrate [them]﴾ i.e., competing with the believers. The meaning of their competition is their opposition to them and their contesting with them: whenever the believers sought to make the truth manifest, these people sought to nullify it. Its origin is from "ʿājazahu, fa-ʾaʿjazahu" and "ʿajjazahu," when one competes with another and outdoes him, for each of the two competitors wants to make the other unable to catch up.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, al-Jahdari, Abu al-Sammal and al-Za'faranI read "(muʿajjizīn)" with a shadda (tashdid), i.e., discouraging people from faith.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "Attributing the Muslims to incapacity (ʿajz)," just as you say: "fasaqtu fulānan" when you attribute someone to wickedness (fisq). This is what fits His words, exalted is He: ﴿They ask you to hasten the punishment﴾.

Ibn al-Zubayr read "(muʿjizīn)" with a sukun on the ʿayn and a lightened zāy, from "aʿjazaka" when he outran you and escaped you. The author of al-Lawami said: "What is meant here is those who think that they will defeat us, because they think they will not be raised." The reading of the majority, "(muʿājizīn)," was interpreted in the same way. The description, in all readings, is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the pronoun in (saʿaw), and it is not a future (muqaddarah) state in any of them, as becomes clear to the attentive reader. ﴿Those﴾, described as mentioned, ﴿are the companions of the Blazing Fire﴾, i.e., those who remain constantly in the intensely blazing fire; and it has been said that it is the name of one of the levels (darakāt) of the Fire.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 52:

﴿And We did not send before you any messenger or prophet but that when he wished, Satan cast into his wish.﴾ The first "min" (in "min qablika") is for the beginning of the extent (ibtida'iyyah), and the second "min" (in "min rasulin") is extra (mazidah) for the comprehensiveness of the category. The clause introduced by "idha" (when) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) according to Abu Hayyan. It has also been said that it is in the position of a qualifying clause (sifah). The pronoun is given in the singular with regard to "each one," or with the implied presence of a clause similar to the one mentioned, as has been said regarding His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 62]. The apparent reading is that "idha" is conditional, and al-Hawfi stated this explicitly. However, they said that "illa" in negation is either followed by a present-tense verb, as in "ma Zaydun illa yaf'alu" and "ma ra'aytu Zaydan illa yaf'alu," or followed by a past-tense verb on condition that a verb precedes it, as in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And there did not come to them any messenger but that they mocked him﴾ [al-Hijr: 11], etc., or the past tense is accompanied by "qad," as in "ma Zaydun illa qad qama." This verse presents a difficulty for this view, since neither a present-tense verb nor a past-tense verb follows "illa" in it, but rather a conditional clause. If what they said is correct, then interpretation is needed. In al-Bahr it was interpreted that "idha" has been stripped of its conditional force for the sense of time (zarfiyyah), and it has been separated, together with what it is attached to, between "illa" and the past-tense verb which is "alqa." This separation is permissible, so "illa qad" is followed by a past-tense verb in estimation, and the condition is fulfilled.

The conjunction of "nabiyyin" over "rasulin" indicates the difference between them, and this is the common view. The difference is also indicated by what has been narrated: that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the prophets, and he said: "One hundred and twenty-four thousand." It was said: "And how many of them were messengers?" He said: "Three hundred and thirteen, a great throng." This has been transmitted, as al-Suyuti said, by Ahmad and Ibn Rahawayh in their Musnads, from the hadith of Abu Umamah, and Ibn Hibban transmitted it in his Sahih, and al-Hakim in his Mustadrak from the hadith of Abu Dharr.

Ibn al-Jawzi claimed that it is fabricated (mawdu'), but this is not so. Yes, it was said that there is weakness in its chain, which is compensated by corroborating narrations (al-mutaba'ah). In one narration it came: "The messengers were three hundred and fifteen."

Here they differed over the explanation of each of the two terms. It was said: The messenger (rasul) is a free male whom Allah, exalted is He, sent with a new law (shar') which he calls people to, and the prophet (nabi) is more general than him, and includes the one sent to affirm a previous law, like the prophets of the Children of Israel who were between Musa and Isa, peace be upon them. It was also said: The messenger is a free male whom Allah, exalted is He, sent to a people with a law that is new with respect to them, even if it is not new in itself, like Isma'il, peace be upon him, since he was sent first to Jurhum. The prophet is more general than him, and includes the one sent with a law that is not new in this way. It was also said: The messenger is a free male who has a message (tabligh) in general, even if it is an explanation and elaboration of a previous law, and the prophet is one to whom revelation is sent but who is not commanded to convey it at all, or he is more general than that and than the messenger. It was also said: Among the prophets, the messenger is one who combined with a miracle a book revealed to him, and the prophet is other than the messenger, one who has no book. It was also said: The messenger is one who has a book or abrogation (naskh) in general, and the prophet is one who has no book and no abrogation. It was also said: The messenger is one to whom the angel comes with revelation while awake, and the prophet is the term applied to one to whom revelation comes in a dream only. This is the strangest of the views, and it implies that some of the prophets, peace be upon them, were not revealed to except in dreams, and this is far-fetched, and such a thing is not said by opinion alone.

You know that the well-known view is that "nabi" in the usage of the Shari'ah is more general than "rasul," for he is one to whom revelation is sent, whether or not he is commanded to convey it, while the "rasul" is one to whom revelation is sent and who is commanded to convey it. It is not valid to intend this here, because when the general is compared with the specific, the general is intended to mean what is other than the specific. So whenever "nabi" is intended to mean other than "rasul," it means one who has not been commanded to convey, and wherever sending (irsal) is attached to him, he becomes commanded to convey, and so he is a messenger. Thus, in the verse, after sending is attached, there remains no messenger with a prophet opposed to him. Therefore, to realize the opposition, it is necessary that "rasul" be intended to mean one sent with a new law, and "nabi" one sent to affirm the law of one before him. Or "rasul" may be intended as one sent with a book, and "nabi" as one sent without a book, or something similar by which the opposition is realized, while sending is attached to both of them.

"Tamanni" (wishing), according to what Abu Muslim said, is the end of estimation (nihayat al-taqdir), and from it comes "al-maniyyah," the death of a person at the time that Allah, exalted is He, has decreed. "Al-umniyyah," according to what al-Raghib said, is the image formed in the soul from wishing. Many others said: "Tamanni" is recitation, and likewise "umniyyah." They recited the verse of Hassan about Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him:

He wished for the Book of Allah on the first night, / Just as Dawud wished for the Zabur with a steady pace.

In al-Bahr, it is said that this goes back to the origin transmitted from Abu Muslim, for the reciter estimates the letters and imagines them, then mentions them one by one. What is meant here, according to many, is recitation. The verse is brought to console the Prophet (ﷺ) that the striving to nullify the verses is a familiar matter, and that this striving is rejected. The meaning is: We did not send before you any messenger or prophet but that, in his state, when he recited some of the verses, Satan cast doubts and fancies into what he recited to his allies, so that they might dispute with him in falsehood and reject what he brought, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed the devils inspire to their allies that they may dispute with you﴾ [al-An'am: 121], and He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy: devils of mankind and jinn, inspiring one another with decorated speech as deception﴾ [al-An'am: 112]. This is like their saying, when they heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recite: ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ [al-Baqarah: 173; al-Nahl: 115], that he makes lawful what he slaughters himself and makes unlawful what Allah slaughters. And their saying, as in some narrations, when they heard his recitation, peace and blessings be upon him: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya': 98], that Isa was worshipped besides Allah, and the angels, peace be upon them, were worshipped besides Allah.

﴿Then Allah abolishes what Satan casts﴾, that is, He nullifies what he casts of those doubts and removes it, through the granting of success to the Prophet (ﷺ) to refute it, or by sending down what refutes it. ﴿Then Allah makes His verses firm﴾, that is, He brings them firm and established, not accepting refutation in any way whatsoever. ("Thumma," then) is for the gradation of rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), for making firm is higher in rank than abrogation. The present-tense form in both verbs is to indicate continuity and renewal. Mentioning the Divine Name (al-Jalalah) in the place of the pronoun is for the increase of confirmation, and to signal that divinity is among the requirements of the firmness of His dazzling verses, exalted is He. Similar to this for the increase of confirmation is the mention of Satan. ﴿And Allah is Knowing﴾, emphatic in knowledge of everything that is appropriate to be known, and among that is what proceeds from Satan and his allies. ﴿Wise﴾ in every thing He does, and among that is His enabling Satan to cast doubts and His allies to dispute with them, and His manifesting its refutation. The explicit mention here is for what has been mentioned, and also with what it contains of emphasizing the independence of the concluding parenthetical objection (al-i'tiraḍ al-tadhyili).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 53:

﴿So that He may make what Satan casts﴾, i.e., that which he casts. It was said: his casting is ﴿a trial﴾, i.e., a punishment. In al-Bahr (Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit), it is a testing and an examination ﴿for those in whose hearts is a disease﴾, i.e., doubt and hypocrisy. This suits His saying, exalted is He, about the hypocrites: ﴿in their hearts is a disease﴾. Specifying the disease as being in the heart supports this, since their disbelief is not made apparent, unlike the open disbeliever. ﴿And those whose hearts are hardened﴾, i.e., the open disbelievers. It was said: what is meant by the first group is the disbelievers in general, and by the latter, their elites, such as Abu Jahl, al-Nadr and Utba. The first group was taken to mean disbelievers absolutely, and the latter to mean the hypocrites, because they are more deserving of the attribute of hardness, since the rust of their hearts is not polished away by the burnishing of mixing with the believers. This is nothing.

﴿Indeed the wrongdoers﴾, i.e., the two groups mentioned. The apparent noun was placed in the position of their pronoun to record wrongdoing against them, along with what they were described with of disease and hardness. ﴿Are in a far-off schism﴾, i.e., intense enmity and complete opposition. The schism is described as "far-off," though the one truly described as such is its bearer, for emphasis (mubalaghah). The sentence is a concluding parenthetical aside (i'tiraḍ tadhyili, an afterthought that closes the statement), confirming what precedes it.

The lām of li-yaj'ala is the lām of purpose (lam al-ta'lil). According to al-Hawfi, it is connected to yuhkimu; according to Ibn 'Atiyya, to yansakhu; and according to others, to ulqiya. However, the causation pertains to what the casting of Satan indicates of His, exalted is He, enabling him to do that in regard to the Prophet (ﷺ) specifically, due to the coordination (ʿaṭf)

[Page 175 is a page marker in the source and is not part of the commentary.]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That those who have been given knowledge may know that it is the truth from your Lord﴾. The pronoun in (أنَّهُ) may refer to the Qur'an. It was also said there is no need for specification (*takhsis*, restricting the reference to one thing), and that the pronoun in (أنَّهُ) refers to God's granting Satan power to cast (suggestions). That is, ﴿that those who have knowledge may know﴾ that this granting of power is the truth, containing far-reaching wisdom, because it is among the things in which God's custom has proceeded concerning the human species since Adam, peace be upon him. The two pronouns in (بِهِ) and (لَهُ) in His saying, ﴿so that they may believe in it﴾, mean: they may remain firm in faith or increase in faith. ﴿And their hearts may humble themselves to it﴾ through submission and fear, to the Qur'an according to the specification, and to the Lord according to the generalization (*ta'mim*, applying the reference broadly). He made both pronouns refer to God's granting Satan power, and the second in particular has no basis.

He preferred what Ibn 'Atiyya said, because the wording of the causal clause (*al-ta'lil*) points to it more clearly. That is, God abrogates (*naskh*, the cancellation of a ruling or text by a later one) what Satan casts and removes it, so that by this removal, and by the manifestation of the corruption of holding to it, it becomes a punishment (*'adhab*) for the hypocrites and disbelievers, meaning a cause of their punishment, since they went along with it even though its corruption was manifest. Or it is a test for them, to see whether they will turn back from it. And ﴿that those who have been given knowledge may know﴾ that the Qur'an is the truth, since what was brought against it of doubts was refuted while it itself was not refuted. Something similar may be said according to the view of al-Hawfi. It is not far-fetched that His saying, ﴿that He may make﴾ and so on, is connected to an omitted element, meaning: He did that so that He may make (لِيَجْعَلَ) and so on, and the reference is to abrogation and making firm. Thus (لِيَجْعَلَ) is the cause of the abrogation, and (وَلِيَعْلَمَ) is the cause of the act of bringing the verses as firmly established. It is also possible that the reference is to the granting of power understood from what preceded, together with the abrogation and making firm, and that (لِيَجْعَلَ) is the cause of the act of granting power, while what follows is the cause of what follows. It is also possible that the pronouns in (أنَّهُ)، (بِهِ) and (لَهُ) refer to the revelation that every one of the Messengers and Prophets, peace be upon them, recited, which is understood from the speech, so there is no need for specification. Whichever of these is the case, His saying, ﴿Indeed God guides those who believe to a straight path﴾, is a parenthetical clause confirming what precedes it. By ﴿those who believe﴾ is meant the believers of this community according to the specified reading, or believers in general according to the generalized reading. By "the straight path" is meant the sound reasoning that leads to the clear truth. That is, He, exalted is He, guides the believers in religious matters, especially in slippery and difficult matters, among which is the refutation of the doubts of the devils concerning the verses of God, mighty and majestic.

Abu Haywa and Ibn Abi 'Absa read (لَهادٍ) with tanwin.

﴿And those who disbelieve will not cease to be in doubt﴾ about it, meaning in doubt ﴿concerning it﴾, meaning concerning the Qur'an. It has also been said that it refers to the Messenger. It is permissible for the pronoun to refer to the one who conveys the revelation, as you have heard. The "min" (from/concerning) in all of these readings is ibtida'iyyah (indicating the starting point). It has also been allowed that the pronoun refers to "what Satan cast," and it has been preferred for this reading that "min" is sababiyyah (indicating causation). The doubt of the disbelievers regarding what the messengers, peace be upon them, brought is caused by what Satan cast into the revelation of doubts and imaginings. So reflect on this. ﴿Until the Hour comes upon them﴾, meaning the Resurrection itself, as is indicated by His words, exalted is He: ﴿suddenly﴾, meaning unexpectedly, for it is the Hour that is described as coming in this manner. It has also been said that what is meant is its signs, with an ellipsis of the genitive (idafah) or by metonymy (tajawwuz). It has also been said that what is meant is death, with the definite article in "the Hour" being for specific reference (al-'ahd). ﴿Or there comes upon them the punishment of a barren day﴾, meaning a day singular and set apart from all other days, with no equal in its severity, or a day after which there is no day, as if every day gives birth to the days that follow it, so the day after which there is no day is barren. What is intended by it is also the Hour, in the sense of the Day of Resurrection. It is as if it were said: "or its punishment comes upon them." That is why this is placed in the position of its pronoun, for the sake of greater awe and warning. The "aw" (or) here is for the difference between the Hour and its punishment, and it serves to prevent the absence of both, the intent being to emphasize their persistence in doubt. It has also been said that what is meant by a barren day is the day of their death, for there is no day after it with respect to them. It has also been said that what is meant is a day of war in which they are killed. It is described as barren because the sons of women are killed in it, so the women become as though they were barren and had never given birth. Or it is because fighters are called "sons of war," so when they are killed the day of war is described as barren. In the first reading there is majaz in the predication (majaz fi al-isnad) and majaz in the single word, by making bereavement into barrenness. The same applies to the second reading, because the fertile and the barren here refer to war by way of isti'arah bil-kinayah (metaphor by allusion). So when the day of war is described with this, it is majaz in the predication. For this reason it has been said that it is majaz muwajjah (a figure with two faces), from the expression "a garment with two faces" (thawb muwajjah), meaning it has two aspects. It has also been said that barren means that which has no good in it. It is said, "a barren wind," when it brings no rain and fertilizes no trees. In this reading there is isti'arah tab'iyyah (a dependent metaphor), because the quality in the day that prevents good is treated as barrenness. Many have specified this day as the Day of Badr, for it was a day of war in which the arrogant disbelievers were killed, and it was a day with no good for them. It is also valid that its description as barren refers to the fact that the angels, peace be upon them, uniquely fought in it. You know that the apparent meaning, from what follows, God willing, determines that this day is to be interpreted as the Day of Resurrection.

This is the end of the discussion. It has also been permitted that "Satan" here means the devil among humans, like al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who used to cast doubts to his people and to the visitors, discouraging them from Islam by them. It has also been said that the pronoun in ﴿his wish﴾ refers to Satan, and what is meant by it is the image that forms in the soul from wishing for something. The "fi" (in) is sababiyyah here, like its use in his (ﷺ) saying: "A woman entered the Fire because of a cat." That is, Satan cast doubts by reason of his wish and displayed them in order to nullify the verses. It has also been said that "tamanna" means "recited," and "umniyyatuhu" means "his recitation," and the pronoun refers to the Prophet or the Messenger. The "fi" (in) is then in its apparent sense. What is meant by "what Satan casts" is what happens to the reciter: replacing a word with another word, a letter with another letter, or changing the i'rab (grammatical inflection) by mistake. It has also been said that what is meant is what he casts into the ambiguous verses of possible meanings that are not what God, exalted is He, intends. It has also been said that "tamanna" means "he prepared and determined in his soul what he desires," and "umniyyatuhu" means "his recitation." The meaning is that when he wished for the faith and guidance of his people, Satan cast doubts to his allies, and God, exalted is He, abrogates those doubts (yansakh) and makes the verses that refute them firm (yuhkim). It has also been said that "tamanna" means "he determined in his soul what he desires," and "umniyyatihi" is a simile (tashbih). What Satan casts is what causes him to be occupied with worldly affairs. Making this a trial is in light of what appears from him of occupation with worldly affairs, and its abrogation (naskh) is its nullification, by His protecting him from inclining toward it and by guiding him to what adorns it.

It has also been said that "tamanna" means "he recited," and "umniyyatihi" means "his recitation." What Satan casts are words resembling the revelation, which Satan speaks in such a way that the listener thinks they are from the Prophet's recitation. It has been reported that this verse was revealed when he (peace be upon him) recited: ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza﴾ ﴿and Manat, the third, the other﴾. Then Satan cast into his pause, imitating his tone, so that those around him heard: "Those are the exalted cranes, and their intercession is indeed to be hoped for." The polytheists thought that he (peace be upon him) was the one who said this, so they rejoiced and prostrated with him when he prostrated at the end of the sura. It has also been said that the one who said this was some of the polytheists, and the rest thought that he (peace be upon him) was the one who said it. It has also been said that he (may God bless him and grant him peace) was the one who said this, intentionally, but in the form of a question, as a denunciation and an argument against the polytheists. It is attributed to Satan's casting because of what followed from it, namely the polytheists' assumption that it was praise for their gods. This does not preclude that he (peace be upon him) was praying, because speech during prayer was permitted at that time. It has also been said: rather, he was heedless. 'Abd ibn Humayd reported through the route of Yunus, from Ibn Shihab, who said: Abu Bakr ibn 'Abd al-Rahman told me that "the Messenger of God (may God bless him and grant him peace), while in Mecca, recited to them al-Najm, and when he reached ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza﴾ ﴿and Manat, the third, the other﴾ [al-Najm 19–20], he said: 'Their intercession is indeed to be hoped for,' and the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) forgot, so the polytheists rejoiced at that. Then he (may God bless him and grant him peace) said: 'Surely that is from Satan.' Then God revealed ﴿And We did not send﴾ until ﴿the punishment of a barren day﴾." Al-Jalal al-Suyuti said: this is a mursal report (a report in which the Successor omits the Companion from the chain), with a sound chain.

It has also been said: he said it while drowsy. Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah, who said: "While the Prophet of God (may God bless him and grant him peace) was praying near the Station (maqam), he dozed, and Satan cast a word upon his tongue, and he spoke it: ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza﴾ ﴿and Manat, the third, the other﴾, and indeed their intercession is to be hoped for, and indeed they are with the exalted cranes." The polytheists memorized it, and Satan informed them that the Prophet of God (may God bless him and grant him peace) had recited it. So their tongues slipped, and God revealed ﴿And We did not send﴾ the verse.

It has also been said: "tamanna" means "he determined in his soul what he desires," and "umniyyatihi" means "his recitation," and what Satan casts are words resembling the revelation. Ibn Abi Hatim reported through the route of Musa ibn 'Uqbah, from Ibn Shihab, who said: "Surat al-Najm was revealed, and the polytheists used to say: 'If this man mentioned our gods with good, we would acknowledge him and his companions. But he does not mention those who oppose his religion among the Jews and Christians with the same kind of abuse and evil that he speaks of our gods.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was greatly distressed by what his companions suffered from their harm and denial, and their misguidance grieved him, so he used to wish for their guidance. When God revealed Surat al-Najm, he said: ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza﴾ ﴿and Manat, the third, the other﴾, Satan cast at that point words, and he said: 'Indeed they are the exalted cranes, and their intercession is indeed the one to be hoped for.' That was from Satan's rhyming and his temptation. These two words fell into the heart of every polytheist in Mecca, their tongues slipped with them, and they rejoiced at them and said: 'Muhammad has returned to his original religion and the religion of his people.' When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) reached the end of al-Najm, he prostrated, and everyone present, Muslim or polytheist, prostrated too. That word spread among the people, and Satan publicized it until it reached the land of Abyssinia. Then God revealed ﴿And We did not send﴾ the verses."

It has also been said that when Satan cast it, the Prophet (ﷺ) spoke it, thinking it was revelation, until Gabriel (peace be upon him) alerted him. Al-Suyuti, in al-Durr al-Manthur, reported that Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim, through a sound chain, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, said: "The Messenger of God (may God bless him and grant him peace) recited al-Najm in Mecca, and when he reached ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza﴾ ﴿and Manat, the third, the other﴾, Satan cast upon his tongue: 'Those are the exalted cranes, and indeed their intercession is to be hoped for.' They said: 'He has not mentioned our gods with good before today.' So he prostrated, and they prostrated. Then Gabriel (peace be upon them both) came to him after that and said: 'Present to me what I brought you.' When he reached 'Those are the exalted cranes, and indeed their intercession is to be hoped for,' Gabriel (peace be upon them both) said to him: 'I did not bring you this. This is from Satan.' Then God revealed ﴿And We did not send﴾ the verse."

Al-Bazzar, al-Tabari, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah reported, through a route whose narrators are trustworthy, from Sa'id, from Ibn 'Abbas, something similar, but without the account of the prostration, and it contains some other minor differences. The account of the prostration appears in another report from him, which al-Bazzar and Ibn Mardawayh also reported through the route of Umayyah ibn Khalid, from Shu'bah. However, in its chain he said: "from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, as I think," so he doubted its continuity (wasl). In Abu Hatim's report from al-Suddi: "When Gabriel (peace be upon him) said to him, when this was presented to him: 'God forbid that I recited this to you,' it weighed heavily upon him (peace be upon him), so God revealed and comforted his soul: ﴿And We did not send﴾ the verse."

It has been said: the resemblance is between what Satan cast and the revelation that was sent down, and its occurrence in the midst of it. The term naskh (abrogation), which is commonly applied to what is truly revelation, has been used for its nullification. However, it is not hidden that legal abrogation (al-naskh al-shar'i) does not apply to reports like those mentioned. Therefore, a reinterpretation of these reports is necessary. Many verifying scholars (muhaqqiqun) have rejected this story. Al-Bayhaqi said: "This story is not established through transmission." Qadi 'Iyad said in al-Shifa': "It is sufficient to weaken this hadith that none of the people of authentic reports has recorded it, nor has any trustworthy narrator transmitted it through a sound, unbroken chain. It was only the exegetes and historians, who are fond of everything strange and who take from the pages every sound and unsound report, who became attached to it and to the like of it."

It is also mentioned in *al-Bahr* that Imam Muhammad ibn Ishaq, compiler of the Prophetic biography (*al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah*), was asked about this story and said: "This is a fabrication of the zanadiqa (heretics)," and he wrote a book on that matter. Shaykh Abu Mansur al-Maturidi mentioned in *Hasis al-Atqiya'* that the correct view is that his saying, "Those are the exalted cranes (*gharaniq*), whose intercession is hoped for," is part of what Satan inspired to his allies among the zanadiqa, in order to cast it among the weak and the feeble in faith, so that they would doubt the soundness of the religion. The sanctity of the Message is free of such a report. Several scholars have mentioned that, according to the view that the one who uttered this was the Prophet (ﷺ), because of Satan's casting disguised as the angel, there follow several matters:

First, that Satan had power over him (peace be upon him), whereas he (ﷺ) is by consensus (*ijma'*) protected from Satan, especially in matters of revelation, conveyance and belief. Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them﴾ [al-Hijr 15:42; al-Isra' 17:65]. And He the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe﴾ [al-Nahl 16:99], and other such verses.

Second, that he (ﷺ) added to the Qur'an what was not part of it, which is impossible for him (peace be upon him) because of his infallibility.

Third, that the Prophet (ﷺ) believed that what was not Qur'an was Qur'an, although it is incoherent, self-contradictory, and mixes praise with blame. This is a grave error, and one should not be lax in attributing it to him (ﷺ).

Fourth, that when he (peace be upon him) uttered it, he either believed what the polytheists believed, namely the praise of their gods with those words, and this is impossible for him (ﷺ) as disbelief; or he believed a different meaning contrary to what they believed and contrary to the apparent wording, and did not clarify it to them, although they rejoiced and claimed that he had praised their gods. Thus he would be approving of them in falsehood, and far be it from him (ﷺ) to approve of that.

Fifth, that what Satan cast became confused for him (ﷺ) with what the angel cast upon him. This implies that he (peace be upon him) was not certain about what was revealed to him. It also implies the permissibility of Satan appearing in the form of an angel, deceiving the Prophet. This is not valid, as he (ﷺ) said in *al-Shifa'*, neither at the beginning of the prophethood nor after it. The reliance in this matter is the evidence of the miracle.

Ibn al-Arabi said: Satan's appearing in the form of an angel to deceive the Prophet is like his appearing in the form of the Prophet to deceive people, and Allah's empowering him in this is like His empowering him in that. How then can it be permissible for a sound mind to deem this acceptable?

Sixth, that he (ﷺ) forged words against Allah the Exalted, whether deliberately, by mistake, or through forgetfulness. All of this is impossible for him (peace be upon him). The Ummah has agreed, as al-Qadi Iyad said, on his infallibility (ﷺ) in what was his path of conveying of statements, regarding reporting contrary to reality, neither intentionally nor through forgetfulness.

Seventh, that it undermines trust in the Qur'an, so that alteration and change cannot be ruled out. This is not resolved, as al-Baydawi said, by the words of the Exalted: ﴿Then Allah abolishes what Satan casts, then Allah establishes His verses﴾ [al-Hajj 22:52], because this also admits of other interpretations.

Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar, in his commentary on al-Bukhari, held the soundness of the report, and cited chains from Ibn Abbas and others. Then he said: "All of them, apart from the chain of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, are either weak or disconnected (*munqati'*). But the abundance of chains indicates that it has a basis. Moreover, there is a connected chain with a sound isnad, which al-Bazzar narrated, and two other mursal chains whose narrators meet the conditions of the Two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim). One of them is what al-Tabari narrated through Yunus ibn Zayd from Ibn Shihab, and the second is what he also narrated through al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman and Hammad ibn Salama, both from Dawud ibn Abi Hind, from Abu al-'Aliyah." Then he began to refute Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi and al-Qadi Iyad in their denial of its soundness.

Also holding the soundness of the story was the last of the later scholars, Shaykh Ibrahim al-Kurani, then al-Madani. After a lengthy discussion, he concluded that the hadith was narrated by more than one of the people of authentic transmission, and that trustworthy narrators related it with a sound, connected isnad from Ibn Abbas, and with three sound chains from three of the Successors (*tabi'un*), leading imams of tafsir who took from the Companions: Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu Bakr ibn Abd al-Rahman, and Abu al-'Aliyah.

Al-Suyuti said in *Lubab al-Nuqul fi Asbab al-Nuzul*: Al-Hakim said in *'Ulum al-Hadith*: "When a Companion who witnessed the revelation and the sending down reports about a verse of the Qur'an that it was revealed concerning such-and-such, it is a musnad (traced-back) hadith." Ibn al-Salah and others followed this. Then he said: "What we have classed as musnad from a Companion, if it comes from a Successor, is also marfu' (attributed to the Prophet) but mursal. It may be accepted if the chain to him is sound and he was among the leading imams of tafsir who took from the Companions, such as Mujahid, Ikrimah and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, or if it is reinforced by another mursal or the like. Accordingly, the report in this story is musnad through the connected chain to Ibn Abbas, and mursal and marfu' through the three chains. The addition in it, which trustworthy narrators related from Ibn Abbas in narrations other than that of al-Bukhari, does not contradict what is in al-Bukhari from him, so it is not shadh (anomalous). Therefore, the blanket attack on it from the standpoint of transmission is not well placed."

He also answered what is implied under the assumption that the one who uttered it was the Prophet (ﷺ). As for the first, the authority denied over the sincere servants is misguidance, meaning deception that undermines the affair of religion. This is what consensus has agreed upon: that the Prophet (peace be upon him) is protected from it. As for what does not undermine, there is no evidence for its negation, and no consensus on protection from it. What is here does not undermine, since it does not contradict monotheism (*tawhid*), as will be explained, God willing. Rather, in it there is discipline, purification, and elevation for the Greatest Beloved (ﷺ). This is because he (peace be upon him) wished for the guidance of all, and that was not the will of Allah the Exalted. The most perfect form of servanthood is the annihilation of one's will in the will of the Truth, glorified is He. So the casting upon him (peace be upon him) at the moment of his wishing for the guidance of all, which conflicts with the Decree and contradicts what is most perfect, was not an imposition on him, so that he might ascend to what is more perfect. This was achieved on this occasion, and for this reason the deception did not occur again. Rather, guards were sent before him and behind him, so that it might be known that they had conveyed the Message of their Lord, glorified is He. The ordering of the casting after the wishing implies a reproach for it.

As for the second, the impermissible thing that contradicts infallibility is that he (peace be upon him) add to it from his own self, that is, add to it what he knows is not from it. What is here is not like that, because he (peace be upon him) only followed in it the casting that was disguised upon him, in a specific state only, as discipline, lest he return to such a state.

As for the third, it is possible that the Prophet (ﷺ) uttered it understanding it as a rejecting interrogative in which the hamzah was omitted, or as a quotation of them with the saying omitted. In that case it would be neither incoherent, nor self-contradictory, nor mixing praise with blame. One of the two options must be upheld, assuming the report is sound, because of infallibility. The purpose of expressing it in this way is to make those in whose hearts is a disease, and whose hearts are hardened, think that he (peace be upon him) praised their gods. This achieves the will of Allah the Exalted indicated by His words, glorified is He: ﴿So that He may make﴾, and so on.

As for the fourth, we choose the second option, on the basis that it is an interrogative with the hamzah omitted, or a quotation with the saying omitted. In both cases he (peace be upon him) believed in a meaning contrary to what they believed. It does not follow from this that he approved of falsehood, because he clarified the invalidity of their belief by the words of the Exalted afterward: ﴿They are nothing but names you have named, you and your fathers, for which Allah has sent down no authority﴾ [al-Najm 53:23]. For what Allah the Exalted has not sent down any authority for, its intercession is not hoped for, since there is no intercession except after divine permission, according to His words after that: ﴿And how many an angel in the heavens whose intercession will avail nothing except after Allah permits for whom He wills and approves﴾ [al-Najm 53:26].

As for the fifth, this confusion in a specific state for the sake of discipline does not imply that Allah bless him and grant him peace was not certain about what was revealed to him in other than that state. As for the statement of al-Qadi Iyad: "It is not valid that Satan appear in the form of an angel and that he (peace be upon him) be deceived," if he means that it is not valid that he be deceived in a damaging way, then this is accepted, but it did not occur. If he means absolutely, even if it did not undermine, then there is no evidence for it. The evidence of the miracle only negates the confusion that undermines the affair of prophethood, contradicts monotheism, and damages infallibility. What is mentioned is not undermining. Rather, in it is discipline, comprising purification and elevation to what is more perfect in servanthood.

As for what Ibn al-Arabi mentioned, it is an analogy with a difference, because Satan's appearing in the form of the Prophet absolutely is negated by sound text, whereas his appearing in the Prophet's form to deceive creation is a pervasive misguidance, and that is an authority negated by the text concerning the sincere ones. As for his appearing in the form of an angel in a specific state, deceiving the Prophet in a way that does not contradict monotheism, for what Allah the Exalted wills by it, as discipline, and because it implies the opposite of the intended meaning as a trial for a people, it is neither from the negated authority nor from the prohibited appearance, since it does not undermine the station of prophethood.

As for the sixth, forging speech (*taqawwul*) is affectation of speech, and whoever follows only what is cast to him from Allah the Exalted, either in reality or as a belief arising from a deception that does not undermine, has no affectation of speech in his case. So there is no forgery against Allah the Exalted at all. This story is similar to what was contained in the hadith of Dhu al-Yadayn. The deception upon him (peace be upon him) in the casting during the state of wishing was for discipline, like the occurrence of forgetfulness upon him (ﷺ) in prayer while believing it complete, for legislation. Uttering what Satan cast in a specific state, which does not contradict monotheism, as Qur'an on the basis of the belief that the one casting was an angel, is deception for discipline, like uttering the greeting. Then, with "I did not forget," he believed it corresponded to reality, on the basis of believing the prayer complete through forgetfulness. And the occurrence of clarification through the tongue of Gabriel (peace be upon him), then the naskh (abrogation) and ihkam (firming), is like the occurrence of clarification through the tongue of a Companion, then correction and prostration of forgetfulness. Just as forgetfulness for legislation does not undermine the station of prophethood, so the confusion in the casting for discipline does not undermine it. And just as the utterance "I did not forget," while it becomes clear that he (peace be upon him) had forgotten, is truthful on the basis of believing the prayer complete through forgetfulness, so the utterance of what Satan cast in that state as Qur'an, on the basis of believing that the one casting was an angel, is truthful. Truthfulness contains nothing of forgery. Therefore nothing of the utterance of what Satan cast in that state is forgery.

What was mentioned from al-Qadi Iyad, about relating a consensus on the impermissibility of forgetfulness entering conveyance statements, is, as al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said, open to critique.

As for the seventh, there is no undermining of trust in the Qur'an for those who were given knowledge and for those who believe, because the trust of each of them

[Page 181]

...following the reliability of their followed authority, the truthful and trustworthy one. So if he affirmed something to be such-and-such, they affirmed it too, and if he retracted something after affirming it, they retracted too, as is their habit regarding the abrogation of other verses that are the speech of God Most High, both in wording and meaning. For it is said: when the wording of something is abrogated, they were certain that they were under obligation to recite it, and after the abrogation they became certain that they were not under obligation to recite it. And when the ruling of something is abrogated, they were certain that they were obligated by its ruling, and after the abrogation they became certain that they were not obligated by it. Therefore, al-Baydawi's statement that this is not resolved by God's words ﴿Then God abrogates﴾ etc., because it too admits of this possibility, is not valid. Its explanation is this: if he means that it admits of this possibility among the four groups mentioned in the verses, namely those in whose hearts is a sickness, those whose hearts are hardened, those who have been given knowledge, and those who believe, then this is impermissible, because of the indication in God Most High's words ﴿that He may make it a trial﴾... (the words ﴿and that those who have been given knowledge may know﴾) etc., that the possibility is excluded for two of the four groups after the abrogation and the establishing. If he means that it admits of this possibility in general, i.e., among some but not others, then this is granted and is not harmful, since it does not undermine the reliance on the Qur'an among those who have been given knowledge and those who believe. As for its undermining the matter in relation to the other two groups, that is what God, Mighty and Majestic, intends.

This is what has been said. It has been objected to the first answer that the confusion, to the point that the matter is made unclear to the Prophet ﷺ so that he believes Satan to be an angel, is a flaw against the station of prophethood and a deficiency in it. For the saint, who is far below him by many ranks, is not hidden from the obedient person from the disobedient one; he perceives the light of obedience and the darkness of disobedience. How then could one who is the master of the prophets and the light of the eyes and hearts of the saints have what is pure light confused for what is pure darkness? As for Gabriel's (peace be upon him) being confused about him ﷺ on some occasions, to the point that he did not recognize him until he departed, and he said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, I was never confused (about 'Ali) since he came to me before this time, and I did not recognize him until he turned away" — if it is sound, it is not of the kind of Satan's confusion with him (peace be upon him), since it is possible that it was the confusion of one angel with another, and both are luminous beings. Indeed, other noble angels besides Gabriel used to come to him ﷺ. It is also possible that it was the confusion of an angel with one of the luminous humans whom he had not seen before that, such as al-Khidr and Elias, for example, if we say they are alive.

Also, the scholars who verify matters have said: the prophets (peace be upon them) do not have a satanic thought. The claim that this was not from him but was merely a casting upon the tongue and not upon the heart is impermissible. Do you not see that He said, Exalted is He, ﴿Satan cast into his wish﴾, not "Satan cast upon his tongue"? The naming of recitation as a "wish" is because the reciter first measures out the letters in his heart and then mentions them one by one. Moreover, his ﷺ retention of that until the evening, as comes in some narrations, and Gabriel's (peace be upon both of them) alerting him to it, makes it unlikely that the casting was upon the tongue alone. Furthermore, even if we concede that and say that Satan cast upon his tongue ﷺ and did not cast into his heart, as is the case with the revelation referred to in God Most High's words ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down﴾ ﴿upon your heart, that you may be among the warners﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 26:193-194], and we say that this is conceivable, then he ﷺ would have to know, from the emptiness of his heart and the occupation of his tongue, that this is not from the revelation at all, and he would not need Gabriel (peace be upon him) to inform him. The claim that the state was made confused for him (peace be upon him) is for discipline and for elevating him to the most perfect station of servanthood, which is the annihilation of his will in the will of his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, in that he wished for the faith of all and was eager for it, and that was not what God Most High intended. This is not worth paying attention to, because the one who holds it claims that the discipline by that occurred after God Most High's words ﴿And if their aversion is hard upon you, then if you are able to seek a tunnel in the earth or a ladder into the sky to bring them a sign — but if God had willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance; so do not be among the ignorant﴾ [Al-An'am 6:35]. There is no doubt that the discipline by this has not remained, has not been left, and was not accompanied by anything of consolation at all. So if it is said, God forbid, that this did not benefit him, how then would what is lesser than it benefit? Furthermore, what indication is there in the verse of discipline, when it did not come in the manner of reproach, but rather in the manner of consolation in the most eloquent form, regarding what the polytheists used to do in striving to nullify the signs? We do not concede that the ordering of the casting upon the wish, together with what is in the context and the sequence that indicates consolation regarding that, is of any benefit in this matter, as is not hidden from people of understanding.

It is objected to his statement that after the discipline by what was mentioned, a watch was sent before him and behind him to protect him from Satan's casting, that no evidence indicates the restriction of the sending to what came after that. Rather, the apparent meaning is that this was at all times. Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim, regarding God Most High's words ﴿except him whom He has approved of the messengers, for indeed He sends before him and behind him a watch﴾ [Al-Jinn 72:27], that he said: "When the angel was sent to the Prophet ﷺ with the revelation, angels were sent with him to guard him from before him and behind him, lest Satan take the form of the angel." It has been mentioned that "kāna" in that is for continuity. Ibn Abi Hatim reported with a sound chain from Sa'id ibn Jubayr who said: "Gabriel (peace be upon him) did not bring the Qur'an to the Prophet ﷺ except that with him were four angels as guardians." This is explicit on that. There is no doubt that this casting, according to those who hold it, was at the time of the descent of revelation. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported through al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas that "while the Prophet ﷺ was praying, the story of the gods of the Arabs was revealed to him, and he began to recite it. The polytheists heard him and said: 'We hear him mentioning our gods favorably.' So they drew near to him, and while he was reciting it and saying ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza﴾ ﴿and Manat, the third, the other﴾, Satan cast: 'Those are the exalted cranes, whose intercession is hoped for.'" Accordingly, in this and similar cases, the watch exists together with the non-effect of its consequence upon him. As for the claim that Gabriel (peace be upon him) and those with him withdrew from him until Satan cast what he cast, based on what Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said regarding the verse of the watch: "The Prophet ﷺ, before Satan cast into his wish, used to draw near to him. When Satan cast into his wish, He commanded them to withdraw from him a little." The meaning of his words "fīhi" ("in it") and "falammā alqā" ("when he cast") is "when he intended to cast," in the sphere of prevention. And likewise the soundness of this report is questionable. Then, what benefit is there in sending a watch if protection is not achieved by it? How could it be called a "watch"?

From what has been mentioned in this objection, what is in the second answer of objection is known, and it is evident. It may be said that the inimitability (i'jaz) of the Qur'an is known to him ﷺ necessarily, as Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari held. Indeed, al-Qadi said: every eloquent person who has encompassed the methods of the Arabs and the rare features of composition necessarily knows its inimitability. It has been mentioned that the inimitability relates to a sūrah or to an amount of speech equal to it, such that a clear superiority of strong eloquence is shown in it. So if there were a verse equal in letters to a sūrah, even if it were like the sūrah of al-Kawthar, it would be inimitable. On this basis, it is impossible for jinn and humankind, even if they were to support one another, to produce, in an amount of the shortest sūrah of it, something resembling it in eloquence. Whenever anyone brings what he claims to be such, his merchandise is not marketed before the Messenger of God ﷺ, nor before any eloquent person who has encompassed what was mentioned earlier. The Messenger (peace be upon him) would not be unaware of this, nor would that eloquent person be unaware of its non-inimitability; so it is not confused with the Qur'an at all. There is no doubt that what Satan cast, according to some narrations, has letters equal to the letters of the sūrah of al-Kawthar, or even more if the doubled letter is counted as two letters. That is: "wa-annahunna lahunna al-gharāniqu al-'ulā, wa-inna shafā'atahunna lahiya allatī turtajā," as reported by Ibn Abi Hatim through Musa ibn 'Uqba from Ibn Shihab.

It also came in the narration of Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim with a chain — al-Suyuti said: "it is sound" — from Abu al-'Aliyah that he cast: "tilka al-gharāniq al-'ulā, wa-shafā'atuhunna turtajā" (turtadā), and "mithluhunna lā yunsā." Its letters are more than its letters if the doubled letter is not counted as two in any of them. If the doubled letter is counted, its letters are more by one. So if what was mentioned is among the things to which inimitability relates, then it must be from God Most High and not from the casting of His enemy, since it would be impossible for him, like the rest of jinn and humankind, to produce that. And if it is not among the things to which inimitability relates, then it is speech of no small amount, which a skilled eloquent person, on hearing it in the midst of speech far above it by many ranks, would notice, because it is not from it. It is therefore utterly unlikely that the deficiency of its eloquence compared with the eloquence of any of the verses of the Qur'an would be hidden from him (peace be upon him), whether we say that the verses differ in eloquence, as Abu Nasr al-Qushayri and a group chose, or we say that there is no difference, as al-Qadi chose. Then he would believe it to be Qur'an until Gabriel (peace be upon him) alerted him, especially since the verses had repeatedly passed over his noble hearing and mingled with his flesh and blood. Even one of us, though not of great eloquence, when he is familiar with a poet's poetry and it has repeatedly passed over his hearing, knows, if a verse or a hemistich is inserted into a qaṣīdah of his, that it is not his. He may be asked for proof, and he does not go beyond saying: "Because the breath differs." This improbability is firmly established in my view if what was cast is what is in the common narration, namely "tilka al-gharāniq al-'ulā, wa-inna shafā'atahunna la-turtajā." Likewise, especially according to the view of a group that inimitability relates to the few and the many of the Qur'an's sentences that convey a complete meaning, based on God Most High's words ﴿then let them produce a discourse like it﴾. As for the claim that the Prophet (may God Most High bless him and grant him peace) was unaware of that for the sake of discipline, there is much to be said about it, and it is not unlikely that the one who holds it deserves rebuke.

[Page 183]

As for his answer to the third objection, that the statement must be read as a question or that the verb "said" must be understood as elided, which is weaker than the first answer: "If the report is sound, then it is sound. But establishing the soundness of the report is harder than plucking thorns from the mimosa (kharṭ al-qatād). Those who criticize it on the basis of its transmission are eminent scholars, expert in distinguishing the worthless from the valuable among reports. They have exerted their utmost effort to establish the truth concerning it, and they have not transmitted it except as rejected. Satan has cast nothing to his allies that is not counted, and those who criticize it are more numerous than those who accept it, and among them are some who are more knowledgeable than him. It is likely that they examined its transmitters through all the chains and found them to be weak (majrūḥūn), and that this was missed by the one who accepts it. By my life, the claim that this report is among what Satan cast upon some of the tongues of the narrators, and then God Most High guided a group of His elect to refute it, is easier to accept than the claim that the Hadith of the Cranes is among what Satan cast upon the tongue of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and then He, glory be to Him and exalted, abrogated it (naskh). Especially since it is not a matter on whose authenticity any religious ruling depends, nor the meaning of any verse, but only that it leads to doubts arising in the hearts of many weak believers, which can hardly be repelled except with great effort.

Its unreliability is further supported by its contradiction of the apparent meanings of the verses. He, glory be to Him, said concerning the Qur'an: ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or behind it; it is a revelation from One who is Wise, Praiseworthy﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 42]. The meaning of "falsehood" here is that which is false in itself, and that which was cast is so, even though the Prophet's (ﷺ) utterance of it could be interpreted in one of two ways. The phrase "cannot approach it" means the continuing negation, not the negation of continuity.

He, glory be to Him, also said: ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed We will be its guardian﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 9]. Here the nominal sentence is emphasized by two emphatics, and the guarding, whose object is omitted to indicate generality, is attributed to the pronoun of majesty. In this there is an indication of the great care given to the matter of the Qur'an. Those who have derived from this verse the preservation of the Qur'an from addition and omission have used it as evidence, and what has been said about that does not concern us. As for the claim that the casting mentioned does not contradict preservation because it was abrogated and remained only a short time, this is not free from examination. The apparent meaning is that even if it does not contradict preservation in general, it does contradict the preservation indicated in the verse, as that care requires.

Moreover, if it is said, in accordance with what is reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk that the whole of Sūrat al-Ḥajj is Medinan, then what Satan cast would have remained, in the belief of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the believers, as Qur'an for a long time, and this claim is extremely reprehensible. He, exalted and majestic, said: ﴿It is nothing but a revelation that is revealed﴾ [al-Najm: 4]. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun refers to what he (peace be upon him) utters concerning religion. From here [al-Dārimī] transmitted from Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr that he said: "Jibrīl (peace be upon him) used to descend with the Sunnah just as he descended with the Qur'an."

What is understood from the implication of the discourse is that all that he (peace be upon him) utters of this kind is not from a satanic casting, just as it is not from desire. There remain other verses on this subject whose apparent meanings also indicate the claim. Interpreting all these numerous apparent meanings in order to accommodate the view of a small group that a report is sound, when it contradicts them, against the view of a great multitude after a thorough investigation that it is not sound, is something that the sound heart does not incline to and that the upright nature does not approve.

The claim of its authenticity is further made unlikely by the fact that none of the major senior scholars included it in any of the Six Books, although it contains a strange story, and human nature tends to hear and transmit the strange. Also, they included the report of the prostration of the polytheists with him (ﷺ) when he prostrated at the end of al-Najm. Al-Bukhārī, Muslim, Abū Dāwūd, al-Nasā'ī and others related from Ibn Mas'ūd that "the Prophet (ﷺ) recited al-Najm and prostrated in it, and everyone who was with him prostrated, except that an old man from Quraysh took a handful of pebbles or dust and raised it to his forehead, and said: 'This is enough for me.'"

Al-Bukhārī also related, and al-Tirmidhī, from Ibn 'Abbās that "the Messenger of God (ﷺ) prostrated with al-Najm, and the Muslims, the polytheists, the jinn and mankind prostrated with him," and other reports besides these.

Nobody may say that the prostration of the polytheists indicates that the sūrah contained something whose apparent meaning praised their gods, for otherwise they would not have prostrated. We say: it is possible that they prostrated out of bewilderment that came upon them and fear that seized them upon hearing the sūrah, because of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And that He destroyed the first 'Ād﴾ ﴿and Thamūd, and spared none﴾ ﴿and the people of Nūḥ before, indeed they were more unjust and more rebellious﴾ ﴿and the overturned cities He hurled down﴾ ﴿and covered them with what covered﴾ [al-Najm: 50–45], to the end of the verses. So they sensed that the like of this was descending upon them. Perhaps they had never heard the like of it from him (ﷺ) before, while he was standing before his Lord, glory be to Him, in a momentous station and before a great assembly. They also supposed, from the arrangement of the command to prostrate after what preceded it, that their prostration, even if not from faith, would be sufficient to avert what they imagined. Nor is their fear from hearing such a thing from him (ﷺ) to be considered unlikely, for the sūrah of Ḥā Mīm al-Sajdah was revealed after that, as is clearly stated in a report from Ibn 'Abbās mentioned by al-Suyūṭī at the beginning of al-Itqān. When 'Utbah ibn Rabī'ah heard His saying in it: ﴿So if they turn away, say: I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of 'Ād and Thamūd﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 13], he placed his hand over the mouth of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), appealed to him by the ties of kinship, and excused himself to his people when they suspected that he had become an apostate. He said: "How could that be, when you know that Muḥammad, when he says something, does not lie? I feared that punishment would descend upon you." This was related by al-Bayhaqī in al-Dalā'il, and by Ibn 'Asākir in a long report from Jābir ibn 'Abd Allāh, may Allah be pleased with him.

It is possible to say, though far-fetched, that their prostration was due to their sensing praise of their gods, and this does not imply the authenticity of that report, since that sensing could have come from His saying: ﴿Have you considered al-Lāt and al-'Uzzā?﴾ ﴿and Manāt, the third, the other?﴾ [al-Najm: 19–20], on the basis that the object is omitted, which they supposed as they wished; or on the basis that the object is ﴿For you the male and for Him the female?﴾ [al-Najm: 21], and they imagined that the point of the denial lies in these deities being females. Love for a thing blinds and deafens. This is not more remote than their interpreting the words "the exalted cranes, whose intercession is indeed hoped for" as praise, to the point that they prostrated for it at the end of the sūrah, even though it occurs between two blames, so that the barrier against interpreting it as praise is present in the context, as is not hidden from one whose inner eye has been spared the defect (al-ghayn).

As for the fourth answer, it has been objected that their prostration with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) came last, after hearing His saying: ﴿They are nothing but names that you and your fathers have named, for which God has sent down no authority﴾ [al-Najm: 23]. So there should have been a warning after the prostration. Perhaps they referred the pronoun in "they" (hiya) to the names, which are their saying "al-Lāt, al-'Uzzā and Manāt," as is one of the two possibilities mentioned by al-Zamakhsharī. Then the meaning would be: "These are nothing but names that you have named by your desire and your lust, for which you have no proof to rely on for their naming." In that case, there is no evidence in it for refuting what they understood from the satanic casting of praise for their gods as "the exalted cranes." It is possible they interpreted it in another way, and the door of interpretation is wide.

It has also been objected to his statement in the fifth answer: "This confusion, in a particular situation, for the sake of discipline, does not require that he (ﷺ) be without insight regarding what is revealed to him in other situations." The objector did not mean that if the matter became confused for him (peace be upon him) once, it would follow that he is without insight regarding what is revealed to him at other times. Rather, he meant that what befits the station of the Prophet (ﷺ) is that he have insight into all that is revealed to him, and that whenever it becomes confused for him (peace be upon him) in any state, the universality of the universal is not preserved, and that is contrary to what is intended.

In al-Tanqīḥ, it is stated that revelation is either apparent or hidden. The apparent is of three kinds. The first is what is established through the tongue of the angel, so that it reaches his (ﷺ) hearing after he knows the conveyor by a definite proof. As Ibn Malak said, what is meant is the necessary knowledge that the conveyor is an angel descending with revelation from God Most High, and the Qur'an is of this kind. The second is what becomes clear to him (ﷺ) through the angel's indication without explanation in speech, as he (peace be upon him) said: "The Holy Spirit breathed into my heart that no soul will die until it has completed its provision," the hadith. This is called the thought of the angel (khāṭir al-malak). The third is what appears to his noble heart without any doubt, by inspiration from God Most High, by which He made him see by a light from Him, as God Most High said: ﴿So that you may judge between the people by what God has shown you﴾ [al-Nisā': 105]. All of these are proof absolutely, unlike the inspiration given to a saint (walī), which is not a proof for others. As for the hidden, it is what is attained by opinion and ijtihād, and there is disagreement about it, and so on to the end of what he said. This is clear that he (ﷺ) has insight into everything of the Qur'an revealed to him, for he placed it in the first kind of the apparent revelation. It is also known from this that the claim that he (ﷺ) uttered what Satan cast is not established, for according to the claimant he would have held it to be Qur'an and revelation from God Most High, and so, as you have heard, he (peace be upon him) would have known that by necessary knowledge. Since in reality it is not so, the knowledge would turn into ignorance. The exception of this matter from the generality is something for which the claimant has no evidence except the report whose soundness he asserts, and upon which he based his interpretation of the verse in the way he explained it, and that is the first point of dispute.
