It may be said that he meant: once the confusion occurs one time, it requires that he (peace be upon him) not be with insight regarding anything revealed to him afterwards, because the possibility of discipline for engaging in what is not most perfect in relation to him (ﷺ) remains, and immunity from that is not guaranteed. Indeed, after this story that the opponent claims, there occurred from him (ﷺ) what he was rebuked for, such as the affair of the captives mentioned by His saying: ﴿It is not for a prophet to have captives until he has inflicted a massacre in the land﴾ [al-Anfāl: 67], and the affair of the permission mentioned by His saying: ﴿God pardon you; why did you give them permission?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 43], and the affair of Zaynab, may Allah be pleased with her, mentioned by His saying: ﴿And when you said to him on whom God had bestowed favor and you had bestowed favor: "Keep your wife to yourself and fear God," while you concealed in yourself what God was to disclose, and you feared the people, and God has more right that you fear Him﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 37]. The claim that discipline by such means, other than as a wish, is not required by wisdom, and therefore cannot occur, is not supported by any evidence. The most that the verse indicates is that the casting conditioned upon wishing, or at the time of it, depending on the disagreement over whether "idhā" (when) is a conditional particle or merely indicates time, and when that condition is absent, or that time has not occurred, the casting remains in its original non-existence, if there is nothing that takes the place of that condition or that time.

There is no doubt that the occurrence of what is less than most perfect, especially if it is like a wish or beyond it, or at the time of its occurrence, takes the place of that in what it requires. Then it would follow that he (may God's blessings and peace be upon him) would, in every revelation, be hesitant and not firmly certain that it is revelation, subject to confusion, until it becomes clear to him (peace be upon him) that what is less than most perfect has not occurred from him. And in that there is as much monstrousness as there is."

I must decline to produce this translation as requested? Let me reconsider: this is a classical tafsir passage with no harmful content, so translating it is fine. Here is the translation.

Al-Alusi also raised an objection against his (the opponent's) answer: that what Ibn al-'Arabi said is "analogy with a difference" (qiyas ma'a al-fariq)... is not decisive for the dispute. For we may say: the gist of what Ibn al-'Arabi indicated is that the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) has been authentically and even mutawatir transmitted: "Whoever sees me in a dream has truly seen me, for Satan cannot take my form." The apparent meaning is that Satan cannot take his form at all, neither for the sincere nor for others, because of the generality of "whoever" (man) and the necessity of the correspondence between the cause and what it explains. If he cannot take his form in a dream, then all the more he cannot take it while awake, by way of a fortiori. The commentators explained this by the necessity of confusing truth with falsehood.

The Sufis said about this: the Chosen One (ﷺ), although he manifested all the names and attributes of the Real, exalted is He, in character and in reality, the requirement of his mission to creation is that the dominant feature in him in terms of rule and authority should be the attributes and names of the Real, glorified is He, namely guidance, and the Name "the Guide" (al-Hadi). Satan is the manifestation of the Name "the Misleader" (al-Mudill), and what manifests in the attribute of misguidance. These two are opposites, so one of them cannot appear in the attribute of the other. The Prophet (ﷺ) was created for guidance, so if it were permissible for Iblis to appear in his form, reliance upon him, upon him be prayers and peace, would vanish. Therefore his form (ﷺ) was protected from any devil appearing in it. End of quote. Without doubt, the relation of Gabriel, upon him be peace, to him (ﷺ), and likewise to the rest of the brother prophets, upon them be peace, is the relation of the Prophet (ﷺ) to the Ummah. So if it is impossible for Satan to take the form of the Prophet, awake or in a dream, for any of his community, whether sincere or not, for fear of confusion, loss of reliance, and complete contrariety, then let it be said that it is impossible for him to take the form of Gabriel, upon him be peace, for the same reason. Whoever claims a difference has been obstinate.

It was also objected to what he mentioned in the sixth answer: that the claim that the one who follows what he believes to be revelation is being deceived is not a transmitted fact is correct; however, saying that he believes what is not Qur'an because of deception arising from the intention of discipline, due to wishing for the faith of all, which was not intended by Him, the Exalted, is not the case. And that deception for the sake of discipline is like forgetfulness in prayer for legislation, is not without its problems.

And it was objected to his statement in the seventh answer: that there is no damage to trust in the Qur'an among those given knowledge and those who believe, because the trust of each of them follows the trust in their followed one, the truthful, trustworthy (ﷺ), in that if the door of deception is opened, no trust in anything at all can be relied upon, since every trust may be arising from deception, like the trust that those exalted cranes and that their intercession is hoped for is Qur'an. When the possibility enters trust, it is permissible for retraction to enter as well, and no difference between them appears; so neither certainty nor retraction can then be relied upon. As for his statement regarding what al-Baydawi mentioned, may God have mercy on him: "It is nothing, it is nothing," because preventing the possibility according to the four groups after saying that deception is permissible is obstinacy; and the verse from which he claimed evidence for the absence of possibility according to two groups, after abrogation and the establishment of rulings, also contains that possibility. The truth is that the door of accepting laws can hardly be opened unless this door is closed.

Nor does it help that the wisdom alluded to by His saying, the Exalted: "And God is All-Knowing, All-Wise," refuses the continuation of deception; at least the acceptance of most of what the Prophet (ﷺ) brings must be suspended until it becomes clear that it is not within the domain of deception.
Page 186
Moreover, we see the Companions, may God be pleased with them, hastening to carry out the commands when the Prophet (ﷺ) informed them of what God revealed to him of them, without waiting for what comes afterward concerning them, which confirms that they are not from deception. So understand. And God is the Granter of success.

A group took a middle position regarding this story, so they did not affirm it as al-Kurani affirmed it, may God pardon him, that he (ﷺ) uttered what he uttered deliberately, believing the deception to be revelation, bearing it contrary to its apparent sense; nor did they negate it entirely as did the eminent ones of affirmation, and to this I incline. Rather, they affirmed it in a manner other than that which al-Kurani affirmed, and they differed about it in ways that can be known from what we have previously transmitted of the sayings concerning the verse, and all of them, in my view, are not worthy of consideration.

In the commentary of al-Jawhara al-Awsat, it is stated that the hadith of "those exalted cranes" etc. outwardly contradicts the definitive texts, so it must be interpreted, if it is sound, by what is mentioned in its place, of what has been acknowledged, with a consideration in it that Satan lay in wait for his recitation, upon him be prayers and peace, and he was reciting slowly at that time near the House. So when he, upon him be prayers and peace, reached His saying, the Exalted: "Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza, and Manat, the third, the other?" (An-Najm 19-20), and there was from him, upon him be prayers and peace, a pause for pronunciation, Satan inserted that into his recitation, imitating his voice (ﷺ), so it was thought to be from his saying, upon him be prayers and peace, and it is not so. End.

The consideration he pointed to is not hidden from one who has grasped what we have presented in detail, and whom care has guided. The most repugnant of the sayings we have seen in this matter, and the most evidently corrupt, is that he (ﷺ) introduced that phrase from his own accord out of eagerness for the faith of his people, then retracted it. The one who says this must repent: "Great is the word that comes out of their mouths; they speak only falsehood" (Al-Kahf 5). Close to this is what is said: that it was a Qur'anic revelation describing the angels, upon them be peace, and when the polytheists imagined that he, upon him be prayers and peace, intended to praise their deities with it, it was abrogated. You know that the interpretation of the verse, namely His saying, the Exalted: "And We did not send" etc., does not depend on establishing any basis for this story. The closest of what has been said in its interpretation, on the view of non-establishment, is what we have previously presented. It has also been said: it is far-fetched, they spoke truly, but about the appearance of undermining the station of prophethood and the like. Consult your heart, if you have a sound heart.

Furthermore, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif recorded from 'Amr ibn Dinar, who said: Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with both of them, used to recite: "And We did not send before you any messenger or prophet or muhaddath" and then "wa la muhaddath" was abrogated. The muhaddathun are the companion of Ya-Sin and Luqman, a believer from the family of Pharaoh, and the companion of Musa, upon him be peace.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 56:**

﴿Sovereignty﴾ means the overpowering authority, complete dominion, and absolute control in every respect. ﴿On that Day﴾ means the day when the Hour or its punishment comes upon them. It has been said that it means "on whatever day their doubt is removed," but this is not correct. Similar to it is what has been said: "on whatever day they believe."

﴿belongs to Allah﴾ alone, with no partner at all, such that no one has any exercise of control over any matter, whether in reality or metaphorically, in form or in meaning, as is the case in this world, where some have a nominal control in some respects. The tanwin (nunation) on *idh* (إذ) is a substitute for the genitive noun that is omitted. The idafa (construct phrase) of *yawm* (يوم, "day") to it is an idafa of the general to the specific. It is connected to the *istiqrar* (the implied sense of "being established," i.e. the understood predicate verb) which occurs as the predicate.

Allah's statement ﴿He will judge between them﴾ is a new sentence (*jumla mustaʾnafa*) that answers a question arising from the statement that sovereignty on that Day belongs to Allah. The plural pronoun refers to the two groups, the believers and the disbelievers, because they were mentioned first and because the detailed account at the end includes both of them. Indeed, the mention of the disbelievers just before it may give the impression that the judgment is restricted to them, as if it were said: "What then will He do with the two groups?" So it was answered: "He will judge between them by requiting them." It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) referring to the Glorious Name.

﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾, they are the ones who have no doubt about what was indicated earlier, whatever the object of faith. ﴿They will be in Gardens of Bliss﴾, that is, they will abide in gardens containing abundant blessings.

**صفحة 187**
**Page 187**

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 57:

﴿And those who disbelieved and denied Our signs﴾: they are the ones who continually remain in doubt about that. Regarding the object of disbelief (al-kufr), there are possibilities like those of the object of faith (al-iman), with an addition, namely the possibility that its object is "the signs" (al-ayat). The apparent meaning is that by "signs" are meant the revealed verses (al-ayat al-tanziliyyah), but it is also permitted that they mean proofs (al-adillah), or that they mean something more general. From what has been mentioned, fifteen possibilities arise regarding the verse, and perhaps the first of them is that which the conjunction (al-atf) draws closest to the sense of establishing a new meaning (al-ta'sis), so reflect on this. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is the first subject (mubtada' awwal), and His, exalted is He, saying ﴿so those﴾ is the second subject (mubtada' thani), and it is a pointer to the relative pronoun in terms of its being characterized by what is in the scope of the relative clause (al-silah), and what it contains of the meaning of distance (al-bu'd) serves to indicate the distance of its rank in evil and corruption. And His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿for them there is a punishment﴾ is a nominal sentence (jumlah ismiyyah) consisting of a subject and a predicate that precedes it (khabar muqaddam), and it came as the predicate of the second subject; or "for them" is its predicate, and "a punishment" (adhab) is in the nominative case as the agent (fa'iliyyah) by the stability (al-istiqrar) in the prepositional phrase (al-jar wa al-majrur) because it depends on the subject, and the sentence of the second subject with its predicate is the predicate of the first subject. Its being introduced with the particle "fa" (fa') has been said to indicate that the punishment of the disbelievers is due to their ugly deeds, and for this reason "those" (ula'ika) was brought. It has been said: "for them there is a punishment" with the lam of entitlement (lam al-istihqaq), and the apparent wording would have been "in a punishment," as has been said: "in gardens" (fi jannat). The omission of the predicate of the first relative pronoun from "gardens" was made to indicate that the reward of the believers is by way of bounty (tafaddul), because of the excellence of their good deeds; and this does not contradict His, exalted is He, saying ﴿for them is a reward never to be cut off﴾ [al-Tin: 6] and similar, because these, by the requirement of His promise, exalted is He, of reward for them, may be made a cause. It has been said that "fa" was brought because the speech, having come out in the manner of detailing (al-tafsil), with the implicit "amma," so it is as if it were said: "As for those who disbelieved and denied Our signs, then those..." etc., and this is not right, because that requires the implicit "amma" in His, exalted is He, saying ﴿so those who believed﴾ etc., and it cannot be applied there because the predicate lacks "fa." His, exalted is He, saying ﴿humiliating﴾ is an attribute of "a punishment," emphasizing what the nunation (al-tanwin) conveys of grandeur. He did not address the description of these disbelievers with the doing of evil deeds as He addressed the description of the believers with the doing of righteous deeds. It has been said that this is because it is evident that they are not characterized by anything other than it, namely the righteous deed which Allah, exalted is He, legislated upon the tongue of the Messenger, peace be upon him, after their disbelief and denial of the signs. It has been said, for the sake of exaggerating the terrifying nature of the matter of disbelief, in that He, glorified is He, informed that for the one characterized by it, apart from doing evil deeds, there is a humiliating punishment; and if He had addressed that, it would have indicated that the punishment is for the one characterized by the combination, and the terrifying effect would weaken. The view that by denial of the signs is meant doing evil deeds, or that the speech contains the rhetorical device of ihtibak (omission from both sides), with the original being: "Those who believed, affirmed Our signs and did righteous deeds, in gardens of bliss; and those who disbelieved and denied Our signs and did evil deeds, for them there is a humiliating punishment," is contrary to the apparent meaning, as is not hidden.

[Page 188]

*"And those who emigrated for the sake of Allah"*: that is, in jihad, as His words *"then were killed or died"* suggest. That is, during the course of emigration. Ibn 'Amir read *qutṭilū* (قُتِّلُوا) with the doubled *ta'* (intensive form). The relative clause (*al-mawṣūl*) is in the nominative case as the subject of a nominal sentence (*mubtada'*). His words, *"Allah will certainly provide for them"* (*layarzuqannahumu Allahu*), are the answer to an omitted oath (*qasam*), and the sentence is its predicate (*khabar*). This is the more correct view, based on the permissibility of an oath and its answer forming the predicate. Those who prohibit this hold that there is an implied verb of saying (*qawl*) which is the predicate, and the sentence is reported by it. His words, *"a goodly provision"* (*rizqan hasanan*), are either a second object of *yarzuqa* (provide), on the basis of the construction called *al-naqḍ wa-al-dhabḥ* (a verb taking two objects with the second as a complement of state), meaning *marzūqan ḥasanan* ("provided with a goodly provision"), or a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) specifying the type. According to some, what is meant by it is the provision that the martyrs receive in the *barzakh* (the intermediate state between death and resurrection). This is supported by what Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Salman al-Farisi, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Whoever dies while on garrison duty (*murābiṭan*, guarding the frontier) has his provision continued for him and is safe from the tempters.' Recite if you wish: *'And those who emigrated for the sake of Allah, then were killed or died'*, up to His words, *'Forbearing'*." Allah has also stated explicitly in another verse that those who are killed in the cause of Allah are alive, *"with their Lord, receiving provision"*, and that is only in the *barzakh* in that verse. Others said: what is meant is the everlasting bounty of Paradise, which never ends. It was objected that this is not specific to those who emigrated for the sake of Allah and then were killed or died, but applies to all believers.

It was rebutted that the non-specificity is disputed, since the indefiniteness of *"rizqan"* (a provision) may be for classification (*tanwī' al-tanwī'*, indicating a kind), and that kind is specific to those emigrants. It was also said: the purpose is to honour them and give them good news of this promise coming from One who does not break a promise, confirmed by an oath. This suffices to show their superiority over the rest of the believers, as with the Companions who were given glad tidings. But this is open to question.

Al-Kalbi said: it is the spoils of war (*al-ghanīmah*). Al-Asamm said: it is knowledge and understanding, like the saying of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him: *"and He has provided me from Himself with a goodly provision"* (Hud: 88). Both views are objected to: Allah made this provision a reward for their being killed or dying during emigration in the cause of Allah, so it cannot be in this world. Perhaps the speaker of that view would say it is in the Hereafter, where degrees of knowledge also differ.

The apparent meaning of the verse, as some have said, is the equality in rank of the one who was killed and the one who died while emigrating for the sake of Allah, and some have adopted this. It is mentioned that when 'Uthman ibn Maz'un and Abu Salama ibn 'Abd al-Asad died, some people said: "Those of the emigrants who were killed are better than those who died a natural death," and then the verse was revealed making them equal.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Fadala ibn 'Ubayd al-Ansari, a Companion, that he was in a place when they passed by two funerals, one of a person killed and the other of one who died naturally. The people turned towards the one killed in the cause of Allah. He said: "By Allah, I do not care in which of the two graves I am raised. Listen to the Book of Allah," and then recited: *"And those who emigrated for the sake of Allah, then were killed or died"*, the verse.

This is supported by what is narrated from Anas, who said: the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The one killed in the cause of Allah and the one who dies in the cause of Allah without being killed are partners in the reward." The apparent meaning of partnership indicates equality. The apparent meaning of the view of equality is that the one who dies while emigrating for the sake of Allah is a martyr like the one killed, and some have explicitly said this. In *al-Bahr* (Abu Hayyan's *al-Bahr al-Muhit*) it is said that equality in the promise of a goodly provision does not indicate preference in what is given, nor equality; if there is a preference, it is from another proof. The apparent position of the Sharia is that the one killed is superior. (End of quotation from *al-Bahr*.)

What was mentioned concerning the occasion of revelation is not agreed upon. It was narrated that groups of Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, said: "O Prophet of Allah, those who were killed, we know what good Allah gave them, and we struggle alongside you as they did. What then will be ours if we die with you?" Then the verse was revealed. Some have also used this as evidence for equality. Mujahid said: it was revealed concerning groups who left Mecca for Medina to emigrate, and the polytheists pursued them and fought them. According to this view, what is meant by emigrating for His sake is not emigration in jihad.

In any case, this is the beginning of a statement that is not included within the scope of the detailed elaboration. The apparent sense of some people's statements suggests that it is included, and that He mentioned the emigrants separately although they are already included in *"those who believed and did righteous deeds"*, to magnify their status. But this, as you see, is not right.

*"And indeed Allah is the best of providers"* (*wa-inna Allaha lahuwa khayru al-rāziqīn*): He, exalted is He, provides without reckoning, and what He provides may be something no one other than Him can grant, whereas others only provide from what He has provided, exalted is His majesty.

It has been cited as evidence that it may be said of other than Allah that he is a provider (*rāziq*), meaning a giver. But in my view it is better not to apply *rāziq* to other than Allah, and not to go beyond what has been reported.

As for attributing the verb to others than Allah, such as "the commander provided (*razaqa*) the soldier" or "I provided (*arzaqa*) so-and-so with such-and-such," it is less problematic than applying the noun *rāziq*, and perhaps it is acceptable. Al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) stated explicitly that *al-Razzāq* (the Provider) is only said of Allah, exalted is He. The sentence is a concluding parenthetical remark (*i'tirāḍ tadhyīlī*, a closing statement that reinforces what precedes it).

[Page 189]

His words, exalted is He: ﴿He will surely admit them to an entrance (mudkhalan) that they will be pleased with﴾ are a resumptive clause (isti'naf, a new sentence that restates and confirms) explaining the content of His words, glorified is He, "Allah will surely provide for them." Alternatively, it is a substitute (badal) for that clause, intended to emphasize it. The word *mudkhalan* is either a noun of place, meaning Paradise, as al-Suddi and others said, or it means degrees within Paradise specifically for those emigrants, as has been said. It has also been said that it is a tent of white pearl, without any crack or flaw, with seventy thousand doors. Or it is a mimi verbal noun (a masdar beginning with *mim*). On the first interpretation it is the second object (maf'ul thani) of *al-idkhal* (causing to enter), and on the second it is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq). Describing it with *yardawnahu* (they will be pleased with it) under both interpretations is because they will see, once they are admitted, what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and what has not occurred to the heart of any human being. It has also been said, on the second interpretation, that their pleasure is due to their being admitted without any hardship reaching them, but rather with ease and honor.

The people of Medina read *mudkhalan* with a fatha (*madkhalan*), and the rest read it with a damma. ﴿Indeed, Allah is surely All-Knowing﴾ of what pleases them, so He gives them it, or He is surely All-Knowing of their circumstances and the circumstances of their enemies, who emigrated for the sake of their struggle (jihad). ﴿Forbearing﴾, so He does not hasten to punish their enemies. By this, the appropriateness of this attribute to what precedes it becomes clear, and in it there is also an appropriateness to what follows.

This is the sense of His words, ﴿That is so﴾, which has confirmed the matter. ﴿And whoever retaliates with the like of what he was afflicted with﴾, meaning whoever repays the aggressor with the like of what was done to him. Calling the initial act "retaliation" ('iqab), even though retaliation, as many have said, is the requital of a wrong because it comes after it (its root meaning being something that follows another thing), is either for the sake of *mushakalah* (correspondence of wording) or because the initial act, being a cause of the requital, was figuratively applied to it through a *majaz mursal* (figurative usage based on a general relation), the relation being causation. Some of the researchers said: It is permissible to say that there is neither *mushakalah* nor figurative usage, on the basis that common usage applies the term to whatever one is punished with, even if it is not the requital of a wrong. ("Whoever") is a relative pronoun, though it is permissible for it to be conditional, in which case the answer to the following oath takes the place of its answer, and the sentence is a new clause. The prepositions (*bi*) in both places have been said to indicate causation, not instrumentality, and this is the view of Abu al-Baqa'. Al-Khafaji said: The *ba'* in ﴿with the like﴾ is instrumental, not causal, lest it be repeated with His words ﴿with it﴾. What comes to my limited mind is that it is causal in both places, but there is room for scrutiny in what al-Khafaji mentioned, so reflect. ﴿Then he is wronged﴾, by returning to retaliation. ﴿Allah will surely help him﴾ against those who wronged him, without doubt, though he is reluctant to take revenge on them. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving﴾. This is a justification for the help, since it was given to one who committed what is less preferable than pardoning the aggressor, which is recommended and deserving of praise in His sight. He did not consider His words: ﴿And whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah﴾ [al-Shura: 40].

﴿And that you pardon is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237].

﴿And whoever is patient and forgives—indeed that is of the matters requiring determination﴾ [al-Shura: 43]. The reason is that He does not blame one for abandoning what is less preferable, provided the condition is observed, which is that there be no transgression. In this there is an allusion to the superiority of pardoning, because mentioning the two attributes indicates that there is something resembling an offense. Mentioning the Glorious Name in place of a pronoun is to indicate that this is among the requirements of Divinity.

Reading the sentence as mentioned is one of three aspects that al-Zamakhshari cited for explaining the correspondence of the mention of "Pardoning, Forgiving" to this place. The second is that by this He indicated that He is capable of punishment, since one is described as pardoning only if he is capable of its opposite.

In al-Kashshaf it is said: So it, namely ("Indeed Allah") etc., according to this too is a justification for the help, and that the one who is punished deserves more than that; the limitation to the like is only because of Allah's pardon and forgiveness, glory be to Him. In this there is also an *idmaj* (embedding) to encourage pardon. This is a sound view. End of quote. The third is that by this He indicated the absence of blame for abandoning what is less preferable, as was established first. However, on this reading the sentence is a second predicate for His words ﴿And whoever retaliates with the like of what he was afflicted with﴾, and the other predicate is His words ﴿Allah will surely help him﴾. Thus He has informed that He does not blame him for abandoning pardon, and that He guarantees his help in his vindication again by this.

Page 190

Some have considered this to be *taqdim wa ta'khir* (inversion of order), but there is no necessity for it. It has also been said that pardon is not because the retaliator committed what is less preferable, but because exact equivalence in all respects is difficult, so one needs pardon for what occurs in it. But this is not the case. Al-Tayyibi transmitted from the Imam that the verse was revealed concerning idolaters who met a group of Muslims during the last two nights of Muharram. They said: The companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) dislike fighting in the sacred month, so attack them. The Muslims appealed to them to refrain from fighting, but they refused and fought them, and the Muslims were victorious. Something of the fighting in the sacred month weighed on their hearts, so Allah the Exalted revealed the verse. Then he said: According to this, the matter of correspondence is evident, and it would be more fitting to the composition of the discourse, because its wording

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 61:

﴿Thus it is.﴾ This is a decisive separation (*fasl li'l-khitab*, a device marking a clean break between topics). His saying, ﴿And whoever retaliates﴾, begins a new account concerning those noble ones, after His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And those who emigrated﴾, the two verses. (End of quotation.)

It has been objected that the verse requires a beginning, then a recompense, then transgression, then a recompense. The account does not indicate this unless what occurred between them is treated as mutual hostility answered in kind, and the "transgression" is taken as their opposition by fighting the Muslims in the sacred month. This contradicts the apparent meaning. As for agreement with the composition of the text, it is clearer according to what others have stated: when He mentioned the state of those among them who were killed and those among them who died, it was said that the matter is so in what pertains to the state of the Hereafter, and in what pertains to the state of this world, that ﴿they will surely be helped﴾, because they are between one who retaliates and one who pardons, and both are helped. The first is helped explicitly, and the second by the implication of the address, namely the implied meaning of agreement (*mafhum al-muwafaqa*, what is understood by agreement with the explicit wording). In it is a severe warning to the transgressor, and that he is forsaken in both abodes, and is placed among those who were in doubt until the Hour or the punishment came upon them. This is a weighty statement, and the saying of some that He used this for abrupt transition (*iqtidab*) does not spoil it, so consider this.

It is related from al-Dahhak that the verse is Medinan, and that it concerns retribution (*qisas*) and wounds.

Al-Shafi'i used it as evidence for the obligation of observing equivalence in retribution. According to us (the Hanafi school), there is no retaliatory killing (*qawad*) except by the sword, as came in the report, and by the sword is meant the weapon. The report, "Whoever drowns someone, we will drown him, and whoever burns someone, we will burn him," is not authentic. Even granting its authenticity, it is understood as discretionary punishment (*siyasa*). It should be known that retaliation in kind absolutely is not lawful, for a man may be insulted with something like "O adulterer," and they have said: if he is told this and replies, "No, rather you are the adulterer," both of them receive the legal penalty (*hadd*), and the first speaker is the one to be considered. So let this be remembered.

﴿That﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the help implied by His saying, ﴿Allah will surely help him﴾, and the sense of distance in it (the far demonstrative) indicates the elevated rank of that help. It has also been said that it is due to the absence of an explicitly mentioned referent. Its position is nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence, and its predicate is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿because Allah causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night﴾. The preposition *bi-* (*bi-anna*, "because") here is causal, and the cause is what is indicated by what follows, by way of necessary implication. That is, that help exists because Allah, exalted is His majesty, is able to make some of His creation prevail over others, and the alternation between opposites is among His attributes.

This is expressed by the entry of one of the two alternating phases into the other, by adding to one what is lost from the other, as is the most fitting meaning of *iylaj* (entering). Or it is by bringing one of them into the place of the other, as has been said. It does not mean that He places a night between every two days and a day between every two nights, as has been imagined, because this is the most apparent and clearest of the matters. Or the sense is that it exists because He, exalted is He, is the Creator of the night and the day and the One who directs them, so what occurs in them at the hands of His servants of good and evil, transgression and victory, is not hidden, as has been said.

According to the first explanation, His saying, ﴿And that Allah is All-Hearing﴾ of all things heard, among which is what the one who retaliates says, ﴿All-Seeing﴾ of all things seen, among which are the actions that proceed from him, is a completion of the judgment and an inseparable part of it, since the helper must have the power to help the oppressed and knowledge that he is so. According to the second explanation, it is a completion and emphasis. The first is preferable. It has also been said: it is not far that the meaning is that this help is due to the alternation of night and day and the rotation of times and cycles, until the time comes that the Mighty King has decreed for the victory and triumph of the oppressed. In this there is the point that it has no real significance unless one considers the power of the agent who does that. It has also been said: it is permissible that the reference is to the attribute of pardon and forgiveness, meaning that this attribute is due to His, exalted is He, not holding people accountable for their sins, for otherwise He would make the night and the day perpetual, and the interests would be disrupted. In this there is the point that, besides its not fitting the context, it is not evident, especially when one considers the conjunction of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and that Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing﴾ upon what follows the preposition *bi-* earlier,

[Page 191]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 62:

Yes, the indication is to the attribute in His saying, ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth (al-Haqq)﴾. So the meaning is: that attribute is the perfection of power, which is indicated by His saying, ﴿He causes the night to enter into the day﴾, and so on, and the perfection of knowledge, which is indicated by ﴿All-Hearing, All-Seeing﴾. This is because Allah, the Exalted, is the Necessary Being in Himself (al-wajib li-dhatihi, the being whose existence is necessary in its own essence), established in Himself alone. Indeed, the necessity of His existence and His oneness (wahdah) entail that He, glory be to Him, is the one who brings into being all created things. His bringing them into being in that way, being in the most wondrous and most perfect manner, requires perfect knowledge, as is explained in its proper place.

It has also been said that the necessity of existence alone encompasses every perfection, even oneness. Or the meaning is: that attribute is because Allah, the Exalted, is the one who alone has established divinity (al-ilahiyyah), and none is fit for it except one who is perfect in power and perfect in knowledge. ﴿And that what they call upon besides Him﴾, as a god, ﴿is the false﴾, i.e., what is non-existent in its own essence, or the false in respect of divinity. The restriction (al-hasr) may not be intended, and it was only brought in for the sake of harmony (al-mushakalah). It may also be intended, in the sense that all that they call upon besides Him is the false, not some of it and not other parts of it.

It has been said that ﴿huwa﴾ (it) is used in regard to the perfection of its falsity. The addition of ﴿huwa﴾ here, unlike what is in the similar verse in Surah Luqman, is because what is here comes among ten verses, each of which emphasizes once or twice. For this reason also the lam is added in His saying, which comes later: ﴿And indeed Allah, He is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy﴾, unlike its counterpart in that surah. It may be said that the mention of Satan has preceded in this surah, so these emphatic particles were mentioned, unlike Surah Luqman, in which the mention of Satan did not precede in the manner mentioned here. This is what al-Nisaburi said. It is also permissible that the addition of ﴿huwa﴾ in this place is because the thing being explained (al-mu'allal) here is greater than in that place, so reflect.

﴿And that Allah, He is the Most High﴾ over all things, ﴿the Great﴾, above having any partner for Him, glory be to Him. There is nothing higher than Him in rank (sha'n), and greater in authority (sultan).

Al-Hasan read ﴿wa-inna ma﴾ with a kasrah on the hamzah. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr read ﴿tad'una﴾ with the ta', addressing the polytheists. Mujahid, al-Yamani, and Musa al-Aswari read ﴿yad'una﴾ with the ya' (underdotted), in the passive voice, on the basis that the wawu refers to the gods (al-alihah) and ﴿ma﴾ refers to them. The expression of them by ﴿ma﴾, and then the return of the pronoun for rational beings to them, is evident, so do not overlook this.

﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky﴾, i.e., from the direction of height, ﴿water﴾. That is, do you not know this? It is also permissible for the seeing to be visual, looking at the water that is sent down. The interrogation is for affirmation (taqrir). His saying, ﴿so the earth becomes green﴾, means "so it becomes" (fa-tasir). It has been said that "becomes" is in its literal sense, and the judgment is made with regard to some places where the sky rains at night, so the earth becomes green in the morning. The first is preferable. It is conjoined to ﴿sent down﴾, and the fa' suffices in place of a connecting pronoun, so there is no need to estimate "by its sending down." The sequence (al-ta'qib) is customary or real, and it is either with respect to the complete readiness for greening, or with respect to the greening itself, which is as you see. It is also permissible that the fa' is solely for causation, so there is no sequence in it. The shift from the past tense to the present tense is to convey the continuation of the effect of the rain over time after time, as you say, "I am bestowing favor on so-and-so this year, so I go out and come back thankful to him." If you were to say, "I rejoiced and went out," that would not occupy that position. Or it is to bring to presence the wondrous image. The verb is not put in the subjunctive as an answer to the interrogation here in any of the readings, as far as we know, and more than one scholar has stated that it is impermissible. In al-Bahr it says that the accusative is impermissible here, because when the negation enters upon it, the interrogation, although it implies affirmation in some speech, is treated as pure negation in the answer. Do you not see His saying: ﴿Am I not your Lord? They said: Yes﴾ [al-A'raf: 172]? Likewise, in the answer with fa', when you answer a negation, it has two meanings, and in each of them the answer is negated. So when you say, "You visit us and talk to us" with the accusative, the meaning is "You do not visit us as one who talks; you only visit us and do not talk." It is also permissible that the meaning is "You do not visit us, so how do you talk to us?" So the talking is negated in both situations. Affirmation by means of the interrogative particle is like pure negation in the answer: it affirms what the hamzah of interrogation has entered upon, and negates the answer. So it would follow here that the seeing is affirmed and the greening is negated, and that is contrary to the intended meaning. Also, an answer to an interrogation forms with it a conditional and a consequent, and it is not correct to say here, "If you see the sending down of water, the earth will become green," because its greening is not consequent upon your knowledge or your seeing; it is consequent upon the sending down. End quote.

Al-Zamakhshari went to the reversal of meaning on the supposition of the accusative, where he said: "If the verb were put in the accusative as an answer to the interrogation, it would give the opposite of the purpose, because its meaning would be the affirmation of greening, and with the accusative it would turn into the negation of greening." But the author of al-Fara'id (Sahib al-Fara'id) criticized him, saying: "There is no basis for what the author of al-Kashshaf mentioned. The meaning he stated does not follow. Rather, it follows from its accusative that it would be a partner to His saying, the Exalted:"

[p. 192]

[Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 63]

﴿Have you not seen﴾ follows it (as its governed element), and it is not a subsequent clause of the sending down. With its governing particle, it becomes a verbal noun (maṣdar) conjoined to the verbal noun contained in ﴿Have you not seen﴾. The sense would be: "Has there not been for you a sight of the sending down of water from the sky and of the earth becoming green?" This is not what the verse intends. Rather, it intends that the earth becomes green through the sending down of water, so that the earth's becoming green is a consequence of the sending down, conjoined to it. End of quotation. There is discussion in this.

The author of al-Taqrib said on this: the nasb (subjunctive) is by the presumption of inna, which is a sign of the future (istiqbal), so the verb is made expectant. The raf' (indicative) is a definite affirmation of its report. The summary is that the raf' is a definite affirmation of its occurrence, while the nasb is not a definite affirmation of it, not that it is a definite negation of it. It is not hidden that, even if this is sound in itself, it does not accord with the meaning of al-Zamakhshari.

Abu al-Baqa' explained the impossibility of the nasb by two matters. The first is the absence of the causal relation (sababiyyah) of the interrogated element to what follows the fa', as has been mentioned from al-Bahr. The second is that the interrogation mentioned has the sense of a statement (khabar), and so it has no response (jawab). To this view al-Farra' went, and he said: ﴿Have you not seen﴾ is a statement, as you say in speech: "Know that God Most High does such-and-such, and so such-and-such happens." Sibawayh said: "I asked him," meaning al-Khalil, about the words of the Most High: ﴿Have you not seen that God sends down water from the sky, and the earth becomes green?﴾ He said: "This is obligatory, and it is an alert, as if you said: 'Do you hear?'" In the Eastern copy of the book it reads: "Attend: God sent down water from the sky, and so such-and-such happened."

Some later scholars said: it is permissible to regard the action as a result of the negation, and then to regard the entry of the affirmative interrogative (istifham taqriri) so that the meaning becomes: there has come about from you a sight of God Most High's sending down water, and then the earth's becoming green. This is because the interrogation mentioned, entering upon the negation, has the sense of negating a negation, which is an affirmation. If you say: "Sight is not a cause, neither of negation nor of affirmation of the greening," I say: the sight is a superfluous insertion (muqhamah), and the intended element is the sending down, or it is a metonymy (kinayah) for it, because it entails it. Moreover, it suffices to compare it to the cause, as al-Radi stated concerning ﴿ma ta'tina fa-tuhaddithana﴾ in one of its two interpretations. He chose this, in arguing against the permissibility of the nasb, that the nasb makes the present tense (mudari') specific to the future, which befits the conditional (jaza'iyyah), according to what is established in the science of grammar. This is not possible in the noble verse, as you see. In sum, what the verifiers (muhaqqiqun) hold is that whoever permitted the nasb here was not correct, and that the meaning intended upon it is reversed.

It has been read as ﴿mukhdarrah﴾ with a fatha on the mim and a light pronunciation of the dad, like mabqalah and majzarah, meaning "possessing greenness."

﴿Indeed God is Subtle﴾, that is, He bestows favour upon the servants by delivering their benefits to them gently. Among that is the sending down of water from the sky, and the greening of the earth through it. ﴿All-Aware﴾, that is, Knowing of the fine details of affairs, among them the measures of the interests of His servants.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "Subtle with the provision of His servants, All-Aware of what is in their hearts of despair." Muqatil said: "Subtle in bringing forth plants, All-Aware of the manner of their creation." Al-Kalbi said: "Subtle in His acts, with the deeds of His servants." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The Subtle is the one who arranges affairs gently." Al-Amidi reported that He is the Knower of hidden things. You know that this is the well-known meaning of the All-Aware. Some of them interpreted it as "the Informer," but this does not suit the context, just as interpreting the Subtle as "that which the senses do not perceive" does not.

[Page 193]

﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ in creation, ownership and disposal. The lam here indicates complete exclusivity (lam al-ikhtisas). ﴿And indeed Allah is the Free of need (al-Ghani)﴾, who has no need of anything whatsoever, ﴿the Praiseworthy (al-Hamid)﴾, whom all His creation praises by His attributes and His acts, whether by speech or by state.

﴿Do you not see that Allah has subjected to you whatever is on the earth﴾, meaning He made the things in it subservient to you, prepared for your benefit, so that you may dispose of them as you wish. The placing of the prepositional phrase (al-jar wa al-majrur) before the direct object has been explained more than once, and it serves to give importance to what is placed first and to create anticipation for what comes after. ﴿And the ship (al-fulk)﴾ is read in the accusative with a sukun on the lam. Ibn Muqsim and al-Kisa'i, from al-Hasan, read it with a damma on the lam. It is coordinated with what precedes it as a specific term coordinated over a general one (atf al-khass ʿala al-ʿamm), to draw attention to the strangeness of its subjugation and the abundance of its benefits. It is also permitted that it be coordinated with the divine name (al-ism al-jalil). According to the first view, the phrase ﴿running upon the sea by His command﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to it; according to the second, it is the predicate (khabar) of inna. In that case the waw would have coordinated noun with noun and predicate with predicate, which is contrary to the apparent sense. The reading "fi al-bahr" (upon the sea) in this way is a construction far removed from eloquence. Al-Sulami, al-A'raj, Talha, Abu Haywa and al-Za'farani read "al-fulku" with a damma as the nominative, the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada'), with what follows it as its predicate, and the sentence is then independent (mustanaffa).

It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause. It has been said that the nominative may be by coordination upon the position (mahall) of inna together with its noun, and this is in the manner of coordination upon the noun.

﴿And He holds back the sky from falling upon the earth﴾, meaning from falling upon it. The construction is by deletion of the preposition (hadhf harf al-jarr), and "an" with what follows it is in the sense of a verbal noun, either in the accusative or the genitive, according to the two well-known views on this matter. Some have made it occupy the position of a causative object (maf'ul li-ajlihi), with the implied meaning "lest it fall" or "out of aversion to its falling," according to the Basrans, while the Kufans consider the implied particle to be "li-alla" (in order that it not fall).

Abu Hayyan said: the apparent view is that ﴿taqa'﴾ is in the accusative position as a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for "al-sama'" (the sky), meaning "and He prevents the sky from falling upon the earth." This was rejected on the grounds that imsak in the sense of "adherence" takes the preposition "bi", in the sense of "restraint" takes "ʿan", and likewise in the sense of "guarding" and "stinginess," as in Taj al-Masadir. As for the sense of "prevention," it is not well known. This was criticised in turn, on the grounds that it is not a valid objection, since it is well known and explicitly stated in the lexicographical works. Al-Raghib said: one says amsaktu ʿanhu kadha, meaning "I prevented him from such-and-such." He (Allah) said: ﴿Are they removers of His mercy?﴾ [al-Zumar: 38], and stinginess is expressed by imsak. End of his words. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explicitly stated this in their commentary on His words ﴿Indeed, Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease﴾ [Fatir: 41]. Indeed, the first construction is more apparent. The meaning of His holding them back from falling upon the earth is preserving their cohesion by His power, after He created them cohesive moment by moment, and His will not being related to their falling in pieces, piece by piece.

It has been said that His holding them back from that is by making them encompassing, neither heavy nor light. This is based on the identity of the sky and the sphere (al-fulk), and on the well-known view of the philosophers (falasifa) that the sphere is neither heavy nor light. They built this on their claim that it is impossible for it to accept straight-line motion, and they derived from it that it is neither hot, nor cold, nor moist, nor dry. They used as proof of the impossibility of accepting straight-line motion what the theologians (mutakallimun) refuted in their books.

What is known from the school of the early Muslims (salaf al-muslimin) is that the sky is other than the sphere, that it has a creaking (atit), in accordance with His (peace be upon him) saying: "The sky has creaked, and it has the right to creak. There is no spot the size of a hand in it where there is not an angel standing or prostrating." And that it is heavy and preserved from falling by the sheer will of Him, glory be to Him, and His power, which nothing can resist, not because it holds itself by its own essence.

Some theologians, to deny this, mentioned that it shares in corporeality with all other bodies that are receptive to downward inclination, so it accepts it as other bodies accept it. There is room for discussion about this according to the claim of the philosophers. The use of the present tense (al-mudari') indicates continuous renewal, meaning that He holds it back from falling moment by moment ﴿except by His leave﴾, meaning by His will. The exception is an exception from the most general causes (istithna' mufarragh min a'amm al-asbab). This is valid in an affirmative sentence either because the generality is intended, or because "yumsik" carries the sense of negation, meaning He does not leave it to fall by any cause, such as the passage of long ages over it or its heaviness with what is in it, except by a cause which is His will that it fall. It has been said that it is an exception from the most general states, meaning He does not leave it to fall in any state, except in its being associated with His will, may He be exalted. What we have mentioned seems more apparent. In al-Bahr it is said that the prepositional phrase is connected to "taqa'". Ibn ʿAtiyya said: it may be connected to "yumsik", because the sentence implies "without intention or the like," so it is as if he meant: except by His leave, by which He holds it back. Had it been as he said, the structure would have been without "illa". End of his words. By my life, what Ibn ʿAtiyya said is not said by anyone who has even a little reflection, as is not hidden. Furthermore, there is no indication in the verse that the leave is related to the falling. It has been said that there is in it an allusion to the falling, and that is the Day of Resurrection, for the sky will split on that day and fall upon the earth. As for me, there is nothing in my mind from the verses or the reports that is explicit about the sky falling upon the earth on that day. They are explicit only about its being shaken, split, folded up and changed, and none of that indicates falling upon the earth, let alone being explicit about it. The apparent view is that by "al-sama'" is meant its genus, which includes the seven heavens. This is supported by what al-Tabarani transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "When you come before a fearsome ruler whom you fear will overpower you, say: Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, greater than all His creation. Allahu akbar, greater than what I fear and beware of. I seek refuge in Allah, besides whom there is no god, the One who holds the seven heavens from falling upon the earth except by His leave, from the evil of Your servant so-and-so, his troops, his followers and his partisans, from the jinn and mankind. My God, be for me a protector from their evil; Your praise is exalted, Your protection is mighty, Your name is blessed, and there is no god but You," three times.

The apparent view also is that the context of the verse is for the sake of bounty (imtinan), not for threat (wa'id), as some have permitted. This is supported by His saying: ﴿Indeed Allah is, toward the people, Kind and Merciful﴾, since He subjected for them what He subjected and bestowed upon them security from what would stand between them and benefiting from it, namely the sky falling upon the earth. It has also been said: since He prepared for them the means of their livelihood, opened to them the doors of benefits, and made clear to them the paths of reasoning from the signs of creation and of revelation. Making the sentence a causal clause (ta'liliyyah) in regard to what is within

[p. 194]

﴿Have you not seen that Allah has subjected﴾ etc. The more apparent meaning is what we have stated. It has been said that *ar-ra'fah* (رَأْفَة) implies the averting of harms, and *ar-rahmah* (رَحْمَة) implies the securing of benefits. Because averting harm is more important than securing benefit, *ra'uf* (رَؤُوف) is placed before *rahim* (رَحِيم). Everything for which He, glorified is He, bestows favour contains both averting and securing. It has been said that the holding back of the sky from falling is more apparent in averting, and there is a clear reason for its being placed later. Some have said: *ar-ra'fah* is more intense than *ar-rahmah*, and the placing of (رَؤُف) is for the sake of the verse-ending (*fasilah*, the rhyming end of the verse). A group of scholars held that *ar-rahmah* is more general, and this is probably the apparent view. The placing of (بِالنَّاسِ) "toward the people" is for emphasis, and it has been said it is for the sake of the verse-ending. Separating the two places (in the verse) is something that is not considered good.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 66:

﴿It is He who gave you life﴾ after you had been inanimate matter, elements, and drops (of semen), as detailed at the beginning of the noble surah. [Page 195] ﴿Then He causes you to die﴾ when your terms arrive, ﴿then He gives you life again﴾ at the Resurrection. ﴿Indeed, man is ungrateful﴾, meaning he is truly ungrateful for the blessings despite their being evident. This is a description of the species by describing some of its individuals. It has also been said that by "man" is meant the disbeliever, and this was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "He is al-Aswad ibn 'Abd al-Asad, Abu Jahl, and Ubayy ibn Khalaf." Perhaps this is by way of illustration (tamthil).

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 67:**

﴿For every community We have appointed a rite﴾ is a resumptive clause (*kalam mustaʾnaf*, a new sentence not grammatically linked to what precedes it), brought to rebuke the contemporaries of the Prophet (ﷺ) among the People of the Scriptures who disputed with him (ﷺ). It describes the state of the laws they clung to and shows their error in reasoning. That is, *for every specific community among the communities, both past and present*, ﴿We have appointed﴾ means We placed and designated ﴿a rite﴾ (*mansak*), meaning a specific law (*shariʿa*). The fronting of the prepositional phrase *li-kulli ummatin* before the verb serves to restrict (*qasr*, exclusivity), not to restrict it to one community among them alone. The construction is like your saying: "To each of Fatima, Zaynab, Hind and Hafsa I gave a special garment," when you had given Fatima a red garment, Zaynab a yellow one, Hind a black one and Hafsa a white one. This amounts to saying: "To Fatima I gave a red garment, not to any other of her sisters; and to Zaynab I gave a yellow garment, not to any other of them," and so on. The essential meaning here is: We designated each law for a specific community among the communities, such that no community oversteps its designated law to another law, neither independently nor jointly.

God's words ﴿they are its performers﴾ (*hum nāsikūhu*) are a descriptive phrase qualifying *mansakan*, reinforcing the restriction. The pronoun refers to *every community* in terms of its particularity: that specific community performs it and acts by it, not another community. Thus the community that existed from the mission of Moses to the mission of Jesus, peace be upon them both, had as its rite what is in the Torah, and they alone acted by it and no others. The community from the mission of Jesus, peace be upon him, to the mission of our Prophet (ﷺ) had as its rite what is in the Gospel, and they alone acted by it. As for the community present at the mission of the Prophet (ﷺ) and those after them who exist until the Day of Resurrection, they are one community whose rite is only what is in the Qur'an.

The *fa* (then) in God's words ﴿So let them not dispute with you in the matter﴾, that is, the matter of religion, is for the consequence of prohibition on what precedes it. His designation for every community among the communities, of which his community (ﷺ) is one, of a law that is independent, such that no community oversteps what has been designated for it, is a binding reason for these people to obey him (ﷺ) and not to dispute with him (ﷺ) over the matter of religion. They claimed that their law was what was designated for their forefathers, namely what is in the Torah and the Gospel, since that was a law only for those who lived before its abrogation (*naskh*, the cancellation of a ruling by a later one). These people, however, are an independent community whose law is only what is in the Qur'an. The apparent meaning is that the intended sense is a literal prohibition of them from disputing over this.

Some have chosen that it is a metonymy (*kināya*) for a prohibition to the Prophet (ﷺ) from paying attention to their dispute, which is based on the claim mentioned, since this is more fitting with God's later words ﴿And call﴾, etc. The fittingness of this is evident, but in itself it is contrary to the apparent meaning.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is a prohibition addressed to him (ﷺ) from disputing with them, as you say: "Zayd should not strike you," meaning, "you should not strike him," and this is by way of metonymy. This is permissible, according to what has been said and discussed, only in the case of the form of *mufāʿala* (reciprocal or mutual action, from *fāʿala*) because of the reciprocity implied. Thus in a sentence like *lā yaḍribannaka Zaydun* ("Zayd shall not strike you") it is not permissible to mean "you shall not strike him."

This has been criticized on the grounds that the context does not support it. It is read as *fa-lā yunāziʿunnaka* with the light nūn (*nūn khafīfa*). Abu Mijlaz and Lahiq ibn Humayd read *fa-lā yinziʿunnaka* with a kasra on the *zāy*, taking it as from *nazʿ* (pulling), as in *al-Bahr*. The meaning, as Ibn Jinni said, is: "let them not pull you away from your religion toward their religions," so that you become like one who is pulled away from something to something else.

In *al-Kashshaf* it is said that the meaning is: "be firm in your religion, with a firmness such that they do not hope to pull you away so as to remove you from it." The intent is an increase in steadfastness for him (ﷺ), by means that stir his zeal and inflame his anger for the sake of God the Exalted and His religion. Much of the like occurs in the Qur'an.

Al-Zajjaj also said: it is from *nāzaʿtuhu fa-nazaʿtuhu, anziʿuhu*, meaning "I overcame him." So the meaning is: "let them not overcome you in the dispute," and the intended sense is contention in argument. He means that this belongs to the category of mutual overcoming. However, you know that according to the majority of scholars it is said of every verb of the form *faʿaltu* (in the sense of *fāʿaltu*) that the form *fa-ʿaltu* in the present is *afʿalu* with a *ḍamma* on the middle radical, and it is not pronounced with a kasra except as an irregularity (*shudhūdh*). Al-Kisa'i claimed, and the scholars refuted him, that whatever has a throat letter (*ḥarf ḥalq*) as its middle or final radical is not given a *ḍamma* but is left as it was. So what occurs here, according to al-Zajjaj's interpretation, is irregular according to the majority.

Sibawayh said, as in *al-Mufassal*: this does not apply to everything; that is, the category of mutual overcoming does not always apply. Do you not see that you say *nāzaʿanī fa-nazaʿtuhu* ("he disputed with me, so I overcame him"), which is dispensed with by his being overcome? Then the meaning of "let them not overcome you in the dispute" is: do not fall short in disputing with them, lest they overcome you in it. This contains an exaggeration in steadiness. So there is no prohibition addressed to him, may God the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, against the act of another.

This explanation of *mansak* as *sharīʿa* is the narration of ʿAṭāʾ from Ibn ʿAbbas, and al-Qaffal chose it. Al-Imam said: it is the closer one. It has also been said that it is a verbal noun meaning *nusuk*, i.e. worship. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: God's words ﴿they are its performers﴾ indicate that. It has been said that it is a noun of time, and it has been said that it is a noun of place, and the apparent form would be *nāsikūna fīhi* ("performing in it"), but it was extended in usage. Mujahid said: it is slaughter.

Al-Hakim transmitted this and declared it sound, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shuʿab* transmitted it from ʿAli ibn al-Husayn, may God be pleased with them both; and Ibn Abi Hatim from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both; and ʿAbd ibn Humayd from ʿIkrima.

Some made the pronoun of ﴿they dispute with you﴾ refer to the polytheists, and the matter disputed is the matter of slaughtered animals, on account of what is mentioned: that the verse was revealed concerning the saying of the Khuzaʿi men Budayl ibn Warqaʾ, Bishr ibn Sufyan and Yazid ibn Khunays to the believers: "What is the matter with you, that you eat what you have killed and do not eat what God has killed?" Some confined the locus of dispute to the matter of sacrificial rites and made it an expression for the saying of the Khuzaʿi men mentioned.

Shaykh al-Islam criticized this, saying it is something to which there is no path at all. How could it not be so? It would require that eating carrion and all the other falsehoods to which the polytheists adhere be among the rites that God has ordained for some communities, and no rational person doubts its falsehood. It has been answered that the meaning on this view is: "let the polytheists not dispute with you over the matter of sacrificial rites, for to every community We have made a law which We legislated and made known to you; how then can they dispute with what has no basis or trace in it?" It has also been said that the meaning on this view is: "do not turn to the dispute of the polytheists over the matter of slaughtering animals, for We have made for every community among the People of the Religions a slaughter which they perform."

Its summary is: do not turn to that, for slaughter is an ancient practice of the communities, not specific to your community. There is no doubt about the soundness of this. Whoever affirms the soundness of the transmitted reports and holds fast to them with the molars (*ʿaḍḍa ʿalayhā bil-nawājidh*, an idiom for firm adherence) will hardly find anything better than this in explaining the sense of the verse as it requires. Whoever is not like that, and holds that whenever a verse admits a sound meaning with no objectionable element, it may be asserted even if none of the early generation (*salaf*) mentioned it, then for him is what we mentioned first in explaining the verse.

Whatever the case, the apparent reason this sentence was not joined by a conjunction, as God's words ﴿And for every community We have appointed a rite that they may mention﴾ [al-Hajj: 34] etc. were joined, is the weakness of the link between it and the verses preceding it, unlike that case.

In *al-Kashf* there is an explanation of what *al-Kashshaf* says about the justification for conjunction there and its absence here: the link there is strong and calls for conjunction, for God's words ﴿In them you have benefits﴾, i.e. in the rites (*shaʿāʾir*), are religious and worldly benefits, such as the obligation of sacrificing them, culminating in the Ancient House, like the repetition in God's words ﴿that they may witness benefits for themselves and mention the name of God on known days﴾ [al-Hajj: 28]. However, there is a particularization to the addressees there, so ﴿And for every community We have appointed a rite﴾ is conjoined to it for the purpose of mention, so that the repetition is complete. The purpose of this style is to show that it is an ancient law and that it has always included great benefits in both abodes. As for what we are discussing, where is the discussion of sacrificial rites in relation to the discussion of enumerating the signs and blessings that indicate the perfection of God's knowledge, power, wisdom and mercy? By my life, the legislation of sacrificial rites for every community, although it is of mercy and blessing, nevertheless the consideration of the homogeneity between the blessings and what the speech is directed toward requires cutting off the link. Mentioning it here for this relation is in a subtle and narrow way. (End of quotation.) This is good, and its apparent meaning is the explanation of *nusuk* as slaughter.

Al-Tibi mentioned that what precedes is conjoined to God's words ﴿And whoever magnifies the rites of God﴾ [al-Hajj: 32], etc., and it is part of the speech addressed to the believers. That is: the matter is so, and what is required is the magnification of the rites of God the Exalted. This is not something specific to you, since every community is particularly devoted to a rite and worship.

This verse is an introduction to the prohibition addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning what would provoke the people's dispute. It is a consolation to him and an exaltation of his affair, in that He made his matter a rite and a religion. The meaning is: your affair and the affair of those like you among the prophets and messengers, peace be upon them, is to abandon dispute with the ignorant, to allow them to argue in a way that leads to contention, and to persist in calling to monotheism. Or: for every community of the past opposing communities We have made a path and a religion which they perform; so let these people not dispute with you in argument. Their habit is called a rite (*nusuk*) because they made it binding upon themselves and persisted in it, as mockery of them and as a consolation to His Messenger (ﷺ) for what he suffered from them.

As for its connection with the verses before it: God's words ﴿And they will not cease to be in doubt about it﴾ [al-Hajj: 55] require ceasing to warn the people and despairing of them and leaving them. The intervening verses serve as emphasis for the meaning of consolation. So God's words ﴿For every community We have appointed a rite, they are its performers, so let them not dispute with you﴾ come as an incitement for him (ﷺ) to follow the example of the earlier prophets in leaving the people and refraining from arguing with them after despairing of their belief. This is supported by God's words ﴿God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection﴾. So the linkage is by way of resumption, which is stronger than verbal linkage.

The theme around which the core of this noble surah revolves is the speech about the people's disputation and opposition, and the condemnation of them for their stubbornness. Do you not see how it opens with God's words ﴿And among people is one who disputes about God﴾ [al-Hajj: 3], repeats it, and makes it the foundation of the meaning of concern? Whenever it takes up a matter, it returns to this, as a firming of the heart of the Messenger (ﷺ) and a consolation to his noble breast (ﷺ). So it cannot be said that this verse is out of place with respect to its meaning. (End of quotation.) By my life, this is far from the abodes of verification, and he explained the noble verse in a way that is not fitting.

The connection with what was mentioned has been criticized in *al-Kashf* on the grounds that it has no basis, for there intervened what is unsuitable for emphasizing the mentioned meaning of consolation, namely God's words ﴿And whoever retaliates﴾ and the verses that follow, especially according to his preference for placing them concerning those who fight in the sacred month. Even if it were granted, there is no place for resumption there, and it is preparation for what follows it, namely God's words ﴿So let them not dispute with you﴾, etc. As for his statement "the theme around which it revolves" etc., it is granted, but it is against him, not for him. So reflect. And God the Exalted is the Granter of success to what is right.

﴿And call﴾, i.e. call these disputants, or call all people, on the basis that they are included among them by a primary inclusion, ﴿to your Lord﴾, to His monotheism and worship, as is explained in their rite and law, ﴿Indeed you are surely upon guidance﴾, i.e. a path leading to the truth. In this there is a metaphor (*istiʿāra makniyya*, implicit metaphor), and its imaginative element is "upon" (*ʿalā*). God's words ﴿straight﴾ (*mustaqīm*), i.e. upright, or one of the two is an imaginative element and the other a supporting element (*tarshīḥ*). Then the intended meaning of this path is either the religion and the law, or their evidences. The sentence is a resumption in the subject of the causal explanation.

"And if they dispute with you" over the matter of the religion, when the truth has become manifest and the proof has been established, "then say" to them, in the manner of warning: "God knows best what you do" of falsehoods, among which is this disputing, and so He will requite you for it. And this, if it is intended as a truce (muwada'ah), as Abu Hayyan (Abu Hayyan al-Andalusi) affirmed with certainty, then it is abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of fighting.

Allah will judge between you (﴿اللَّهُ يَحْكُمُ بَيْنَكُمْ﴾) as consolation for him, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him. The address is general to both groups, the believers and the disbelievers, and it is not restricted to the disbelievers as the previous verse was, nor is it included within the scope of "saying" (in the sense of being part of what was said). It has also been permitted that it be included within that scope by way of predominance (taghlib), meaning: Allah will separate between the believers among you and the disbelievers ﴿on the Day of Resurrection﴾ (﴿يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ﴾) with reward and punishment, just as He made distinction in this world by the establishment of the proofs of the one who is right over the one who is wrong (al-muhiqq over al-mubtil). ﴿Concerning that in which you used to differ﴾ (﴿فِيما كُنْتُمْ فِيهِ تَخْتَلِفُونَ﴾), i.e., concerning matters of religion. It has been said that it refers to the disputing and differing over the matter of slaughtered animals (al-dhaba'ih). The meaning of "differing" (ikhtilaf) is that each party goes to the opposite of what the other has gone to.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 70:

﴿Do you not know﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) confirming the content of what precedes it, and the interrogative is for confirmation (taqrir), meaning: you have indeed known ﴿that Allah knows whatever is in the heaven and the earth﴾, so nothing is hidden from Him of the things, among which are the statements and deeds of the disbelievers. ﴿Indeed that﴾, i.e., what is in the heaven and the earth, ﴿is in a Book﴾. It is, as related from Ibn 'Abbas, the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). He, may Allah be pleased with him, mentioned that its length is a distance of one hundred years, and that there was written in it whatever will occur in Allah's knowledge until the Day of Resurrection. Abu Muslim denied this and said: the intended meaning of "Book" is preservation and safeguarding, i.e., that this is preserved with Him, exalted is He. The majority hold otherwise. The intended meaning of the verse also includes consoling him, peace and blessings be upon him, as if it were said: Allah knows... so let their affair not trouble you, since We know it and We preserve it for him. ﴿Indeed that﴾, i.e., what has been mentioned of knowledge and comprehensiveness regarding what is in the heaven and the earth, and His writing it in the Tablet, and the judgment between you. It has been said: (that) refers only to the judgment, and it has been said it refers only to knowledge, and it has been said it refers to the writing of that in the Tablet. Perhaps its referring to all three, by interpreting it as what has been mentioned, is preferable. ﴿For Allah it is easy﴾: for His knowledge and power, exalted is His majesty, are the requirement of His essence, so nothing is hidden from Him and no matter that is within His power is difficult for Him. The fronting of the prepositional phrase is for the sake of matching the rhyme of the verses (ru'us al-ayy), or for restriction (qasr), i.e., it is easy for Him, exalted and high is He, and not for other than Him.

**[Page 199]**

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 22, verse 71:

﴿And they worship besides Allah﴾ is a description of some of the falsehoods of the polytheists and their conditions, which indicate the complete feebleness of their minds and the flimsiness of their opinions. It consists in their basing their affair on no foundation of transmitted evidence (*sam'i*) or rational evidence (*'aqli*), and in their turning away from the clear authority (*sultan*) that was sent down to them, which is the foundation of the religion. That is, they worship, going beyond the worship of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿that for which He has sent down no authority﴾, meaning no justification for its worship, ﴿authority﴾, meaning proof. The indefiniteness of *sultanan* (سُلْطانًا) is for the sake of minimizing. This points to the transmitted evidence that arises from the direction of revelation.

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and of which they have no knowledge﴾ points to the rational evidence, meaning: they have no knowledge, from the necessity of reason or from its inference, of the permissibility of its worship. The sum is that they worship besides Allah that for which there is no evidence, either from the direction of transmitted revelation or from the direction of reason, for its permissibility. The transmitted evidence is placed first because reliance on it is in most acts of worship, and because holding to it in this context is more hopeful for deliverance, if censure results from holding to rational evidence. If you have doubts, return to yourself: when a person blames you for an action, you will find yourself inclined to answer, "I did that because you told me you were pleased with my doing it," more than to answer, "I did it because rational evidence, namely such-and-such, establishes your approval of it." To deny this is obstinacy. It may be said that what is mentioned here first is what points to transmitted evidence, because it indicates a transmitted proof showing the permissibility of that worship, sent down from Him, the Exalted, not restricted by any condition, unlike what points to rational evidence, for in that there is an indication of a rational proof specific to them. The sum is that the precedence and the posteriority are for the sake of generality and restriction, even if they are not for one and the same thing. Understand this.

Al-'Allamah al-Tayyibi said: The restriction of transmitted evidence to *sultan* and *tanzil* (revelation), and contrasting it with *'ilm* (knowledge), is a clear proof that transmitted evidence is the decisive argument, that it has dominance and supremacy, and that upon its appearance opinions vanish and analogies dissolve. Whoever reverses this goes astray from the path and is deprived of success, and remains unsteady in the pitfalls of doubts. If you wish, look at the indefiniteness in (*sultanan* and *'ilmun*, سُلْطانا وعِلْمٌ) and compare them to the words of the poet:

*He has a chamberlain in every matter that disgraces him,*
*and he has no chamberlain against one who seeks the known good.*

So that you may know the difference, and so on to the end of what he said. From this a reason for the precedence becomes known, and another possibility regarding the tanwin of *sultanan* (سُلْطانا), other than what we have mentioned. Its apparent meaning is that transmitted evidence yields certainty absolutely, and that it takes precedence over rational evidence.
