The position of the Mu'tazilah (a theological school that gave reason primacy) and the majority of the Ash'ariyyah (a theological school that followed al-Ash'ari) is that it does not yield certainty absolutely, because that depends on matters all of which are speculative, so its indication is also speculative, since the branch cannot exceed the root in strength. The truth is that it may yield certainty in matters of the law (*shar'iyyat*) but not in rational matters (*'aqliyyat*), by means of observed or widely transmitted indicators that point to the exclusion of possibilities.

The virtuous al-Rumi mentioned in his glosses on the commentary of *al-Mawaqif*, after an investigation, that the truth is that it may yield certainty in rational matters too. As for its precedence over rational evidence, what our scholars hold is the opposite. Whenever rational evidence contradicts transmitted evidence, the transmitted evidence must be interpreted in a way that does not conflict with rational evidence, since it is impossible to act on both or on neither of them. Giving precedence to revelation over reason is the invalidation of the root by the branch, and in it is the invalidation of the branch. When establishing a thing leads to its invalidation, it contradicts itself and is void. However, the apparent meaning of the words of Muhyi al-Din ibn al-'Arabi, may his secret be sanctified, in several places of his *Futuhat* is that it takes precedence. Among that is his saying in the three hundred and fifty-eighth chapter, in verses:

*Every knowledge that the law bears witness to*
*is knowledge, so hold fast to it.*
*And if reason contradicts it, say:*
*Keep to your own station, for you have no footing in it.*

And his saying in the four hundred and seventy-second chapter:

*Upon revelation we relied, and so we became people of intellect,*
*and there is no knowledge in what does not come from revelation.*

And other than that. He is, like most of his speech, beyond the bounds of the station of reason.

﴿And for the wrongdoers﴾, that is, they have nothing, but it has been turned to the apparent form (*zahir*), registering upon them the wrongdoing together with giving the ruling a cause. It is also permitted that there is no turning here, and that what is meant includes them and others, though their inclusion is more appropriate. The *min* (from) in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿any helper (min nasir)﴾ is a strengthening particle. The meaning is the negation that there be for them, because of their wrongdoing, anyone who assists them in this world by supporting their doctrine and confirming their opinion, and repelling what opposes it, and in the hereafter by averting punishment from them.

﴿And when Our verses are recited to them﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with (yaʿbudūna, "they worship"), and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause (iʿtirāḍ). The use of the present tense (ṣīghat al-muḍāriʿ) indicates continuity and recurrence. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿clear proofs﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "the verses," meaning clear in their indication of the true beliefs and sound rulings, or clear in indicating the falsity of what they hold of worshipping other than Allah, Exalted is He. ﴿You will recognize in the faces of those who disbelieve﴾ means in their faces. The shift from what came before, and the address, is either to the master of those addressed, ﷺ, or to anyone who may be made to recognize, whoever he may be. ﴿The denial﴾ means the act of denying, taking it as a mīmī verbal noun (maṣdar mīmī), and what is meant is the sign of denial, or the disliked matter, such as the scowling, the frowning, and the appearances that indicate what they intend. This is the most fitting reading in light of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They almost assault those who recite Our verses to them﴾

[Page 200]

That is, they rush upon and attack them out of extreme rage and anger, over falsehoods they took up by blind imitation (taqlīd). The great ignorance in this is not hidden. It is also said that what is meant is that they are constantly on the verge of doing this throughout their lives; otherwise, they did in fact assault some of the reciting Companions at certain times, as in al-Bahr (al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ, the tafsir of Abū Ḥayyān). The clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the genitive noun (muḍāf ilayhi). It was also permitted that "the faces" be understood as the people themselves, but this is not the preferred reading.

ʿīsā ibn ʿUmar read «yuʿraf» in the passive voice, and «al-munkar» in the nominative case. ﴿Say﴾ in the manner of a warning and rebuke: ﴿Shall I inform you of something worse than that?﴾ That is, shall I address you, or will you listen so that I may tell you ﴿of worse than that﴾ which is within you of your rage against the reciters and your assault upon them, or of what befalls you of vexation because of what is recited to you. ﴿The Fire﴾ — that is, it is the Fire, taken as the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtadaʾ). The sentence is an answer to an implied question, as if it was said: "What is it?" It was also said that it is the subject (mubtadaʾ) whose predicate is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah has promised it to those who disbelieve﴾. According to the first reading, this is a resumptive sentence (jumla mustaʾnafa). It was also permitted that it be a predicate following a predicate (khabar baʿda khabar).

Ibn Abī ʿAbla, Ibrāhīm ibn Yūsuf (on the authority of al-Aʿshā), and Zayd ibn ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with them both, read «al-nār» in the accusative case as a restrictive object (ikhtiṣāṣ). The clause «waʿadahā» and so on is either a resumptive sentence or a circumstantial clause from «al-nār», with or without the particle qad, according to the difference of opinion. They did not permit the circumstantial reading in the nominative reading according to the first grammatical analysis, since there is nothing in the sentence that can govern the circumstantial clause. In the accusative reading it was permitted that it be of the type of ishtighāl (the verb being occupied with a pronoun referring to the noun), in which case the clause is then explanatory (mufassira). Ibn Abī Isḥāq and Ibrāhīm ibn Nūḥ, on the authority of Qutayba, read «al-nāri» in the genitive case as a substitution (ibdāl) for «sharr». In the clause there are two possibilities: that it is a resumptive sentence or a circumstantial clause. Apparently, in meaning, the pronoun in «waʿadahā» is the second object, and the first object is the relative pronoun, meaning: those who disbelieved promised it (the Fire) to themselves. Apparently, in wording, the first and second objects are the relative pronoun, as if the Fire had been promised to the disbelievers so that it would consume them. ﴿And wretched is the destination﴾ — the Fire.

﴿O mankind, a parable has been coined﴾ means: a strange situation or a wondrous, striking account has been set forth for you, truly deserving to be called a parable and to travel through the cities and the ages. The expression of that clarification in the past tense is for the certainty of its occurrence. The original meaning of mathal is "likeness," and then it became specific to a saying likened to its source, until it became a technical term, and then it was borrowed for what has been mentioned. It was said that mathal is in its literal sense, and «ḍuriba» means "was made," that is, a likeness was made for Allah, glorified is He, in the entitlement to worship. This is reported from al-Akhfash. The discourse is connected to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those you invoke besides Allah﴾ up to its end, as an explanation of the parable and an elucidation of it according to the first view, and as a justification for the invalidity of their making their false objects of worship a likeness of Allah, Exalted is His majesty, in the entitlement to worship according to the second view. Some have taken it, in accordance with what we have mentioned and what is reported from al-Akhfash, as an explanation: either, according to the first view, for the parable itself in its figurative meaning, or, according to the second view, for the situation of the parable in its literal meaning, since the meaning is: the disbelievers made a likeness for Allah, so listen to its situation and what is said about it. The truth, which none denies except a stubborn person, is that interpreting the verse by what has been reported in it is a departure from the apparent meaning.

Apparently, the address in

[Page 201]

**"O mankind"** [﴿يا أيُّها النّاسُ﴾] addresses all those who are legally responsible (mukallafun). However, the address in "**you call upon**" [تَدْعُونَ] is directed at the disbelievers. Some scholars have inclined to the view that the address in both places is directed at the disbelievers, and the evidence that the first is specifically for them is the second. It has also been said that the address in the first place is directed at the believers, whom Allah addressed in order to show them the error of the disbelievers. And it has been said that the address in both places is general, and that the second is like your saying, "You, O Banu Tamim, killed so-and-so." But this requires examination.

Al-Hasan, Ya'qub, Harun, al-Khaffaf and Mahbub, from Abu 'Amr, read **yad'una** [يَدْعُونَ] with a *ya'* (the third-person masculine prefix) in the active voice, as in the reading of the majority. Al-Yamani and Musa al-Aswari read **yud'awna** [يُدْعَوْنَ] also with a *ya'*, in the passive voice. The returning pronoun (al-rajiʿ) to the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) in the two previous readings is omitted: [the verse reads] **"those whom they call upon besides Allah will never create a fly"** [﴿لَنْ يَخْلُقُوا ذُبابًا﴾], meaning: they are not able to create it, despite its smallness and insignificance. What shows that the intended meaning is the negation of ability is the context, together with His words, exalted is He: **"even if they gathered together for it"** [﴿ولَوِ اجْتَمَعُوا لَهُ﴾], that is, for its creation. For custom dictates that one does not say, "The Zaydun will never carry such-and-such, even if they gather together to carry it," except when the intention is to negate the ability to carry it.

It has also been said that this negation with **lan** [لَنْ] is what is meant, since it is a particle conveying emphatic negation (nafy mu'akkad). It therefore indicates a contradiction between what is negated, namely creation, and that of which it is negated, namely the false objects of worship, and so it conveys their incapacity to do so. Apparently, the matter cannot dispense with the aid of the context as well. You should know that there is a difference of opinion on whether **lan** conveys emphatic negation. Al-Zamakhshari held that it conveys this, and that the emphasis of the negation here is to show that the creation of a fly by them is impossible. In his *Unmudhajuh* he said that it conveys perpetuity (al-ta'bid).

[Page 202]

The majority, and Abu Hayyan said it is the correct view, held that it does not convey this. For them, **lan** is a sister of **la** [لا] for negating the future when used without any indication of emphasis or perpetuity. If this is understood, it is from outside the particle and through contextual indicators. It may also be understood in this way even when the negation is with **la**. So if it were said here, "They do not create a fly, even if they gather together for it," this would be understood. They say regarding every proof that al-Zamakhshari uses for his claim that the conveyance of this meaning comes from outside and they do not concede that it comes from the particle itself. He will never be able to prove it. His defence, that **sa-yaf'alu** [سَيَفْعَلُ] (he will do) has an absolute and general force, and **lan yaf'ala naqidahu** [لَنْ يَفْعَلَ نَقِيضَهُ] (he will never do its opposite) therefore has the force of an absolute perpetual statement, cannot be achieved except by conveying perpetuity through **lan**. This is nothing at all, as is not hidden. What led al-Zamakhshari into error, so that he said what he said, relying on what cannot stand as a proof, is his extreme partisanship for his false school and his corrupt belief. We ask Allah, exalted is He, to protect us from abandonment.

**Dhubab** [الذُّبابُ] is a collective noun (ism jins). Its plurals are **adhibbah** [أذِبَّةٍ] and **dhibban** [ذِبّانٍ], with a kasra on the *dhal* in both. The *Bahr* also reports a damma on it in **dhubban**. It is derived either from **dhabb**, meaning driving away and repelling, or from **dhabb** in the sense of alternation, that is, going and returning. The latter is more suited to the state of the fly, because of its alternation, so much so that it has been said it is a compound (manhut) from *dhabba aba*, meaning it was driven away and so returned.

The answer (jawab) of **law** [لَوِ] is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it. The clause is conjoined (ma'tufa) to another conditional clause that is omitted, relying on this one to indicate it: that is, "If they did not gather together for it and cooperate in it, they would never create it, and even if they gathered together for it and cooperated in it, they would never create it." Both are in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), as if it were said, "They will never create a fly in any circumstance."

Some have said: the **waw** is for the circumstantial clause, and **"even if they gathered together for it"** [﴿ولَوِ اجْتَمَعُوا لَهُ﴾] together with its answer is a circumstantial clause. Others said: **law** here does not need an answer, because it has been stripped of the meaning of conditionality and purified to indicate supposition and assumption. The meaning is: "They will never create a fly, even supposing they gathered together." **"And if the fly should snatch anything from them"** [﴿وإنْ يَسْلُبْهُمُ الذُّبابُ شَيْئًا﴾] is an explanation of their incapacity regarding another matter besides creation, that is: if the fly takes anything from them, **"they could not rescue it from it"** [﴿لا يَسْتَنْقِذُوهُ مِنهُ﴾], meaning they would not be able to rescue it from it, despite its extreme weakness.

It is apparent that **istanqadha** [اسْتَنْقَذَ] here has the meaning of **naqadha** [نَقَذَ] (to rescue). In the verse there is, regarding their ignorance in associating others with Allah, the Mighty who is able over all possible things, the One who alone originates all existing things, an incapacity: they cannot create even the smallest and most abject of living creatures, even if they gathered together for it, nor can they rescue from the fly what it snatches from them. This is clear.

Although the verse was revealed concerning the idols, it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that they used to smear them with saffron and their heads with honey, and lock them in, so the fly would enter through the openings and eat it. It has also been said that they used to perfume them with various kinds of scent, and the fly would take that away. However, the ruling is general for all false objects of worship.

**"The seeker and the sought are weak"** [﴿ضَعُفَ الطّالِبُ والمَطْلُوبُ﴾] is a concluding statement (tadhyil) to what precedes it, either a report or an expression of wonder. The seeker is the worshipper of other than Allah, exalted is He, and the sought is the gods, as reported from al-Suddi and al-Dahhak. The worshipper of these is a seeker, since he calls upon them and believes in their benefit, and his weakness lies in seeking benefit from other than its source. The other being sought is apparently weak in the same way. It has also been said: the seeker is the fly, which seeks what it snatches from the gods, and the sought is the gods, in the sense of the one from whom what is snatched is sought.

Ibn Mardawayh, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, and al-Zamakhshari preferred, that the seeker is the idols and the sought is the fly. In this concluding statement, then, there is the appearance of equality, and it establishes that the seeker is weaker, because the creation, the smallest, is the one who snatches, while that (the idol) is a seeker who has failed to achieve its aim. Since He made the snatched property belong to them and treated them as rational beings, He attributed to them a seeking. And since He showed that they are weaker than the most abject of animals, He drew attention thereby to the place of mockery in this. Some people preferred the first view, because it is more suited to the context, as the context concerns their ignorance and the belittling of their gods, so it fits both their intent and their gods within this concluding statement.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 74 (part 1 of 2):

﴿They have not esteemed God with the esteem due to Him﴾. Al-Hasan and al-Farra' said: that is, they did not magnify Him, glorified be He, with the magnification due to Him. Magnifying Him, exalted be He, as He deserves, means describing Him with what He has described Himself with, and worshipping Him as He commanded to be worshipped. These people did not do that, for they worshipped besides Him one who is not at all fit for worship. In that is a description of Him, glorified be He, with what He is free of, namely the existence of a partner for Him, mighty and majestic is He.

Al-Akhfash said: that is, they did not know Him with the knowledge due to Him. Knowing God Most High as He should be known is affirming Him, glorified be He, as described by what He described Himself with. These people did not affirm Him in this way, because of their association of partners with Him and their worship of others besides Him, whose condition you have heard. It was also said: the knowledge due to Him is that He be known in His true reality (kunh). This is what is meant by his words, upon him be blessings and peace: "Glory be to You, we have not known You as You truly should be known."

You know that the apparent meaning of His words, exalted be He, ﴿They have not esteemed﴾ and so on, is a report about the polytheists and a censure of them. If the intended meaning is the negation of knowledge of the essence, the matter would be shared between them and the monotheists, for knowledge of the essence has not been attained by any of the monotheists either, according to the researchers (al-muhaqqiqun). The aforementioned report also points to this, since it indicates that this knowledge was not attained by the most perfect of the prophets, upon him and upon them be blessings and peace. If it was not attained by him (ﷺ), then its non-attainment by others is all the more certain. The suggestion that the knowledge negated in it refers to comprehending the attributes has a condition that is not hidden. Likewise, the suggestion that knowledge of the essence was attained by him, upon him be blessings and peace, after the aforementioned report, is also weak. And his saying (ﷺ): "Reflect upon the blessings of God Most High, and do not reflect upon His essence, for you will never measure His true measure." The apparent meaning is the generality of the ruling, not its restriction to those being addressed at that time. Also the words of al-Siddiq al-Akbar, may God Most High be pleased with him: "Inability to grasp the grasping is itself a grasping." And the words of Ali, may God Most High honour his face, completing a line of verse: "Probing into the secret of God's essence is an association (of partners)."

Indeed, Hujjat al-Islam al-Ghazali, his teacher Imam al-Haramayn, the Sufis and the philosophers have said that knowledge of Him, glorified be He, in His true reality is impossible. It is related from Aristotle (Arisṭū) that he said on this: "Just as darkness and haze afflict the eye when it gazes at the body of the sun, preventing it from complete sight, so too does bewilderment and confusion afflict the intellect when it wishes to comprehend His essence, exalted be He, preventing it from comprehending Him, glorified be He."

[p. 203]

It is not hidden that this does not serve as a proof of impossibility. The most that can be said is that it is a rhetorical (khitabi) argument, which yields only a conjecture that is insufficient in a matter of this kind. Similar to it is the argument that all human souls, whether refined or not, are more deficient in their immateriality and freedom from the Necessary Being (al-Wajib), exalted be He, than others, and the more deficient cannot comprehend what is more immaterial and more free from it, just as material things cannot comprehend immaterial ones. Likewise is the argument that He, exalted be He, is nearer to us than the jugular vein, so His perception is impossible just as the eye cannot perceive what is in direct contact with it. And better than all of that is what has been said: knowledge of His essence is not self-evident (badihi) by necessity with respect to a particular person or a particular time, so it is not attained by anyone at any time by necessity, and so it is acquired (kasbi). Acquisition is either through a complete definition (hadd tamm) or an incomplete one, and both are impossible, since it entails composition in the Necessary Being, because a definition must be composed of a genus, either proximate or remote, and a differentia. Moreover, an incomplete definition does not yield the essence. As for a simple definition by a single term, it is impossible by evident reasoning, for if that term is the very essence of the thing, it would follow that knowledge of the thing depends on knowledge of itself, with no distinction between the two, even in general terms and in detail, as is the case with a composite definition together with its complete definition. And if it is other than the essence, then it is not a definition but a description (rasm) or another concept that is not predicated of it. As for a complete or incomplete description, neither of them yields the essence by necessity.

It has been objected that the impossibility of self-evidence with respect to all persons and all times requires proof. Perhaps it is attained after the soul has been refined by true revealed laws and purified of human impurities and bodily hindrances. Even if we grant that self-evidence is impossible in that way, we may choose to say that knowledge is among the things acquired through a complete definition composed of genus and differentia, and the most that follows from this is rational composition, which is not impossible unless we say that it entails external composition, which entails need of parts, contrary to necessary existence. We do not say that, because according to a group the preferred view is that the parts of a quiddity are taken from a single simple matter, and they are unified in quiddity and existence, so they are mental abstractions and not its reality, and so there is no entailment. Yes, there would be such an entailment if we said that the parts are taken from matters that are distinct in external reality. But we do not say that either, for if it is said then that the parts themselves are distinct in quiddity and existence, as one group held, it follows that they cannot be predicated of one another, since two things existing with two distinct existences cannot be predicated one of the other, like Zayd and 'Amr. And if it is said that they are distinct in quiddity but not in existence, so that predication is possible, as another group held, it follows that one single existence subsists in a single individual while being multiple things distinct in quiddity. Even if we grant the entailment between rational composition and external composition, we may say: we do not concede that no description yields the essence by necessity. How could it not, when it does yield it in cases where the essence is necessarily entailed by the description, in a clear sense of the more specific kind? Indeed, it is possible for every description to yield it, according to the principle of al-Ash'ari that all possible things are dependent upon Him, exalted be He, without condition. Even if that yielding never actually occurs, since the discussion concerns the impossibility of attaining the essence through acquisition. Thus they said.

(Mulla Sadra argued for the denial of rational parts in Him, exalted be He, by saying: His reality, glorified be He, is pure quiddity-less existence (anniyya mahda) and sheer being. So if He, mighty and majestic, had a genus and a differentia, then His genus would be in need of the differentia, not in its concept and meaning but in being existent and actualized. Then it is said: that genus is either pure existence or a quiddity other than existence. If the first, then what we supposed to be a differentia is not a differentia, since a differentia is that by which the genus exists. This can only be conceived if the reality of the genus is not the reality of existence. If the second, then it follows that the Necessary Being would have a quiddity, whereas it has been established that existence itself is His reality without generality. Also, if He, exalted be He, had a genus, He would be included under the category of substance and would be one of the substantial species, sharing with the rest of them in the genus. He has demonstrated the possibility of such species, and established that the possibility of a species entails the possibility of the genus, which entails the possibility of each of the individuals of that genus insofar as each is an instance of it. For if existence were impossible for the genus as genus, that is absolutely, it would be impossible for every individual. Thus it follows from this that the Necessary Being would be possible, exalted be He high above that. The basis of this is that the reality of the Necessary Being, exalted be He, is pure existence, which the philosophers and eminent researchers have held. This existence is not meant as the verbal noun (masdari) meaning, which no one is ignorant of, for it is certain that it is impossible for that to be the reality of the Necessary Being, glorified be He. Rather it is meant in the sense of the source of effects, as Jalal al-Dawani verified, and he extended discussion of it in his glosses on the commentary on the Tajrid, in his commentary on the Hayakil al-Nuriyya, and in other of his treatises. Mulla Sadra has a long and broad discourse on this point and on al-Jalal's discussion, and he verified the matter in another style that may be sought in his book al-Asfar. However, we will mention here from his words a question and answer relevant to what we are dealing with. He said: "If you say: how can the essence of the Creator, glorified be He, be the very reality of existence, when existence is self-evident in conception and the essence of the Creator is unknown in its reality? I say: it has already been explained that the intensity of manifestness and the confirmation of existence there, together with the weakness of the power of perception and the weakness of existence here, have become two sources of His concealment from us, exalted be He. Otherwise His essence, exalted be He, is in extreme radiance and illumination. If you return and say: if the essence of the Creator is existence itself, then either existence is the reality of the essence, as is apparent, or it is predicated of it accidentally, as the concept of 'thing' is predicated of Him, exalted be He. In the first case, either this is meant as this general, self-evident concept abstracted from existents, or another meaning. The first is obviously false, and the second requires that His reality, exalted be He, be other than what is understood from the word 'existence', like the other quiddities, except that you have named that reality 'existence', as when a man is named 'existence'. Clearly this naming has no effect on the rulings, and this type returns to the Necessary Being, not the existence under discussion, and it would follow that the Necessary Being, exalted be He, has a quiddity, and it has been demonstrated that everything with a quiddity is caused. As for the second, namely that it be predicated of Him, exalted be He, accidentally, it is not hidden that this does not free Him from a cause but rather requires that He be existent. For this reason, most of the later philosophers held that existence is non-existent. I say: the source of this problem is the assumption that the meaning of this general, shared concept being accidental is that the subject has one existence and the accident has another existence, like the walker in relation to the animal and the laughing in relation to the human. This is not so. Rather, this concept is a label and a representation of the external existences, and its relation to them is like the relation of humanity to the human and animality to the animal. Just as the concept of humanity may be said to be the very essence of the human, because it is a mirror for considering him and a representation of his aspect, it may also be said to be other than him, because it is a relational matter, whereas the human is a substantial quiddity. In sum, existence is not like possibility, such that there is nothing corresponding to it, so that the verbal noun is a representation of it. Rather it is like blackness, which is sometimes meant as the relational meaning itself, namely blackness-ness, and sometimes meant as that by which a thing is black, namely the specific quality. Just as blackness, when supposed to subsist in itself, may be said that its essence is the very blackness-ness, but when supposed to be in a body characterized by it, it is not permissible to say that its essence is the very blackness-ness, even though that notion, being a mental consideration, is additional to all of them. Having established this, we say in response to the first disjunction: we choose the first part, that existence is the reality of the essence. As for your statement in the second disjunction: either that existence is what is understood from the word existence, and so on, we choose...")

[p. 204]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 74 (part 2 of 2):

Among them is that which corresponds to what is understood from this term, I mean the reality of external existence (wujud khariji), of which this concept is a representation. For we hold that existence has a reality in every existent, just as blackness has a reality in every black thing. However, in some existents it is mixed with deficiencies and nonexistence, and in others it is not so. Just as blacknesses vary in degree of blackness, some stronger and more intense, others weaker and less, so existents vary in degree of existence, in perfection and imperfection.

We may also choose the second part of the first disjunction, but this general concept, although it is accidental in the sense that, as a concept with a title (mafhum 'unwani), it has no existence in the external world such that it could be identical with some thing, nevertheless it is a representation of the very reality of existence, which subsists through itself. It applies to it in such a way that the source of its truth and the instance of its predication upon it is that very reality, not some other thing that inheres in it, as with the other accidentals in their predication upon things. Thus the predication of this concept upon particular existence resembles the predication of essentials in this respect. Accordingly, your statement does not object to us: "The predication of existence upon it does not make it independent of a cause," because it would not be independent of a cause if its existence were due to this meaning's accidence or to the subsistence of a portion of existence. But that is not the case. Rather, that particular existence is existent by its very self, just as it is existence by its very self, whether or not the concept of existence is predicated of it. What the philosophers (hukama') held to be nonexistent is not the particular existences, but this general mental matter which applies to the 'ayniyyat (specific individual instances) and the particular existential characteristics. End.

What he (al-Alusi's source) pointed to regarding the plurality of existences was held by the Peripatetics (al-Mashsha'un), and according to most of them they are distinct realities, multiple in themselves, not merely by the accidental relation to quiddities (mahiyyat), so that they would be of one reality, nor by differentiae, so that absolute existence would be their genus. Some held the difference is in reality, such that among them there is a difference by gradation (tashkik), like the existence of the Necessary (wajib) and the existence of the contingent (mumkin), and likewise the existence of immaterial beings (mujarradat) and the existence of bodies. A group of the qualified philosophers (hukama' al-mutaʾahhilin) said that in external reality there is only one particular existence whose essence is unknown, and it is the essence of the Necessary Being, exalted is His majesty. As for the observed contingent beings, they have no existence of their own, but only a connection (irtibat) with the true existence, which is the Necessary by essence, and a relation to Him. Yes, it is said of them that they are existent, in the sense that they have a relation to the Most High. So the concept of existence is more general than the existent that subsists through itself and than the matters related to Him in some manner of relation. The predication of a derived term (mushtaqq) does not contradict the subsistence of the source of derivation (mabda' al-ishtiqaq) in itself, the meaning of which returns to its not subsisting in another. Nor does it contradict that what it applies to is something related to the source, not something in which the source inheres in any way, as in "the iron-worker" (al-hiddad) and "the one who faces the sun" (al-mushmis). Furthermore, the usage of the people of language and the masters of speech carries no weight in establishing realities.

They also said: that a derived term is among the second intelligibles (ma'qulat thaniyya) and the primary self-evident truths does not conflict with the source being a rooted (muta'assila), individuated (mutashakhkhisa) reality whose essence is unknown; the secondness of the intelligible and its rootedness may vary in relation to matters. The defects in this are not hidden. A similar view circulated on the tongues of some of the Sufis: that the reality of the Necessary Being is absolute existence, holding that it cannot be nonexistence or a nonexistent, which is evident, nor an existing quiddity by existence or with existence, whether as a cause or a restriction, because of the dependence and composition that this entails. Thus it is necessarily existence, and not the particular existence, because if it is taken together with the absolute it is composite, and if it is merely the thing qualified (al-ma'ruḍ) it is dependent, necessarily with the dependence of the restricted upon the absolute. Their argument is weaker than a spider's web.

What I have verified from the books of the Greatest Shaykh (al-Shaykh al-Akbar, Ibn 'Arabi), may his secret be sanctified, and the books of his companions, is that God, glorified is He, is not the same as absolute existence in the sense of the universal natural (al-kulli al-tabi'i) existing in external reality within its individuals, nor in the sense of being a concept in the mind corresponding to each of its particulars in external reality, such that what is in the mind would exist in any one of the external individuals and that individual would be exactly that, without any difference at all.

[Page 206]

Rather, it is in the sense of not being restricted by anything else while being existent by itself. In the second section of al-Futuhat (al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya) it is stated that the Truth, exalted is He, is existent by Himself through His essence, absolute existence, not restricted by another, nor an effect of anything, nor a cause of anything; rather, He is the creator of effects and causes, the King, the Holy, who has never ceased. In "al-Nusus" of Sadr al-Din al-Qunawi, the conception of the absoluteness of the Truth must be understood as a negative attribute, not in the sense that its opposite is restriction. Rather, it is absoluteness from the known unity and plurality, and from confinement in absoluteness and restriction, and in combining all that with transcendence (tanzih) above it. Thus all of that is correct regarding Him while He is transcendent above all of it.

Some eminent scholars mentioned that God, according to the Sufi masters, is the particular existence, the Necessary Being by His essence, subsisting through Himself, determined by His essence, combining every perfection, transcendent above every deficiency, manifesting Himself in whatever manifestations He wills while transcendence remains. Then he said: This is also what al-Ash'ari's statement that existence is the very essence necessarily implies, together with his final statement in his book al-Ibana, regarding letting the ambiguous verses (mutashabihat) pass as they are in their apparent meaning, with transcendence: ﴿there is nothing like unto Him﴾.

The verification of this: it has been established by demonstration that the Necessary Being by essence is existent. So He is either pure existence stripped of quiddity, determined by His essence; or existence conjoined with quiddity, determined according to it; or quiddity which is the thing qualified by existence, determined according to it; or the composite of quiddity and existence determined according to it. There is no way to the fourth, because composition entails dependence; nor to the third, because quiddity needs existence in its external realization; nor to the second, because existence needs quiddity for its individuation according to it. And dependence in all of these contradicts essential necessity. So the first is determined. Thus the One who is existent by His essence, glorified is He, is pure existence stripped of quiddity, determined by His essence. Then He is either absolute with true absoluteness, which has no opposing restriction, being the one that accepts every absoluteness and restriction; or He is restricted by a specific restriction. There is no way to the second, because the composite of a restriction and what it qualifies entails dependence, which contradicts essential necessity. So the first is determined. Therefore the Necessary Being by essence is pure existence stripped of quiddity, subsisting through itself, determined by its essence, absolute with true absoluteness.

The proponents of this view held that in external reality there is only one existence, which is true existence, and that there is no existent other than it. The quiddities of contingent beings are nonexistent matters distinguished in themselves by an essential distinction. They are established in knowledge, never having smelled the scent of existence nor ever smelling it, but their effects appear in the supposed existence, which is the attached light, called 'ama' (the cloud, the void), and the Truth through which the created things were created. These are the ones known as the Advocates of Unity (ahl al-wahda).

Perhaps the view we cited from some of the qualified philosophers returns to their saying that it is a state beyond the state of the intellect. Because of it, groups went astray and left the bond of Islam. In sum, the view that the reality of the Necessary Being, exalted is He, is not known to anyone with a comprehensive, encompassing, intellectual or sensory knowledge is, in my opinion, undoubtedly correct, and the scholars who investigated (al-muhaqqiqun), including the Advocates of Unity, held it. The view contrary to this, which is attributed to some of the theologians (mutakallimun), should not be given any attention at all. I do not know whether knowledge of the reality is possible or not possible, though perhaps the view that it is not possible is more fitting to His greatness, exalted is His majesty, and whose sovereignty the intellects cannot encompass.

As for seeing the Necessary Being with the eye, there is a disagreement among the People of the Sunna regarding its occurrence in this world. In the Hereafter there is no disagreement about it, except that some Sufis said that it occurs only through some manifestation, and not through the absolute reality. As for seeing Him, glorified is He, with the heart, it has been said that it occurs in this world, but in the sense of witnessing His holy light, and this varies according to the difference in readiness. It is not in the sense of witnessing the very essence and reality. Whoever claims that has been confused about the matter and claimed what he claimed.

[Page 207]

Some people say: there is no barrier to ﴿with His true measure﴾ meaning the true knowledge of Him, and "the true knowledge of Him" meaning the knowledge that grasps His essence. That this is not attained by anyone, believer or otherwise, does not harm what we are discussing, because the purpose is to affirm His greatness, exalted is He, which contradicts what the polytheists hold. And the fact that no one knows the essence of His reality demands greatness in its most perfect form. So reflect on all of that. And God, exalted is He, is the Granter of success toward what is correct.

﴿Indeed, God is Powerful﴾ over all possible things, ﴿Mighty﴾, prevailing over all things. You have known the state of their gods, which are subdued by the most abject of the weak. The sentence is in the position of giving a reason (ta'lil) for what precedes it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 75:

﴿Allah chooses﴾, i.e., selects, ﴿from among the angels messengers﴾ who act as intermediaries between Him, exalted is He, and the prophets, peace be upon them, with the revelation; ﴿and from among mankind﴾, i.e., and He selects from mankind messengers who call whomever He wills to Him, exalted is He, and convey to them what has been sent down to them. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best where He places His message. The mention of the messengers from among the angels first is because they are intermediaries between Him, exalted is He, and the messengers from among mankind. The conjunction of ﴿from among mankind﴾ to ﴿from among the angels﴾, while it is in fact preceded (in its sense) by ﴿messengers﴾, does not require any supposition, even though the messengers of each group are described by attributes other than those of the other group, as we have indicated. It has also been said that the meaning is: Allah chooses from the angels messengers to the rest of them in conveying what He has charged them with of acts of obedience, and from mankind messengers to the rest of them in conveying what He has charged them with likewise. This is the beginning of establishing messengership after the demolition of the foundation of polytheism and the filling-in of the pillars of monotheism.

It is related in some reports that the verse was revealed because of the statement of al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah: ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down upon him from among us?﴾ [Sad: 8], and the verse, in it, is a refutation of the saying of the polytheists that the angels are the daughters of Allah and of similar falsehoods of theirs. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Hearing﴾ of all things heard, and this includes the words of the messengers; ﴿Seeing﴾ of all things seen, and this includes the conditions of those to whom they were sent. It has also been said that hearing and seeing are a metaphor for His knowledge, exalted is He, of all things, by the indication of the context.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 76:

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾, because it is like an explanation of that. Perhaps the first (view) is preferable, and this is a generalization after a specification. The plural pronoun refers to the accountable beings (al-mukallafun), as has been said; that is, He knows their future states and their past states. It is narrated from al-Hasan that (it means) the first of their deeds and the last of them. It is narrated from Ali ibn Isa that the pronoun refers to the messengers, the angels and the people, and the meaning according to him is: He knows what was before the creation of the messengers and what will be after their creation. ﴿And to Allah are all matters returned﴾, all of them, not to other than Him, glorified is He, neither jointly nor independently, because He is the owner of them in essence. So He, may He be exalted and high, is not questioned about what He does, including choosing (whom He wills) and other things; so it has been said. From this it is known that it is connected with His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Allah chooses﴾ etc., and likewise is the aspect of the connection. It is also permissible that it be connected with His, glorified is He, saying: (He knows) etc., in the sense of: and to Him, exalted is He, all matters return on the Day of Resurrection, so there is no command or prohibition for anyone other than Him, exalted is His majesty, there, and He will recompense each according to what is known of his deeds. And perhaps this is preferable to what preceded. It may be said that it is connected with what has been mentioned, but in another manner, namely that it is an indication of another generalization of the knowledge: that is, to Him, exalted is He, all matters return, because He, glorified is He, is the agent of them all, both through intermediaries and without intermediaries, or without intermediaries in all of them, according to what al-Ash'ari says; so He, glorified is He, is knowing of them.

The basis of this, as some have established, is that He, exalted is He, knows Himself in the most complete manner, and His essence, exalted is He, is a cause that necessitates what is other than Him. Complete knowledge of the cause, or of the aspect of its being a cause, necessitates complete knowledge of its effect. Thus His, exalted is He, knowledge of all that is other than Him is necessary consequent upon His knowledge of His essence, just as the existence of what is other than Him follows the existence of His essence, glorified is He. On this there is a long and broad discussion.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 22, verse 77:**

﴿O you who have believed, bow (irkaʿū) and prostrate (usjudū)﴾, i.e., pray. He referred to the prayer by these two because they are its greatest pillars (arkān) and most excellent parts.

[Page 208]

The meaning is that the two together are like this, and this does not preclude that one of them is superior to the other, nor that standing or prostration is superior to each individual pillar. It has been said: the meaning is, "Submit to Allah, the Exalted, and fall down before Him in prostration." It has also been said: the intended meaning is the command to the ruku' (bowing) and sujud (prostration) in their legal sense in the prayer, for at the beginning of their Islam they used to bow in their prayer without prostrating at times, and prostrate without bowing at other times, so they were commanded to perform both acts together. This is what Abu Hayyan reported in al-Bahr, though I have not found it in any transmission on which one may rely. Ṣāḥib al-Mawāhib (Ibn Ḥajar al-Haytamī, in al-Mawāhib) expressed doubt about it, and al-Farrāʾ mentioned it without a chain of transmission. ﴿And worship your Lord﴾, by all the acts of worship with which He has charged you, as the omission of the object indicates. It has also been said: the intended meaning is the command to perform the obligatory duties.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do good﴾ is a generalization after a specification, or it is restricted to the voluntary acts. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he interpreted it as the command to maintain ties of kinship and noble character. ﴿That you may succeed﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun of the addressees; that is, do all of this while hoping thereby for success, not certain of it, and not relying on your deeds.

The verse is a verse of prostration according to al-Shafiʿī, Aḥmad, Ibn al-Mubārak and Isḥāq, may Allah be pleased with them all, because of the apparent command to prostrate in it, and because of what has preceded: "It is reported from ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, has the Surah of al-Ḥajj been given preference over the rest of the Qur'an by two prostrations?' He said: 'Yes. So whoever does not prostrate in them, let him not recite them.'" ʿAlī, may Allah honour his face, ʿUmar, his son ʿAbd Allah, ʿUthmān, Abu al-Dardāʾ, Abu Mūsā and Ibn ʿAbbās in one of the two reports from him, may Allah be pleased with them all, said the same. Abu Ḥanīfah, Mālik, al-Ḥasan, Ibn al-Musayyab, Ibn Jubayr and Sufyān al-Thawrī, may Allah be pleased with them all, held that it is not a verse of prostration. Ibn al-Humām said: because it is coupled with the command to bow, and what is customary in such a Qur'anic context, by inductive observation, is that it is a command to do what is a pillar of the prayer, like His words: ﴿Prostrate yourself and bow down﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 43]. When possibility enters, the argument from it falls away. As for the hadith of ʿUqbah, al-Tirmidhī said: "Its chain is not strong," and Abu Dāwūd and others said the same. End of quotation.

Al-Ṭībī defended his imam al-Shafiʿī, may Allah be pleased with him, and said: "The bowing (rukūʿ) is a metaphor for the prayer because it is specific to it. As for the prostration, since it is not specific to it, it is taken in its literal sense because of the generality of benefit. Moreover, shifting to a metaphor without a diverting factor or a special purpose is impermissible, and the coupling does not necessitate that." The author of al-Kashf (Ṣāḥib al-Kashf) criticized him, saying: one may say that coupling is appropriate, and the agreement of the two commands in obligation or requirement, according to both schools, is also one of the implications. Then he returned to defending the position, saying: "The truth is that prostration, wherever it is established, does not follow from the specific content of this verse, because the verse's indication is not restricted to the state of recitation. Rather, that comes only from the act or the saying of the Messenger (ﷺ). So there is no obstacle to the verse indicating the obligation of prostration in the prayer, and yet prostration is legislated when reciting it, on the basis of the authentic transmission." This has a problem: if he means that what is established is an independent proof for its legislation, without any role for the verse, then that is, with its own problems, a position neither al-Shafiʿī nor anyone else has held; and if he means that the verse indicates it just as it indicates the obligation of prostration in the prayer, and what is established reveals that indication, then that is a claim that the indication is hidden, and a commitment that the command to prostrate is for general demand, which includes what is required, as in the demand for prostration in the prayer, and what is recommended, as in the demand for prostration of recitation. For this is a sunnah according to al-Shafiʿī, may Allah be pleased with him. Perhaps this is what is necessarily meant in his view, and there is no objection to it; indeed there is no alternative to it, if the hadith is authentic. But you have already heard what has been said about it. You may say that it has been strengthened by what Abu Dāwūd, Ibn Mājah, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqī reported from ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) taught him fifteen prostrations in the Qur'an, three of them in al-Mufaṣṣal.

[Page 209]

In Surah al-Ḥajj there are two prostrations. And there is the practice of many of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, which apparently was based on hearing from him (ﷺ) or seeing his act of doing so.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 22, verse 78 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And strive for Allah with the striving due to Him﴾. That is, for the sake of Allah, the Exalted, or in His way, glorified is He. Jihad, as al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said, is the exertion of one's full capacity in repelling the enemy, and it has three kinds: striving against the visible enemy, such as the disbelievers; striving against Satan; and striving against the self (nafs), which is greater than the striving against the visible enemy, as is indicated by what al-Bayhaqi and others narrated from Jabir, who said: "A group of warriors came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: 'You have come with the best arrival, from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad.' It was said: 'And what is the greater jihad?' He said: 'The servant's striving against his desire.'" In its chain there is a weakness that is excused in such a case.

Here, according to al-Dahhak, the intended meaning is jihad against the disbelievers until they enter Islam, and this implies that the verse is Medinan, because jihad was only enjoined after the Hijrah. According to Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak, it is jihad against desire and the self. The preferable view is that it means its three kinds, and this is not a combination of the literal and the metaphorical in any way. To this point also refers what a group narrated from al-Hasan, that he recited the verse and said: "Indeed, a man strives for Allah, the Exalted, though he has never struck with a sword." This includes the jihad against innovators and wrongdoers, for they too are enemies, and it is by restraining them from innovation and wrongdoing. ﴿with the striving due to Him﴾, that is, a striving that is truly in Him. So "haqq" (truly) was placed first and the phrase was made an idafah (construct) in the manner of "jard qatifah" (a plain cloak), the preposition was omitted, and "jihad" was made an idafah to His pronoun, in the manner of his saying: "And the day we witnessed him, sound and whole." 

In al-Kashshaf: the idafah is used for the slightest connection and specificity. Since jihad is specific to Allah, the Exalted, in that it is done for His sake and for His purpose, its idafah to Him is valid. In any case, "haqqa" is in the accusative as an infinitive (masdar). Abu al-Baqa' said that it is an adjective of a deleted infinitive, meaning "jihadan haqqa jihadihi" (striving truly, the striving due to Him). In this there is an objection: it is definite, so how can an indefinite be described by it? I do not think anyone would claim that an idafah in the loose sense (ittisa') does not give definiteness, so that neither the construct nor the genitive is made definite by it. The verse indicates the command to jihad in its most complete form, by its being purely for Allah, the Exalted, without fearing the blame of any blamer. And it is muhkam (definitive in its ruling).

As for those who said, like Mujahid and al-Kalbi, that it is abrogated (mansukh) by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [al-Taghabun: 16], they meant by it that He should be obeyed and not disobeyed at all. In this there is a discussion that is not hidden.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said to me: "Did we not used to recite: 'And strive for Allah with the striving due to Him' at the end of time, as you strove at its beginning?" I said: "Yes. So when is this, O Commander of the Faithful?" He said: "When the Banu Umayyah are the rulers and the Banu al-Mughirah the viziers." And al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated it from al-Miswar ibn Makhramah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: Umar said to Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, and he mentioned it. The ruling on this reading is not hidden from you. Al-Nisaburi said: The scholars said, if this narration is sound, then perhaps this addition is from his (ﷺ) explanation and not from the Qur'an itself; otherwise it would have been transmitted by mass transmission (mutawatir). And it is as you see.

﴿He has chosen you﴾, that is, He, may His majesty be exalted, chose you, not another, glorified is He. The sentence is a new clause (mustaanifah) explaining the reason for the command to jihad, for one who chooses only chooses one who serves him, and from his great nearness it is required that one repel his enemies and strive against one's own self by abandoning what He does not approve. So in it is an alert to the cause that calls for jihad. In His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and He has not placed upon you in the religion﴾, that is, in all its affairs, and jihad enters into this first and foremost, ﴿any hardship﴾, that is, narrowness, by imposing what is very difficult to uphold upon you, indicating that there is no obstacle for them in it. The summary is that He, the Exalted, commanded them to jihad and made clear that there is no excuse for them in abandoning it, since the cause exists and the obstacle is removed.

Page 210

It is also possible that this is an indication of the dispensation (rukhsah) in abandoning some of what He, glorified is He, commanded them, when it became difficult for them, based on his (ﷺ) saying: "If I command you with something, then do of it what you are able." So the negation of hardship on this view, after its establishment, is by the permission to abandon in accordance with the requirement of the Shari'ah; and on the first view the negation of hardship is from the outset. It was also said: the absence of hardship means that He made for them a way out from every sin, by permitting them in narrow situations, opening for them the door of repentance, and prescribing for them expiations (kaffarat) for the rights of Allah and compensations (arsh) and blood-money (diyat) for the rights of the servants. It is not hidden that generalizing it to repentance and the like is contrary to the apparent meaning, even though this has been narrated through Ibn Shihab from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

In al-Hawashi al-Shihabiyyah: the apparent meaning is that ﴿the striving due to Him﴾, since it is difficult, he followed it with this to clarify that the intended meaning is what is according to their capacity, not what befits Him, exalted is He, in every respect.

Al-Jalal al-Suyuti mentioned that this verse is the origin of the principle "hardship brings facilitation" (al-mashaqqah tajlib al-taysir), and this agrees best with the second view in it.

﴿The religion of your father Ibrahim﴾. It is in the accusative as an infinitive, governed by a verb indicated by what precedes it, namely the negation of hardship, after deleting a modifier: "Your religion was made wide with the breadth of the religion of your father," or in the accusative by specification (ikhtisas), with the estimate "I specify the religion" or similar. Al-Zamakhshari followed both views. Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' said it is in the accusative by incitement (ighra'), with the estimate "follow" or "adhere to" or the like. Al-Farra' said it is in the accusative by removing the preposition, that is, "like the religion of your father." The word "millah" (religion) is meant either as what includes the roots and the branches, or what pertains specifically to the roots, so consider this and do not be heedless. "Ibrahim" is in the accusative also by an estimated verb, or in the genitive with a fatha as an appositive (badal) or explanatory apposition (atf bayan). He, peace be upon him, was made their father because he is the father of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he is like a father to his community in that he is the cause of their eternal life and of their existence in the manner counted in the Hereafter. Or because most of the Arabs were of his offspring, peace be upon him, so they were given precedence over all the people of his religion (ﷺ).

﴿He (named you Muslims)﴾, that is, Allah, the Exalted, as was narrated from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Qatadah and Sufyan, and what comes after in the verse supports it, as well as the reading of Ubayy, may Allah be pleased with him: "Allah named you Muslims before" (min qablu), that is, before the revelation of the Qur'an, and that is in the heavenly books such as the Torah and the Gospel. ﴿And in this﴾, that is, in the Qur'an. The clause is a new one. It was also said that it is like a substitute for his saying, the Exalted: ﴿He has chosen you﴾, and therefore it was not joined by a conjunction. It is narrated from Ibn Zayd and al-Hasan that the pronoun refers to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and Abu Hayyan preferred this for its proximity. His naming them with this from before, in His saying: ﴿Our Lord, make us Muslims to You and from our descendants a Muslim nation to You﴾ [al-Baqarah: 128], and his saying here is the cause of their being named thereby in this, since most of them entered into the descendants, so he was made to name them in it metaphorically. This requires combining the literal and the metaphorical, and on its permissibility there is a well-known disagreement. Abu al-Baqa' said: the meaning according to this, "and in this," is an explanation of His naming you with this name, in that He related his statement in the Qur'an. Ibn Atiyyah said: it is estimated as "and I named you in this, the Muslims." And there is no hiding the artificiality in all of this.

Whoever argued from the verse that naming with "the Muslims" is specific to this community has an argument that needs examination.

﴿That the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿that he has conveyed to you﴾. This statement from Him, the Exalted, indicates the acceptance of his testimony for himself (peace be upon him), relying on his infallibility, and perhaps this is among his particular privileges on that day; otherwise the infallible is required in this world to produce two witnesses if he claims something for himself, as the story of the horse and the testimony of Khuzaymah, may Allah be pleased with him, indicates. Also, if every infallible person's testimony for himself in that matter were accepted, there would be no need for the testimony of this community over the nations, when their prophets bear witness against them and they deny it, as many commentators mentioned in explaining His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and that you may be witnesses over the people﴾. It was objected that the nations and their prophets will be brought, and it will be said to the prophets: "Did you convey to your nations?" They will say: "Yes, we conveyed to them," and they will deny it. Then this community will be brought and will testify that they conveyed, and the nations will say to them: "From where do you know?" They will say: "We know this by Allah's informing in His Book, the speech upon the tongue of His truthful Prophet." Or, he is a witness over you by your obedience to the one who obeyed and your disobedience to the one who disobeyed. Perhaps his knowledge of that is by Allah's making known to him through signs that appear to him at that time, which make his testimony lawful for him (peace be upon him). And that the deeds of his community are presented to him, peace be upon him, while he is in the barzakh every week or more or less, if this is sound, does not give knowledge of the particular persons whose deeds are witnessed; otherwise there would be a problem with what Ahmad narrated in his Musnad and al-Shaykhan narrated from Anas and Hudhayfah, who both said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Some of my companions will certainly come to me at the Pool, until when I see them and recognize them, they will be driven away from me. So I will say: O Lord, my companions, my companions! It will be said to me: You do not know what they innovated after you.'" This is perhaps more problematic on the assumption of the soundness of the hadith of the presentation, whether it gives knowledge of the particular persons or not. And if one maintains the soundness of that hadith and that he (ﷺ) did not summon the deeds of those peoples when he recognized them, and so he said what he said, and that the meaning of "You do not know" etc. is merely the magnifying of the matter of what they innovated after his death, peace be upon him, and not the negation of knowledge of it, then there remains those of his community who died, obedient or disobedient, during his lifetime, about whom no knowledge existed at all, like one who believed and died without hearing of him (ﷺ). For the presentation of deeds in his regard has not come in any report at all, and saying there is no such person is far-fetched. And whoever claims that he (ﷺ) knows the deeds of his community and recognizes them, one and all, living and dead, and that therefore his testimony over them of obedience and disobedience on the Day of Resurrection is valid, has not brought a proof. The verse is not fit as proof for him except by this interpretation, and that is the very point under discussion. Moreover, in the hadith of the slander (ifk) there is what indicates the opposite.

Some have claimed that his (ﷺ) knowledge of the obedient and the disobedient of his community is because they are present at their questioning in the grave concerning him, peace be upon him, as is indicated by what has been reported, that it is said to the one in the grave: "What do you say about this man who was sent to you?" The demonstrative "this" requires a sensible, witnessed referent, and that, as you see, is not so. Some chose that the testimony by that is over some of the community, namely those who were present in his time (ﷺ) and whose state of obedience and disobedience he knew. The address in "over you" is either specific to them or general by way of predominance, and there is in this what there is, so reflect. It was also said that "ʿalā" in "ʿalaykum" means "lam" (for), as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and what was sacrificed on the stone altars﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], so the meaning is "a witness for you." The intended meaning of his testimony for them is his commendation of them when they bear witness against the nations. And its remoteness is not hidden. The "lam" is connected to "named you" on both readings of the pronoun, and it is for consequence according to what was said. Al-Khafaji said: there is no objection to its being for causation, for Allah's naming them, or Ibrahim's naming them, as "Muslims," is a ruling of their Islam and their uprightness, and it is a cause for the acceptance of the testimony of the Messenger (ﷺ), who is included among them by way of primary inclusion, and for the acceptance of their testimony over the nations. And in this there is a kind of obscurity.

﴿So establish the prayer and give the zakat﴾, that is, draw near to Him, the Exalted, for what He has distinguished you with of this favor and nobility, by all kinds of obedience. The mention of these two matters specifically is for their eminence and excellence. ﴿And hold fast to Allah﴾, that is, trust in Him, the Exalted, in all your affairs. ﴿He is your Protector﴾, your helper and the one who manages your affairs. ﴿How excellent a Protector and how excellent a Helper!﴾ He is, for there is no equal to Him, the Exalted, in guardianship and support, for whoever takes Him as protector is not lost, and whoever seeks His help is not forsaken; rather, in reality there is no protector nor helper other than Him, may He be mighty and majestic. And in

Page 212

This is an indication that the utmost perfection is holding fast to God Most High and realizing the station of servanthood, which lies beyond naming and selection. It is permissible that ﴿He is your Protector﴾ be a completion of the selection, but this is not the most fitting reading.
* * *
Among the indications in the verses is ﴿Surely God defends those who believe﴾ against the plot of their enemy, namely Satan and the soul (nafs). ﴿Surely God does not love any treacherous ingrate﴾. Satan and the soul are included in this, and the truth of both descriptions applies to them clearly. Indeed, there are no traitors and no ingrates like them. ﴿Those who, if We establish them in the land, establish prayer﴾, etc. In this is an indication of the state of the people of tamkin (the established station, i.e., those whom God has firmly established in spiritual realization), that they are guided and guiding. Therefore there is no excess (shatah, ecstatic utterance) with them, and no one goes astray through their words. ﴿How many a town We destroyed while it was wrongdoing, so it lies in ruins over its roofs, and [how many] a well abandoned and a lofty palace﴾. It has been said: the wrongdoing town is an indication of the heart heedless of God Most High, the abandoned well is an indication of the mind from which pure thoughts have not been extracted, and the lofty palace is an indication of the body containing the chambers of the faculties.
﴿For it is not the eyes that are blinded, but it is the hearts within the breasts that are blinded﴾. In this is an indication of the evil state of the veiled and the deniers, for their hearts are blind to seeing the lights of the people of God Most High. For they have lights that are not seen except by the eye of the heart, and by this eye the realities of the visible realm (mulk) and the subtleties of the unseen realm (malakut) are perceived. In a hadith: "Beware the insight of the believer, for he sees by the light of God."
﴿And surely a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count﴾. The discussion of the day and its divisions has already preceded, so recall it.
﴿Then those who believed and did righteous deeds, for them is forgiveness﴾, i.e., a veil from the others (aghyar), so that they do not come to know their reality, as the hadith qudsi indicates: "My friends are beneath My domes; no one knows them but Me." ﴿And a generous provision﴾, which is the knowledge of the divine presence (ladunni), by which the spirits are nourished.
Some of them have said: the provision of the hearts is the sweetness of gnosis (irfan), the provision of the secrets is the contemplation of beauty, and the provision of the spirits is the unveiling of majesty. To this provision he, upon whom be blessings and peace, alludes in his saying: "I spend the night with my Lord; He feeds me and gives me drink."
The indication in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We did not send before you any messenger or prophet but that when he desired, Satan cast into his desire﴾, etc., according to the view of one who claims the authenticity of the hadith of the Gharaniq (the so-called Satanic verses), is that the servant should be annihilated (fana', passing away of the self) in the will of his Master, Mighty and Majestic. Otherwise he is tested with Satan's deception so that he may learn courtesy, and that deception does not persist, because it contradicts wisdom.
﴿And those who emigrated in the way of God﴾ from the homelands of nature in seeking the Truth, ﴿then were slain﴾ by the sword of sincerity and spiritual discipline, ﴿or died﴾ through the attraction (jadhbah) away from the attributes of humanity, ﴿God will surely provide them with a goodly provision﴾. It is the provision of continuous union, as has been said, or it is like the generous provision.
﴿And whoever retaliates with the like of what he was afflicted with, then is wronged, God will surely help him﴾. In this is an indication of the help given to the wayfarer (salik) who punishes his own soul with striving after it has punished him with disobedience, and then it wrongs him by seizing control through its attributes.
﴿And if they dispute with you, say: God knows best what you do﴾. The Sufis have taken from this the abandoning of argument with the deniers. Some have mentioned that arguing with them is futile, like arguing with an impotent man about the pleasure of intercourse.
﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them, you recognize denial in the faces of those who disbelieved﴾, etc. In this is an indication of the blame of the Sufis who, when they hear verses that refute them, show sourness and frowning. They are many in our time. ﴿Surely we belong to God and to Him we return﴾.
In His saying: ﴿Surely those you call upon besides God will not create a fly﴾, etc., is an indication of the blame of the extremists regarding the friends of God Most High, in that they seek help from them in distress, heedless of God Most High, and make vows to them. The intelligent among them say: "They are our means to God Most High, and we only vow to God, Mighty and Majestic, and we give its reward to the saint (wali)." It is not hidden that in their first claim they most resemble the idol-worshippers who said: "We only worship them so that they bring us near to God in closeness." Their second claim is not objectionable if they did not ask those [saints] for this, such as the cure of their sick or the return of their absent ones, or the like. The apparent state of them is asking. What points to this is that if it were said: "Make your vow to God Most High and give its reward to your parents," they would not do so, though your parents are more in need than those saints. I have seen many of them prostrating at the thresholds of the tombs of the saints. Some of them affirm that the saints have full power of action in their graves, though they differ in this according to the differences in their ranks. The scholars among them confine the power of action in graves to four or five [cases], and when they are asked for evidence, they say: "This is established by unveiling (kashf)." May God damn them! How ignorant they are and how much they fabricate! Among them are those who claim that [the dead] come out of their graves and take various forms. Their scholars say: "Only their spirits appear in forms and wander wherever they wish, and sometimes they take the form of a lion, a gazelle, or the like." All of this is false, with no basis in the Book, the Sunnah, or the words of the early community (salaf al-ummah). These people have corrupted the religion of the people and have become a laughingstock for the adherents of the abrogated religions, such as the Jews and the Christians, and likewise for the sects and the materialists (dahriyyah). We ask God Most High for pardon and well-being.
﴿And strive in God with the striving due to Him﴾. It encompasses all kinds of striving. Among them is the striving of the soul (nafs), which is by purifying it through performing the rights [owed to God and others] and abandoning worldly portions. The striving of the heart is by purifying it and cutting its attachment from both worlds. The striving of the spirit is by annihilating existence. It has been said: "Your existence is a sin, with which no other sin can be compared."
﴿And hold fast to God﴾, cling to Him, Exalted is He, in all your conditions. ﴿He is your Protector in truth﴾, ﴿so excellent is the Protector﴾ in annihilating your existence, ﴿and excellent is the Helper﴾ in preserving you. How great is this conclusion for a people who understand. Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe, and peace be upon the messengers, and praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds.

The seventeenth part is complete by the praise of God. It is followed, God willing, by the eighteenth part, whose beginning is the Surah of the Believers.
